method: Eight literature sweeps (energy, protein, goals, endurance fuelling, adaptation, dietary patterns, safety, food data and licences); each source read from PubMed/PMC, the publisher or the official report, findings paraphrased with exact numbers, and a second agent re-opened each source to confirm, correct or reject every finding. 'findingIndex' is what the diet-1 policy cites as #N.

gaps.parameter: maintenance goal: tolerance band that counts as weight-stable (maintenance/recomposition, all patterns)
gaps.problem: No verified finding defines how much weight drift is still 'maintenance'. NASEM 2023 only says stable weight means intake matches need. Without a band, the adaptive rule cannot tell 'on target' from 'adjust'. The noise findings (about +/-1% daily, 0.35% day-of-week cycle, +1.35% holiday rise) are not a maintenance definition.
suggestedSources: Stevens J et al. 2006, Int J Obes, The definition of weight maintenance (proposes <3% change for long-term maintenance) - doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803175, PMID 16302013
Orsama AL et al. 2014, Obes Facts, weekday/weekend weight rhythm - doi:10.1159/000356147, PMID 24504358

gaps.parameter: adaptation: size of each intake adjustment, the deviation that triggers it, and the shortest weigh-in window before adjusting (all goals)
gaps.problem: The findings give only qualitative rules: NASEM (monitor weight, adjust in small steps), a weekly readjustment with no step size (Ribeiro 2019), a >=3-day drift trigger (Byrne 2018), and a 100-200 kcal/d taper (Helms 2014, narrative). Sanghvi 2015 gives the error of weight-derived intake change but no decision rule. The app has no cited step size, trigger threshold or minimum window.
suggestedSources: Hall KD, Chow CC 2011, Am J Clin Nutr (simulations: daily weights over more than 28 d needed for a 95% CI under 300 kcal/d on intake change) - doi:10.3945/ajcn.111.014399, PMID 21562087
Martin CK et al. 2016, JMIR mHealth uHealth, SmartLoss (adherence judged from weight against a model trajectory) - doi:10.2196/mhealth.5027, PMID 26983937
Thomas DM et al. 2015, Am J Clin Nutr, POUNDS Lost: early deviation from expected weight predicts 1-year success - doi:10.3945/ajcn.114.091520, PMID 25733628

gaps.parameter: selfMonitoring: model of weigh-in noise and confounders (glycogen/water after carbohydrate changes, menstrual cycle)
gaps.problem: The luteal-phase gain of more than 2 kg and the 1:3-4 glycogen:water ratio appear only second-hand (ACSM 2007; Martins 2020 citing others). No primary menstrual-phase data were opened. Carbohydrate refeeds, diet breaks and switching from low-carb or keto will move scale weight in ways the adaptive rule could misread as fat change.
suggestedSources: Kreitzman SN et al. 1992, Am J Clin Nutr, glycogen stored with 3-4 parts water - doi:10.1093/ajcn/56.1.292S, PMID 1615908
Fernandez-Elias VE et al. 2015, Eur J Appl Physiol, muscle water vs glycogen recovery - doi:10.1007/s00421-015-3175-z, PMID 25911631
Benton MJ et al. 2020, PLoS One, meta-analysis of menstrual phase and RMR (small luteal rise; not significant in post-2000 studies) - doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0236025, PMID 32658929
White CP et al. 2011, Obstet Gynecol Int, self-reported fluid retention across 765 cycles (peaks on first day of flow; not measured weight) - doi:10.1155/2011/138451, PMID 21845193

gaps.parameter: exercise energy expenditure input (needed for energy availability, and for choosing PAL for lifters and endurance users)
gaps.problem: The EA formula needs exercise energy expenditure. The only method named is MET x body mass x hours from the 2011 Compendium, and it is cited second-hand in the Triad statement. The Compendium itself was not opened. NASEM PAL examples use walking, cycling and tennis, and no finding maps resistance-training sessions onto PAL. There is also no finding on how accurate wearable or HealthKit energy estimates are, if the app uses them.
suggestedSources: Herrmann SD et al. 2024, J Sport Health Sci, 2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities (1114 activities, ages 19-59) - doi:10.1016/j.jshs.2023.10.010, PMID 38242596
Ainsworth BE et al. 2011, Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2011 Compendium - doi:10.1249/MSS.0b013e31821ece12, PMID 21681120

O'Driscoll R et al. 2020, Br J Sports Med, meta-analysis of wrist/arm monitor energy-expenditure validity (accuracy varies by activity; high heterogeneity) - doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099643, PMID 30194221

gaps.parameter: fat-free mass input when the user has no body-composition measurement (EA floor, Cunningham/ten Haaf FFM equations, protein per kg FFM)
gaps.problem: Several floors and targets are stated per kg FFM: EA of 30/45 kcal/kg FFM, fat-loss protein of 2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM, and FFM-based RMR equations. No verified finding says how to estimate FFM from inputs an app has, or how much error consumer smart scales add. Tinsley 2019 only notes that non-DXA FFM moved predicted RMR by -30 to +74 kcal/d.
suggestedSources: Deurenberg P et al. 1991, Br J Nutr, body fat % from BMI, age and sex (adult SEE 4.1%; overestimates in obesity) - doi:10.1079/bjn19910073, PMID 2043597
Gallagher D et al. 2000, Am J Clin Nutr, BMI-linked healthy body-fat ranges by ethnicity (SEE 2.8-5.4%) - doi:10.1093/ajcn/72.3.694, PMID 10966886
Frija-Masson J et al. 2021, JMIR mHealth uHealth, smart-scale fat/lean errors vs DXA (median fat-mass error -2.2 to -4.4 kg) - doi:10.2196/22487, PMID 33929337

gaps.parameter: surplusRate: energy surplus and weekly gain rate for muscleGain (trained vs novice; men vs women)
gaps.problem: Support is weak. Iraki 2019 (10-20% surplus; 0.25-0.5%/wk) and Slater 2019 (359-478 kcal/d; says the optimal surplus is not established) are narrative reviews. The other data are small trials (Ribeiro 2019; Garthe 2013, planned surplus not stated). NASEM's EER + 1.96 x SEPV is a worked example, not a validated gain prescription. No finding separates novice from advanced lifters or women from men.
suggestedSources: Helms ER et al. 2023, Sports Med Open, randomized maintenance vs 5% vs 15% surplus in trained lifters over 8 wk (faster gain mainly raised skinfolds, not muscle thickness or squat 1RM) - doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00651-y, PMID 37914977
Bray GA et al. 2012, JAMA, inpatient overfeeding RCT (~954 kcal/d surplus; fat gain similar across protein levels; lean gain only with 15-25% protein) - doi:10.1001/jama.2011.1918, PMID 22215165
Aragon AA et al. 2017, J Int Soc Sports Nutr, ISSN position stand on diets and body composition - doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0174-y, PMID 28630601

gaps.parameter: deficitRate: rule tying weekly loss rate to body-fat level or BMI (fatLoss)
gaps.problem: Several sources say leaner users should lose more slowly (Helms 2014, Roberts 2020, ISSN), but none gives a numeric fat-level cut-off. The 0.5-1%/wk evidence comes from lean trained athletes. The obesity evidence gives kcal deficits (AHA 500-750, NICE 500-800) but no %BW/wk ceiling. The app cannot choose a rate from body composition.
suggestedSources: Forbes GB 2000, Ann N Y Acad Sci, share of weight change that is lean tissue depends on initial body fat - doi:10.1111/j.1749-6632.2000.tb06482.x, PMID 10865771
Heymsfield SB et al. 2014, Obes Rev, critique of the quarter-FFM rule - doi:10.1111/obr.12143, PMID 24447775

Aragon AA et al. 2017, J Int Soc Sports Nutr (a higher baseline fat level permits a more aggressive deficit; slower loss preserves lean mass in leaner people) - doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0174-y, PMID 28630601

gaps.parameter: safety: absolute maximum weekly weight loss for users with obesity
gaps.problem: Johansson 2013 links very-low-calorie diets and larger losses to gallstones but reports no rate threshold. No verified finding gives a kg/week ceiling for users with obesity, whose %BW/wk rates can be large in absolute terms.
suggestedSources: Weinsier RL et al. 1995, Am J Med, gallstone risk rises exponentially above about 1.5 kg/week of loss - doi:10.1016/S0002-9343(99)80394-5, PMID 7847427

gaps.parameter: protein: per-kg denominator and target for users with overweight/obesity (fatLoss/maintenance)
gaps.problem: Most g/kg targets come from lean, trained samples. Applied to actual body weight at high BMI they inflate intake, and none of the findings covers which body weight to use. The only overweight-specific figure (1.2-1.5 g/kg) is second-hand in a JSCR narrative review. KDIGO uses ideal body weight, but only for CKD.
suggestedSources: Wycherley TP et al. 2012, Am J Clin Nutr, meta-analysis of 24 energy-restricted RCTs, high vs standard protein (FFM +0.43 kg; fat mass -0.87 kg) - doi:10.3945/ajcn.112.044321, PMID 23097268
Weijs PJ, Wolfe RR 2016, Clin Nutr, obese older adults losing weight: >=1.2 g/kg BW or >=1.9 g/kg FFM linked to muscle accretion (exploratory) - doi:10.1016/j.clnu.2015.02.016, PMID 25788405

gaps.parameter: dietaryPattern: protein adjustment for vegan/vegetarian users
gaps.problem: The findings conflict. IOM, WHO, AND 2016 and Hevia-Larrain 2021 (1.6 g/kg) give no adjustment. Neufingerl 2022 reports proposals of about 20% more. Pinckaers 2021 calls the question unresolved. Only 9 of 74 RCTs in Nunes 2022 used plant protein.
suggestedSources: Mariotti F, Gardner CD 2019, Nutrients, review of protein and amino-acid adequacy in vegetarian diets - doi:10.3390/nu11112661, PMID 31690027

gaps.parameter: protein: daily target for the endurance goal
gaps.problem: The findings disagree: 1.2-2.0 (ACSM 2016), 1.3-1.7 (IAAF 2019), 1.6-2.1 up to 2.5 (ISSN ultra), and 1.2-1.6 (T1D consensus). None is a direct requirement measurement in endurance athletes.
suggestedSources: Kato H et al. 2016, PLoS One, indicator-amino-acid-oxidation study in endurance-trained men (estimated average requirement 1.65, recommended intake 1.83 g/kg/d after a 20 km run; n=6) - doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0157406, PMID 27322029

gaps.parameter: dietaryPattern: cuisine preference (food suggestions and adherence)
gaps.problem: No verified finding covers cuisine preference at all. The dietaryPattern findings cover omnivore, vegetarian and vegan nutrients only. Gardner/Yancy 2015 shows that choosing a macronutrient pattern did not change weight loss, which is a different question. There is no evidence base for cuisine-specific suggestions, and no licensed non-US food composition data (see the dataset licence gap).
suggestedSources: Brown T et al. 2015, Int J Environ Res Public Health, meta-analysis of diet/activity interventions in South Asians (adult weight MD -1.82 kg in two baseline-adjusted trials) - doi:10.3390/ijerph120100566, PMID 25584423
Estruch R et al. 2018, N Engl J Med, PREDIMED Mediterranean-pattern RCT - doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1800389, PMID 29897866
Celis-Morales C et al. 2017, Int J Epidemiol, Food4Me: personalised advice improved diet quality vs generic advice - doi:10.1093/ije/dyw186, PMID 27524815

gaps.parameter: foodSelection: bundle-able food composition dataset under the repository licence policy (AGENTS.md rule 5)
gaps.problem: Of the verified licences, only USDA FoodData Central (CC0) is on the allowlist. AFCD (a CC BY-SA 3.0 AU based licence) and Open Food Facts images (CC BY-SA) are explicitly prohibited. The Open Food Facts database (ODbL share-alike), CNF (OGL-Canada) and CoFID (OGL v3) use licences that are not on the allowlist. So cuisine coverage beyond US foods, mixed dishes and portion weights has to come from FDC (Foundation, SR Legacy, FNDDS), and no finding documents those subsets or their portion data.
suggestedSources: Fukagawa NK et al. 2022, Am J Clin Nutr, the five FoodData Central data types - doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqab397, PMID 34893796
Ahuja JKC et al. 2013, J Nutr, USDA databases (SR, FNDDS, FPED) in the public domain - doi:10.3945/jn.112.170043, PMID 23269654

gaps.parameter: foodSelection: protein-quality (DIAAS/amino-acid score) data for plant-protein suggestions
gaps.problem: The DIAAS method and example values come from the FAO 2013 report, which is all rights reserved. Mathai 2017 and Pinckaers 2021 values are journal data with no bundle licence. The IOM 2005 and FAO scoring patterns are usable as facts, but no licensed digestibility coefficients were found. A bundle can compute an amino-acid score from CC0 FDC amino-acid data, but not a digestibility-corrected score. No CC0 digestibility dataset was verified, so this stays unknown.
suggestedSources: Fukagawa NK et al. 2022, Am J Clin Nutr (FDC amino-acid fields, CC0) - doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqab397, PMID 34893796

gaps.parameter: foodSelection: nutrient-density ranking and processing (NOVA) classification of bundle foods
gaps.problem: The UPF findings (Hall 2019; Lane 2024) and the energy-density findings support down-weighting some foods. But no verified finding gives a validated ranking score, or a way to assign NOVA groups to FDC items, which carry no NOVA label.
suggestedSources: Fulgoni VL et al. 2009, J Nutr, Nutrient-Rich Foods index (NRF9.3 per 100 kcal and per serving validated against HEI) - doi:10.3945/jn.108.101360, PMID 19549759
Monteiro CA et al. 2019, Public Health Nutr, how to identify ultra-processed foods - doi:10.1017/S1368980018003762, PMID 30744710
Steele EM et al. 2023, J Nutr, reference approach for NOVA-coding WWEIA/NHANES (FNDDS) foods - doi:10.1016/j.tjnut.2022.09.001, PMID 36913457

gaps.parameter: safety: exclusion or referral for glucose-lowering drugs (insulin, sulfonylureas), GLP-1 therapy and bariatric history
gaps.problem: The verified exclusions cover CKD, T1D, eating disorders, pregnancy and adolescents. Nothing covers adults with type 2 diabetes on hypoglycaemia-risk drugs who start a deficit, or GLP-1 users, whose reduced intake and lean-mass loss make automated deficit and protein targets unsafe. The NICE flag list names T1D but not these.
suggestedSources: American Diabetes Association 2025, Diabetes Care, Standards of Care Section 8: Obesity and weight management - doi:10.2337/dc25-S008, PMID 39651976
Mozaffarian D et al. 2025, Am J Clin Nutr, joint advisory on nutritional priorities with GLP-1 therapy - doi:10.1016/j.ajcnut.2025.04.023, PMID 40450457

gaps.parameter: safety: lactation (energy deficit while breastfeeding)
gaps.problem: IOM 2009 covers pregnancy weight gain only. No finding addresses whether a fatLoss goal is allowed during lactation, or at what rate.
suggestedSources: Lovelady CA et al. 2000, N Engl J Med, RCT: about 0.5 kg/week loss (500 kcal/d cut plus exercise) in overweight exclusively breastfeeding women from 4 to 14 wk postpartum did not affect infant growth - doi:10.1056/NEJM200002173420701, PMID 10675424

gaps.parameter: safety: harm from calorie-counting and tracking features in at-risk users
gaps.problem: The safety findings cover self-weighing only (no psychological harm in trials). No finding covers harm from calorie logging itself, which the app requires. The SCOFF findings cover screening, not the risk created by the feature.
suggestedSources: Simpson CC, Mazzeo SE 2017, Eat Behav, calorie-tracker use linked to higher eating concern and restraint - doi:10.1016/j.eatbeh.2017.02.002, PMID 28214452
Levinson CA et al. 2017, Eat Behav, most eating-disorder patients using a calorie app felt it contributed to their disorder - doi:10.1016/j.eatbeh.2017.08.003, PMID 28843591

gaps.parameter: fat: minimum fat intake (g/kg or % energy) protecting sex-hormone status, by sex
gaps.problem: The floors conflict (see contradictions). The testosterone point rests on one cited study within narrative reviews (Ruiz-Castellano 2021; Slater 2019). No verified finding covers women's reproductive-hormone response to low fat intake apart from energy availability.
suggestedSources: Whittaker J, Wu K 2021, J Steroid Biochem Mol Biol, meta-analysis of 6 intervention studies: low-fat vs high-fat diets lowered total testosterone in men (SMD -0.38) - doi:10.1016/j.jsbmb.2021.105878, PMID 33741447

gaps.parameter: safety: energy-availability floor as a hard threshold vs a continuous risk
gaps.problem: The app would apply a single EA cut-off. The findings give 30 kcal/kg FFM (Loucks 2003, women) and about 9-25 in men (IOC 2023, low certainty). IOC 2023 says the zones are a guide, not a diagnostic endpoint. No finding tests whether any threshold exists.
suggestedSources: Lieberman JL et al. 2018, Med Sci Sports Exerc, RCT: menstrual disturbance odds fell 9% per unit of EA, with no threshold - doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000001451, PMID 29023359

gaps.parameter: energyRequirement: RMR equation choice by training status and ethnicity (definition of 'trained'; ages over 35; non-white muscular users)
gaps.problem: The findings support Mifflin-St Jeor for the general population, and ten Haaf, Cunningham or Tinsley equations for trained users. No finding sets the threshold that moves a user from one to the other. ten Haaf's derivation criterion (>=3 h/wk and >=2 sessions/wk, ages 18-35) is the only candidate, and athlete-equation evidence stops at 35 y. The Sabounchi Asian male intercept looks like a transcription error and needs checking. Evidence in non-white muscular users is almost absent.
suggestedSources: Joseph M et al. 2017, Indian J Endocrinol Metab: in 30 Indian male weightlifters all eight equations underestimated measured REE by 375-636 kcal/d. The paper's new LBM equation prints an implausible coefficient, so use it only as a bias signal - doi:10.4103/ijem.IJEM_563_16, PMID 28670532

gaps.parameter: recomposition: energy target for the maintenance/recomposition goal in trained users
gaps.problem: Support is weak. Barakat 2020 is a narrative review, and Murphy 2022 shows a deficit blunts lean-mass gain. No verified trial compares maintenance energy with a small surplus for recomposition in trained people.
suggestedSources: Helms ER et al. 2023, Sports Med Open (includes a maintenance-energy arm alongside 5% and 15% surpluses) - doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00651-y, PMID 37914977

gaps.parameter: foodSelection: allergen and intolerance exclusions
gaps.problem: No verified finding covers excluding foods for allergy or intolerance. The only related finding is the low-FODMAP/gluten statement (IAAF 2019). The suggestion engine needs an allergen taxonomy and a hard-exclusion rule.
suggestedSources: Muraro A et al. 2014, Allergy, EAACI food allergy and anaphylaxis guidelines: diagnosis and management - doi:10.1111/all.12429, PMID 24909706

gaps.parameter: safety: sodium and potassium reference values (current DRI)
gaps.problem: The 2019 NASEM sodium/potassium DRI (CDRR of 2,300 mg/d; potassium AI 3,400/2,600 mg/d) appears only as an update note inside the IOM 2005 finding. The 2019 report itself was not opened. A PubMed title search did not find it, so no PubMed-verified source can be offered. Open it directly at doi:10.17226/25353 before using those numbers.

contradictions: RMR equation for trained users: Frankenfield 2005/2013 prefer Mifflin-St Jeor (82% within +/-10% overall) (10.1016/j.jada.2005.02.005; 10.1016/j.clnu.2013.03.022). The athlete meta-analysis says avoid it (52% precision) (10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z), and Tinsley 2019 finds it underestimates muscular men by up to 393 kcal/d (10.1139/apnm-2018-0412). The app needs a cited training-status switch.

Direction of Cunningham and Harris-Benedict bias: EP087512 cites both as overestimating (HB 5%, Cunningham 14-15%), and Mifflin 1990 has HB 5% high. Jagim 2018 and the collegiate study find all equations, Cunningham included, underpredict athletes (Cunningham -165 kcal/d). HB is significantly low in heavier male athletes (ES -0.91).

PAL category cut-offs disagree: FAO sedentary 1.40-1.69 and active 1.70-1.99; IOM 2005 sedentary 1.0-<1.4 and active 1.6-<1.9; NASEM 2023 inactive 1.00-<1.53, active 1.68-<1.85, very active 1.85-<2.50. The same activity label maps to different multipliers.

Starting fat-loss deficit: NASEM's example gives EER - 1.96 x SEPV (about -670 kcal/d men, -472 women). ACSM 2016 gives 250-500 kcal/d, AHA 2013 500-750, NICE trials 500-800, and Murphy 2022 says avoid more than ~500 kcal/d to preserve lean mass. The %BW/wk sources give 0.5-1% (Helms 2014; Ruiz-Castellano 2021), <1% (ACSM), and 0.7% as better than 1.4% (Garthe 2011).

Surplus size for muscleGain: 10-20% above maintenance (Iraki 2019), about 359-478 kcal/d (Slater 2019), 200-300 kcal/d preferred for highly trained people (Garthe via Iraki), and NASEM's EER + 1.96 x SEPV example (+670/+472 kcal/d). Ribeiro 2019 at about 67.5 kcal/kg/d gained more fat for little extra muscle.

Fat-loss protein denominator and range: ISSN 2017 prints 2.3-3.1 g/kg with no source, in the unit it defines per kg body weight. Helms 2014 gives the same range per kg FFM/LBM (10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054; 10.1186/1550-2783-11-20). Other sources: IAAF 2019 >1.6-2.4 g/kg BW, with >2.5 g/kg/d giving no advantage; Ruiz-Castellano 2021 2.2-3.0 g/kg BW; ACSM >=2.0 g/kg; JSCR 2021 1.2-1.5 (overweight) and 1.2-2.0 (lean).
Vegan protein: no adjustment (IOM 2005; AND 2016; Hevia-Larrain 2021 at 1.6 g/kg) vs about 20% higher proposed (Neufingerl 2022 citing others) vs unresolved (Pinckaers 2021).
Endurance protein: 1.2-2.0 (ACSM 2016), 1.3-1.7 (IAAF 2019), 1.6-2.1 up to 2.5 (ISSN ultra 2019), 1.2-1.6 g/kg/d (T1D consensus 2017).

Carbohydrate floor: IOM RDA 130 g/d and EAR 100 g/d. EFSA 2015 sets 30 g/d for total diet replacements. AHA 2013 accepts about 20 g/d low-carb for weight loss. Henselmans 2022 finds no minimum for strength. Ruiz-Castellano 2021 warns ketogenic intakes may reduce FFM retention, and ACSM/Helms advise against very-low-carb diets for athletes.

Fat floor: ACSM 2016 discourages chronic intake below 20% of energy, and Slater 2019 discourages below 15-20%. Helms 2014 accepts 15-20% in a cut, JSCR 2021 allows 10-25%, and Ruiz-Castellano 2021 sets at least 0.5 g/kg/d. EFSA minimums are 11 g linoleic acid and 1.4 g ALA per day, and Johansson 2013 says 7-10 g/d is needed for gallbladder emptying.

Energy availability threshold: 30 kcal/kg FFM (Loucks 2003; IOC 2014/2018; Triad) vs about 9-25 in males (IOC 2023) vs no threshold at all, with risk rising linearly (Lieberman 2018, 10.1249/MSS.0000000000001451).

Absolute energy-intake floor: 1,200 kcal/d (Campbell 2021 trial rule; AHA women 1,200-1,500), men 1,500-1,800 (AHA), <800 kcal/d VLED only under specialist care (NICE/AHA), 600 kcal/d minimum for total diet replacements (EFSA 2015), and >=2,000 kcal/d during low-EA treatment (Triad 2014).
BMI floor for allowing fat loss: 17.5 kg/m2 as the low-energy-store flag (Triad 2014; IOC 2018) vs 18.5 as the lower healthy bound and the restoration target (FAO 2004; Triad 2014).

Energy per kg of weight change in the adaptive rule: 7,700 kcal/kg static rule (overestimates loss; Thomas 2013) vs 24.7-32.2 MJ/kg depending on initial fat (Hall 2008) vs 4,858 kcal/kg at week 4 and 6,041 at week 6 (Heymsfield 2012) vs rho 8,840 kcal/kg (Sanghvi 2015) vs 9,500/1,020 kcal/kg FM/FFM (Thomas 2014) vs 9,300/1,100 (Hall 2019). For gain, Slater 2019 gives 5,000-5,200 kJ stored per kg muscle.

Adaptive thermogenesis magnitude: about 220 kcal/d (NASEM 2023) vs about 120 kcal/d (Muller 2013) vs 70-100 kcal/d (Trexler/JSCR citing Minnesota) vs 79-504 kcal/d (Helms 2014 citing) vs -92 kcal/d that shrank to non-significant after stabilisation and did not predict regain (Martins 2020).

Diet breaks: MATADOR (2 wk off / 2 wk on) gave more weight and fat loss than continuous restriction (Byrne 2018). Peos 2021 found no body-composition difference with 1-wk breaks, and the meta-analyses cited in JSCR 2021 found no weight-loss difference for intermittent vs continuous restriction.

Per-meal protein ceiling: maximal MPS at 20 g (Moore 2009) and >40 g not shown to add (ACSM 2016) vs no ceiling up to a 100 g bolus (Trommelen 2023). Older vs younger per-meal need: 0.40 vs 0.24 g/kg (Moore 2015).

Intra-exercise carbohydrate for very long events: up to 90 g/h beyond 2.5-3 h (ACSM 2016; Jeukendrup 2014) and >90 g/h (Stellingwerff 2014) vs 30-50 g/h, with 90 g/h judged unrealistic for races over 6 h (ISSN ultra 2019).
In-exercise hydration rule: drink to thirst (Goulet 2013; NATA when sweat rate unknown) vs a planned intake keeping loss below 2% of body mass (ACSM 2007/2016; IAAF 2019 says <2-3%).

Serum vitamin D target: IOM 2011 treats >=50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) as sufficient for practically all and finds no consistent benefit above 75 nmol/L. IOC 2018 and Triad 2014 target above 30 ng/mL, or 32-50 ng/mL.

Sodium upper value: the IOM 2005 UL of 2.3 g/d was replaced by the NASEM 2019 CDRR (reduce if above 2,300 mg/d), which was only seen second-hand, while KDIGO 2024 sets <2 g/d in CKD. The app must not cite the superseded UL as current.

paceResearch.summary:
BOTTOM LINE
Q1: A person's sense of having a "slow" or "fast" metabolism does not predict their measured metabolic rate. Real differences do exist once body size and composition are accounted for, but self-report cannot detect them; only measurement can, and for this app that means the weight trend.
Q2: How precise an intake-change estimate from daily weights is depends on how many days the window covers, not on how often it is recomputed. The literature gives numbers only for 28 days; the 14-, 21- and 35-day figures below are my own calculation from the paper's published equation. No trial compared adjustment frequencies head to head.

Q1 EVIDENCE: SELF-PERCEPTION VS MEASUREMENT
- Wallhuss 2010 (full postprint read; n=56): 44 people who believed their metabolism was "high" and 12 who believed it was "low".
  - Resting metabolic rate did not differ: 7230 vs 7430 kJ/d, P=0.6.
  - The "low" group had a higher BMI (27.8 vs 20.4) and reported eating less (8339 vs 11435 kJ/d).
  - Step counts and thyroid tests did not differ.
  - The highest resting rate in the whole study belonged to someone in the "low" group.
  - Limitations: small sample; no body-composition adjustment.
- Lichtman 1992 NEJM (abstract only): 10 people with self-described diet resistance.
  - Total and resting energy expenditure were within 5% of the values predicted from body composition.
  - They under-reported intake by 47±16% and over-reported activity by 51±75%.
- Clark 1995 (abstract only; 18 women): women who saw themselves as small eaters had a higher, not lower, FFM-adjusted resting rate.

Q1 EVIDENCE: HOW BIG REAL DIFFERENCES ARE
- Johnstone 2005 (abstract only): FFM explains 63% of the variance in basal metabolic rate, FM 6% and age 2%; 26% is unexplained. Within-person variation is only 2%.
- Pontzer 2021 (n=6421, doubly labelled water): FFM explains 83% of total expenditure. Even after controlling for FFM, FM, sex and age, individuals vary by more than ±20%; adults aged 20–25 have an adjusted SD of about 18%.
- Anthanont 2016 (n=757):
  - About 70% of people had a basal rate within roughly −173 to +169 kcal/d of the value predicted for their body composition, age and sex.
  - People in the lowest and highest 15% (1510 vs 2001 kcal/d at matched body composition) gained weight at the same rate over about 10 years (0.3 vs 0.5 kg/y, P=0.16).
- Ravussin 1988 and Bogardus 1986 (abstracts only): some adjusted-metabolism differences run in families (family explained 11% of variance), and one population showed a link to later weight gain.
- Frankenfield 2005 systematic review (abstract only): even Mifflin-St Jeor, the best of the four common equations, gives noteworthy errors in individuals.

Q1 OWNER DECISION (the literature gives no number)
Perceived metabolism should not shift the starting calorie estimate or the size of a calorie change. The only justification for offering "faster" or "slower" is how much noise the user will tolerate: faster means a shorter window and less certainty. I suggest labelling the choice that way rather than as a metabolism type. No study was found in which users chose adaptation speed based on perceived metabolism.

Q2: PRECISION BY WINDOW LENGTH (Hall & Chow 2011)
Reported in the paper (daily weights, 28 days):
- With the paper's inputs (weight fluctuation SD 0.5 kg; 9100 kcal/kg; 22 kcal/kg/d), the estimate's SD is 180 kcal/d, i.e. a 95% CI of ±350 kcal/d.
- In simulations with realistic day-to-day noise, the 95% CI was 290–300 kcal/d.
- Windows longer than 28 days are needed for a 95% CI under 300 kcal/d.

Derived by me from the paper's Equation 3 (not reported in the paper), 95% CI of the intake-change estimate:

| Window (daily weights) | Weight SD 0.5 kg | Weight SD 0.35 kg |
|---|---|---|
| 7 days | ±1769 kcal/d | ±1238 kcal/d |
| 14 days | ±710 kcal/d | ±497 kcal/d |
| 21 days | ±457 kcal/d | ±320 kcal/d |
| 28 days | ±352 kcal/d | ±247 kcal/d |
| 35 days | ±295 kcal/d | ±207 kcal/d |
| 42 days | ±260 kcal/d | ±182 kcal/d |

The CI scales linearly with the user's own weight noise. The appendix says using each person's own measured scatter gives results similar to the generic assumption, so users who weigh consistently could reach a usable precision sooner.

Q2: NOISE IN DAILY WEIGHTS
- Turicchi 2020 (n=1421): weight follows a weekly cycle of about 0.35% (~0.3 kg), highest on Monday and lowest on Friday; 0.41% in men vs 0.29% in women.
- Orsama 2014: the same weekly pattern.
- Implication (owner decision): windows should cover whole weeks.
- Bhutani 2017: in people not trying to change weight, the SD of a 2-week weight change was 1.1–1.3 kg. That change was 84% fat-free mass and water, about 2380 kcal/kg. The authors say weight alone over 2 weeks cannot separate energy balance from an imbalance under 500 kcal/d.

Q2: WHAT TRIALS ACTUALLY DID
- MATADOR (Byrne 2018):
  - During the 4-week maintenance baseline, intake was adjusted after at least 3 days of consistent weight change. Weight still changed −1.6±1.4 kg over that baseline.
  - During energy restriction, the prescription was recalculated every 4 weeks from measured resting expenditure.
- SmartLoss RCT: participants weighed daily and were compared against a model-predicted zone. Counsellors gave feedback at least weekly, but on behaviour, not calorie targets. Weight loss was −9.4% vs −0.6%.
- Sanghvi 2015 (CALERIE): a model using only weights estimated intake change within 40 kcal/d on average, but within 215 kcal/d root-mean-square for individuals.
- Garthe 2011 (abstract only): diets were set to hit 0.7% vs 1.4% weekly weight loss targets. Energy intake was cut 19% vs 30%; the slow group lost 0.7%/wk and the fast group 1.0%/wk (target 1.4%).

Q2 OWNER DECISION
Recomputing weekly over a rolling window of at least 21–28 whole-week days fits these precision data. A 21-day minimum can only detect large discrepancies (about ±460 kcal/d at 0.5 kg noise). The current policy of about 5 weeks gives about ±295 kcal/d.

SOURCES I COULD NOT READ IN FULL
Johnstone, Lichtman, Clark, Garthe, Ravussin, Bogardus and Frankenfield were read as abstracts only (paywall, 403 errors or bot checks; no CAPTCHA was bypassed). Their findings rely on the abstract alone. Pontzer was read from the PMC author manuscript.

findings.citation: Wallhuss A, Isik M, Nystrom FH. Comparison of the subjective sense of high or low metabolism and objectively measured resting metabolic rate. Scand J Clin Lab Invest. 2010;70(5):334-337.
findings.design: Cross-sectional observational study (advertised recruitment of self-perceived extremes); ventilated-hood indirect calorimetry; n=56
findings.question: Q1: Does self-perceived metabolism predict measured RMR?
findings.finding: Participants were recruited because they believed their metabolism was 'high' (n=44; 29 men, 15 women) or 'low' (n=12; 5 men, 7 women). Fasting RMR did not differ: 7230±1233 kJ/d in the 'high' group vs 7430±1422 kJ/d in the 'low' group (P=0.6). This was despite a BMI of 20.4 vs 27.8 and reported intake of 11435 vs 8339 kJ/d (P=0.001). Steps per day (6168 vs 7127), reported exercise, TSH and T4 did not differ. Several 'high' participants had a lower RMR than the lowest 'low' participant, and the highest RMR in the study was in the 'low' group. Across the cohort RMR correlated with BMI (r=0.52) and inversely with age. Limitations: RMR was not adjusted for FFM (no body composition was measured), the sample was small and the sexes were unbalanced. Derived by this reviewer from Table I: reported intake divided by RMR was about 1.12 in the 'low' group vs 1.58 in the 'high' group, which is consistent with under-reporting in the 'low' group; the paper does not report this ratio.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results; Table I (participant characteristics, RMR, intake, steps, T4); Figure 1; Discussion paragraphs 1-2 (Linköping University postprint, DiVA diva2:345844)

findings.citation: Lichtman SW, Pisarska K, Berman ER, et al. Discrepancy between self-reported and actual caloric intake and exercise in obese subjects. N Engl J Med. 1992;327(27):1893-1898.
findings.design: Clinical physiology study with controls; doubly labelled water, indirect calorimetry and body composition over 14 days; 10 diet-resistant subjects vs 80 comparison subjects drawn from 224 consecutive obese patients
findings.question: Q1: Do people who believe their metabolism is abnormally low actually have low energy expenditure?
findings.finding: In 10 obese people who reported diet resistance (failing to lose weight on under 1200 kcal/d), total energy expenditure and RMR were within 5% of the values predicted from body composition. The thermic effects of food and exercise did not differ from the comparison group. The diet-resistant subjects under-reported intake by 47±16% (mean±SD) and over-reported physical activity by 51±75%. They also more often attributed their obesity to genetics and used thyroid medication more frequently (P<0.05). Low energy expenditure was therefore excluded as the explanation.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results and Conclusions); full text not accessible (NEJM paywall)

findings.citation: Clark DG, Tomas FM, Withers RT, et al. Differences in substrate metabolism between self-perceived 'large-eating' and 'small-eating' women. Int J Obes Relat Metab Disord. 1995;19(4):245-252.
findings.design: Comparative physiology study; repeated indirect calorimetry; 9 vs 9 women
findings.question: Q1: Does self-perception of eating little (an implied 'slow metabolism') match measured RMR?
findings.finding: FFM-adjusted RMR, averaged over 10 measurements at 30-minute intervals, was 3891±93 J/min in women who saw themselves as small eaters vs 3375±107 J/min in self-perceived large eaters. The group who believed they eat little therefore did not have a lower adjusted RMR; it was about 15% higher. RQ was 0.81 vs 0.78. The authors attribute the small eaters' weight control to high activity levels. The sample is very small and only the abstract was read.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results)

findings.citation: Johnstone AM, Murison SD, Duncan JS, Rance KA, Speakman JR. Factors influencing variation in basal metabolic rate include fat-free mass, fat mass, age, and circulating thyroxine but not sex, circulating leptin, or triiodothyronine. Am J Clin Nutr. 2005;82(5):941-948.
findings.design: Cross-sectional study with repeated BMR measurements (variance partitioning); n=150 white adults, Scotland
findings.question: Q1: How much inter-individual BMR variation remains after adjusting for body size and composition?
findings.finding: Within-subject effects accounted for only 2% of BMR variability, of which 0.5% was analytic error. Of the between-subject variance, FFM explained 63%, FM 6% and age 2%; sex and bone mineral content were not significant. 26% remained unexplained. The residual was unrelated to leptin or T3. T4 explained 25% of the residual in men and was not significant in women. Residual SD in kJ/d was not available because only the abstract could be read.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results); full text blocked (publisher 403 / bot challenge)

findings.citation: Pontzer H, Yamada Y, Sagayama H, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808-812.
findings.design: Pooled analysis of an international doubly labelled water database (n=6421, 29 countries; basal expenditure by indirect calorimetry in n=2008)
findings.question: Q1: How much does total energy expenditure vary between individuals after adjusting for body composition?
findings.finding: Total expenditure scaled with FFM as a power law (TEE=0.677·FFM^0.708; r²=0.83), so body size, mainly FFM, explained 83% of the variation. After controlling for FFM, FM, sex and age, TEE and its components still varied by more than ±20% between individuals. Adjusted TEE in adults aged 20–25 years was 102.7±18.1% of expected (n=314). Adjusted expenditure was stable from about 20 to 60 years and declined by about 0.7% per year after about 60.
findings.locator: Results paragraphs 1 and 4; final paragraph (>±20% residual variation); PMC8370708 author manuscript

findings.citation: Anthanont P, Jensen MD. Does basal metabolic rate predict weight gain? Am J Clin Nutr. 2016;104(4):959-963.
findings.design: Retrospective cohort (research-unit BMR by ventilated hood plus DXA; EMR weight follow-up of at least 3 years, mean about 9.7 years); n=757, follow-up n=163
findings.question: Q1: How large and how stable are body-composition-adjusted BMR differences, and do 'slow metabolism' individuals gain more weight?
findings.finding: Among 757 weight-stable adults, the top and bottom 15% of residual BMR (adjusted for FFM, FM, age and sex) were more than 169 kcal/d above and more than 173 kcal/d below predicted. About 70% of people therefore fell within roughly ±170 kcal/d of prediction. With follow-up data (86 vs 77 people), the high and low groups had BMRs of 2001±317 vs 1510±222 kcal/d despite similar age, BMI, FFM and FM. Weight gain did not differ: 0.5±1.5 vs 0.3±1.0 kg/y (P=0.16), and 4.7% vs 3.9% gained 10 kg. In 33 people measured twice about 1.0±0.9 years apart, the residual was −33±143 kcal/d (−2±9%) and then −61±190 kcal/d (−4±11%), with no significant difference (P=0.40).
findings.locator: Methods (Calculations); Results paragraphs 1-3 and repeat-measurement paragraph; Table 1; Figure 1

findings.citation: Ravussin E, Lillioja S, Knowler WC, et al. Reduced rate of energy expenditure as a risk factor for body-weight gain. N Engl J Med. 1988;318(8):467-472.
findings.design: Prospective cohort; respiratory chamber 24-h EE and resting metabolic rate; Pima Indians (n=95, n=126, and 94 siblings)
findings.question: Q1: Do body-composition-adjusted differences in expenditure exist and matter?
findings.finding: Adjusted 24-h EE correlated with the rate of weight change over 2 years (r=−0.39). People 200 kcal/d below predicted had about 4 times the estimated risk of gaining more than 7.5 kg compared with people 200 kcal/d above predicted. The 15 people who later gained more than 10 kg had a lower initial adjusted resting rate (1694±103 vs 1764±109 kcal/d). Adjusted 24-h EE aggregated in families (intraclass correlation 0.48). This finding contrasts with the null result of Anthanont 2016 in a Western cohort.
findings.locator: Abstract; full text not accessible

findings.citation: Bogardus C, Lillioja S, Ravussin E, et al. Familial dependence of the resting metabolic rate. N Engl J Med. 1986;315(2):96-100.
findings.design: Cross-sectional family study; indirect calorimetry; n=130 adults from 54 families
findings.question: Q1: How much RMR variance is explained by body composition, and is the residual individual-specific?
findings.finding: FFM, age and sex together accounted for 83% of the variance in RMR, with FFM the dominant factor. Family membership explained a further 11% (P<0.0001). People from lower-RMR families were not more obese.
findings.locator: Abstract; full text not accessible

findings.citation: Frankenfield D, Roth-Yousey L, Compher C. Comparison of predictive equations for resting metabolic rate in healthy nonobese and obese adults: a systematic review. J Am Diet Assoc. 2005;105(5):775-789.
findings.design: Systematic review (ADA evidence analysis) of RMR prediction equations validated against indirect calorimetry using individual-level data
findings.question: Q1: How closely do body-size equations predict an individual's measured RMR?
findings.finding: Of the four commonly used equations (Harris-Benedict, Mifflin-St Jeor, Owen, WHO/FAO/UNU), Mifflin-St Jeor predicted RMR within 10% of measured in more nonobese and obese individuals than any other and had the narrowest error range. The review still reports noteworthy individual errors. Older adults and US ethnic minorities were underrepresented. The exact percentages within 10% are in the full text, which was not read, so they are not quoted here.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results and Conclusions)

findings.citation: Hall KD, Chow CC. Estimating changes in free-living energy intake and its confidence interval. Am J Clin Nutr. 2011;94(1):66-74.
findings.design: Mathematical modelling study, validated on inpatient controlled-feeding data and simulated free-living 'virtual subjects'
findings.question: Q2: How precise is an intake-change estimate from daily weights over a given window?
findings.finding: The intake-change estimate is ε(BW_i − BW_0) + ρ·a, where a is the least-squares slope of weight. Its variance (Eq. 3) falls as the number of daily points n grows, and daily weighing (T=1 d) is optimal. With n=28, ρ=9100 kcal/kg, ε=22 kcal/kg/d and a weight fluctuation SD of about 0.5 kg, SD(ΔEI)=180 kcal/d, giving a 95% CI of ±350 kcal/d. In simulations with 20% day-to-day variation in intake, sodium and carbohydrate, the 95% CI at n=28 was 290 kcal/d for a 90-kg man (mean residual 90 kcal/d), 290 for a 120-kg woman and 300 for an active 70-kg man. The largest errors occurred just after diet transitions because of fluid shifts. An unknown added exercise of about 240 kcal/d biased the estimate by −220 kcal/d. Because ρ/ε exceeds 365 d, a linear weight fit is adequate over windows shorter than about 60 d. Weights over more than 28 d are needed for a 95% CI under 300 kcal/d. The weight residual variance can be the empirical value or the stationary fluctuation, which give similar results.
findings.locator: Abstract; Methods, 'Estimating changes in EI and its 95% CI' (Equations 2-3); Results, computational-model sections (Figures 3-6); Appendix A (variance derivation)

findings.citation: Hall KD, Chow CC. Estimating changes in free-living energy intake and its confidence interval. Am J Clin Nutr. 2011;94(1):66-74. (Derived values: Equation 3 applied by this reviewer)
findings.design: Reviewer calculation using the published Equation 3 and the published parameters (ρ=9100 kcal/kg, ε=22 kcal/kg/d, T=1 d); not reported in the paper
findings.question: Q2: Precision of intake-change estimates from daily weights over 14, 21 and 28 days
findings.finding: DERIVED, not stated in the paper. 95% CI (1.96×SD) of the intake-change estimate from daily weights with a weight fluctuation SD of 0.5 kg: 7 d ±1769; 14 d ±710; 21 d ±457; 28 d ±352 (this reproduces the paper's ±350); 35 d ±295; 42 d ±260; 56 d ±216 kcal/d. With a weight SD of 0.35 kg: 14 d ±497; 21 d ±320; 28 d ±247; 35 d ±207 kcal/d. The CI scales linearly with the individual's weight-residual SD. Only T=1 d (daily weighing) was computed, because the last term of Eq. 3 is written with T² and its scaling for other weighing intervals is ambiguous.
findings.locator: Equation 3 (Methods; formula image ajcn941066equ3) with the parameters stated in the same paragraph

findings.citation: Hall KD, Chow CC. Estimating changes in free-living energy intake and its confidence interval. Am J Clin Nutr. 2011;94(1):66-74.
findings.design: Modelling study (Discussion citing doubly labelled water data)
findings.question: Q1: How uncertain is a person's baseline energy requirement without measurement?
findings.finding: Using Institute of Medicine equations, the 95% CI for baseline energy intake exceeds 450 kcal/d. In DLW data from 1399 adults (cited by the authors), the SD of energy expenditure was about 500 kcal/d among people within a 5-kg body-weight range, for both men and women. Even with individual DLW at baseline, the SD of initial intake is still about 100 kcal/d. The authors therefore recommend using weight data to estimate changes in intake, not absolute intake. The 1399-adult figure is a secondary report of Swinburn 2009.
findings.locator: Methods (paragraph after Equation 3); Discussion, final paragraphs

findings.citation: Sanghvi A, Redman LM, Martin CK, Ravussin E, Hall KD. Validation of an inexpensive and accurate mathematical method to measure long-term changes in free-living energy intake. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(2):353-358.
findings.design: Validation study within an RCT (CALERIE 2-year 25% caloric restriction); model vs DLW/DXA intake-balance; n=140 (112 with complete data)
findings.question: Q2: How accurate are weight-based intake-change estimates in real free-living people?
findings.finding: Using only baseline demographics and clinic weights (months 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 24), the NIDDK model's mean intake-change estimate was within 40 kcal/d of DLW/DXA in every interval (weeks 0–26, 26–52, 52–78 and 78–104; all P≥0.11). For individuals, the RMS deviation was 215 kcal/d. Most estimates were within 132 kcal/d and three-quarters within 250 kcal/d; averaged per subject, most were within 158 kcal/d. Limits of agreement spanned about 800–1000 kcal/d. Model parameters were ρ=8840±450 kcal/kg and ε=25.8±1.0 kcal/kg/d. The authors note that the DLW/DXA reference is also imprecise for individuals and that more frequent weights would improve the model's precision.
findings.locator: Abstract; Methods (mathematical modelling paragraph); Results paragraphs 2-3; Table 1; Figure 3; Discussion paragraphs 2 and 5

findings.citation: Bhutani S, Kahn E, Tasali E, Schoeller DA. Composition of two-week change in body weight under unrestricted free-living conditions. Physiol Rep. 2017;5(13):e13336.
findings.design: Observational study of two free-living cohorts (TBW by isotope dilution, n=24; DXA, n=22); n=46
findings.question: Q2: How noisy and what composition are 2-week weight changes when people are near energy balance?
findings.finding: Two-week weight change was 0.18±1.1 kg in cohort 1 and 0.35±1.3 kg in cohort 2 (combined 0.26±1.2 kg), consistent with energy balance. Each 1 kg of 2-week weight change was 84% FFM (r=0.80), mostly water, so its energy density was about 2380 kcal/kg rather than the value for fat tissue. The authors conclude that in free-living people, weight change alone over 2 weeks cannot distinguish energy balance from an imbalance of less than 500 kcal/d, because weight will not move by more than 1–2 kg. They also cite typical short-term (days to 3 weeks) fluctuations of 1–2 kg.
findings.locator: Results paragraphs 2-3 (Figure 1); Introduction paragraph 3; Discussion (paragraph on limits of weight change alone)

findings.citation: Turicchi J, O'Driscoll R, Horgan G, et al. Weekly, seasonal and holiday body weight fluctuation patterns among individuals engaged in a European multi-centre behavioural weight loss maintenance intervention. PLoS One. 2020;15(4):e0232152.
findings.design: Secondary analysis of smart-scale weights within an RCT (NoHoW); LOESS-detrended; weekly analysis n=1421 (mean 220 weighings over 566 days)
findings.question: Q2: Day-of-week weight variability that trend estimates must handle
findings.finding: After LOESS detrending (span 0.5), weight was highest on Monday, then Sunday and Tuesday, and lowest on Friday. The within-week fluctuation was about 0.35% of body weight (about 0.3 kg): 0.41% in men vs 0.29% in women. It was larger in healthy-weight people (0.39%) than in class 2–3 obesity (0.26%), and largest at age 30–45 (0.43%). Christmas raised weight by 1.35±1.74% (about 1.1 kg), which was not fully reversed by March (still at least 0.35% above). Scale use averaged about 4 times per week at first, falling to about 2.5 per week.
findings.locator: Methods (detrending paragraphs); Results, 'Weekly patterns of body weight' and Christmas paragraph; Discussion paragraphs 1-2

findings.citation: Orsama AL, Mattila E, Ermes M, van Gils M, Wansink B, Korhonen I. Weight rhythms: weight increases during weekends and decreases during weekdays. Obes Facts. 2014;7(1):36-47.
findings.design: Retrospective pooled analysis of self-recorded morning weights from 4 studies; semi-parametric mixed models; n=80 adults, 4657 measurements over 15–330 days
findings.question: Q2: Weekly weight cycles in daily self-weighing data
findings.finding: After a 7-day moving-average detrend, day of week significantly predicted weight in all groups (P≤0.002). Weight was highest on Sunday and Monday, fell through the week, bottomed on Friday and rose from Saturday. In people losing weight, 60% of weekly minima fell on Friday or Saturday and 59% of maxima on Sunday or Monday. Read approximately from Figure 1 (normalised units), the Monday-to-Friday amplitude was about 0.25% of body weight for the whole sample and about 0.4% in the weight-loss group. The pattern was weakest in people gaining weight.
findings.locator: Methods (Derivation of Variables); Results (Table 3 and text); Figure 1 (amplitude read from the plot, approximate); Conclusion

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138.
findings.design: Randomised controlled trial with food provided (continuous vs intermittent 2-week blocks of energy restriction); n=51 randomised, 36 per protocol; obese men
findings.question: Q2: How often did a well-controlled trial adjust energy prescriptions from weight or expenditure data?
findings.finding: Maintenance needs were estimated as measured REE times a self-reported activity factor. During the 4-week baseline, participants self-weighed at home and received adjustment instructions after gaining or losing weight consistently for at least 3 days. Even so, baseline weight changed by −1.6±1.4 kg (−1.4±1.2%). During restriction (67% of maintenance), the prescription was recalculated every 4 weeks from newly measured REE to keep the same relative deficit. The absolute deficit shrank from −4142 and −4009 kJ/d (weeks 1–4) to −3810 and −3740 kJ/d (weeks 13–16). Home weights were requested at least weekly, and daily weighing was also instructed. Weight changed 0.0±0.3 kg across the 2-week energy-balance blocks.
findings.locator: Methods: 'Determination of weight maintenance energy requirements', energy-restriction paragraph, 'Body height, weight and composition'; Results (baseline paragraph; Figure 1b legend and text)

findings.citation: Martin CK, Miller AC, Thomas DM, Champagne CM, Han H, Church T. Efficacy of SmartLoss, a smartphone-based weight loss intervention: results from a randomized controlled trial. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2015;23(5):935-942.
findings.design: Pilot randomised controlled trial, 12 weeks; model-based weight-graph adherence coaching vs attention-matched health education; n=40
findings.question: Q2: Adaptive coaching trials that act on daily weight trends
findings.finding: Each participant's expected weight curve was generated from a dynamic energy-balance model. An adherence zone was set from the model's validation mean absolute error. Participants weighed daily on wireless scales (on average 5.75 times per week; data transmitted on 79% of days) and counsellors sent feedback at least weekly. The adjustments were behavioural and counselling-based; the calorie prescription stayed fixed at 1200 kcal/d for women and 1400 kcal/d for men. Weight loss at 12 weeks was −9.4±0.5% vs −0.6±0.5% (P<0.001); 80% lost more than 5% and 50% more than 10%.
findings.locator: Methods (SmartLoss intervention paragraphs; Figure 2); Results; weighing-frequency paragraph

findings.citation: Garthe I, Raastad T, Refsnes PE, Koivisto A, Sundgot-Borgen J. Effect of two different weight-loss rates on body composition and strength and power-related performance in elite athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2011;21(2):97-104.
findings.design: Randomised controlled trial; elite athletes doing 4 resistance-training sessions per week; slow (0.7%/wk target) vs fast (1.4%/wk target) weight loss; n=24
findings.question: Q2: Trials that prescribed diets to hit a weekly rate of weight change
findings.finding: Energy-restricted diets were set to produce a predetermined weekly loss. Intake was cut by 19±2% in the slow group vs 30±4% in the fast group. Both lost about 5.5% of body weight, at 0.7±0.8 vs 1.0±0.4% per week; the fast group did not reach its 1.4% target. Time in intervention was 8.5±2.2 vs 5.3±0.9 weeks. Lean mass rose 2.1% in the slow group and was unchanged (−0.2%) in the fast group (P<0.01). How often intake was adjusted is not stated in the abstract, and the full text was not accessible.
findings.locator: Abstract; full text paywalled

findings.citation: Pieper C, Redman L, Racette S, et al. Development of adherence metrics for caloric restriction interventions. Clin Trials. 2011;8(2):155-164.
findings.design: Modelling of weight trajectories from CALERIE phase 1 (DLW plus DXA/BodPod intake-balance); n=77
findings.question: Q2: Over what horizon can short-term body-store changes be trusted?
findings.finding: The authors state that body energy-store changes are too small to quantify accurately with DXA within about 1 month. Intake, and therefore adherence, could only be determined accurately over months of negative balance. They built individual percentile normograms (10th to 90th) of expected percent weight change under 25% caloric restriction for real-time adherence monitoring. Weight change varied widely between individuals, and some regained after about 6 months.
findings.locator: Introduction paragraph 3; Methods (normogram development); Figure 3 legend; Discussion

findings.citation: Frankenfield D, Roth-Yousey L, Compher C. Comparison of predictive equations for resting metabolic rate in healthy nonobese and obese adults: a systematic review. J Am Diet Assoc. 2005;105(5):775-89. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2005.02.005
findings.population: Healthy non-obese and obese adults in validation studies reporting individual-level data
findings.parameter: RMR equation default (healthy non-obese and obese adults)
findings.value: Mifflin-St Jeor preferred over Harris-Benedict, Owen and WHO/FAO/UNU; accuracy criterion = share of individuals predicted within ±10% of RMR measured by indirect calorimetry (percentages not given in abstract)
findings.finding: Among the four equations most often used in practice, Mifflin-St Jeor was the most reliable: it brought the largest share of lean and obese people within 10% of their measured RMR and showed the tightest spread of error. Sizeable errors in individuals still occur.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 15883556), Results and Conclusions paragraphs

findings.citation: Frankenfield D, Roth-Yousey L, Compher C. Comparison of predictive equations for resting metabolic rate in healthy nonobese and obese adults: a systematic review. J Am Diet Assoc. 2005;105(5):775-89. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2005.02.005
findings.parameter: WHO/FAO/UNU RMR equation individual-level validation
findings.value: No individual-level validation studies identified
findings.finding: The reviewers found no validation studies of the WHO/FAO/UNU equation that looked at errors for individual people. Its accuracy for one person is therefore unestablished by this review. Choosing it not to be the app default is our inference, not the paper's statement.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 15883556), Results paragraph

findings.citation: Frankenfield D, Roth-Yousey L, Compher C. Comparison of predictive equations for resting metabolic rate in healthy nonobese and obese adults: a systematic review. J Am Diet Assoc. 2005;105(5):775-89. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2005.02.005
findings.population: Healthy non-obese and obese adults; older and ethnic-minority adults underrepresented
findings.parameter: RMR estimate confidence flag (age and ethnicity coverage)
findings.value: Older adults and US-resident ethnic minorities underrepresented in equation derivation and validation; treat estimates as lower-confidence for these groups; measured RMR (indirect calorimetry) preferred when prediction fails an individual
findings.finding: Few older people or US ethnic-minority participants were in the samples used to build or test these equations. The expert panel urges strong doubt about predicted RMR for such groups, clinician judgement, and indirect calorimetry where the estimate clearly misfits a person.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 15883556), Results and Conclusions paragraphs

findings.citation: Frankenfield DC. Bias and accuracy of resting metabolic rate equations in non-obese and obese adults. Clin Nutr. 2013;32(6):976-82. doi:10.1016/j.clnu.2013.03.022
findings.population: Ambulatory, community-living non-obese and obese adults
findings.parameter: Mifflin-St Jeor bias (estimated minus measured RMR)
findings.value: Unbiased; 95% CI of difference −26 to +8 kcal/day
findings.finding: In a cross-sectional validation against indirect calorimetry, the Mifflin-St Jeor equation showed no systematic bias, with the 95% confidence interval of estimate-minus-measured spanning zero.

findings.citation: Frankenfield DC. Bias and accuracy of resting metabolic rate equations in non-obese and obese adults. Clin Nutr. 2013;32(6):976-82. doi:10.1016/j.clnu.2013.03.022
findings.population: Ambulatory, community-living non-obese and obese adults
findings.parameter: Mifflin-St Jeor accuracy (share within ±10% of measured RMR)
findings.value: 82% overall; 87% non-obese vs 75% obese
findings.finding: About four in five people were predicted within 10% of measured RMR by Mifflin-St Jeor. Accuracy was lower in obese than non-obese participants for every equation tested, so estimates for people with obesity warrant wider uncertainty.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 23631843), Results paragraph

findings.citation: Frankenfield DC. Bias and accuracy of resting metabolic rate equations in non-obese and obese adults. Clin Nutr. 2013;32(6):976-82. doi:10.1016/j.clnu.2013.03.022
findings.population: Ambulatory, community-living non-obese and obese adults
findings.parameter: Livingston RMR equation bias and accuracy
findings.value: Underestimates: 95% CI −63 to −25 kcal/day; 79% of estimates within ±10% of measured
findings.finding: The Livingston equation had accuracy similar to Mifflin-St Jeor but systematically underestimated measured RMR.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 23631843), Results paragraph

findings.citation: Frankenfield DC. Bias and accuracy of resting metabolic rate equations in non-obese and obese adults. Clin Nutr. 2013;32(6):976-82. doi:10.1016/j.clnu.2013.03.022
findings.population: Ambulatory, community-living non-obese and obese adults
findings.parameter: Bias direction of Harris-Benedict, WHO, Oxford (WHO variant), Muller and Vander Weg equations
findings.value: All tended to overestimate measured RMR (magnitudes not reported in abstract)
findings.finding: Apart from Mifflin-St Jeor (unbiased) and Livingston (underestimating), every other equation tested, including Harris-Benedict and WHO/Oxford, tended to overestimate resting metabolic rate.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 23631843), Methods and Results paragraphs

findings.citation: Frankenfield DC. Bias and accuracy of resting metabolic rate equations in non-obese and obese adults. Clin Nutr. 2013;32(6):976-82. doi:10.1016/j.clnu.2013.03.022
findings.population: Ambulatory, community-living non-obese and obese adults (the proposed equation targets the obese subgroup; the subgroup n is not given in the abstract)
findings.parameter: Obesity-specific RMR equation (Frankenfield 2013)
findings.value: Proposed; coefficients not given in abstract; author states it requires validation before clinical adoption
findings.finding: Because accuracy was lower in obesity, the author proposed an obesity-specific equation but said it needs validation before clinical use. The app should therefore not use it as a default.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 23631843), Conclusions paragraph

findings.citation: Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, Hill LA, Scott BJ, Daugherty SA, Koh YO. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241-7. doi:10.1093/ajcn/51.2.241
findings.population: Healthy adults aged 19-78 y (mean 45±14); 247 women, 251 men; 264 normal-weight, 234 obese
findings.parameter: RMR equation (Mifflin-St Jeor)
findings.value: Men: REE = 10×weight(kg) + 6.25×height(cm) − 5×age(y) + 5; Women: REE = 10×weight(kg) + 6.25×height(cm) − 5×age(y) − 161. Unified form: 9.99×weight + 6.25×height − 4.92×age + 166×sex (male=1, female=0) − 161; R²=0.71. Output unit not printed in abstract.
findings.finding: Multiple regression on indirect-calorimetry REE gave a weight-height-age equation with a sex term; simplifying coefficients and splitting by sex did not reduce predictive value.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 2305711), sentences 3-4 (sample description in sentences 1-2)

findings.citation: Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, Hill LA, Scott BJ, Daugherty SA, Koh YO. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241-7. doi:10.1093/ajcn/51.2.241
findings.population: Healthy adults aged 19-78 y, normal-weight and obese, both sexes
findings.parameter: FFM-based RMR equation (Mifflin)
findings.value: REE = 19.7×FFM + 413; R²=0.64 (FFM and output units not stated in abstract)
findings.finding: Fat-free mass was the strongest single predictor of resting energy expenditure, explaining about 64% of its variance.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 2305711), sentence 7 (second-to-last)

findings.citation: Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, Hill LA, Scott BJ, Daugherty SA, Koh YO. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241-7. doi:10.1093/ajcn/51.2.241
findings.population: Healthy adults aged 19-78 y, normal-weight and obese, both sexes
findings.parameter: Weight-only RMR equation (Mifflin)
findings.value: REE = 15.1×weight + 371; R²=0.56 (units not stated in abstract)
findings.finding: Body weight alone correlated closely with resting energy expenditure but explained less variance than the full weight-height-age-sex equation.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 2305711), final sentence

findings.citation: Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, Hill LA, Scott BJ, Daugherty SA, Koh YO. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241-7. doi:10.1093/ajcn/51.2.241
findings.population: Healthy adults aged 19-78 y, normal-weight and obese, both sexes
findings.parameter: Harris-Benedict bias vs measured REE
findings.value: Overestimated measured REE by 5% (p<0.01)
findings.finding: In this sample, the 1919 Harris-Benedict equations gave REE values about 5% above those measured by calorimetry.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 2305711), sentence 6

findings.citation: Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, Hill LA, Scott BJ, Daugherty SA, Koh YO. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241-7. doi:10.1093/ajcn/51.2.241
findings.population: Healthy adults aged 19-78 y, normal-weight and obese, both sexes
findings.parameter: Extra RMR predictors (relative body weight, body-weight distribution)
findings.value: No significant improvement in predictive value
findings.finding: Adding relative body weight or body-weight distribution measures did not significantly improve the equations. By our inference, the app need not collect them to estimate RMR.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 2305711), sentence 5

findings.citation: Cunningham JJ. A reanalysis of the factors influencing basal metabolic rate in normal adults. Am J Clin Nutr. 1980;33(11):2372-4. doi:10.1093/ajcn/33.11.2372
findings.population: Normal adults from the Harris-Benedict (1919) metabolism dataset
findings.parameter: LBM-based BMR equation (Cunningham 1980)
findings.value: BMR = 500 + 22×LBM (abstract prints the unit as cal/day; LBM unit not stated in abstract; LBM was estimated, not measured)
findings.finding: Using multiple regression on 223 Harris-Benedict subjects, the author identified estimated lean body mass as the one variable needed to predict BMR and proposed a simple intercept-plus-slope LBM equation.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 7435418), sentences 1 and 4-6

findings.citation: Cunningham JJ. A reanalysis of the factors influencing basal metabolic rate in normal adults. Am J Clin Nutr. 1980;33(11):2372-4. doi:10.1093/ajcn/33.11.2372
findings.population: Normal adults from the Harris-Benedict (1919) metabolism dataset
findings.parameter: Sex and age as additional BMR predictors when LBM is known
findings.value: Add little beyond LBM
findings.finding: Once lean body mass was included, sex and age contributed little further to BMR prediction in this reanalysis.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 7435418), final sentence

findings.citation: Owen OE, Kavle E, Owen RS, Polansky M, Caprio S, Mozzoli MA, et al. A reappraisal of caloric requirements in healthy women. Am J Clin Nutr. 1986;44(1):1-19. doi:10.1093/ajcn/44.1.1
findings.population: Healthy lean and obese women aged 18-65 y, 43-143 kg (36 non-athletes, 8 trained athletes)
findings.parameter: RMR equation, non-athletic women (Owen)
findings.value: RMR = 795 + 7.18×weight(kg) (output unit not printed in abstract)
findings.finding: In this sample of healthy women, weight tracked RMR closely and adding further variables through stepwise regression gave no better prediction, so a weight-only equation was fitted for non-athletes.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 3728346), sentences 1, 3-4, 7 and 9

findings.citation: Owen OE, Kavle E, Owen RS, Polansky M, Caprio S, Mozzoli MA, et al. A reappraisal of caloric requirements in healthy women. Am J Clin Nutr. 1986;44(1):1-19. doi:10.1093/ajcn/44.1.1
findings.population: Trained female athletes within a sample of healthy women aged 18-65 y
findings.parameter: RMR equation, athletic women (Owen)
findings.value: RMR = 50.4 + 21.1×weight(kg) (output unit not printed in abstract; derived from 8 athletes; sport type not stated in abstract)
findings.finding: The slope of RMR against weight differed significantly between athletic and non-athletic women, so a separate athlete equation was fitted. It rests on only eight trained women, and the abstract does not say what sport they did.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 3728346), sentences 8-9

findings.citation: Owen OE, Kavle E, Owen RS, Polansky M, Caprio S, Mozzoli MA, et al. A reappraisal of caloric requirements in healthy women. Am J Clin Nutr. 1986;44(1):1-19. doi:10.1093/ajcn/44.1.1
findings.population: Healthy lean and obese women aged 18-65 y, including 8 athletes
findings.parameter: Bias of earlier RMR tables/equations in women
findings.value: Overestimate RMR of healthy women by 7-14%
findings.finding: Tables and regression equations available at the time overestimated measured RMR in healthy women by roughly 7 to 14 percent.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 3728346), sentence 6

findings.citation: Owen OE, Holup JL, D'Alessio DA, Craig ES, Polansky M, Smalley KJ, et al. A reappraisal of the caloric requirements of men. Am J Clin Nutr. 1987;46(6):875-85. doi:10.1093/ajcn/46.6.875
findings.population: Lean and obese men aged 18-82 y, 60-171 kg
findings.parameter: RMR equation, men (weight-based)
findings.value: RMR (kcal/d) = 879 + 10.2 x body weight (kg)
findings.finding: Regression built from measured RMR in 60 lean and obese men. Body weight alone predicted RMR about as well as other markers of metabolically active tissue.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 3687821); full text not opened

findings.citation: Owen OE, Holup JL, D'Alessio DA, Craig ES, Polansky M, Smalley KJ, et al. A reappraisal of the caloric requirements of men. Am J Clin Nutr. 1987;46(6):875-85. doi:10.1093/ajcn/46.6.875
findings.population: Lean and obese men aged 18-82 y, 60-171 kg
findings.parameter: RMR equation, men (fat-free-mass-based)
findings.value: RMR (kcal/d) = 290 + 22.3 x fat-free mass (kg, by densitometry)
findings.finding: Alternative Owen equation for men when fat-free mass is known. FFM was measured by densitometry, and the abstract says nothing about using FFM from other methods such as consumer scales.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 3687821); full text not opened

findings.citation: Owen OE, Holup JL, D'Alessio DA, Craig ES, Polansky M, Smalley KJ, et al. A reappraisal of the caloric requirements of men. Am J Clin Nutr. 1987;46(6):875-85. doi:10.1093/ajcn/46.6.875
findings.population: Lean and obese men aged 18-82 y
findings.parameter: bias and covariates of RMR prediction in men
findings.value: Classic equations/tables overestimate men's RMR; age effect trivial; regional fat distribution no effect; 95% confidence limits broad (numeric limits not in abstract)
findings.finding: Older standard equations overpredicted RMR in men. Age added almost nothing and fat distribution added nothing. Individual 95% limits were wide, so any single prediction is uncertain.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 3687821)

findings.citation: Schofield WN. Predicting basal metabolic rate, new standards and review of previous work. Hum Nutr Clin Nutr. 1985;39 Suppl 1:5-41.
findings.population: Pooled literature BMR data, all ages, both sexes
findings.parameter: individual-level error of BMR equations
findings.value: Prediction error for an individual judged necessarily high; error tables for individuals vs group means exist in the paper (values not read)
findings.finding: The author argues that individual BMR predictions must carry large error, because BMR mixes separate effects of sex, age and body size. The paper gives separate error tables for individuals and for group means.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 4044297); full text not opened

findings.citation: Schofield WN. Predicting basal metabolic rate, new standards and review of previous work. Hum Nutr Clin Nutr. 1985;39 Suppl 1:5-41.
findings.population: Pooled literature BMR data (screened, ~50 years of studies)
findings.parameter: BMR equation predictors
findings.value: Weight alone, or weight + height, within sex- and age-banded equations; more complex equations added little
findings.finding: Equations predict BMR from weight, or from weight and height, separately by sex and age band. More complex models gave little practical improvement.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 4044297)

findings.citation: Schofield WN. Predicting basal metabolic rate, new standards and review of previous work. Hum Nutr Clin Nutr. 1985;39 Suppl 1:5-41.
findings.parameter: population differences in BMR per kg
findings.value: Subjects from developing countries had lower BMR per kg body weight than European/North American subjects (magnitude not given in abstract)
findings.finding: Beyond being smaller, people from developing countries had lower BMR per kg than Western subjects. This suggests the equations may not transfer across populations.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 4044297)

findings.citation: Henry CJK. Basal metabolic rate studies in humans: measurement and development of new equations. Public Health Nutr. 2005;8(7A):1133-52. doi:10.1079/phn2005801
findings.population: Pooled published and measured BMR data, all ages, both sexes, broad geographic origin
findings.parameter: BMR equation adults, weight only (Oxford)
findings.finding: Oxford equations fitted to 10,552 BMR values. They exclude all Italian subjects and include 4,018 people from the tropics, which makes them an alternative to Schofield for users from more varied populations.
findings.locator: Table 12, p.1144; Abstract

findings.citation: Henry CJK. Basal metabolic rate studies in humans: measurement and development of new equations. Public Health Nutr. 2005;8(7A):1133-52. doi:10.1079/phn2005801
findings.population: Oxford BMR database, adults by age band
findings.parameter: BMR equation adults, weight + height (Oxford)
findings.finding: Height-inclusive Oxford equations. Adding height gave no significant improvement over weight alone (Table 17), so height is optional.
findings.locator: Table 15 and Table 17, p.1146

findings.citation: Henry CJK. Basal metabolic rate studies in humans: measurement and development of new equations. Public Health Nutr. 2005;8(7A):1133-52. doi:10.1079/phn2005801
findings.parameter: BMR equation older adults (Oxford, 60-70 and 70+)
findings.finding: Separate weight-based BMR equations for adults aged 60-70 and 70+. They split the 60+ group more finely, and the single 60+ equations in Table 12 remain an option.
findings.locator: Table 14, p.1145

findings.citation: Henry CJK. Basal metabolic rate studies in humans: measurement and development of new equations. Public Health Nutr. 2005;8(7A):1133-52. doi:10.1079/phn2005801
findings.population: Children and adults 3-60 y from tropical/non-European ethnic groups (Henry and Rees compilation)
findings.parameter: bias of FAO/WHO/UNU (Schofield) BMR equations by sex and ethnicity
findings.value: Mean overestimate of measured BMR: males 3-60 y +9.0% (n 2053); females +5.4% (n 769); overall +8.0% (n 2822). By ethnicity (M/F): Indian +12.8%/+12.9%; Chinese +7.6%/+3.8%; Japanese +5.8%/+4.6%; South American +9.4%/+4.8%; Filipino +9.5%/+1.1%; Ceylonese +22.4%/+12.5%
findings.finding: In Henry and Rees's compilation of data from tropical and non-European groups, the Schofield equations overpredicted measured BMR by 8% on average. Overestimates were largest in some groups, such as Ceylonese and Indian subjects. This matters for users outside the European reference data.
findings.locator: Tables 4 and 5, p.1138 (data from Henry and Rees)

findings.citation: Henry CJK. Basal metabolic rate studies in humans: measurement and development of new equations. Public Health Nutr. 2005;8(7A):1133-52. doi:10.1079/phn2005801
findings.parameter: Oxford vs FAO/WHO/UNU difference in estimated requirement
findings.value: Oxford BMR lower than FAO for men 18-30 and 30-60 y and all women >18 y; for ages 18-30 at 55-105 kg, TEE lower by 396-841 kJ (95-201 kcal)/d in men (PAL 1.55-2.10) and 202-863 kJ (48-206 kcal)/d in women (PAL 1.56-1.82)
findings.finding: Switching from Schofield to Oxford BMR lowers estimated daily needs by about 50-200 kcal for adults aged 18-30. In men the gap is largest at low body weight (<60 kg); in women it grows as weight rises.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results); p.1144 text (BMR differences, Tables 18-20); p.1145 text; Tables 21-22, p.1148

findings.citation: Henry CJK. Basal metabolic rate studies in humans: measurement and development of new equations. Public Health Nutr. 2005;8(7A):1133-52. doi:10.1079/phn2005801
findings.population: Schofield database adults 18-30 y excluding Italians
findings.parameter: Schofield 18-30 y equations recalculated without Italian subjects
findings.finding: Italians supplied 3,388 of 7,173 (47%) Schofield data points. Henry reports Schofield's own refits for ages 18-30 without Italians. Applied to the Italian subjects, those refits fit very poorly, which marks the Italians as a distinct high-BMR group.
findings.locator: p.1140 (Schofield refit as reported by Henry); Abstract

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: TEE factorial equation
findings.value: TEE (energy requirement) = BMR x PAL; PAL = 24-h TEE / 24-h BMR
findings.finding: For healthy adults, the daily energy requirement is BMR multiplied by the physical activity level. PAL itself is 24-hour TEE divided by BMR.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, sections 5.1 and 5.3; section 2.6 glossary (y5686e07.htm, y5686e04.htm)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.population: Adults by sex and age band
findings.parameter: BMR equations adults (Schofield, retained by FAO/WHO/UNU)
findings.finding: The consultation kept the 1985 Schofield weight-based equations. Newer equations had some merits but were not judged robust enough to adopt. Annex 3 confirms that no update was made.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, section 5.2, Table 5.2; Annex 3 (y5686e0e.htm)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: PAL lifestyle categories
findings.value: Sedentary/light 1.40-1.69; active/moderately active 1.70-1.99; vigorous/vigorously active 2.00-2.40; PAL >2.40 hard to sustain long term
findings.finding: Three lifestyle bands, each defined by a PAL range and used the same way for men and women. Lifestyle means habitual activity over about a month or more, including discretionary activity, not occupation alone.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, section 5.3.1, Table 5.3

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: PAL mid-points, spread and sustainable range
findings.value: Mid-point e.g. 1.85 for moderately active; +/-8 to +/-10% variation around category mid-points; sustainable free-living PAL ~1.40-2.40; values apply to groups, individuals need own TEE/BMR-based estimate
findings.finding: Requirements are calculated at category mid-points and vary by about 8-10% around them. They are meant for population groups. An individual's needs should come from their own expenditure or habitual activity.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, sections 5.3 and 5.4.1

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: BMR share of TEE
findings.value: BMR = about 45-70% of daily TEE in adults
findings.finding: Basal metabolism accounts for roughly 45-70% of adults' daily energy expenditure. The share depends on age and lifestyle.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, section 5.2; Ch. 2, section 2.3

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: thermic effect of food (FAO)
findings.value: ~10% of BMR over 24 h on a mixed diet
findings.finding: The metabolic response to eating a mixed diet adds about one-tenth of BMR to daily expenditure.
findings.locator: Ch. 2, section 2.3

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University.
