Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: metabolizable energy factors per gram
findings.value: Carbohydrate 16.7 kJ (4 kcal)/g; protein 16.7 kJ (4 kcal)/g; fat 37.7 kJ (9 kcal)/g; ethanol 29.3 kJ (7 kcal)/g
findings.finding: General energy conversion factors per gram of macronutrient and alcohol. Use them to turn logged grams into energy, including alcohol energy.
findings.locator: Ch. 2, section 2.2

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: averaging window for daily energy intake/expenditure
findings.value: 7-day periods commonly used (convention; no biological basis for a specific number of days)
findings.finding: A daily requirement is an average over several days, not an amount to eat every day. A week is the usual window for estimating it.
findings.locator: Ch. 2, section 2.1.1

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: energy recommendation level (no safety margin)
findings.value: Recommend the estimated average requirement; do not add 2 SD (unlike protein safe level = mean + 2 SD)
findings.finding: Unlike nutrients with safety margins, energy should be set at the average requirement. Intakes above requirement produce positive balance and, over time, overweight.
findings.locator: Ch. 2, section 2.1.2

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: BMI range for maintenance energy recommendations
findings.value: Individual BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m2; population median BMI 21.0
findings.finding: Energy intake should let a healthy population keep an adequate BMI at its usual expenditure. Tables 5.4-5.9 list requirements by body weight and PAL, with the heights that give BMI 18.5, 21.0 and 24.9 at each weight.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, section 5.4.2, Tables 5.4-5.9 (y5686e08.htm)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: age-related BMR decline
findings.value: 1-2% per decade (older estimate); 2.9% (men) and 2.0% (women) per decade at BMI 18.5-25; 3.1%/1.9% if overweight; breakpoint ~40 y men, ~50 y women; ~5% lower in older adults after FFM adjustment
findings.finding: BMR falls with age, partly through loss of fat-free mass, and the decline is not linear. Requirements for older adults are still calculated from PAL, so accuracy depends on the BMR estimate.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, section 5.5 (y5686e09.htm)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: exercise effect on PAL and health-associated PAL threshold
findings.value: ~1 h/day moderate-to-vigorous exercise raises PAL from 1.55 to 1.75; habitual PAL >=1.70 associated with lower risk of overweight/obesity and chronic disease
findings.finding: About an hour of daily moderate-to-vigorous exercise moves a sedentary person into the moderately active band. Expert consensus links a habitual PAL of 1.70 or more with lower chronic-disease risk.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, sections 5.3.2 and 5.6

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Health Organization, United Nations University. Human energy requirements: report of a Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome, 17-24 October 2001. FAO Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series No. 1. Rome: FAO; 2004.
findings.parameter: energy cost of sports (PAR, multiple of BMR)
findings.value: Male/female average PAR: circuit training 6.96/6.29; running long distance 6.34/6.55; running sprint 8.21/8.28; high-intensity aerobic dance 7.93/8.31; low-intensity 3.51/4.24; rowing 6.7/5.34; tennis 5.8/5.92; swimming 9 (male, range 8.5-9.4); walking quickly 3.8 (male)
findings.finding: Tabulated energy costs of activities, as multiples of BMR per unit time, for factorial activity estimates. No resistance-training entry is listed; circuit training is the closest.
findings.locator: Annex 5, Energy costs of activities (y5686e0e.htm)

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.population: US/Canadian general population incl. overweight/obesity; men 19+ y
findings.parameter: EER equations, men 19+ y (NASEM 2023)
findings.value: EER kcal/d (age y, height cm, weight kg): inactive 753.07 - 10.83A + 6.50H + 14.10W; low active 581.47 - 10.83A + 8.30H + 14.94W; active 1,004.82 - 10.83A + 6.52H + 15.91W; very active -517.88 - 10.83A + 15.61H + 19.11W. R2 0.73; RMSE 339 kcal/d; MAPE 9.4%
findings.finding: Current US/Canada DRI equations built from 8,600 doubly-labelled-water observations. They replace the 2005 equations and apply across BMI categories, because slopes did not differ between normal-weight and overweight/obese groups.
findings.locator: Summary Table S-1 p.4 and Table S-3 pp.7-8; Ch. 5 pp.68 (8,600 observations) and 87 (BMI slope test)

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.population: US/Canadian general population incl. overweight/obesity; non-pregnant women 19+ y
findings.parameter: EER equations, women 19+ y (NASEM 2023)
findings.value: EER kcal/d (age y, height cm, weight kg): inactive 584.90 - 7.01A + 5.72H + 11.71W; low active 575.77 - 7.01A + 6.60H + 12.14W; active 710.25 - 7.01A + 6.54H + 12.34W; very active 511.83 - 7.01A + 9.07H + 12.56W. R2 0.71; RMSE 246 kcal/d; MAPE 8.7%
findings.finding: Female counterparts of the 2023 DRI equations. External validation used 65 studies (144 cohorts, 5,056 people). The predicted-vs-observed correlation was 0.93 for women, 0.92 for men and 0.96-0.97 for children.
findings.locator: Summary Table S-3 pp.7-8; Ch. 5 external validation and Table 5-10 p.92

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.population: Adults 19-70 y in combined DLW database
findings.parameter: PAL category cut-offs, adults 19+ y (NASEM 2023)
findings.value: Inactive 1.00 <= PAL < 1.53; low active 1.53 <= PAL < 1.68; active 1.68 <= PAL < 1.85; very active 1.85 <= PAL < 2.50
findings.finding: Adult bands are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of PAL, using observed plus predicted DLW data for ages 19-70 (n 4,299), and apply to all adult ages. They differ from the 2005 IOM and FAO cut-offs.
findings.locator: Ch. 5, p.80 (derivation); Tables 5-3 and 5-4, p.82

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: PAL category selection guide (activity examples)
findings.value: Inactive (PAL ~1.4): daily living only (~30 min walking + ~90 min light-moderate chores); low active (~1.6): + 60-80 min walking at 3-4 mph; active (~1.75): + 30-50 min walking + 45 min moderate cycling + 40 min doubles tennis; very active (~2.05): + 45 min cycling + ~25 min jogging (10 min/mile) + 60 min doubles tennis
findings.finding: A descriptive guide for choosing a category. Step counts and questionnaires correlate only weakly with DLW PAL, and meeting activity guidelines cannot place a person in a category. Weight monitoring is the correction.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: individual prediction error of EER (SEPV)
findings.value: SEPV men 19+ 342 kcal/d; women 19+ 241 kcal/d; ~68% of individuals within +/-1 SEPV, ~95% within +/-1.96 SEPV
findings.finding: A person's true requirement can differ substantially from the EER. For example, a woman with an EER of 2,275 kcal has a 95% range of 1,803-2,747 kcal/d.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: starting energy intake for weight loss
findings.value: EER - 1.96 x SEPV (men: EER - 670 kcal/d; women: EER - 472 kcal/d, computed from SEPV 241); report example for a 45-y, 100-kg low-active man: 3,041 - (1.96 x 342) = 2,371 kcal/d
findings.finding: EER equations target maintenance, not weight change. Subtracting 1.96 SEPV gives an intake predicted to cause loss in almost all similar people. The report offers it as a possible starting point to adjust afterwards.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: starting energy intake for weight gain
findings.value: EER + 1.96 x SEPV (men: EER + 670 kcal/d; women: EER + 472 kcal/d, computed from SEPV 241); report example for a man: 2,368 + (1.96 x 342) = 3,038 kcal/d
findings.finding: Adding 1.96 SEPV to the EER gives an intake predicted to cause gain in almost all similar individuals. The report treats it as a starting value, to be modified as required.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: adaptive adjustment rule from body weight
findings.value: Two-step process: (1) compute EER; (2) monitor body weight over time and adjust intake incrementally; stable weight = requirement met, gain/loss = intake above/below requirement
findings.finding: Body-weight trend, not reported intake, is the valid indicator of energy adequacy. The DRI tells planners to recalibrate intake from weigh-ins, which directly supports weight-driven adaptive targets.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.population: Adults and athletes in DLW validation studies
findings.parameter: accuracy of self-reported energy intake
findings.value: Underreporting vs DLW: 24-h recall 8-30%; FFQ 4.6-42%; food records 11-41%; diet history 1.3-47%; athletes' food records ~19% below DLW on average (11 studies)
findings.finding: Self-reported intake runs systematically low, more so in women and in some higher-BMI groups. Logged meals should not be used alone to judge whether intake meets requirement.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.population: Adults in a year-long intake study (cited)
findings.parameter: days of intake records for an individual's usual energy intake
findings.value: ~31 days of records to estimate an individual's mean energy intake within 10% (Basiotis et al. 1987, 29 people, 1 year)
findings.finding: Short food records, such as 3 days, can differ from usual intake. In the cited year-long study, estimating one person's average within 10% took about a month of records.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: adaptive thermogenesis magnitude during weight loss
findings.value: REE falls further than tissue loss predicts; the report gives the shortfall as 12-44% less than predicted, equating to about 220 kcal/d
findings.finding: Several systematic reviews found REE drops beyond what tissue loss predicts during weight loss. The size varies widely, so a fixed maintenance estimate will drift during a deficit.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: rate of weight loss vs REE reduction
findings.value: Gradual loss ~0.5 kg/week produced less REE reduction than rapid loss ~1.1 kg/week (systematic review: 7 studies, 361 participants)
findings.finding: One systematic review cited by the committee found that slower weight loss preserved REE better than faster loss. This supports a moderate weekly loss rate over an aggressive one.
findings.locator: Ch. 4, p.47 (Ashtary-Larky et al. 2020)

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.population: Individuals with extremely high activity (e.g., elite athletes)
findings.parameter: upper validity limit of EER equations
findings.value: Equations exclude PAL > 2.5; heavy-training athletes often exceed it, so even the very-active EER underestimates their needs
findings.finding: DLW data with PAL above 2.5 were excluded as unsustainable. Very high-volume endurance users need another method, and their intake should not be capped at the very-active EER.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: thermic effect of food fraction and by macronutrient
findings.value: TEF ~10% of daily energy expenditure; DIT ~0-3% of energy for fat, 5-10% carbohydrate, 20-30% protein, 10-30% alcohol; REE ~60-70% of TEE; activity 15-50% of TEE
findings.finding: The committee's breakdown of expenditure components. Protein has the largest thermogenic effect, and activity is the most variable component.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: tissue-specific metabolic rates
findings.value: Adipose/fat mass ~5 kcal/kg/d vs fat-free mass ~20 kcal/kg/d; FFM explains 60-80% of REE variance vs ~50% for body weight alone
findings.finding: Fat-free mass drives REE far more than fat mass does. Weight change made of lean tissue shifts expenditure differently from change made of fat.

findings.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2023. doi:10.17226/26818
findings.parameter: weight cycling risk
findings.value: 20-55% of adults with overweight/obesity report weight cycling; one systematic review (23 studies, 441,199 participants) linked cycling with +41% all-cause and +36% CVD mortality; no standard definition of a cycle
findings.finding: Repeated loss and regain is common and, in observational syntheses, linked with worse outcomes. Mechanisms and definitions remain unclear, so it can only inform cautious messaging.
findings.locator: Summary p.15; Ch. 8, pp.191-192

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: EER equations adults 19+ y, normal weight (IOM 2005, superseded)
findings.value: Men: EER = 662 - 9.53 x age + PA x (15.91 x weight kg + 539.6 x height m), PA 1.00/1.11/1.25/1.48; women: EER = 354 - 6.91 x age + PA x (9.36 x weight + 726 x height), PA 1.00/1.12/1.27/1.45 (sedentary/low active/active/very active)
findings.finding: The 2005 EER equations are still widely used but have been replaced by the NASEM 2023 equations. The PA coefficient multiplies the combined weight-and-height term.
findings.locator: Ch. 5 Energy (pp.107-264); cited p.185 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: PAL categories (IOM 2005)
findings.value: Sedentary 1.0-<1.4; low active 1.4-<1.6; active 1.6-<1.9; very active 1.9-2.5 (PAL = TEE/BEE)
findings.finding: The 2005 PAL bands used with the 2005 EER PA coefficients. They differ from the NASEM 2023 cut-offs, so the two systems should not be mixed.
findings.locator: Ch. 5 Energy (pp.107-264); cited pp.157-158 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: recommended daily physical activity (IOM 2005)
findings.value: 60 min/day of moderate-intensity activity on top of sedentary daily living; corresponds to the 'active' DRI category (PAL 1.6-1.89)
findings.finding: The DRI recommends this amount to prevent weight gain and gain further health benefits of activity.
findings.locator: Ch. 12 Physical Activity (pp.880-935); cited p.880 and Summary p.4 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: protein EAR and RDA, adults
findings.value: EAR 0.66 g/kg/d; RDA 0.80 g/kg/d, men and women 19+ y (56 g/d and 46 g/d at reference body weights)
findings.finding: The RDA covers nearly all (97-98%) healthy adults. It is a floor for adequacy, not a performance target. Gram amounts equal the per-kg value multiplied by the reference weight.
findings.locator: Ch. 10 Protein and Amino Acids (pp.589-768) and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.643-645 and p.1324 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: protein AMDR and upper limit
findings.value: AMDR 10-35% of energy (adults); no UL set for protein or amino acids
findings.finding: Protein at 10-35% of energy is the range associated with reduced chronic-disease risk that still supplies essential nutrients. No UL was set, and missing data do not show that chronic high intakes are tolerated.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.12, 15 and p.1325 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: carbohydrate AMDR
findings.value: 45-65% of energy (adults 19+)
findings.finding: The acceptable share of energy from carbohydrate: the range associated with reduced chronic-disease risk that still supplies essential nutrients.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited p.15 and p.1325 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: total fat AMDR
findings.value: 20-35% of energy (adults 19+); no AI/EAR/RDA or UL for total fat in adults
findings.finding: Adult fat intake falls between 20% and 35% of energy. Total fat has no adult RDA or AI, so the AMDR is the only numeric bound.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.4, 9, 15 and p.1325 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: n-6 and n-3 PUFA AMDR
findings.value: Linoleic acid 5-10% of energy; alpha-linolenic acid 0.6-1.2% of energy; up to ~10% of the n-3 range may come as EPA/DHA
findings.finding: Essential fatty-acid ranges within total fat intake. Up to one-tenth of the alpha-linolenic range may be supplied as EPA and/or DHA.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.15-16 and p.1325 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: essential fatty acid Adequate Intakes
findings.value: Linoleic acid AI: men 17 g/d, women 12 g/d (19-50 y); men 14, women 11 g/d (51+ y). Alpha-linolenic acid AI: men 1.6 g/d, women 1.1 g/d (19+ y)
findings.finding: Gram-per-day Adequate Intakes for essential fats, based on observed intakes of apparently healthy people. They are useful as minimums, especially on very low-fat plans.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.8-11 and p.1324 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: carbohydrate EAR/RDA (minimum)
findings.value: EAR 100 g/d; RDA 130 g/d for adults 19+ y (non-pregnant)
findings.finding: The minimum daily carbohydrate for adequacy in adults. It is a lower bound, not an optimal or performance intake.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited p.4, p.6, pp.1324, 1330 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: total fiber Adequate Intake
findings.value: 14 g per 1,000 kcal; men 38 g/d and women 25 g/d (19-50 y); men 30 g/d and women 21 g/d (51+ y)
findings.finding: The fiber AI is 14 g per 1,000 kcal, multiplied by median energy intakes to give the gram values. An app can scale it from the user's calorie target.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.4, 7-8 and p.1324 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: added sugars upper level
findings.value: No more than 25% of total energy from added sugars (suggested maximum; no UL set)
findings.finding: A suggested maximum to stop added sugars displacing micronutrient-rich foods. It is not a toxicity limit.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.13, 16 and p.1325 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: saturated fat, trans fat, dietary cholesterol
findings.value: As low as possible while consuming a nutritionally adequate diet; no AI/EAR/RDA/UL set
findings.finding: No requirement or UL values exist for saturated fat, trans fat or dietary cholesterol. The guidance is to keep them as low as possible within a nutritionally adequate diet.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.4, 12-13 and p.1325 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.parameter: protein requirement for vegetarians/vegans
findings.value: No separate protein requirement for vegetarians who eat complementary mixtures of plant proteins
findings.finding: Mixed plant proteins can match the quality of animal protein, so the standard RDA applies to vegetarians who combine plant sources.
findings.locator: Ch. 10 Protein and Amino Acids (pp.589-768); cited pp.661-662 not verified

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Macronutrients, Food and Nutrition Board. Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10490
findings.population: Reference pattern based on EARs of 1-3-year-olds (applies age 1 y and older)
findings.parameter: protein quality scoring pattern (indispensable amino acids)
findings.value: mg per g protein: histidine 18; isoleucine 25; leucine 55; lysine 51; methionine + cysteine 25; phenylalanine + tyrosine 47; threonine 27; tryptophan 7; valine 32
findings.finding: Reference amino-acid pattern for scoring food protein quality by PDCAAS. It helps when judging plant-protein combinations for vegetarian or vegan users.
findings.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited Table S-8 p.14 not verified

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.population: Adult athletes (recreational to elite), studies in 18-35 y; ten Haaf-specific pooled sample 204
findings.parameter: RMR equation for trained users: pooled accuracy of ten Haaf (2014) age/weight/height equation
findings.value: Effect size 0.04 (95% CI -0.16 to 0.23), 4 studies, 7 comparisons, 204 participants, I2 = 0%; after adding 2 post-search studies: ES -0.02 (95% CI -0.17 to 0.14), mean difference -2.6 kcal/24 h (95% CI -29.6 to 24.4)
findings.finding: Of 11 equations meta-analysed in adult athletes, the ten Haaf weight-based equation had the smallest pooled bias versus indirect calorimetry and no heterogeneity. Adding two later studies left the result essentially unchanged. The evidence base is small, and the authors ask for more comparisons.
findings.locator: Results, 'Meta-analysis Accuracy—Heterogeneity Summary'; Discussion, 'Emerging Research and Practical Implications' (updated pooled estimate); Conclusion

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.population: Adult athletes in 10 studies (225 F, 272 M), mean age 27.3 y
findings.parameter: RMR equation precision (% of individuals predicted within ±10% of measured RMR)
findings.value: Weighted mean precision: ten Haaf (age, wt, ht) 80.22% (3 studies, n=177); De Lorenzo 63.69% (3, n=190); Cunningham 1980 LBM 54.08% (7, n=233); Harris-Benedict 1918 53.67% (8, n=490); Mifflin-St Jeor (age, wt, ht) 52.17% (6, n=414); WHO/FAO/UNU (age, wt, ht) 51.64% (4, n=335); Mifflin-St Jeor FFM 44.88% (3, n=303); Owen weight 41.24% (4, n=354); WHO/FAO/UNU (age, wt) 40.67% (3, n=150)
findings.finding: In pooled precision data, the ten Haaf weight-based equation put about 80% of athletes within 10% of measured RMR, but one of its three studies was the derivation cohort. Other equations managed roughly 41-64%, so many users' estimates will miss by over 10%.
findings.locator: Results, 'Meta-analysis Precision—Overall Result'; Table 3 (Overall rows); Discussion, 'Precision' (derivation-study caveat)

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.population: 23 studies in the accuracy meta-analysis, adult athletes (671 F, 387 M)
findings.parameter: RMR equations to avoid for athletic users
findings.value: Avoid: Mifflin-St Jeor (1990, age/wt/ht), Owen (1988, weight), FAO/WHO/UNU (1985, age/wt/ht and age/wt), Nelson (1992, FFM/FM). Significant pooled bias (p<0.05) also for Koehler. Non-significant pooled bias: Cunningham 1980, Harris-Benedict 1918, Cunningham 1991, De Lorenzo, ten Haaf
findings.finding: Mifflin-St Jeor, Owen, both FAO/WHO/UNU versions and Nelson were consistently inaccurate and imprecise in athletes, and the authors advise against them. Predictions from these equations, and from Koehler, differed significantly from measured RMR. Five equations showed no significant pooled bias.
findings.locator: Abstract Results; Results, 'Meta-analysis Accuracy—Results'; Discussion, 'Equations that Performed Poorly'

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.population: Adult athletes, mixed sports and levels
findings.parameter: Pooled accuracy and heterogeneity of Cunningham (1980) and Harris-Benedict (1918) in athletes
findings.value: Cunningham 1980 (LBM): ES 0.15 (95% CI -0.26 to 0.57), 18 studies, 30 comparisons, 846 participants, I2 = 93%. Harris-Benedict 1918: ES -0.14 (95% CI -0.52 to 0.25), 17 studies, 29 comparisons, 892 participants, I2 = 93%. Cunningham single-study ES ranged 3.08 to -2.11
findings.finding: Cunningham and Harris-Benedict show little average bias in athletes. Heterogeneity is very high, though, and individual studies range from large over-estimation to large under-estimation. Their group-level mean accuracy does not make them reliable for an individual user.
findings.locator: Results, 'Meta-analysis Accuracy—Heterogeneity Summary'; Discussion, 'Energy Availability Status, Body Composition Method and Prior Exercise Avoidance' (ES range)

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.population: Male athletes in 11 studies; heavy subgroup 71
findings.parameter: Harris-Benedict bias in male and heavier male athletes
findings.value: Males overall: ES -0.53 (95% CI -0.93 to -0.13), 11 studies, 357 participants, I2 = 84%. Males >=78.9 kg: ES -0.91 (95% CI -1.25 to -0.56), 4 studies, 71 participants, I2 = 0%. Males <78.9 kg: ES -0.33 (95% CI -0.85 to 0.20), 7 studies, 286 participants. Heavy vs light subgroup trend p = 0.07. By athlete tier (sexes combined): Tier 3 ES -0.42 (95% CI -0.82 to -0.02); Tier 1 (female-only studies) ES +1.50 (95% CI 1.26 to 1.73)
findings.finding: Harris-Benedict tended to under-predict RMR in male athletes, most clearly in groups averaging 78.9 kg or more (for example bodybuilders and rugby players). In recreational female exercisers it over-predicted. The authors advise caution when applying it to heavier males.
findings.locator: Results, 'Sex', 'Athlete Status', 'Heavy and Light Males and Females'; Discussion, 'Body Weight'

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.population: Adult athletes; 93 F, 266 M in subgroup analyses
findings.parameter: De Lorenzo equation sex-specific bias
findings.value: Females: ES +0.93 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.23), 4 studies, 93 participants, I2 = 0%. Males: ES -0.31 (95% CI -0.73 to 0.11), 6 studies, 266 participants, I2 = 81%. Subgroup difference I2 = 95.4%, p < 0.0001
findings.finding: The De Lorenzo equation, derived in 51 larger male athletes, substantially over-predicted RMR in female athletes. It showed trivial-to-small bias in males similar in size to that group, while clearly heavier males were under-predicted. The authors advise taking sex into account but do not explicitly rule out use in women.
findings.locator: Results, 'Sex'; Discussion, 'Sex Differences' and 'Body Weight'

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.population: Methodological convention across cited athlete and general-population studies
findings.parameter: Accuracy criterion for an RMR prediction
findings.value: Accurate = predicted RMR within ±10% of indirect-calorimetry value; justified by indirect calorimetry measurement error of <=5%
findings.finding: Across the athlete and general-population literature, an RMR prediction counts as accurate when it falls within 10% of the measured value. This is the threshold the app should use when it states the uncertainty of an estimated RMR.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Inclusion Criteria'

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.parameter: Use of measured/predicted RMR ratio to flag low energy availability
findings.value: RMR ratio <0.9 is commonly used as a proxy for low energy availability; the review advises against using it from a single measurement with an arbitrary or commonly used equation
findings.finding: A measured-to-predicted RMR ratio below 0.9 is widely used to suggest low energy availability. The review warns that equation error alone can exceed 10%, so a single ratio is unreliable. Longitudinal RMR relative to body weight or FFM is preferred. The app should not infer energy deficiency from predicted RMR.
findings.locator: Introduction (para 2); Discussion, 'Energy Availability Status, Body Composition Method and Prior Exercise Avoidance'; Key Points 3; Conclusion

findings.citation: O'Neill JER, Corish CA, Horner K. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023;53(12):2373-98. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01896-z
findings.parameter: Validated age range for athlete RMR equation evidence
findings.value: Eligible studies covered adults 18-35 y only; no equation performance data by age for 35-65 y athletes
findings.finding: The review allowed ages 18-65, but every eligible study involved 18-35-year-olds, so equation accuracy in athletes over 35 is unvalidated. The app should mark RMR estimates for older users as lower confidence. The review also advises picking an equation derived in people similar to the user.
findings.locator: Discussion, 'Methodological Considerations' (generalisability paragraph); Key Points 2

findings.citation: ten Haaf T, Weijs PJM. Resting energy expenditure prediction in recreational athletes of 18-35 years: confirmation of Cunningham equation and an improved weight-based alternative. PLoS One. 2014;9(9):e108460. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0108460
findings.population: Dutch recreational athletes, 53 M / 37 F, 18-35 y, training 9.1 ± 5.0 h/wk
findings.parameter: RMR equation (weight-based) for trained users: ten Haaf 2014
findings.value: REE (kcal/d) = 11.936 × weight(kg) + 587.728 × height(m) − 8.129 × age(y) + 191.027 × sex(M=1, F=0) + 29.279; equivalently REE (kJ/d) = 49.940 × weight + 2459.053 × height − 34.014 × age + 799.257 × sex + 122.502. Within ±10%: M 83.0%, F 75.7% (derivation sample, not cross-validated)
findings.finding: The equation needs no body-composition input and was derived by regression in 90 Dutch recreational athletes. In that cohort it matched Cunningham's accuracy, and the authors recommend it when FFM is unavailable. It was not cross-validated in the source, but a later meta-analysis found it the most accurate and precise equation in athletes.
findings.locator: Abstract Results; Results, weight-based equation (kcal form read from the published formula image, equation e004); accuracy in Results para 2 / Fig 3

findings.citation: ten Haaf T, Weijs PJM. Resting energy expenditure prediction in recreational athletes of 18-35 years: confirmation of Cunningham equation and an improved weight-based alternative. PLoS One. 2014;9(9):e108460. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0108460
findings.population: Dutch recreational athletes, 53 M / 37 F, 18-35 y
findings.parameter: RMR equation (FFM-based) for trained users: ten Haaf 2014
findings.value: REE (kcal/d) = 22.771 × FFM(kg) + 484.264; REE (kJ/d) = 95.272 × FFM(kg) + 2026.161. Within ±10%: M 83.0%, F 72.3%; RMSE M 0.62 MJ/d, F 0.57 MJ/d (lowest of all equations tested); FFM by air-displacement plethysmography
findings.finding: When fat-free mass is known, this single-predictor equation gave the lowest prediction error in the derivation cohort. The app should use it only when the user supplies a measured FFM. It must not estimate FFM itself.
findings.locator: Abstract Results; Results (FFM-based equation, kcal form from the published formula image e006; RMSE in Results para 4)

findings.citation: ten Haaf T, Weijs PJM. Resting energy expenditure prediction in recreational athletes of 18-35 years: confirmation of Cunningham equation and an improved weight-based alternative. PLoS One. 2014;9(9):e108460. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0108460
findings.population: Dutch recreational athletes, 53 M / 37 F, 18-35 y
findings.parameter: Cunningham equation form and accuracy in recreational athletes
findings.value: Cunningham REE (kcal/d) = 22 × FFM(kg) + 500; within ±10%: M 84.9%, F 78.4% (highest of all equations tested); RMSE comparable to the new weight-based equation
findings.finding: In this Dutch recreational athlete sample, Cunningham gave the highest share of predictions within 10% (M 84.9%, F 78.4%), supporting it when FFM is measured. Pooled across seven studies in O'Neill 2023, however, it reached only about 54% and showed very high heterogeneity.
findings.locator: Table 4 (equation form); Results para 2 (accuracy); Conclusions

findings.citation: ten Haaf T, Weijs PJM. Resting energy expenditure prediction in recreational athletes of 18-35 years: confirmation of Cunningham equation and an improved weight-based alternative. PLoS One. 2014;9(9):e108460. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0108460
findings.population: Dutch recreational athletes, 53 M / 37 F, 18-35 y
findings.parameter: Performance of general-population RMR equations in recreational athletes
findings.value: Harris-Benedict (1919, 1984), FAO/WHO, Schofield, Mifflin and Owen (including their height or FFM variants): <50% of predictions within ±10%; RMSE >0.95 MJ/d (~227 kcal/d). Negative proportional bias (higher measured REE under-predicted) shown for the six equations plotted in Fig 4: new weight-based, new FFM-based, De Lorenzo, Cunningham, Owen FFM, Harris-Benedict 1984
findings.finding: Standard population equations, including Mifflin-St Jeor, placed fewer than half of recreational athletes within 10% of measured REE, with RMSE above about 227 kcal/d. Among the six equations checked for proportional bias, all under-predicted people with higher REE. This argues against Mifflin as the default for trained users.
findings.locator: Abstract Results; Results paras 2-5; Fig 3 and Fig 4

findings.citation: ten Haaf T, Weijs PJM. Resting energy expenditure prediction in recreational athletes of 18-35 years: confirmation of Cunningham equation and an improved weight-based alternative. PLoS One. 2014;9(9):e108460. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0108460
findings.population: Dutch recreational athletes, 53 M / 37 F, 18-35 y
findings.parameter: De Lorenzo equation accuracy in recreational athletes
findings.value: De Lorenzo REE (kcal/d) = 9 × wt(kg) + 1170 × ht(m) − 857; within ±10%: M 77.4%, F 59.5%; RMSE M 0.74, F 0.77 MJ/d; bias negative in males, positive in females
findings.finding: The De Lorenzo equation was developed in elite male athletes training at least 3 h a day. It did worse than Cunningham and the new ten Haaf equations, especially in women, where it over-predicted.
findings.locator: Table 4 (equation); Results paras 2-4; Discussion para 3

findings.citation: ten Haaf T, Weijs PJM. Resting energy expenditure prediction in recreational athletes of 18-35 years: confirmation of Cunningham equation and an improved weight-based alternative. PLoS One. 2014;9(9):e108460. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0108460
findings.parameter: Derivation range (applicability limits) of ten Haaf equations
findings.value: Age 18-35 y; height 1.61-2.05 m; weight 52.8-100.3 kg; BMI 17.9-27.0 kg/m2; body fat 1.5-32.2%; training >=3 h/wk and >=2 sessions/wk (mean 9.1 ± 5.0 h/wk)
findings.finding: The ten Haaf equations come from lean, young, regularly training adults. The app should treat users outside these age, weight, BMI and training ranges as outside the equation's validated domain and widen or flag the uncertainty. The authors note that validation in other cohorts is needed.
findings.locator: Methods para 1 (inclusion); Table 2 (subject characteristics); Discussion para 3

findings.citation: Thompson J, Manore MM. Predicted and measured resting metabolic rate of male and female endurance athletes. J Am Diet Assoc. 1996;96(1):30-4. doi:10.1016/S0002-8223(96)00010-7
findings.population: Trained endurance athletes, 24 M / 13 F (running and cycling appear only in the PubMed MeSH indexing)
findings.parameter: Cunningham equation prediction error in endurance athletes
findings.value: Cunningham most accurate of Harris-Benedict, Owen, Mifflin, Cunningham; predicted measured RMR within 158 kcal/d (men) and 103 kcal/d (women). The abstract names root mean squared prediction error as the comparison method but does not explicitly label these figures
findings.finding: In trained endurance athletes, the FFM-based Cunningham equation predicted measured RMR better than Harris-Benedict, Owen or Mifflin. Typical error was about 158 kcal/d in men and 103 kcal/d in women. This is early, small-sample support for FFM-based equations in endurance users.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results and Conclusions); full text paywalled, not accessed

findings.citation: Thompson J, Manore MM. Predicted and measured resting metabolic rate of male and female endurance athletes. J Am Diet Assoc. 1996;96(1):30-4. doi:10.1016/S0002-8223(96)00010-7
findings.parameter: Best single predictor of RMR in endurance athletes by sex
findings.value: Men: fat-free mass was the best predictor; women: energy intake was the best predictor (exploratory maximum R2 procedure over combinations of four variables; R2 values not in abstract)
findings.finding: In an exploratory maximum-R2 analysis, fat-free mass best predicted RMR in male endurance athletes, whereas energy intake did so in the 13 women. The authors call for athlete-specific equations and for testing predictors beyond weight, height and age.
findings.locator: Abstract (Methods, Results and Conclusions); full text paywalled, not accessed

findings.citation: Jagim AR, Camic CL, Kisiolek J, Luedke J, Erickson J, Jones MT, Oliver JM. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes. J Strength Cond Res. 2018;32(7):1875-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002111
findings.population: Athletes aged ~20 y: 22 F (63.5 ± 7.3 kg, 23.4% BF) and 28 M (94.5 ± 16.2 kg, 15.1% BF); collegiate status not stated in the abstract
findings.parameter: Direction and size of RMR equation bias in athletes (Jagim 2018 sample)
findings.value: All 5 equations significantly under-predicted RMR (p <= 0.05); Cunningham had the smallest mean difference, -165 kcal/d. The five equations are not all named in the abstract
findings.finding: In 50 young athletes, all five equations tested under-predicted measured RMR; the best, Cunningham, averaged about 165 kcal/d low. This single-sample result differs from the O'Neill 2023 pooled estimate, in which Cunningham showed no significant average bias.
findings.locator: Abstract; full text paywalled, not accessed

findings.citation: Jagim AR, Camic CL, Kisiolek J, Luedke J, Erickson J, Jones MT, Oliver JM. Accuracy of resting metabolic rate prediction equations in athletes. J Strength Cond Res. 2018;32(7):1875-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002111
findings.population: Athletes aged ~20 y, 22 F / 28 M (men mean 94.5 kg); collegiate status not stated in the abstract
findings.parameter: Sex-specific best equation and RMSE in athletes (Jagim 2018 sample)
findings.value: Men: Harris-Benedict best, root-mean-square prediction error 284 kcal/d; women: Cunningham best, RMSE 110 kcal/d
findings.finding: Harris-Benedict gave the lowest error in heavy male athletes, though still about 284 kcal/d. Cunningham gave the lowest error in female athletes, at about 110 kcal/d. Individual error bands for men are wide.
findings.locator: Abstract; full text paywalled, not accessed

findings.citation: Fields JB, Magee MK, Jones MT, Askow AT, Camic CL, Luedke J, Jagim AR. The accuracy of ten common resting metabolic rate prediction equations in men and women collegiate athletes. Eur J Sport Sci. 2023;23(10):1973-82. doi:10.1080/17461391.2022.2130098
findings.population: NCAA Division III athletes, 97 M / 90 F
findings.parameter: Direction of bias of 10 common RMR equations in collegiate athletes
findings.value: Men: all 10 equations (Cunningham, De Lorenzo, Freire, Harris-Benedict, Mifflin-St Jeor, Nelson, Owen, Tinsley, Watson, Schofield) significantly under-predicted RMR (p < 0.001). Women: all except De Lorenzo and Watson under-predicted (those two p = 1.00 vs measured)
findings.finding: In 187 collegiate athletes, all ten equations under-estimated RMR in men, and eight of ten did so in women. The authors conclude that predicted values may understate athletes' true energy needs and should be interpreted cautiously.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results, highlights and conclusion); full text paywalled, not accessed

findings.citation: Fields JB, Magee MK, Jones MT, Askow AT, Camic CL, Luedke J, Jagim AR. The accuracy of ten common resting metabolic rate prediction equations in men and women collegiate athletes. Eur J Sport Sci. 2023;23(10):1973-82. doi:10.1080/17461391.2022.2130098
findings.population: NCAA Division III athletes, 97 M / 90 F
findings.parameter: Lowest RMSE equations by sex in collegiate athletes
findings.value: Men: Tinsley RMSE 404 kcal/d, Freire 412 kcal/d (lowest); women: De Lorenzo 171 kcal/d, Watson 211 kcal/d (lowest)
findings.finding: Even the best equations for male athletes carried typical errors of about 400 kcal/d, while the best for women were about 170-210 kcal/d. The app should present RMR-based targets for athletic men with a wide uncertainty band.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results); full text paywalled, not accessed

findings.citation: Freire R, Pereira GR, Alcantara JMA, Santos R, Hausen M, Itaborahy A. New predictive resting metabolic rate equations for high-level athletes: a cross-validation study. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022;54(8):1335-45. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002926
findings.population: High-level Brazilian athletes, 58 M / 44 F, multiple sports
findings.parameter: Agreement of new Freire equations in high-level athletes
findings.value: Equation 1 / Equation 2: mean difference 3 / -15 kcal/d; RMSE 200 / 192 kcal/d; R2 0.71 / 0.74; 61% of subjects within ±10% of measured RMR. Coefficients not given in the abstract and not verified from the primary text
findings.finding: Two new equations for national- and Olympic-level athletes showed near-zero mean bias and about 200 kcal/d typical error. Only 61% of athletes were within 10%. The coefficients could not be verified from the primary source, so the app should not implement them yet.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results); full text paywalled, not accessed

findings.citation: Freire R, Pereira GR, Alcantara JMA, Santos R, Hausen M, Itaborahy A. New predictive resting metabolic rate equations for high-level athletes: a cross-validation study. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022;54(8):1335-45. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002926
findings.parameter: Existing equation to prefer and to avoid in high-level athletes
findings.value: Cunningham best existing equation for males and females; Jagim equation worst in males (mean difference -335 kcal/d; RMSE 386 kcal/d); most equations heteroscedastic (p <= 0.05), mainly in males
findings.finding: Among existing equations, Cunningham performed best in elite athletes of both sexes. The Jagim equation should not be used for high-level men. This is the corrected version. The retracted 2021 original (PMID 34974500) had named Harris-Benedict as worst, so only this version should be cited.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results, Conclusions); PubMed record flags 'Corrected and Republished Article'; retracted original PMID 34974500 abstract compared; full text paywalled, not accessed

findings.citation: Tinsley GM, Graybeal AJ, Moore ML. Resting metabolic rate in muscular physique athletes: validity of existing methods and development of new prediction equations. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2019;44(4):397-406. doi:10.1139/apnm-2018-0412
findings.population: Resistance-trained male (n=17) and female (n=10) physique athletes, 18-50 y, mostly off-season
findings.parameter: RMR equation, muscular resistance-trained adults, body-weight based
findings.value: RMR (kcal/d) = 24.8 x BW (kg) + 10; R2 0.849; SEE 169, total error 177, leave-one-out total error 188 kcal/d; constant error +13 +/- 180 kcal/d; 95% LOA +/-352 kcal/d. Sex, age and height were not significant predictors, so there is one equation for both sexes
findings.finding: In very muscular lifters, a single weight-only equation derived by stepwise regression predicted measured RMR with near-zero mean bias and no significant proportional bias. It performed better than all the existing weight-based equations tested. It still needs external cross-validation.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript apnm-2018-0412.R1 (U Toronto TSpace hdl:1807/93913): Abstract; Results p.12; Table 1; Table 6

findings.citation: Tinsley GM, Graybeal AJ, Moore ML. Resting metabolic rate in muscular physique athletes: validity of existing methods and development of new prediction equations. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2019;44(4):397-406. doi:10.1139/apnm-2018-0412
findings.population: Resistance-trained male and female physique athletes, 18-50 y
findings.parameter: RMR equation, muscular resistance-trained adults, FFM based
findings.value: RMR (kcal/d) = 25.9 x DXA FFM (kg) + 284; R2 0.851; SEE 166, total error 173, leave-one-out total error 187 kcal/d; constant error -3 +/- 176 kcal/d; 95% LOA +/-346 kcal/d. Sex, age, height and weight were excluded as non-significant
findings.finding: An FFM-only equation built on DXA fat-free mass matched measured RMR about as well as the new weight-only equation. Males still showed significant proportional bias (B -0.484), so predictions for very large, high-RMR men are less reliable.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript R1: Results p.12; Table 6; Discussion p.15

findings.citation: Tinsley GM, Graybeal AJ, Moore ML. Resting metabolic rate in muscular physique athletes: validity of existing methods and development of new prediction equations. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2019;44(4):397-406. doi:10.1139/apnm-2018-0412
findings.parameter: Validity of existing FFM-based RMR equations in muscular adults
findings.value: Cunningham 1980 (22 x FFM + 500): CE -53 +/- 188 kcal/d, TE 192, LOA +/-368. ten Haaf 2014 FFM (0.239 x (95.272 x FFM + 2026.161)): CE -16 +/- 184, TE 181, LOA +/-360. These two were acceptable. Cunningham 1991 (21.6 x FFM + 370): CE -210; Owen: -273; Mifflin FFM (19.7 x FFM + 413): -296 kcal/d. Figures are for the combined n=27
findings.finding: Of the published FFM equations, only Cunningham 1980 and ten Haaf 2014 gave acceptable estimates in muscular men and women. The others underestimated RMR by 10.2-17.4%, and every FFM equation showed significant negative proportional bias in males.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript R1: Results p.11-12; Tables 1, 3, 4, 5

findings.citation: Tinsley GM, Graybeal AJ, Moore ML. Resting metabolic rate in muscular physique athletes: validity of existing methods and development of new prediction equations. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2019;44(4):397-406. doi:10.1139/apnm-2018-0412
findings.parameter: Bias of standard weight-based RMR equations (Mifflin-St Jeor, Harris-Benedict, FAO, De Lorenzo, ten Haaf) in muscular adults
findings.value: Combined n=27: weight-based equations underestimated RMR by 4.5-15.1%. Mifflin CE -310 +/- 232 kcal/d (TE 385); Harris-Benedict -199 (TE 286); FAO -203; De Lorenzo -108; ten Haaf BW -92. Males: all except ten Haaf underestimated by >=10.1%, with Mifflin up to -393 kcal/d. Females: ten Haaf BW CE 0 +/- 142 kcal/d (TE 142)
findings.finding: The common weight-based equations, Mifflin-St Jeor included, underestimate RMR in very muscular people, by several hundred kcal/d in men. Only the ten Haaf weight equation was acceptable, and only in women.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript R1: Results p.11; Discussion p.15-16; Tables 1, 3, 4, 5

findings.citation: Tinsley GM, Graybeal AJ, Moore ML. Resting metabolic rate in muscular physique athletes: validity of existing methods and development of new prediction equations. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2019;44(4):397-406. doi:10.1139/apnm-2018-0412
findings.parameter: Equation input choice: body weight vs estimated FFM
findings.value: Using FFM from non-DXA methods (multi-compartment models, BIA devices, bioimpedance spectroscopy) instead of DXA FFM shifted the FFM-equation RMR by -30 to +74 kcal/d on average (data not shown). The authors judged the BW-based equation the most practical
findings.finding: Scale weight is measured with much less error than fat-free mass, and body-composition estimates vary by device. The authors therefore favour the weight-based equation for everyday use in people who resemble their sample.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript R1: Discussion p.17

findings.citation: Tinsley GM, Graybeal AJ, Moore ML. Resting metabolic rate in muscular physique athletes: validity of existing methods and development of new prediction equations. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2019;44(4):397-406. doi:10.1139/apnm-2018-0412
findings.parameter: Applicability limits of the physique-athlete RMR equations
findings.value: Derivation sample: 18-50 y (mean 25.9 +/- 6.0); >=3 y of resistance training at >=3 sessions/wk (current 5.7 +/- 0.9 d/wk). Males: 94.0 +/- 9.7 kg, BMI 28.8 +/- 2.0, body fat 12.5 +/- 2.7%, FFMI 24.2 +/- 1.3 kg/m2. Females: 63.8 +/- 5.7 kg, BMI 22.8 +/- 1.6, body fat 19.2 +/- 3.4%, FFMI 17.7 +/- 0.9. Off-season (all but one participant); 26% reported current anabolic steroid use
findings.finding: The new equations apply only to people like the derivation sample: highly muscular, lean, experienced lifters who are not in contest preparation. RMR is known to fall during competition dieting, so the equations may overestimate RMR for users in an aggressive cut.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript R1: Methods p.5; Results p.10; Discussion p.17-18; Table 2

findings.citation: Schofield KL, Thorpe H, Sims ST. Resting metabolic rate prediction equations and the validity to assess energy deficiency in the athlete population. Exp Physiol. 2019;104(4):469-475. doi:10.1113/EP087512
findings.parameter: RMR share of total daily energy expenditure and tissue contributions
findings.value: RMR = 50-70% of total daily energy expenditure. FFM is the main contributor, at about 60-70% of RMR; fat mass contributes roughly 5-7%; sex and age contribute little (the review cites Johnstone et al. 2005)
findings.finding: RMR is the largest part of daily expenditure and is driven mainly by fat-free mass, with fat mass contributing little. The review uses this to argue that RMR estimates for athletes should account for FFM.
findings.locator: Section 2 (Measurement of metabolic rate), p.470

findings.citation: Schofield KL, Thorpe H, Sims ST. Resting metabolic rate prediction equations and the validity to assess energy deficiency in the athlete population. Exp Physiol. 2019;104(4):469-475. doi:10.1113/EP087512
findings.population: Athletes; thresholds derived mainly from studies in women
findings.parameter: Energy availability floor kcal/kg FFM/day
findings.value: EA = (dietary energy intake - exercise energy expenditure) / FFM. Adequate: 45; subclinical: 30-45; low energy availability: <30 kcal per kg FFM per day. Threshold evidence in male athletes is sparse
findings.finding: The review tabulates energy-availability cut-offs taken from earlier laboratory studies on hormones, bone markers and RMR. It says EA is only a snapshot, prone to intake under-reporting, and should be read alongside other markers rather than on its own.
findings.locator: Sections 8-9, Equation 1 and Table 2, p.473

findings.citation: Schofield KL, Thorpe H, Sims ST. Resting metabolic rate prediction equations and the validity to assess energy deficiency in the athlete population. Exp Physiol. 2019;104(4):469-475. doi:10.1113/EP087512
findings.parameter: Measured-to-predicted RMR ratio threshold for energy deficiency
findings.value: mRMR/pRMR < 0.90 has been used as a marker of energy deficiency. It was set originally in exercising women using the Harris-Benedict equation, and prevalence depends on which predictive equation is used
findings.finding: A measured-to-predicted RMR ratio below 0.9 is a common flag for energy deficiency. Its validity depends on the prediction equation used, so the authors advise caution in athletes. It also needs a measured RMR, which an app without calorimetry cannot supply.
findings.locator: Section 6 (Using RMR as a marker of energy deficiency), p.472; Section 7

findings.citation: Schofield KL, Thorpe H, Sims ST. Resting metabolic rate prediction equations and the validity to assess energy deficiency in the athlete population. Exp Physiol. 2019;104(4):469-475. doi:10.1113/EP087512
findings.parameter: RMR equation input rule for athletic or muscular users
findings.value: Rule: include FFM in RMR prediction for athletes. Equations without FFM return the same estimate for two people matched on age, height and mass regardless of body composition, and typically underestimate RMR in muscular people
findings.finding: Many standard equations were derived in non-athletes. Trained male athletes were removed from the Cunningham (1980) and Owen (1987) samples, while Owen (1986) gave women athletes a separate equation. The authors recommend FFM-inclusive equations for athletes and rate measured RMR above prediction.
findings.locator: Sections 4-5 and 7, p.471-472; Section 10 (Summary)

findings.citation: Schofield KL, Thorpe H, Sims ST. Resting metabolic rate prediction equations and the validity to assess energy deficiency in the athlete population. Exp Physiol. 2019;104(4):469-475. doi:10.1113/EP087512. Erratum: Exp Physiol. 2026;111(7):3439. doi:10.1113/EP094060
findings.population: Derivation samples of common RMR equations
findings.parameter: Derivation populations and forms of common RMR equations
findings.value: Harris-Benedict: 136 men, 103 women, 21-70 y, 25-124.9 kg, 151-200 cm. Cunningham 1980: 500 + 22 x FFM, re-derived from HB data with FFM estimated and 16 male athletes removed. Mifflin 1990: 251 men, 247 women, 19-78 y. Owen 1986 women: athletes 50.4 + 21 x BM, non-athletes 795 + 7.18 x BM. Owen 1987 men: 879 + 10.2 x BM or 290 + 22.3 x FFM. De Lorenzo 1999, 51 male athletes: -857 + 9.0 x BM + 11.7 x H (kcal/d). HB and Cunningham reportedly overestimated REE by 5% and 14-15%. Caution: the original Table 1 printed the male Mifflin equation without its constant. A 2026 erratum (PMID 42229949) corrects it to 9.99BM + 6.25H - 5A + 5. That is close to the sex-combined form in Tinsley 2019 Table 1 (9.99BW + 6.25H - 4.92age + 166 x sex - 161)
findings.finding: The review lists who each common RMR equation was derived in, showing that most came from general, non-athletic samples. Its male Mifflin equation needed a published erratum, so the app should take coefficients from the original derivation papers.
findings.locator: Section 4 and Table 1, p.470-471; Erratum Exp Physiol 2026;111(7):3439

findings.citation: Jesus F, Nunes CL, Matias CN, Francisco R, Carapeto B, Macias H, et al. Are predictive equations a valid method of assessing the resting metabolic rate of overweight or obese former athletes? Eur J Sport Sci. 2020;20(9):1225-1234. doi:10.1080/17461391.2019.1708974
findings.population: Overweight/obese former athletes; BMI 31.5 +/- 4.0 kg/m2, 95.8 +/- 14.8 kg, 78.6% male, 37.5% obese
findings.parameter: RMR equation error in overweight/obese adults (former athletes), including Katch-McArdle
findings.value: Seven equations (Harris-Benedict, Cunningham, Schofield, FAO/WHO/UNU, Owen, Mifflin-St Jeor, Katch-McArdle) overestimated measured RMR by 70-300 kcal/d (4.3-14.9%). Each explained about 50% of the variance in measured RMR, and limits of agreement were wide. Only Harris-Benedict showed no proportional bias. The abstract gives no per-equation figures (none for Katch-McArdle specifically)
findings.finding: Against indirect calorimetry, every equation tested, Katch-McArdle included, overestimated RMR in heavier retired athletes and agreed poorly at the individual level. Calorie targets built on predicted RMR may therefore be too high for this group.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed 31868121)

findings.citation: Weijs PJM. Validity of predictive equations for resting energy expenditure in US and Dutch overweight and obese class I and II adults aged 18-65 y. Am J Clin Nutr. 2008;88(4):959-70. doi:10.1093/ajcn/88.4.959
findings.population: US adults aged 18-65 y, BMI 25-40 (180 women, 158 men; IOM published data)
findings.parameter: RMR equation for overweight/obese adults (BMI 25-40), US
findings.value: Mifflin-St Jeor was the most accurate and precise equation for the US sample: 79% of people predicted within +/-10% of measured REE, bias -1.0%, RMSE 136 kcal/d. The study included 27 equations (9 FFM-based); the abstract does not say how many could be applied to the US data
findings.finding: For US adults with BMI 25-40, the Mifflin equation was the best alternative to indirect calorimetry. About one in five people still fell outside +/-10% of measured REE.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed 18842782), Results/Conclusion

findings.citation: Weijs PJM. Validity of predictive equations for resting energy expenditure in US and Dutch overweight and obese class I and II adults aged 18-65 y. Am J Clin Nutr. 2008;88(4):959-70. doi:10.1093/ajcn/88.4.959
findings.population: Dutch adults aged 18-65 y, BMI 25-40 (154 women, 54 men), measured by indirect calorimetry
findings.parameter: RMR equation accuracy in non-US overweight/obese adults
findings.value: Overweight Dutch: best was the FAO/WHO/UNU weight equation (68% within +/-10%, bias -2.5%, RMSE 178 kcal/d). Obese Dutch: best was the Lazzer equation (69% within +/-10%, bias -3.0%, RMSE 215 kcal/d). Author's conclusion: no accurate equation exists for this group
findings.finding: The best equation differed by population, and even the best left about 30% of Dutch overweight and obese adults outside +/-10% of measured REE. An app should expect errors of this size and correct its estimates from observed weight change.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed 18842782), Results/Conclusion

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.population: Healthy obese and non-obese white adults 18-57 y (4 pooled studies)
findings.parameter: BMR meta-regression equation, white adults 18-57, weight/height/age
findings.value: Female BMR (kcal/d) = 301 + 10.2W + 3.09H - 3.09A; male = 522 + 10.4W + 3.19H - 3.1A (W kg, H cm, A y). 4 studies; mean R2 0.619 (range 0.449-0.75) for females and 0.671 (0.6-0.75) for males. The same coefficients are listed for white adults >50. Worked example, a 35-y, 75-kg, 165-cm woman: 1467.7 kcal/d, vs Harris-Benedict 1513.8, WHO 1558.7, IOM 1475.9
findings.finding: Inverse-variance pooling of published regressions gives a weight-height-age BMR equation for white adults that agrees within about 90 kcal/d with the Harris-Benedict, WHO and IOM equations in a typical case.
findings.locator: Table 1 (White 18-57 and White >50, structure 1); Results, 'Using the Resulting Equations'

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.parameter: BMR meta-regression equation, white adults, FFM + fat mass
findings.value: 18-57 y: female BMR = 360 + 21.0 FFM + 4.68 FM (5 studies; mean R2 0.804, range 0.526-0.91); male = 361 + 21.1 FFM + 4.77 FM (4 studies, because one reference is female-only; mean R2 0.809, range 0.612-0.91) (kg, kcal/d). >50 y: female 290 + 19.9 FFM + 4.71 FM (mean R2 0.751); male 291 + 20 FFM + 4.64 FM (mean R2 0.789)
findings.finding: When fat-free and fat mass are known, this structure had the highest mean R2 among the multi-study white-adult structures; a single-study log-form equation reported 0.806. The authors name it, with structure 11, as giving a good balance of precision and supporting evidence.
findings.locator: Table 1 (White 18-57 and White >50, structure 4); Results, 'Best Fitting Equations for Subpopulations'

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.population: White adults 18-57 y (same coefficients listed for >50)
findings.parameter: BMR meta-regression equation, white adults, age + FFM + fat mass
findings.value: Female BMR = 682 - 3.08A + 12.9 FFM + 5.9 FM (13 studies; mean R2 0.66, range 0.425-0.88); male = 898 - 3.32A + 14.3 FFM + 6.46 FM (12 studies, because one reference is female-only; mean R2 0.711, range 0.45-0.88) (A y, kg, kcal/d)
findings.finding: This age-plus-body-composition structure had the most pooled studies of any adult structure, and the authors recommend it for white adults. Adding age shrinks the FFM coefficient and raises the intercept.
findings.locator: Table 1 (White 18-57 and White >50, structure 11); Results, 'Impact of Age'

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.parameter: BMR meta-regression equation, white adults, FFM only
findings.value: 18-57 y: female BMR = 473 + 20.1 FFM (9 studies; mean R2 0.675); male = 503 + 18.3 FFM (8 studies, because one reference is female-only; mean R2 0.674) (kg, kcal/d). >50 y: female 429 + 20.9 FFM; male 464 + 18.6 FFM; 4 studies; mean R2 0.669
findings.finding: A simple FFM-only equation pooled from eight to nine studies fits white adults moderately well. It suits an app that has an FFM estimate but no fat-mass value.
findings.locator: Table 1 (White 18-57 and White >50, structure 5)

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.parameter: BMR meta-regression equation, white adults, weight only and weight + age
findings.value: Weight only, 18-57 y: female 632 + 10.9W (4 studies; mean R2 0.645); male 778 + 11.7W (2 studies, because two references are female-only; mean R2 0.745). Weight only, >50 y: female 568 + 11.1W; male 743 + 11.7W (2 studies; mean R2 0.745). Weight + age, 18-57 y: female 781 + 11W - 3.45A; male 1050 + 11W - 3.53A (2 studies; mean R2 0.51 female, 0.645 male). All in kcal/d, W kg, A y
findings.finding: The pooled equations include fallbacks that need only weight, or weight and age, for when height or body composition is missing. In women their mean fit is below the body-composition structures. In men the weight-only mean R2 (0.745, two studies) exceeds the FFM-only and age+FFM+FM structures.
findings.locator: Table 1 (White 18-57 and White >50, structures 3 and 10)

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.population: African American adults 18-50 y (the same equations are largely repeated for >50)
findings.parameter: BMR meta-regression equations, Black adults 18-50
findings.value: FFM + FM: female 397 + 20.6 FFM + 1.9 FM; male 421 + 20.6 FFM + 1.9 FM (1 study; mean R2 0.783). FFM only: female 400 + 16.6 FFM (2 studies; R2 0.748); male 392 + 17.4 FFM (3 studies; R2 0.73). Age + FFM + FM: female 678 - 3.28A + 13.6 FFM + 5.95 FM; male 787 - 3.28A + 13.6 FFM + 5.95 FM (2 studies; R2 0.695). W/H/A: female 883 + 8.7W - 0.342H - 3.9A; male 1100 + 8.7W - 0.342H - 3.9A (1 study; R2 0.675). Weight only: female 302 + 13.2W (R2 0.548); male 500 + 15.6W. All kcal/d
findings.finding: Separate pooled equations exist for Black adults. The authors describe the FFM-based structures as well supported (R2 roughly 0.6-0.8), but each rests on only one to three studies.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Black 18-50 and Black >50 rows); Results, 'Best Fitting Equations for Subpopulations'

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.population: Asian adults 18-30 y (male row 18-50), Hispanic adults >50 y, Pima Native American adults 18-50 y
findings.parameter: BMR meta-regression equations, Asian, Hispanic and Native American adults
findings.value: Asian W/H/A: female -101 + 11.5W + 5.59H - 3.3A; male 883 + 11.5W + 5.59H - 3.3A (1 study; R2 0.834). The male intercept and SE (883, SE 471) are identical to the Black female entry, so verify against the source study. Asian female weight only: 593 + 10.9W. Asian male weight + age: 860 + 11.6W - 3.37A (R2 0.41). Hispanic >50, weight only: female 394 + 13.6W; male 502 + 13.6W (1 study; R2 0.75). Pima 18-50, age + FFM + FM: female 705 - 2.2A + 15 FFM + 4.4 FM; male 829 - 2.2A + 15 FFM + 4.4 FM (1 study; R2 0.88). All kcal/d
findings.finding: Each of these groups has only single-study equations, and the authors say the choices are limited. They are thin support for ethnicity-specific calorie targets.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Asian 18-30, >50 Hispanic, 18-50 Native American rows and footnotes); Results, 'Best Fitting Equations for Subpopulations'

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.parameter: BMR predictor ranking and FFM coefficient
findings.value: FFM is the best single predictor and weight is almost as good; fat mass adds a small independent improvement. The FFM coefficient is about 20 kcal/kg/d without an age term and about 13 kcal/kg/d with one. The age effect is consistently negative and slightly stronger in males
findings.finding: Pooled regressions confirm fat-free mass as the main driver of BMR, with a small independent effect of fat mass and a decline with age. The authors suggest height and BMI may appear significant mainly because some equations lack FFM or weight terms.
findings.locator: Results, 'Impact of Body Composition' and 'Impact of Age'

findings.citation: Sabounchi NS, Rahmandad H, Ammerman A. Best-fitting prediction equations for basal metabolic rate: informing obesity interventions in diverse populations. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(10):1364-70. doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.218
findings.parameter: Uncertainty and within-person change not captured by cross-sectional BMR equations
findings.value: Only 47 of 248 studies (19%) reported enough variance detail for meta-regression. Pooling assumed independent coefficients, so the variance of the meta-coefficients may be underestimated. The analysis uses cross-sectional equations and does not model within-person BMR change. The authors note that rapid weight loss may lower BMR even when FFM is kept (no pooled number)
findings.finding: Pooled BMR equations cannot track how one person's BMR changes during dieting, and their stated precision is probably optimistic. The app should treat equation BMR as a starting estimate and refine it from observed weigh-ins and logged intake.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Overview' (cross-sectional focus); Results (study flow); Conclusions paragraphs 2 and 4

findings.citation: Black AE, Coward WA, Cole TJ, Prentice AM. Human energy expenditure in affluent societies: an analysis of 574 doubly-labelled water measurements. Eur J Clin Nutr. 1996;50(2):72-92. PMID: 8641250
findings.population: People aged 2-95 y in affluent societies; 574 DLW measurements selected from 1614 in 1156 subjects; separate analysis of non-ambulant subjects and elite endurance athletes
findings.parameter: Physical activity level (PAL = TEE/BMR) plausible range
findings.value: A separate analysis of non-ambulant people and elite endurance athletes (both excluded from the main dataset) put the limits of human daily energy expenditure at about 1.2 x BMR and about 4.5 x BMR respectively
findings.finding: Doubly-labelled water data put the lower and upper limits of human daily expenditure at roughly 1.2 and 4.5 times BMR. An app's activity multiplier should stay inside this range, with values near the top reserved for elite endurance training.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed 8641250), Results

findings.citation: Black AE, Coward WA, Cole TJ, Prentice AM. Human energy expenditure in affluent societies: an analysis of 574 doubly-labelled water measurements. Eur J Clin Nutr. 1996;50(2):72-92. PMID: 8641250
findings.population: People aged 2-95 y in affluent societies (DLW)
findings.parameter: Sex difference in energy expenditure after adjustment for body size and age
findings.value: Females expended on average 11% less energy than males for TEE, BMR and activity energy expenditure, after adjusting for weight, height and age
findings.finding: Even at the same weight, height and age, women's measured total, basal and activity expenditure averaged 11% lower than men's, which supports sex-specific energy equations.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed 8641250), Results

findings.citation: Black AE, Coward WA, Cole TJ, Prentice AM. Human energy expenditure in affluent societies: an analysis of 574 doubly-labelled water measurements. Eur J Clin Nutr. 1996;50(2):72-92. PMID: 8641250
findings.population: People aged 2-95 y in affluent societies (DLW)
findings.parameter: PAL model structure (TEE = BMR x PAL) and predictors
findings.value: PAL was confirmed as a valid index of TEE adjusted for BMR. The effect of body weight disappears when expenditure is expressed as PAL, while height and age remain highly significant predictors of PAL. The abstract does not give their direction for PAL; for TEE, BMR and AEE, height is positive and age negative, especially for activity
findings.finding: Multiplying BMR by an activity factor is a valid way to model total expenditure, since body weight no longer predicts PAL once expenditure is scaled to BMR. Height and age still predict PAL, and age lowers activity expenditure in particular.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed 8641250), Results

findings.citation: Black AE, Coward WA, Cole TJ, Prentice AM. Human energy expenditure in affluent societies: an analysis of 574 doubly-labelled water measurements. Eur J Clin Nutr. 1996;50(2):72-92. PMID: 8641250
findings.population: People aged 2-95 y in affluent societies (DLW)
findings.parameter: PAL for active users vs guideline-assumed values
findings.value: Average expenditure was similar to the FAO/WHO/UNU (1985) and UK Department of Health (1991) energy requirement recommendations, but PAL in active people tends to be higher than those assumptions. The abstract gives no numeric PAL for active groups (it is in the tables, which were not read)
findings.finding: Guideline energy requirements matched average measured expenditure. Active people's measured PAL tended to run above the values the guidelines assume, so an app should not cap active users at a low default multiplier.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed 8641250), Conclusions

findings.citation: Pontzer H, Yamada Y, Sagayama H, Ainslie PN, Andersen LF, Anderson LJ, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808-12. doi:10.1126/science.abe5017
findings.population: IAEA DLW database: 6,421 people (64% female) aged 8 d to 95 y from 29 countries; BEE subset n = 2,008
findings.parameter: TEE scaling with fat-free mass (equation form)
findings.value: TEE = 0.677 x FFM^0.708, r2 = 0.83 (TEE in MJ/d as used throughout the paper; FFM in kg; units are not restated next to the equation); n = 6,421 DLW measurements
findings.finding: DLW-measured TEE rises with fat-free mass as a power law with an exponent below 1; body size, mainly FFM, explained 83% of the variance. Energy per kg therefore falls as size rises, so a fixed per-kg ratio misestimates people at the size extremes; the authors adjusted for size by regression instead.
findings.locator: Main text, paragraph beginning 'We found that both total and basal expenditure increased with fat free mass' (Fig. 1; Figs S1-S2; Table S1)
