findings.citation: Pontzer H, Yamada Y, Sagayama H, Ainslie PN, Andersen LF, Anderson LJ, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808-12. doi:10.1126/science.abe5017
findings.population: DLW database adults 20-60 y and >60 y
findings.parameter: age adjustment to size-adjusted TEE in adults
findings.value: No age trend from 20 to 60 y; decline begins at a break point of 63.0 y (95% CI 60.1-65.9); after that adjusted TEE falls by -0.7 +/- 0.1% per year and is about 26% below middle-aged adults by the 90s
findings.finding: With fat-free and fat mass accounted for, TEE showed no age trend between 20 and 60 years, and this held even in pregnancy. A segmented regression put the start of the decline at about 63 years. After that, adjusted TEE fell by roughly 0.7% per year.
findings.locator: Main text, subsections 'Adults (20 to 60 y)' and 'Older adults (>60 y)' (Fig. 2; Fig. S3; Table S4)

findings.citation: Pontzer H, Yamada Y, Sagayama H, Ainslie PN, Andersen LF, Anderson LJ, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808-12. doi:10.1126/science.abe5017
findings.parameter: age at which the adult TEE plateau starts
findings.value: Size-adjusted TEE declines by -2.8 +/- 0.1% per year from childhood to a break point at 20.5 y (95% CI 19.8-21.2); adults aged 20-25 y averaged 102.7 +/- 18.1% of the adult-expected value
findings.finding: Size-adjusted TEE fell through childhood and adolescence and reached the adult plateau at about 20.5 years. This suggests 18-20-year-olds may still sit slightly above adult-equation predictions.
findings.locator: Main text, subsection 'Juveniles (1 to 20 y)' (Fig. 2)

findings.citation: Pontzer H, Yamada Y, Sagayama H, Ainslie PN, Andersen LF, Anderson LJ, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808-12. doi:10.1126/science.abe5017
findings.parameter: sex term in body-composition-adjusted adult TEE
findings.value: Sex had no detectable effect on TEE in adults 20-60 y once FFM and fat mass were in the model
findings.finding: In adults, adding sex did not improve the explanation of TEE once fat-free mass and fat mass were modelled. Sex differences in expenditure were explained by body composition.
findings.locator: Main text, subsection 'Adults (20 to 60 y)'

findings.citation: Pontzer H, Yamada Y, Sagayama H, Ainslie PN, Andersen LF, Anderson LJ, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808-12. doi:10.1126/science.abe5017
findings.parameter: individual residual error of predicted TEE
findings.value: TEE and its components vary by more than +/-20% between individuals even after controlling for FFM, fat mass, sex and age
findings.finding: Even after accounting for fat-free mass, fat mass, sex and age, individual TEE varied by more than plus or minus 20%. Any equation-based starting estimate therefore carries large person-level error. For the app, this argues for calibrating from observed intake and weight trends.
findings.locator: Main text, final paragraph (Figs 1-2; Table S2)

findings.citation: Macena ML, Pereira MR, Carvalho GCO, Santos JVLD, Silva Junior AED, Praxedes DRS, et al. Adequacy of the "pocket formulas" for measuring total energy expenditure in healthy women compared with the new DRI equation: a doubly labeled water study. Nutrition. 2023;116:112183. doi:10.1016/j.nut.2023.112183
findings.population: Healthy adult women, largely sedentary or low-active (Brazil)
findings.parameter: kcal/kg body-weight multiplier for TEE when PAL is unknown (whole sample)
findings.value: x30 kcal/kg: bias -6%, limits of agreement -39.8 to +27.5 (unit not stated in abstract; presumably %), RMSE 373.4 (units not given in abstract), precision 42%; multipliers tested: 20, 25, 30, 35 kcal/kg
findings.finding: Against doubly labelled water in 55 healthy women, 30 kcal/kg body weight gave the lowest mean bias and highest precision of the four multipliers tested. Individual limits of agreement were still wide, about -40 to +28 (apparently percent; the abstract does not state the unit).
findings.locator: Abstract, Results (entire sample)

findings.citation: Macena ML, Pereira MR, Carvalho GCO, Santos JVLD, Silva Junior AED, Praxedes DRS, et al. Adequacy of the "pocket formulas" for measuring total energy expenditure in healthy women compared with the new DRI equation: a doubly labeled water study. Nutrition. 2023;116:112183. doi:10.1016/j.nut.2023.112183
findings.population: Healthy adult women, largely sedentary or low-active (Brazil)
findings.parameter: kcal/kg multiplier by BMI category (women)
findings.value: Normal weight: x35 kcal/kg, bias -4.8%, LoA -41.5 to 31.8; overweight: x30 kcal/kg, bias -2.2%, LoA -25.1 to 20.6; obesity: x30 kcal/kg, bias +4.2%, LoA -21.1 to 29.4 (LoA unit not stated in abstract)
findings.finding: The abstract gives 35 kcal/kg for normal weight and 30 kcal/kg for overweight and obesity, implying these agreed best. Limits of agreement stayed wide in every class, roughly 20-40 either side (apparently percent of measured TEE; the unit is not stated).
findings.locator: Abstract, Results (BMI categories)

findings.citation: Macena ML, Pereira MR, Carvalho GCO, Santos JVLD, Silva Junior AED, Praxedes DRS, et al. Adequacy of the "pocket formulas" for measuring total energy expenditure in healthy women compared with the new DRI equation: a doubly labeled water study. Nutrition. 2023;116:112183. doi:10.1016/j.nut.2023.112183
findings.population: Healthy adult women, largely sedentary or low-active (Brazil)
findings.parameter: fallback rule when the DRI 2023 EER equation lacks a PAL input
findings.value: The DRI 2023 EER equations need a PAL estimate; kcal/kg rules showed reasonable agreement with DLW compared with the DRI proposal. The abstract gives no numeric DRI-equation bias.
findings.finding: The 2023 DRI energy equations require an estimate of physical activity level. The authors propose simple kcal/kg rules as a practical substitute when PAL is unavailable, but only for sedentary or low-active healthy women. The abstract does not report DRI-equation accuracy figures.
findings.locator: Abstract, Introduction and Conclusion

findings.citation: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms E, et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-84. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608
findings.population: Healthy adults, not energy-restricted, doing resistance training for at least 6 weeks
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day plateau for RT-induced FFM gain
findings.value: 1.62 g/kg/day (95% CI 1.03-2.20); biphasic regression of 42 study arms, 723 participants; R2 = 0.19; p = 0.079 (not statistically significant); intakes studied ranged from 0.9 to 2.4 g/kg/day
findings.finding: A two-segment regression put the plateau for training-induced FFM gain at about 1.62 g protein/kg/day of total intake. The estimate was imprecise, and the biphasic model did not reach statistical significance.
findings.locator: Results, 'Break point analysis'; Figure 5

findings.citation: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms E, et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-84. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608
findings.population: Healthy adults, not energy-restricted, resistance training
findings.parameter: upper protein target to maximise FFM gain
findings.value: about 2.2 g/kg/day (the upper 95% CI bound of the 1.62 g/kg/day break point)
findings.finding: Because the break-point confidence interval reached 2.20 g/kg/day, the authors suggested about 2.2 g/kg/day as a prudent target for people trying to maximise FFM gain. They present it as a pragmatic estimate with known error, not a measured optimum.
findings.locator: Discussion, 'Muscle mass', paragraph discussing the two-segment regression

findings.citation: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms E, et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-84. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608
findings.parameter: adequacy of the 0.8 g/kg/day RDA for resistance-training goals
findings.value: RDA 0.8 g/kg/day judged insufficient; mean baseline intake was about 1.4 g/kg/day (75% above the RDA), yet about 35 g/day of added protein still increased FFM and 1RM
findings.finding: Participants who already ate about 1.4 g/kg/day still gained more FFM and strength with extra protein. The authors therefore judged 0.8 g/kg/day insufficient for people seeking strength and FFM gains from training, especially older adults.
findings.locator: Discussion, 'Muscle mass', paragraph beginning 'A goal of this meta-analysis'; Results 'Protein supplementation'

findings.citation: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms E, et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-84. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608
findings.population: 49 RCTs, healthy adults, not energy-restricted, resistance training for at least 6 weeks
findings.parameter: expected body-composition change from added protein during RT
findings.value: FFM +0.30 kg (95% CI 0.09-0.52); fat mass -0.41 kg (-0.70 to -0.13); total body mass +0.11 kg (-0.23 to 0.46, not significant); 1RM +2.49 kg (0.64-4.33); resistance training alone gave about +1.1 +/- 1.2 kg FFM over 13 +/- 8 weeks
findings.finding: Compared with training alone, adding protein raised FFM by 0.30 kg and cut fat mass by 0.41 kg. Total body mass did not change significantly, which is a small recomposition effect on top of the roughly 1.1 kg FFM that training itself produced.
findings.locator: Results, 'Meta-analyses' (Figs 2-3); Discussion, 'Muscle mass'

findings.citation: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms E, et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-84. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608
findings.parameter: age modifier of protein effect on FFM
findings.value: -0.01 kg (95% CI -0.02 to -0.00) per year of age (p = 0.02 in Results and Table 1; the abstract states p = 0.002); under 45 y MD 0.55 kg (0.30-0.81) vs over 45 y MD 0.06 kg (-0.14 to 0.26)
findings.finding: The benefit of protein on FFM got smaller with age. It was clear under 45 years and not significant over 45. Older-adult trials were few (13) and used low supplemental doses of about 20 g/day, so they may not have been given enough protein.
findings.locator: Results, 'Meta-regression' (Table 1; Figure 4); Discussion, 'Muscle mass' (20 +/- 18 g/day dose) and limitations paragraph (13 studies in >45 y)

findings.citation: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms E, et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-84. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608
findings.parameter: training-status modifier of protein effect on FFM
findings.value: Trained: FFM MD 1.05 kg (0.61-1.50); untrained: 0.15 kg (-0.02 to 0.31, not significant); meta-regression advantage for trained status 0.75 kg (0.09-1.40), p = 0.03; 10 studies in trained participants
findings.finding: Extra protein increased FFM more consistently in resistance-trained people than in novices. In novices the effect was small and not significant.
findings.locator: Table 1; Figure 3 caption; Results, 'Meta-regression'

findings.citation: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms E, et al. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376-84. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608
findings.parameter: post-exercise protein dose as modifier
findings.value: Post-exercise dose of 5-44 g (mean 24 +/- 11 g) did not modify the FFM effect (20 studies, 793 participants, p = 0.25)
findings.finding: How much protein was taken after exercise did not change the FFM benefit. Total daily intake, not the size of the post-workout serving, appears to drive the effect.
findings.locator: Results, 'Meta-regression', univariate paragraph (Table 1); Results, 'Protein supplementation' (5-44 g range, 24 +/- 11 g)

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.parameter: daily protein range for exercising adults
findings.value: 1.4-2.0 g/kg body weight/day (stated as a minimum for most exercising individuals); within the IOM AMDR of 10-35% of energy; RDA of 0.8 g/kg/day judged inappropriate for training athletes
findings.finding: The ISSN says most exercising people need at least about 1.4-2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day to build or keep muscle. This fits within the 10-35% protein energy range. It considers the 0.8 g/kg RDA and older nitrogen-balance estimates too low for athletes.
findings.locator: Abstract, position statement 2; 'Recommended intake' key points; Conclusion

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day during a hypocaloric phase (resistance-trained)
findings.value: 2.3-3.1 g/kg/d, written in the same g/kg/d unit that position statement 2 defines per kg body weight; no source is cited for the figure. The identical range in Helms et al. 2014 (not in the stand's reference list) is per kg fat-free mass.
findings.finding: The ISSN says resistance-trained people cutting calories may need 2.3-3.1 g/kg/day, written per kg body weight, to maximise lean-mass retention. Helms 2014 gives the identical range per kg fat-free mass; the stand cites no source, so the app must choose the unit deliberately.
findings.locator: Abstract, position statement 3 (the number appears only in the abstract's position list; the 'Recommended intake' key points say only that more may be needed during energy restriction)

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.parameter: very high protein intake and fat-mass change
findings.value: >3.0 g/kg/day (preliminary evidence)
findings.finding: The ISSN cites early, novel evidence that intakes above 3.0 g/kg/day may help resistance-trained people lose fat mass. It labels this evidence preliminary.
findings.locator: Abstract, position statement 4; Conclusion

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.population: Exercising individuals; older adults for the 40 g figure
findings.parameter: protein per serving
findings.value: 0.25 g high-quality protein/kg body weight, or 20-40 g absolute per dose; about 40 g for older adults; about 70 g needed to further reduce muscle protein breakdown
findings.finding: The general per-serving target is about 0.25 g/kg body weight, or 20-40 g, of high-quality protein. Older adults probably need about 40 g per dose to maximise muscle protein synthesis, and larger doses (about 70 g) further reduce protein breakdown.
findings.locator: Abstract, position statement 5; 'Recommended intake' key points

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.parameter: leucine and EAA content per protein dose
findings.value: 700-3000 mg leucine per dose (the 'Protein quality' key points give 1-3 g leucine per meal); a 20-40 g dose supplies about 10-12 g EAA
findings.finding: Each protein serving should aim for about 0.7-3 g leucine with a complete set of essential amino acids. A 20-40 g serving of high-quality protein provides roughly 10-12 g EAA.
findings.locator: Abstract, position statement 6; 'Protein timing' key points; 'Protein quality' key points

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.population: Young healthy adults (acute MPS study); exercising individuals
findings.parameter: protein feeding interval and minimum per main meal
findings.value: Evenly spaced every 3-4 h; at least 20-25 g (~0.25 g/kg) per main meal with no more than 3-4 h between meals; in an acute study, 4 x 20 g every 3 h beat 2 x 40 g and 8 x 10 g over 12 h
findings.finding: Protein servings should be spread evenly across the day, every 3-4 hours. As a practical rule, eat at least 20-25 g at each main meal. In an acute study, moderate servings every 3 hours raised muscle protein synthesis more than fewer large servings or many small ones.
findings.locator: Abstract, position statement 7; 'Protein ingestion and meal timing', final paragraph

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.parameter: meal pattern during energy restriction
findings.value: 3-4 whole meals per day, each with 20-40 g protein
findings.finding: People cutting calories are advised to eat three to four whole meals a day, each with 20-40 g of protein.
findings.locator: 'Recommended intake' section, paragraph on the MPS 'muscle-full' response

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.population: Individuals increasing energy intake; lean and overweight/obese adults in the cited pacing trials
findings.parameter: meal frequency when increasing energy intake
findings.value: Between-meal snacks combining complete protein with carbohydrate; protein-pacing trials cited used 4-6 meals/day of 20-40 g protein each
findings.finding: For people raising their calories, the stand suggests adding between-meal snacks that combine complete protein and carbohydrate. It cites protein-pacing trials that used four to six meals a day with 20-40 g protein each.
findings.locator: 'Recommended intake' section, paragraph beginning 'For those attempting to increase their calories'

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.population: Young and older men (acute studies); a 12-week training trial in young men
findings.parameter: pre-sleep protein
findings.value: 30-40 g casein about 30 min before sleep
findings.finding: Taking 30-40 g of casein about 30 minutes before sleep raised overnight muscle protein synthesis and next-morning metabolic rate without reducing overnight fat breakdown.
findings.locator: Abstract, final position statement; 'Pre-sleep protein intake' section

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.parameter: relevance of peri-workout protein timing
findings.value: Timing benefit lessens when daily protein is already >=1.6 g/kg/day; immediate post-exercise protein is less needed if a pre-exercise meal was eaten less than about 5 h before the session ends
findings.finding: Protein timing around workouts matters less once daily intake reaches about 1.6 g/kg/day. A pre-workout meal eaten within about five hours of finishing training reduces the need for protein straight after. Total daily protein and energy are what matter most.
findings.locator: 'Protein timing' section, paragraph on daily intake >=1.6 g/kg/day; 'Protein timing' key points

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.parameter: protein during endurance exercise
findings.value: about 0.25 g protein/kg body weight per hour of endurance exercise, added to usual carbohydrate
findings.finding: The stand recommends about 0.25 g protein/kg per hour of endurance exercise, on top of normal carbohydrate, to reduce muscle-damage markers and soreness. Added protein did not improve endurance performance when carbohydrate was adequate.
findings.locator: 'Benefits on exercise performance' > 'Endurance exercise performance', concluding paragraph and key points

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.parameter: daily carbohydrate for endurance athletes (restated reference range)
findings.value: 6-10 g carbohydrate/kg/day (cited as the recommended intake, not the stand's own position); a 7-day diet of 5.9 g/kg carbohydrate plus 3.3 g/kg protein slowed a time trial by 20% versus 7.9 g/kg carbohydrate plus 1.3 g/kg protein
findings.finding: The stand cites 6-10 g/kg/day as the recommended carbohydrate range for endurance athletes. It describes a one-week crossover in which swapping carbohydrate for protein, taking carbohydrate below that range, slowed cyclists' time trial by 20%.
findings.locator: 'Endurance exercise performance', first paragraph

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.population: Trained individuals after hard exercise (cited studies)
findings.parameter: post-exercise carbohydrate plus protein for glycogen recovery
findings.value: Adding 0.4 g/kg protein to 0.8 g/kg carbohydrate increased glycogen replenishment; no added benefit with 1.2 g/kg carbohydrate. The key points state the threshold as '<1.2 g/kg/day', which conflicts with the per-dose units in the text.
findings.finding: Adding protein helped glycogen recovery only when post-exercise carbohydrate was moderate (0.8 g/kg), not when it was higher (1.2 g/kg). The stand's units for this threshold are inconsistent, so it should not be encoded without checking the primary studies.
findings.locator: 'Effects of milk proteins on glycogen replenishment and skeletal muscle damage'; 'Protein timing' key points

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.population: Healthy resistance-trained adults; excludes people with renal disease
findings.parameter: protein intake range without adverse clinical markers (healthy adults)
findings.value: Per the stand's Antonio et al. series: up to 3.4 g/kg/day for 8 weeks with no change in clinical blood markers, including kidney and liver function; 8-week-block crossover (n = 12; habitual 2.6 vs mean 2.9 g/kg/day) with no clinical side effects; 1-year crossover (n = 14; 3.3 vs 2.5 g/kg/day) with no harm to kidney or liver function or blood lipids. A 4.4 g/kg/day, 8-week trial (n = 30, parallel) reported no adverse outcomes but measured body composition only.
findings.finding: Small controlled trials in healthy resistance-trained adults found no harm to kidney or liver markers at up to 3.4 g/kg/day for 8 weeks or 3.3 g/kg/day for a year, with lipids unchanged in the year-long trial. A 4.4 g/kg/day, 8-week trial measured only body composition.
findings.locator: 'Protein safety' section and key points

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.population: Food composition statements (mixed human and animal evidence)
findings.parameter: leucine content by protein source
findings.value: Whey ~11%, casein ~9.3%, dairy 9-11%, egg 8.6%, meat ~8% leucine; plant proteins described as low in leucine; a cited animal-model comparison used wheat 6.8%, soy 8.0%, egg 8.8%, whey 11%; 113.4 g lean beef supplies ~10 g EAA, 3.5 g leucine and 30 g amino acids; one large egg has ~6 g protein and 75 kcal
findings.finding: Dairy and egg proteins carry the most leucine per gram of protein and meat slightly less. The stand calls plant proteins low in leucine, though its soy figure (8.0%) matches meat. This supports ranking protein foods by leucine or EAA density.
findings.locator: 'Criteria for comparing protein sources'; 'Milk proteins'; 'Egg proteins'; 'Beef and other flesh proteins'

findings.citation: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
findings.population: Older men (wheat study); resistance-trained adults (rice trial)
findings.parameter: plant-protein dose adjustment
findings.value: 35 g wheat protein gave lower MPS than 35 g casein in older men, while about 60 g raised myofibrillar synthesis; soy MPS was below whey but above casein; 48 g/day rice protein matched whey over 8 weeks of training
findings.finding: Plant proteins may need larger servings to match animal proteins. Nearly doubling a wheat-protein dose made it effective, and a high daily dose of rice protein matched whey for training adaptations in one 8-week trial.
findings.locator: 'Meat vs. plant based proteins' section; 'Protein timing' section (rice-protein trial)

findings.citation: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, Yau T, Ali MU, Fitzpatrick-Lewis D, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810. doi:10.1002/jcsm.12922
findings.population: Healthy, non-obese adults under 65 doing resistance exercise; weight-loss protocols excluded
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day floor for lean-mass gain with RT, adults under 65
findings.value: >=1.6 g/kg/day: LBM SMD 0.30 (95% CI 0.17-0.43), 23 studies (all in adults under 65), moderate GRADE; 1.2-1.59 g/kg/day in under-65s: SMD 0.15 (-0.02 to 0.31), 15 studies, not significant; <1.2 g/kg/day with RE (all ages, not split by age): SMD -0.14 (-0.56 to 0.27), 4 studies
findings.finding: In adults under 65 doing resistance exercise, more protein increased lean mass significantly only at 1.6 g/kg/day or above. Intakes of 1.2-1.59 g/kg/day showed no significant added gain.
findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 'Effect of additional protein intake on lean body mass'

findings.citation: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, Yau T, Ali MU, Fitzpatrick-Lewis D, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810. doi:10.1002/jcsm.12922
findings.population: Healthy, non-obese adults 65 and over doing resistance exercise
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day for lean-mass gain with RT, adults 65 and over
findings.value: 1.2-1.59 g/kg/day: SMD 0.20 (0.02-0.37), 9 studies, low GRADE; not significant after removing one large trial (SMD 0.12, -0.08 to 0.32); no trials tested >=1.6 g/kg/day in this age group
findings.finding: In adults 65 and over doing resistance exercise, 1.2-1.59 g/kg/day gave a small lean-mass benefit. The result depended on one large trial, and no trials tested 1.6 g/kg/day or more in this age group, so the best intake for older adults is unknown.
findings.locator: Table 2; Results, lean body mass paragraph 2; Table S6 (sensitivity analysis)

findings.citation: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, Yau T, Ali MU, Fitzpatrick-Lewis D, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810. doi:10.1002/jcsm.12922
findings.population: Healthy, non-obese adults 18 and over; about 80% of trials had baseline intake of at least 1.2 g/kg/day
findings.parameter: expected extra lean mass from higher protein (mostly with RT)
findings.value: SMD 0.22 (0.15-0.30 in text; 0.15-0.29 in Table 2), 66 RCTs, 2,665 participants (62 used RE; RE-only SMD 0.22, 0.14-0.30); about 1.3-1.4 kg LBM gain vs about 0.8 kg in controls (about 0.5-0.7 kg difference); 76% of studies lasted 8-12 weeks
findings.finding: Across 66 trials, eating more protein gave a small extra lean-mass gain of about 0.5-0.7 kg over roughly 8-12 weeks compared with controls. This sets a realistic expectation for how much a higher protein target adds.
findings.locator: Results, lean body mass paragraph 1; Table 2

findings.citation: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, Yau T, Ali MU, Fitzpatrick-Lewis D, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810. doi:10.1002/jcsm.12922
findings.population: Healthy, non-obese adults not doing resistance exercise
findings.parameter: effect of higher protein without resistance training
findings.value: LBM SMD 0.21 (-0.15 to 0.58), 6 studies, not significant, low GRADE
findings.finding: Raising protein without resistance exercise did not significantly increase lean mass. Higher protein alone should not be presented as building muscle.
findings.locator: Table 2; Results, lean body mass paragraph 1

findings.citation: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, Yau T, Ali MU, Fitzpatrick-Lewis D, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810. doi:10.1002/jcsm.12922
findings.population: Healthy, non-obese adults doing resistance exercise
findings.parameter: protein intake for lower-body strength gain with RT
findings.value: >=1.6 g/kg/day: SMD 0.40 (0.23-0.57) (Table 4: 19 trials; the Results text says 20; the abstract prints a CI of 0.09:0.35); meta-regression SMD 0.26 per g/kg/day (0.05-0.47) in RE studies; low GRADE
findings.finding: Lower-body strength gains were larger only at 1.6 g/kg/day or above, and in meta-regression they rose with intake. Effects on bench press and handgrip were small or unclear.
findings.locator: Table 4; Results, 'Effect of dietary protein intake on lower-body strength'

findings.citation: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, Yau T, Ali MU, Fitzpatrick-Lewis D, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810. doi:10.1002/jcsm.12922
findings.population: Healthy adults over 18 (official reference values restated)
findings.parameter: adult protein reference intake (RDA/PRI floor)
findings.value: US/Canada RDA 0.8 g/kg BW/day; FAO/WHO 0.83 g/kg BW/day; EFSA PRI 0.83 g/kg BW/day; meant to maintain nitrogen balance in about 98% of individuals; the same for all adults regardless of age or sex
findings.finding: The paper restates the official adult protein reference intakes: about 0.8-0.83 g/kg body weight/day, set to cover nitrogen balance in nearly all healthy adults. These are floors, not targets for training goals. Confirm them against the primary DRI and FAO/WHO reports.
findings.locator: Introduction, paragraph 2

findings.citation: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, Yau T, Ali MU, Fitzpatrick-Lewis D, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2022;13(2):795-810. doi:10.1002/jcsm.12922

findings.value: 65 of 74 RCTs supplied animal protein; 9 used plant-based (mainly soy) protein; 6 used blends
findings.finding: Almost all included trials used animal protein. The g/kg thresholds mainly reflect animal-protein diets, and how well they transfer to vegetarian or vegan patterns is uncertain.

findings.citation: Helms ER, Zinn C, Rowlands DS, Brown SR. A systematic review of dietary protein during caloric restriction in resistance trained lean athletes: a case for higher intakes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2014;24(2):127-38. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054

findings.finding: For lean, energy-restricted, resistance-trained adults, the review recommends 2.3-3.1 g protein per kg fat-free mass per day. Targets move toward the top of the range as the deficit gets larger and the person gets leaner. The unit is fat-free mass, not body mass.

findings.citation: Helms ER, Zinn C, Rowlands DS, Brown SR. A systematic review of dietary protein during caloric restriction in resistance trained lean athletes: a case for higher intakes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2014;24(2):127-38. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054

findings.parameter: observed protein intake that went with FFM retention in lean athletes under substantial restriction
findings.value: 2.5-2.6 g/kg (the abstract does not say whether per kg body mass or FFM)
findings.finding: One group was not high in body fat, was under substantial restriction and had no novel training stimulus, yet avoided meaningful FFM loss. It had the highest protein intake in the review. This is a single-group observation.

findings.citation: Helms ER, Zinn C, Rowlands DS, Brown SR. A systematic review of dietary protein during caloric restriction in resistance trained lean athletes: a case for higher intakes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2014;24(2):127-38. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054

findings.value: Body fat <=23% (men) or <=35% (women); age 18 and over; resistance-trained for more than 6 months
findings.finding: The recommendation comes only from lean, experienced lifters under these body-fat limits. The limits were inclusion criteria, not tested cut-offs for switching an app's protein target.

findings.citation: Helms ER, Zinn C, Rowlands DS, Brown SR. A systematic review of dietary protein during caloric restriction in resistance trained lean athletes: a case for higher intakes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2014;24(2):127-38. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054

findings.parameter: FFM loss during energy restriction in lean resistance-trained athletes
findings.value: Body fat percentage fell by 0.5-6.6% in all 13 groups; FFM fell by 0.3-2.7 kg in 9 of 13 groups; the abstract gives no numeric deficit-rate threshold
findings.finding: Most groups lost some FFM while cutting. Groups that kept FFM tended to have higher body fat, smaller calorie restriction, or a new training stimulus. This supports gentler deficits for leaner users, but no rate is quantified.

findings.citation: Longland TM, Oikawa SY, Mitchell CJ, Devries MC, Phillips SM. Higher compared with lower dietary protein during an energy deficit combined with intense exercise promotes greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss: a randomized trial. findings.finding: Young men ate about 40% below their energy needs and did resistance training plus HIIT 6 days a week for 4 weeks. On 2.4 g/kg/d protein they gained more lean mass than on 1.2 g/kg/d. Performance improved equally in both groups.

findings.citation: Longland TM, Oikawa SY, Mitchell CJ, Devries MC, Phillips SM. findings.parameter: energy deficit size tested with high protein (trial condition, not a recommended rate)
findings.value: ~40% below energy requirement; intake 33 ± 1 kcal/kg LBM/d for 4 wk; fat mass −4.8 ± 1.6 kg (2.4 g/kg/d) vs −3.5 ± 1.4 kg (1.2 g/kg/d)
findings.finding: The trial used an aggressive, short deficit of roughly 40% below requirement (about 33 kcal per kg lean mass per day), with diets provided by the researchers, for only 4 weeks. This is a tested condition, not evidence that such a rate is safe or optimal for longer use.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Design; Results), PMID 26817506

findings.citation: Longland TM, Oikawa SY, Mitchell CJ, Devries MC, Phillips SM. Higher compared with lower dietary protein during an energy deficit combined with intense exercise promotes greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss: a randomized trial. Am J Clin Nutr. 2016;103(3):738-46. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.119339
findings.population: Young men, 4-wk deficit with RT + HIIT 6 d/wk
findings.parameter: lean mass gain with fat loss during a deficit (recomposition feasibility)
findings.value: 2.4 g/kg/d: LBM +1.2 ± 1.0 kg, fat mass −4.8 ± 1.6 kg; 1.2 g/kg/d: LBM +0.1 ± 1.0 kg, fat mass −3.5 ± 1.4 kg; 4 wk; 4-compartment model
findings.finding: With high protein and intense combined training, lean mass went up while fat went down during a large deficit. So short-term recomposition is possible. The higher-protein group also lost more fat. This is one small 4-week trial in young men.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results), PMID 26817506

findings.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA. How much protein can the body use in a single meal for muscle-building? Implications for daily protein distribution. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2018;15:10. doi:10.1186/s12970-018-0215-1
findings.population: Resistance-trained adults (review of acute and longitudinal studies)
findings.parameter: per-meal protein g/kg/meal and minimum meal count
findings.value: 0.4 g/kg/meal across ≥4 meals (to reach ≥1.6 g/kg/d); maximum 0.55 g/kg/meal across 4 meals if targeting 2.2 g/kg/d
findings.finding: For building muscle, the authors suggest at least four protein meals of about 0.4 g/kg each, and no more than 0.55 g/kg per meal for a 2.2 g/kg/d target. The 0.4 comes from a 0.25 g/kg plateau in young men plus two standard deviations.
findings.locator: Conclusions section, final two paragraphs (PMC5828430)

findings.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA. How much protein can the body use in a single meal for muscle-building? Implications for daily protein distribution. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2018;15:10. doi:10.1186/s12970-018-0215-1
findings.population: Resistance trainees, energy balance or surplus
findings.parameter: daily protein g/kg/day for resistance-training gains (non-dieting)
findings.value: ~1.6 g/kg/d; upper 95% CI 2.2 g/kg/d (restated from a cited meta-analysis; eucaloric or hypercaloric conditions)
findings.finding: The review says about 1.6 g/kg/d gets the most out of resistance training when not dieting. It treats that as an average, not a hard limit, and cites a meta-analytic upper 95% CI of 2.2 g/kg/d. This is second-hand, so check the original meta-analysis.
findings.locator: Conclusions section, second (final) paragraph, which opens with the collective evidence on total daily protein intake (PMC5828430)

findings.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA. How much protein can the body use in a single meal for muscle-building? Implications for daily protein distribution. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2018;15:10. doi:10.1186/s12970-018-0215-1
findings.parameter: hard per-meal protein cap rule
findings.value: No upper per-meal threshold quantified; doses > 20 g raise amino acid oxidation but part of the excess is still used for tissue building
findings.finding: Doses above about 20 g increase amino acid oxidation, but some of the extra still builds tissue. Longitudinal studies (intermittent fasting, pulse feeding) do not consistently back a strict per-meal ceiling. The authors say no specific upper limit has been quantified yet.
findings.locator: Longitudinal findings section and Conclusions, last paragraph (PMC5828430)

findings.citation: Moore DR, Robinson MJ, Fry JL, Tang JE, Glover EI, Wilkinson SB, et al. Ingested protein dose response of muscle and albumin protein synthesis after resistance exercise in young men. Am J Clin Nutr. 2009;89(1):161-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.2008.26401
findings.population: Healthy young men, leg-based resistance exercise, randomized-order crossover
findings.parameter: absolute per-meal protein dose (g) for maximal post-exercise MPS
findings.value: 20 g whole egg protein (doses tested 0, 5, 10, 20, 40 g); MPS maximally stimulated at 20 g over 4 h post-exercise (abstract gives no 20 vs 40 g contrast)
findings.finding: Six young men did leg resistance exercise five times, each followed by a different egg-protein dose in random order. Muscle protein synthesis over 4 h rose with dose and was maximal at 20 g. The sample is tiny and only lower-body exercise was used.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Design; Results; Conclusions), PMID 19056590

findings.citation: Moore DR, Robinson MJ, Fry JL, Tang JE, Glover EI, Wilkinson SB, et al. Ingested protein dose response of muscle and albumin protein synthesis after resistance exercise in young men. Am J Clin Nutr. 2009;89(1):161-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.2008.26401
findings.population: Healthy young men after leg resistance exercise
findings.parameter: per-meal protein dose at which amino acid oxidation rises
findings.value: Whole-body leucine oxidation significantly increased after 20 g and 40 g egg protein (abstract names only these doses; comparator not stated in abstract)
findings.finding: Leucine oxidation rose significantly at 20 and 40 g. The authors took this to mean protein beyond what muscle can use gets burned. Trommelen et al. 2023 later argued oxidation is only a minor fate, so this is low certainty.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results; Conclusions), PMID 19056590

findings.citation: Moore DR, Churchward-Venne TA, Witard O, Breen L, Burd NA, Tipton KD, et al. Protein ingestion to stimulate myofibrillar protein synthesis requires greater relative protein intakes in healthy older versus younger men. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2015;70(1):57-62. doi:10.1093/gerona/glu103
findings.population: Healthy younger men (~22 y), pooled tracer studies; n not given in abstract
findings.parameter: per-meal protein g/kg body mass for maximal MPS, younger adults
findings.value: 0.24 ± 0.06 g/kg body mass; 0.25 ± 0.13 g/kg lean body mass (men ~22 y); ± as reported in abstract (abstract labels basal MPS as mean ± 95% CI; error type for breakpoints not separately stated)
findings.finding: A retrospective pooled breakpoint analysis of tracer studies from the authors' laboratories, each giving a single bolus of 0–40 g high-quality protein. In young men, myofibrillar protein synthesis levelled off at about 0.24 g/kg body mass per meal. Men only; single-bolus feeding.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Methods; Results), PMID 25056502

findings.citation: Moore DR, Churchward-Venne TA, Witard O, Breen L, Burd NA, Tipton KD, et al. Protein ingestion to stimulate myofibrillar protein synthesis requires greater relative protein intakes in healthy older versus younger men. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2015;70(1):57-62. doi:10.1093/gerona/glu103
findings.population: Healthy older men (~71 y), pooled tracer studies; n not given in abstract
findings.parameter: per-meal protein g/kg body mass for maximal MPS, older adults
findings.value: 0.40 ± 0.19 g/kg body mass (vs young p = .055); 0.60 ± 0.29 g/kg lean body mass (vs young p < .01) (men ~71 y)
findings.finding: Older men reached the synthesis plateau at a larger relative dose: about 0.40 g/kg body mass per meal (vs 0.24 in young; p = .055, not significant) and 0.60 g/kg lean mass (p < .01). Their low-dose response was also weaker. Men only, abstract-level.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results; Conclusions), PMID 25056502

findings.citation: Areta JL, Burke LM, Ross ML, Camera DM, West DWD, Broad EM, et al. Timing and distribution of protein ingestion during prolonged recovery from resistance exercise alters myofibrillar protein synthesis. J Physiol. 2013;591(9):2319-31. doi:10.1113/jphysiol.2012.244897
findings.population: Resistance-trained young men (~25 y, group mean body mass 80.5–83.6 kg, ≥2 y training); 24 randomized to parallel groups (matched for body mass), 23 analysed
findings.parameter: protein feeding interval and per-feed dose pattern
findings.value: 80 g whey over 12 h: 4 × 20 g every 3 h gave myofibrillar FSR 0.079 %/h vs 0.060 (8 × 10 g every 1.5 h) and 0.053 %/h (2 × 40 g every 6 h); +31% and +48% (P < 0.02). ≈0.25 g/kg per 20 g feed at mean ~80.5 kg (derived)
findings.finding: Trained men did leg-extension exercise and took 80 g whey in one of three patterns. 20 g every 3 h beat 10 g every 1.5 h and 40 g every 6 h for 12-h myofibrillar synthesis. The 12-h protein total was under 1 g/kg; results may suit only 70–80 kg people.
findings.locator: Results, 'Myofibrillar fractional synthetic rate' and Fig. 4B; Methods, 'Subjects', 'Experimental trials' and Table 1; Discussion (body-mass limitation)

findings.citation: Trommelen J, van Lieshout GAA, Nyakayiru J, Holwerda AM, Smeets JSJ, Hendriks FK, et al. The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4(12):101324. doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2023.101324
findings.population: Healthy recreationally active men 18–40 y, BMI 18.5–30, n = 12/group, randomized double-blind placebo-controlled parallel trial
findings.parameter: per-meal protein upper limit (anabolic ceiling)
findings.value: No ceiling detected up to a 100 g single bolus: myofibrillar synthesis over 12 h 100 g > 25 g > 0 g; 100 g vs 25 g ~20% higher at 0–4 h and ~40% higher at 4–12 h
findings.finding: After whole-body resistance exercise, 100 g of milk protein raised muscle protein synthesis more, and for longer (past 12 h), than 25 g, with no visible upper limit. This argues against capping protein at 20–25 g per meal. Acute study, young men only.
findings.locator: Results, 'Prolonged muscle protein synthetic response to protein ingestion' (Fig. 4G, primary outcome); Discussion; STAR Methods 'Subjects' and 'Study design'

findings.citation: Trommelen J, van Lieshout GAA, Nyakayiru J, Holwerda AM, Smeets JSJ, Hendriks FK, et al. The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4(12):101324. doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2023.101324
findings.population: Healthy young men after whole-body resistance exercise
findings.parameter: fraction of ingested protein oxidised
findings.value: Oxidation negligible relative to the rise in whole-body synthesis; re-analysis of earlier dose-response studies: < 15% of the protein increment oxidised, > 85% used for tissue protein synthesis
findings.finding: Larger doses raised whole-body amino acid oxidation only slightly compared with synthesis. Re-expressing earlier dose-response data, the authors estimate under 15% of extra protein is oxidised. That weakens the claim that big protein meals are wasted.
findings.locator: Results, 'Dose-dependent increases in amino acid kinetics and whole-body protein metabolism' (Fig. 2G, 2H, 2J); Discussion, third text paragraph (on the proposal that excess amino acids are oxidised)

findings.citation: Trommelen J, van Lieshout GAA, Nyakayiru J, Holwerda AM, Smeets JSJ, Hendriks FK, et al. The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4(12):101324. doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2023.101324
findings.population: Healthy young men after whole-body resistance exercise
findings.parameter: postprandial amino acid availability duration by protein dose (meal spacing)
findings.value: 25 g: plasma amino acids raised ~first 5 h; 100 g: raised for the full 12 h. Dietary amino acids reaching circulation over 12 h: 16 ± 1 g (66%) vs 53 ± 7 g (53%). Muscle incorporation over 12 h: 18% of 25 g vs 13 g (13%) of 100 g
findings.finding: Bigger protein boluses are digested and absorbed over a longer window. Blood amino acids stayed high about 5 h after 25 g but for 12 h after 100 g. The authors suggest fewer, larger protein meals are a workable alternative to frequent small ones.
findings.locator: Results, 'Sustained hyperaminoacidemia' (Fig. 1D) and 'No limit to protein-derived amino acid bioavailability' (Fig. 6A–6D); Limitations of the study

findings.citation: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, Cesari M, Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Morley JE, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2013;14(8):542-59. doi:10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021
findings.population: Adults aged >65 y; international expert consensus using a Delphi-like process (EUGMS-led)
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day floor, healthy adults aged >65 y
findings.value: at least 1.0-1.2 g/kg body weight/day (average daily intake), versus the general adult RDA of 0.8 g/kg/d
findings.finding: For healthy people over 65, the group says the 0.8 g/kg/d RDA is too low and advises average intake of at least 1.0-1.2 g/kg/d to keep or regain lean mass and function. It expects this range to leave renal function unaffected.
findings.locator: Abstract; box 'PROT-AGE recommendations for dietary protein intake in healthy older adults' p.543; renal paragraph p.545; Table 2 p.547; 'Key PROT-AGE recommendations' box p.554 (read from a PDF copy of the published JAMDA article hosted by ageingmuscle.be; the publisher site returned 403)

findings.citation: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, Cesari M, Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Morley JE, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2013;14(8):542-59. doi:10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day floor, exercising or active adults aged >65 y
findings.value: >=1.2 g/kg body weight/day total intake (from diet or supplements)
findings.finding: Older adults who exercise or are otherwise active should reach a total daily protein intake of at least 1.2 g/kg, raised through food or supplements as needed, alongside endurance and resistance exercise at safe, individualised levels.
findings.locator: Abstract; box 'PROT-AGE recommendations for exercise and protein intake for older adults' p.550

findings.citation: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, Cesari M, Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Morley JE, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2013;14(8):542-59. doi:10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021
findings.population: Adults aged >65 y (expert consensus from short-term metabolic studies)
findings.parameter: per-meal protein threshold, adults aged >65 y
findings.value: 25-30 g protein per meal containing about 2.5-2.8 g leucine
findings.finding: Older adults seem to need more protein per meal than young adults to trigger an anabolic response, about 25-30 g with roughly 2.5-2.8 g leucine. This favours spreading protein across breakfast, lunch and dinner, although midday pulse feeding also helped and neither pattern is settled.
findings.locator: Box 'PROT-AGE recommendations ... healthy older adults' p.543; 'Specific Nutritional Strategies' p.545; Table 1 p.545

findings.citation: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, Cesari M, Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Morley JE, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2013;14(8):542-59. doi:10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021
findings.parameter: post-exercise protein dose, adults aged >65 y
findings.value: >=20 g protein, preferably soon after exercise; amino acid mix containing 2.0-2.5 g leucine
findings.finding: The group suggests a serving of at least 20 g protein, probably right after exercise, when muscle is thought to be more sensitive to amino acids. The protein should provide about 2.0-2.5 g leucine.
findings.locator: Box 'PROT-AGE recommendations for exercise and protein intake' p.550; 'Exercise and Protein Recommendations for Older People' p.551

findings.citation: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, Cesari M, Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Morley JE, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2013;14(8):542-59. doi:10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021
findings.population: Older adults with chronic kidney disease (expert consensus drawing on ISRNM guidance)
findings.parameter: kidney-function exclusion for higher protein targets
findings.value: Severe CKD, eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and not on dialysis: limit protein to 0.8 g/kg ideal body weight/d. Moderate CKD, eGFR 30-60: >0.8 g/kg/d considered safe, with GFR monitored twice a year. Mild CKD, eGFR >60: raise intake to individual needs.
findings.finding: Severe kidney disease without dialysis is the one stated exception to the higher-protein advice: these people need to restrict protein. Moderate CKD allows intake above 0.8 g/kg/d with twice-yearly GFR checks.
findings.locator: Abstract; disease recommendations box p.546; 'Kidney Function and Kidney Disease' pp.549-550; Table 6 p.549

findings.citation: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, Cesari M, Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Morley JE, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2013;14(8):542-59. doi:10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021
findings.population: Older adults (>65 y) with acute or chronic disease
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day, older adults with acute or chronic disease (clinical; outside the app's healthy-adult scope)
findings.value: 1.2-1.5 g/kg body weight/d for most; up to 2.0 g/kg/d with severe illness, injury or marked malnutrition
findings.finding: Most older adults with acute or chronic illness need more protein than healthy peers, around 1.2-1.5 g/kg/d, and severe illness, injury or marked malnutrition may call for up to 2.0 g/kg/d. The extra amount scales with the type and severity of illness and with pre-illness nutritional status.
findings.locator: Abstract; box 'PROT-AGE recommendations for protein levels in geriatric patients' p.546; key recommendations box p.554

findings.citation: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, Cesari M, Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Morley JE, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2013;14(8):542-59. doi:10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021
findings.population: Older adults (>65 y); AMDR figure is a secondary citation of the IOM DRI report
findings.parameter: protein as % of energy / AMDR check
findings.value: 1.0-1.2 g/kg/d is about 13-16% of total energy, inside the IOM protein AMDR of 10-35% of daily energy (cited)
findings.finding: The authors note that their raised older-adult range works out to roughly 13-16% of calories, which still sits well inside the Institute of Medicine's acceptable protein range of 10-35% of energy.
findings.locator: 'Specific Recommendations on Dietary Protein Intake by Healthy Older People' pp.545-546; Table 2 (Gaffney-Stomberg row) p.547

findings.citation: Devries MC, Sithamparapillai A, Brimble KS, Banfield L, Morton RW, Phillips SM. Changes in kidney function do not differ between healthy adults consuming higher- compared with lower- or normal-protein diets: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Nutr. 2018;148(11):1760-75. doi:10.1093/jn/nxy197
findings.population: Adults aged 23-72 y (mean 49), mean BMI 31.1, without CKD; includes people with obesity, hypertension or type 2 diabetes
findings.parameter: kidney safety of higher protein intake in adults without kidney disease
findings.value: Change in GFR, higher vs normal/lower protein: SMD 0.11 (95% CI -0.05 to 0.27; P=0.16; I2=44%; 19 RCT comparisons, 1547 participants in GRADE table; very low certainty). Post-only GFR: SMD 0.19 (0.07 to 0.31; P=0.002; trivial). Higher-protein arms averaged 1.81 +/- 0.60 g/kg/d vs 0.93 +/- 0.51. High protein was defined as >=1.5 g/kg/d, >=20% of energy or >=100 g/d. 28 RCTs, n=1358, 4 d to 104 wk.
findings.finding: In adults without kidney disease, higher-protein diets changed GFR no differently from normal or lower protein. Post-intervention GFR was only trivially higher, which the authors read as normal renal reserve, not harm. The authors graded the evidence low to very low.
findings.locator: Abstract; Methods 'Study inclusion and exclusion criteria'; Results 'Diet protocol characteristics', 'Publication bias, heterogeneity, and risk of bias', 'Overall effect of HP compared with NLP diets on GFR'; Table 3 (GRADE); Discussion

findings.citation: Devries MC, Sithamparapillai A, Brimble KS, Banfield L, Morton RW, Phillips SM. Changes in kidney function do not differ between healthy adults consuming higher- compared with lower- or normal-protein diets: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Nutr. 2018;148(11):1760-75. doi:10.1093/jn/nxy197
findings.parameter: protein dose-response for kidney function (GFR change)
findings.value: Protein intake vs change in GFR: r=0.184, P=0.33. Meta-regression of the between-group protein difference on GFR change: P=0.42. Dose was linearly related only to post-only GFR (r=0.332, P=0.03). No biphasic breakpoint (P=0.38).
findings.finding: How much protein was added did not predict how much GFR changed, so within the intakes tested (higher-protein arms averaging 1.81 +/- 0.60 g/kg/d) the data give no dose threshold for kidney harm. They also do not show safety far above that range.
findings.locator: Results 'Meta-regression', 'Dose-response analysis'; Table 4; Figure 4; Discussion (dose paragraph)

findings.citation: Devries MC, Sithamparapillai A, Brimble KS, Banfield L, Morton RW, Phillips SM. Changes in kidney function do not differ between healthy adults consuming higher- compared with lower- or normal-protein diets: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Nutr. 2018;148(11):1760-75. doi:10.1093/jn/nxy197
findings.population: Adults without CKD in weight-loss vs weight-maintenance RCTs (subgroup analysis)
findings.parameter: kidney safety of higher protein during energy restriction
findings.value: Energy restriction, pre/post GFR change: SMD 0.09 (95% CI -0.15 to 0.34; P=0.46). Energy balance: SMD 0.18 (0.02 to 0.34; P=0.03), driven by the first 8 wk (SMD 0.30); no difference beyond 8 wk.
findings.finding: In trials run during an energy deficit, higher protein did not change GFR differently from lower protein. A trivial rise appeared in energy-balance trials, confined to the first eight weeks.
findings.locator: Results 'Effects of energy intake during HP compared with NLP diets on GFR'; Discussion

findings.citation: Antonio J, Ellerbroek A, Silver T, Vargas L, Tamayo A, Buehn R, et al. A high protein diet has no harmful effects: a one-year crossover study in resistance-trained males. J Nutr Metab. 2016;2016:9104792. doi:10.1155/2016/9104792
findings.population: Healthy resistance-trained men, 26.3 +/- 3.9 y, 8.9 +/- 3.4 y of training
findings.parameter: upper protein intake without adverse clinical markers (trained men)
findings.value: Habitual phase 2.51 +/- 0.69 g/kg/d vs high-protein phase 3.32 +/- 0.87 g/kg/d (self-reported), about 6 months each over 1 year. No significant differences in blood lipids, liver enzymes, BUN, creatinine or GFR.
findings.finding: Fourteen resistance-trained men alternated habitual and higher protein intakes over a year and showed no adverse change in lipids, liver or kidney panels. Intake was self-logged in a phone app three days a week. The sample was small, male-only, and already eating a lot of protein at baseline.
findings.locator: Abstract; 2.1 Participants; 2.2 Food Diary; 2.4 Blood Analysis; 3 Results; 4 Discussion; 4.1 Limitations (PMC text; the data tables were not rendered in the extraction)

findings.citation: Antonio J, Ellerbroek A, Silver T, Vargas L, Tamayo A, Buehn R, et al. A high protein diet has no harmful effects: a one-year crossover study in resistance-trained males. J Nutr Metab. 2016;2016:9104792. doi:10.1155/2016/9104792
findings.parameter: effect of extra protein energy on body composition when training is unchanged
findings.value: Reported energy intake 29.94 +/- 5.65 kcal/kg/d (habitual) vs 34.37 +/- 5.88 kcal/kg/d (high-protein phase); no significant change in body weight, fat mass or lean mass; training volume load unchanged
findings.finding: Extra protein raised reported energy intake by about 4.4 kcal/kg/d, yet with training held constant the men gained neither fat nor lean mass. The authors suggest added protein alone does not change body composition without a new training stimulus. Self-reported intake limits this.
findings.locator: Abstract; 3 Results; 4 Discussion (paragraph on volume load); 5 Conclusions

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.population: Adult athletes; EA thresholds derived mainly from studies in females
findings.parameter: energy availability floor kcal/kg FFM/day
findings.value: EA = (energy intake - exercise energy expenditure) / fat-free mass. About 45 kcal/kg FFM/d is associated with energy balance and good health. Chronic EA below 30 kcal/kg FFM/d is associated with impaired body functions. Raising EA to about 40 kcal/kg FFM/d restored menses in a mean of 2.6 months.
findings.finding: The statement treats energy availability as a foundation of athlete health. About 45 kcal/kg FFM/d supports health, and sustained values under 30 impair many systems (RED-S). Harm builds along a continuum rather than at one cut-off, and low EA can occur at a stable weight.
findings.locator: Theme 1 'Energy Requirements, Energy Balance and Energy Availability', pp.7-8 of the Dietitians of Canada concurrent publication of the same joint position (Feb 2016, rev. Dec 2016); MSSE full text was paywalled

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: RMR/BMR equation and TEE model
findings.value: TEE = BMR + TEF + TEA. Estimate BMR with the Cunningham or Harris-Benedict equation, then apply an activity factor. RMR may run about 10% above BMR. RMR is 60-80% of TEE in sedentary people and can be only 38-47% in elite endurance athletes.
findings.finding: Cunningham or Harris-Benedict equations, multiplied by an activity factor, are accepted for a reasonable basal estimate, though population-specific equations are preferred. Dietary Guidelines and DRI estimates tend to understate athletes' needs because they do not span athletes' body sizes or activity levels.
findings.locator: Theme 1 'Energy Requirements...' p.7 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.population: Adult athletes seeking fat or weight loss
findings.parameter: daily energy deficit kcal/day
findings.value: reduce intake by ~250-500 kcal/d below periodized energy needs, keeping expenditure the same or slightly higher; progress over about 3-6 weeks
findings.finding: For most athletes, a modest daily cut of roughly 250-500 kcal, with activity held or nudged up, is the practical route to short-term body-composition goals. It should be paired with a slow loss rate and higher protein to spare muscle.
findings.locator: 'Principles of Altering Body Composition and Weight' p.11 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: weekly loss % body mass (upper limit)
findings.value: <1% body mass per week (citing Garthe 2011). EAL Q1: slow (0.7%/wk) loss was better for performance than fast (1.4%/wk); Grade II (Fair).
findings.finding: Fat-free mass and performance are more likely to be kept when weekly weight loss stays below 1% of body mass. Planned loss should happen in the base training phase or well before competition.
findings.locator: 'Principles of Altering Body Composition and Weight' p.11; Figure 1, EAL Question #1, p.4 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day, athletes (general range)
findings.value: 1.2-2.0 g/kg/d; higher for short periods of intensified training or reduced energy intake
findings.finding: Protein intake supporting adaptation, repair and turnover generally falls between 1.2 and 2.0 g/kg/d. It should be adjusted to training status, session demands, carbohydrate availability and, above all, energy availability, rather than fixed by a strength or endurance label.
findings.locator: 'Protein Needs' p.17; Summary p.36 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day during energy restriction
findings.value: >=2.0 g/kg/d spread over the day during energy restriction or sudden inactivity. Cited trial: 2.3 vs 1.0 g/kg/d over a 2-week energy-restricted diet retained muscle mass.
findings.finding: During energy restriction, or abrupt inactivity such as after injury, the statement suggests that protein around 2.0 g/kg/d or above, split across several eating occasions, may help limit fat-free-mass loss; the cited 2-week trial retained muscle at 2.3 versus 1.0 g/kg/d.
findings.locator: 'Protein Needs' p.17; 'Principles of Altering Body Composition and Weight' p.11; Summary p.36 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: per-meal protein dose and spacing
findings.value: ~0.3 g/kg body weight per feeding, after key exercise sessions and every 3-5 h across multiple meals
findings.finding: Newer guidance frames protein as regular moderate servings, about 0.3 g/kg after key sessions and every three to five hours over the day, rather than a daily total alone. These amounts can usually be met from food.
findings.locator: 'Protein Timing as a Trigger for Metabolic Adaptation' p.17; Summary p.36 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: post-exercise protein dose
findings.value: 0.25-0.3 g/kg body weight or 15-25 g high-quality protein (~10 g essential amino acids) within 0-2 h after exercise. >40 g not yet shown to raise MPS further. EAL Q8: ~20-30 g protein during or after exercise increased protein synthesis (Grade I, Good).
findings.finding: Muscle protein synthesis after exercise is best supported by about 0.25-0.3 g/kg, roughly 15-25 g of high-quality protein, in the first two hours. Much larger servings over 40 g have not shown extra benefit except perhaps for very large athletes or during weight loss.
findings.locator: 'Protein Timing as a Trigger for Metabolic Adaptation' p.17; Figure 1 EAL Question #8 p.5; Summary p.37 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: daily carbohydrate g/kg/day by training load
findings.value: Light (low-intensity or skill-based): 3-5 g/kg/d. Moderate (~1 h/d): 5-7 g/kg/d. High (1-3 h/d moderate-high intensity): 6-10 g/kg/d. Very high (>4-5 h/d): 8-12 g/kg/d.
findings.finding: Daily carbohydrate targets scale with body mass and training load. They apply when session quality or intensity matters; on other days intake can follow energy goals and preference, or be deliberately lowered for train-low adaptation.
findings.locator: Table 1 'Daily needs for fuel and recovery' p.15; Summary p.36 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: carbohydrate loading before events >90 min
findings.value: 10-12 g/kg body weight per 24 h for 36-48 h before events longer than 90 min of sustained or intermittent exercise, with a training taper
findings.finding: For events longer than about 90 minutes, athletes can supercompensate muscle glycogen by eating 10-12 g/kg of carbohydrate daily for the 36-48 hours beforehand while tapering training.
findings.locator: Table 1 'Acute fuelling strategies' p.15; 'Achieving Adequate Muscle Glycogen Stores' p.26; Summary p.37 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.population: Athletes preparing for competition or key sessions
findings.parameter: general fuelling-up before events <90 min
findings.value: 7-12 g/kg per 24 h (as for daily fuel needs); with an exercise taper this normalises muscle glycogen within ~24 h
findings.finding: Before events under 90 minutes, eating 7-12 g/kg of carbohydrate over the preceding day, with reduced training, is enough to restore normal glycogen stores. Low-fibre, easily eaten carbohydrate sources can help with gut comfort.
findings.locator: Table 1 'Acute fuelling strategies' p.15; p.26; Summary pp.36-37 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: pre-event carbohydrate g/kg
findings.value: 1-4 g/kg eaten 1-4 h before exercise lasting >60 min. At least 1 g/kg in the pre-event meal helps offset insulin-related early fatigue in sensitive individuals.
findings.finding: A pre-event meal or snack of 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate in the one to four hours before longer exercise tops up liver and muscle stores. Low-fat, low-fibre, low-to-moderate-protein foods are preferred to limit gut problems, and the choice should be individually trialled.
findings.locator: Table 1 'Pre-event fuelling' p.16; 'Achieving Adequate Muscle Glycogen Stores' p.26 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: carbohydrate during exercise g/h by duration
findings.value: <45 min: not needed. 45-75 min: small amounts, including mouth rinse. 1-2.5 h: 30-60 g/h. >2.5-3 h: up to 90 g/h, using multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose:fructose).
findings.finding: Carbohydrate during exercise scales with duration: none for short sessions, mouth exposure for sustained 45-75 minute efforts, 30-60 g per hour for one to two and a half hours, and up to 90 g per hour for ultra-endurance. Higher intakes there link to better performance.
findings.locator: Table 1 'During' rows p.16; pp.26-27; Summary p.37 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.population: Athletes with short recovery between sessions
findings.parameter: post-exercise carbohydrate refuelling g/kg/h
findings.value: 1-1.2 g/kg/h for the first 4 h (summary: 4-6 h) when <8 h separate two fuel-demanding sessions, then resume daily needs
findings.finding: Glycogen is rebuilt at only about 5% per hour, so when sessions are less than eight hours apart, eating about 1-1.2 g/kg of carbohydrate per hour early in recovery maximises refuelling. Small regular snacks may help.
findings.locator: Table 1 'Speedy refuelling' p.15; p.27; Summary p.37 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: recovery carbohydrate plus protein co-ingestion
findings.value: 0.8 g/kg carbohydrate + 0.4 g/kg protein gave glycogen repletion and performance recovery similar to 1.2 g/kg carbohydrate alone
findings.finding: When carbohydrate or energy is limited after exercise, adding protein can support glycogen repletion. A mix of 0.8 g/kg carbohydrate with 0.4 g/kg protein matched 1.2 g/kg carbohydrate alone. Evidence that protein directly improves performance is lacking.
findings.locator: 'Protein Intake Guidelines' p.27; Figure 1 EAL Questions #5-7 pp.4-5 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: fat % of energy (range and floor)
findings.value: typically 20-35% of total energy; chronic intake below 20% of energy discouraged; saturated fat <10% of energy per public-health guidelines
findings.finding: Most athletes' fat intake falls at 20-35% of energy, in line with public-health advice. Long-term intake at or below 20% brings no performance benefit and risks shortfalls in fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids. Very low fat is reserved for acute pre-event or loading phases.
findings.locator: 'Fat' pp.18-19; Summary p.36 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: high-fat low-carbohydrate (ketogenic-style) pattern for athletes
findings.value: Rule: not supported for competitive performance. Matches high-carbohydrate strategies only at moderate intensities and impairs high-intensity performance.
findings.finding: Chronic high-fat, carbohydrate-restricted eating raises fat oxidation but appears to down-regulate carbohydrate use, harming high-intensity work. The statement advises competitive athletes against it, while noting that more research with proper periodised control diets is needed.
findings.locator: 'Fat' p.18; Summary p.36 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: glycemic index / glycemic load in carbohydrate food selection
findings.value: Rule: GI and GL did not affect endurance performance or metabolic responses when carbohydrate and energy were matched (EAL Q11, Grade I, Good). Low-GI pre-event choices give no universal benefit.
findings.finding: Once total carbohydrate and energy are accounted for, the glycemic index or load of carbohydrate foods made no difference to training metabolism or endurance performance. GI therefore need not drive food choice, although low-GI options may help when no carbohydrate can be taken during exercise.
findings.locator: Figure 1 EAL Question #11 p.5; 'Carbohydrate' p.14; Table 1 p.16; p.26 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: fluid intake before, during and after exercise
findings.value: Before: 5-10 mL/kg in the 2-4 h pre-exercise. During: keep total deficit <2% body weight; typical intake 0.4-0.8 L/h (sweat rates 0.3-2.4 L/h). After: drink 125-150% of the remaining deficit (1.25-1.5 L per kg lost). Hyponatraemia: plasma Na <135 mmol/L.
findings.finding: Athletes should start exercise euhydrated, drink during exercise to keep losses under about 2% of body weight without exceeding sweat losses, and afterwards replace about one and a half times the fluid lost. Over-drinking, most common in recreational athletes and women, risks hyponatraemia.
findings.locator: 'Hydration Guidelines: Fluid and Electrolyte Balance' pp.23-25; Summary p.37 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: sodium intake during exercise (trigger conditions)
findings.value: Include sodium when sweat rate is >1.2 L/h, sweat is salty, or exercise lasts >2 h. Average sweat sodium is ~50 mmol/L (~1 g/L). Do not restrict sodium after large losses.
findings.finding: Sodium should be taken during exercise when sweat losses are heavy, sweat is salty, or sessions run past two hours. Post-exercise sodium from food or drink helps retain fluid, so athletes with large losses should not be told to cut sodium.
findings.locator: 'During Exercise' and 'After Exercise' p.25 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: weigh-in protocol / interpreting acute body-weight change
