findings.value: Weigh on waking and after voiding. Acute body-weight changes mostly reflect body-water shifts (when in energy balance). Around exercise, 1 kg of body-weight loss is about 1 L of sweat.
findings.finding: Early-morning body weight taken after waking and voiding can track day-to-day hydration because short-term weight swings mainly reflect water. Weighing before and after exercise, corrected for drinks and urine, estimates sweat loss.
findings.locator: 'Hydration Guidelines' pp.23-24 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: food-intake logging method and bias
findings.value: Weighed or measured food records (typically 3-7 days), multi-pass 24-h recall or food-frequency questionnaire; all methods are biased toward under-reporting
findings.finding: Energy intake can be estimated from several days of weighed or measured food records, multi-pass recalls or food-frequency questionnaires. Every method tends to under-report, and educating users on why and how to record intake may improve accuracy.
findings.locator: Theme 1 'Energy Requirements...' p.7 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: vegetarian at-risk nutrient flags
findings.value: At-risk intakes: energy, protein, fat, creatine, carnosine, n-3 fatty acids, iron, calcium, riboflavin, zinc, vitamin B12; possible lower bone mineral density and stress-fracture risk
findings.finding: A vegetarian diet can be adequate, but depending on how restrictive it is, athletes may fall short on energy, protein, fat, n-3 fats, creatine, carnosine and several micronutrients. Comprehensive dietary assessment, and screening for disordered eating behind the restriction, is advised.
findings.locator: Theme 3 'Vegetarian Athlete' p.32; Summary p.37 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.population: Athletes, especially female, vegetarian or endurance
findings.parameter: iron intake target mg/day for at-risk users
findings.value: At-risk athletes (distance runners, vegetarians, regular blood donors): aim above the RDA, i.e. >18 mg/d for women and >8 mg/d for men. Female athletes' needs may be up to 70% above the EAR. A typical diet supplies about 6 mg iron per ~1000 kcal.
findings.finding: Athletes at higher risk of low iron should aim above the RDA and favour well-absorbed sources such as heme iron, or non-heme iron eaten with vitamin C foods, as the first line. Routine unmonitored supplementation is discouraged.
findings.locator: 'Micronutrients of Key Interest: Iron' pp.19-20 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
findings.parameter: alcohol energy density kcal/g
findings.value: 7 kcal/g
findings.finding: Alcohol provides 7 kcal per gram. It also suppresses fat oxidation and encourages unplanned eating, which can undermine body-composition goals. The statement advises minimising alcohol after exercise when recovery is a priority.
findings.locator: 'Alcohol' p.19 (DC concurrent publication)

findings.citation: Garthe I, Raastad T, Refsnes PE, Koivisto A, Sundgot-Borgen J. Effect of two different weight-loss rates on body composition and strength and power-related performance in elite athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2011;21(2):97-104. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.21.2.97
findings.population: Elite athletes (men and women), ~22-24 y, ~72-75 kg, adding 4 resistance sessions/wk
findings.parameter: weekly loss % body mass
findings.value: Target 0.7%/wk (slow) vs 1.4%/wk (fast). Achieved 0.7 +/- 0.8 vs 1.0 +/- 0.4 %/wk. Total body-weight loss 5.6 +/- 0.8% vs 5.5 +/- 0.7%. LBM +2.1 +/- 0.4% (slow, p<.001) vs -0.2 +/- 0.7% (fast); between groups p<.01. Fat mass -31 +/- 3% vs -21 +/- 4%.
findings.finding: Elite athletes doing four strength sessions a week who lost weight slowly, about 0.7% of body weight weekly, gained lean mass, while faster losers held lean mass flat. The authors advise about 0.7% a week when aiming to gain lean mass and 1RM strength while cutting.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only (Results and Conclusion sentences); full text paywalled

findings.citation: Garthe I, Raastad T, Refsnes PE, Koivisto A, Sundgot-Borgen J. Effect of two different weight-loss rates on body composition and strength and power-related performance in elite athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2011;21(2):97-104. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.21.2.97
findings.parameter: energy intake reduction (% of habitual) and duration per loss rate
findings.value: Energy intake cut by 19 +/- 2% (slow) vs 30 +/- 4% (fast), p=.003. Intervention lasted 8.5 +/- 2.2 vs 5.3 +/- 0.9 wk, p<.001.
findings.finding: The slow schedule meant cutting intake by roughly a fifth, against nearly a third for the fast one. It took about 8.5 rather than 5.3 weeks to reach a similar total weight loss.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only (Results sentences); full text paywalled

findings.citation: Garthe I, Raastad T, Refsnes PE, Koivisto A, Sundgot-Borgen J. Effect of two different weight-loss rates on body composition and strength and power-related performance in elite athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2011;21(2):97-104. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.21.2.97
findings.parameter: lean-mass gain during a slow deficit with resistance training
findings.value: LBM +2.1 +/- 0.4% over ~8.5 wk at ~0.7%/wk body-weight loss, alongside 4 resistance sessions/wk; no LBM gain at the faster rate
findings.finding: Trained athletes gained lean mass while losing fat, provided the deficit was mild enough for roughly 0.7% weekly weight loss and resistance training continued. This supports recomposition as feasible in trained people at a slow loss rate.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only; full text paywalled

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.population: Natural bodybuilders in contest preparation (lean, resistance-trained)
findings.parameter: weekly loss % body mass
findings.value: ~0.5-1% body weight per week; preparations longer than 2-4 months at this rate preferred; a slower pace toward the end as leanness increases
findings.finding: To keep muscle, lean dieters should set calories for about 0.5-1% body-weight loss per week and allow enough time. Easing the pace near the end is advised, because the risk of losing lean mass rises as body fat falls.
findings.locator: Abstract; 'Caloric intake for competition'; Table 1

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: protein g/kg lean body mass/day in a deficit
findings.value: 2.3-3.1 g/kg lean body mass/d (per LBM, not body weight); the upper end for leaner people, larger deficits and when keeping LBM is the priority. Cited consensus for athletes at or above energy needs: 1.2-2.2 g/kg.
findings.finding: Lean, resistance-trained people in a calorie deficit likely need more protein than standard athlete ranges. The review suggests 2.3-3.1 g per kg of lean mass, moving higher as body fat falls and the deficit deepens.
findings.locator: Abstract; 'Protein' section; Table 1

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: fat % of energy in a deficit
findings.value: 15-30% of calories; 15-20% acceptable if higher fat would push carbohydrate or protein below ideal ranges
findings.finding: In a deficit, fat can sit at 15-30% of calories. The review accepts the lower end, 15-20%, when a higher share would squeeze protein or carbohydrate, arguing that carbohydrate supports training and lean-mass retention more than extra fat supports testosterone.
findings.locator: Abstract; 'Fat' section; Table 1

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: carbohydrate allocation in a deficit
findings.value: Carbohydrate = remaining calories after protein and fat. Cited strength-sport range 4-7 g/kg is unlikely at its upper end during a contest deficit. If training performance drops, shift calories from fat to carbohydrate.
findings.finding: After protein and fat targets are set, carbohydrate fills the rest of the calorie budget. A practical floor seems to exist below which performance and lean-mass retention suffer, so declining training performance is a cue to move energy from fat to carbohydrate.
findings.locator: Abstract; 'Carbohydrate' section; 'Macronutrient recommendations summary'; Table 1

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: meal frequency and minimum protein per meal
findings.value: 3-6 meals/day, each with at least 20 g protein. Mechanistic leucine rationale: ~0.05 g/kg (~3 g) leucine per meal, about 30-40 g high-quality protein.
findings.finding: Meal frequency in the moderate range of three to six protein-containing meals a day matters little for fat loss or lean-mass retention once daily totals are right. Very low or very high frequencies may harm hunger control and muscle retention. The leucine-threshold idea rests on mechanistic, not long-term, data.
findings.locator: Abstract; 'Meal frequency' section

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: peri-workout protein dose g/kg
findings.value: 0.4-0.5 g/kg body weight of protein in meals both before and after resistance training (citing Aragon and Schoenfeld)
findings.finding: A protein-containing meal of about 0.4-0.5 g/kg before and after training likely covers any theoretical timing benefit. However, total daily macronutrient intake matters far more than timing for long-term adaptation.
findings.locator: Abstract; 'Nutrient timing' section; Figure 1

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.population: Overweight dieters and non-overweight men in semi-starvation (cited studies); bodybuilders not directly studied
findings.parameter: metabolic adaptation magnitude / need to re-adjust intake
findings.value: In overweight dieters, energy expenditure fell 79-504 kcal/d below what weight loss predicted (cited studies). In non-overweight men eating 50% of maintenance for 24 wk (losing a quarter of body mass), expenditure fell 40%: 25% from weight loss, 15% from adaptation. A static 3500 kcal per pound model is inaccurate.
findings.finding: Energy expenditure falls during dieting both because body mass drops and through adaptation beyond that prediction. The starting calorie target will therefore need repeated downward adjustment as weight falls, rather than relying on a fixed 3500-kcal-per-pound rule.
findings.locator: 'Caloric intake for competition' section (first paragraph)

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: deficit taper near target leanness
findings.value: At ~0.5 kg/wk loss (~500 kcal/d deficit) near goal leanness: add 25-50 g carbohydrate per day, shrinking the deficit by ~100-200 kcal/d
findings.finding: Once a dieter is at or near the target level of leanness, the review suggests adding a little carbohydrate to shrink the deficit slightly, aiming to protect performance and lean mass during the final phase.
findings.locator: 'Carbohydrate' section (final paragraph)

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: ketogenic / very-low-carbohydrate pattern during a cut
findings.value: Rule: avoid very-low-carbohydrate diets for contest preparation until more research exists; allow for large individual variability
findings.finding: Most studies reviewed linked lower carbohydrate intake with worse performance and poorer fat-free-mass retention, so ketogenic diets are not recommended for contest dieting. Individual responses vary widely, and some people may do better outside the suggested ranges, so monitoring is advised.
findings.locator: 'Ketogenic diets and individual variability' section

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: disordered-eating and extreme-practice risk in aggressive physique dieting
findings.value: 46% of male drug-free bodybuilders reported post-competition binge eating; 81.5% reported food preoccupation. Dehydration and electrolyte manipulation are dangerous. Access to mental-health professionals is advised.
findings.finding: Prolonged aggressive dieting to very low body fat carries higher risk of binge eating, food preoccupation and body-image disorders. The review advises that competitors be able to reach suitable mental-health support, and warns that fluid or electrolyte manipulation may be dangerous.
findings.locator: Abstract; 'Psychosocial issues' section; 'Peak week' section

findings.citation: Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20
findings.parameter: food variety during a deficit
findings.value: Rule: avoid eliminating food groups and monotonous food choices. Earlier studies found shortfalls in vitamin D, calcium, zinc, magnesium and iron in dieting bodybuilders.
findings.finding: Micronutrient shortfalls seen in dieting bodybuilders were attributed to cutting out food groups and eating the same few foods. Varied food choices are the implied remedy, with a low-dose multivitamin possibly useful but unverified.
findings.locator: 'Micronutrients' section

findings.citation: Roth C, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Lean mass sparing in resistance-trained athletes during caloric restriction: the role of resistance training volume. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022;122(5):1129-1151. doi:10.1007/s00421-022-04896-5
findings.population: Lean, healthy, drug-free resistance-trained adults (60 female, 69 male) in 15 studies, 8 of them case studies; one study used recreationally trained participants
findings.parameter: daily energy deficit observed in trained-athlete caloric-restriction studies (descriptive)
findings.value: estimated -250 to -882 kcal/day; mean -347 kcal/day (females) and -398 kcal/day (males); inclusion required a deficit of at least 200 kcal/day for at least 4 weeks
findings.finding: Across 15 studies of lean, drug-free resistance-trained adults, deficits estimated from weight lost ranged from 250 to 882 kcal/day and averaged about 350-400 kcal/day. Most studies lowered intake gradually over time. These are observed values, not a tested prescription.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Inclusion criteria'; Results, 'Estimated caloric deficit, diet differences, and protein consumption'

findings.citation: Roth C, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Lean mass sparing in resistance-trained athletes during caloric restriction: the role of resistance training volume. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022;122(5):1129-1151. doi:10.1007/s00421-022-04896-5
findings.population: Resistance-trained males (7 studies, 4 of them case studies)
findings.parameter: deficit size associated with lean-mass loss in trained males
findings.value: little or no lean loss at about -260 to -350 kcal/day when training volume rose; about 43% of lost mass was lean in case studies at about -580 and -882 kcal/day
findings.finding: Male studies with small deficits (about 260-350 kcal/day) and rising training volume showed little or no lean loss. Two case studies at about 580 and 882 kcal/day lost roughly 43% of their weight as lean tissue. The authors blame deficit severity in part, but the data are correlational.
findings.locator: Results, lean-mass change paragraphs; Discussion, 'Male resistance-trained athletes'

findings.citation: Roth C, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Lean mass sparing in resistance-trained athletes during caloric restriction: the role of resistance training volume. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022;122(5):1129-1151. doi:10.1007/s00421-022-04896-5
findings.parameter: share of weight lost as lean mass during caloric restriction, by sex
findings.value: males: mean -2.81 kg lean (median -0.9 kg), 28.7% of mass lost (median 39.1%, range 12-54%); females: mean +0.2 kg lean; mean body-mass loss -4.8 kg (F) and -5.0 kg (M)
findings.finding: On average, dieting trained men lost about 29% of their lost weight as lean tissue (range 12-54%). Trained women, on average, kept or slightly gained lean mass. Sex appears to change how much lean mass is kept during restriction.
findings.locator: Results, 'Exercise protocols, volume quantification, lean mass change, and assessment techniques'; Discussion

findings.citation: Roth C, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Lean mass sparing in resistance-trained athletes during caloric restriction: the role of resistance training volume. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022;122(5):1129-1151. doi:10.1007/s00421-022-04896-5
findings.parameter: protein intake in trained-athlete caloric-restriction studies (g/kg FFM/day, descriptive)
findings.value: mean 3.35 g/kg FFM/day (females) and 3.06 g/kg FFM/day (males); range 2.12-4.00 g/kg FFM/day; inclusion floor at least 2.0 g/kg FFM
findings.finding: Every included study used a high-protein diet, since inclusion required at least 2.0 g/kg fat-free mass. Reported intakes averaged about 3.1-3.4 g/kg FFM (range 2.12-4.00). These are observed intakes, not a tested dose-response.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Inclusion criteria'; Results, 'Estimated caloric deficit, diet differences, and protein consumption'

findings.citation: Roth C, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Lean mass sparing in resistance-trained athletes during caloric restriction: the role of resistance training volume. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022;122(5):1129-1151. doi:10.1007/s00421-022-04896-5
findings.population: Male natural bodybuilder (case study) within the review
findings.parameter: body-fat level at which the risk of lean loss rises (males)
findings.value: sharp fall in muscle thickness once body fat went below about 7% (single case study); a speculative threshold that other studies do not consistently show
findings.finding: In one male case study, muscle was kept for about five months and then fell sharply as body fat dropped below about 7%, together with further intake cuts and more aerobic work. The authors speculate that lean loss speeds up near a minimum body-fat level. Findings across studies are inconsistent.
findings.locator: Discussion, 'Male resistance-trained athletes'

findings.citation: Roth C, Schwiete C, Happ K, Rettenmaier L, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Resistance training volume does not influence lean mass preservation during energy restriction in trained males. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023;33(1):20-35. doi:10.1111/sms.14237
findings.parameter: weight-maintenance energy intake used for resistance-trained males (kcal/kg/day)
findings.value: 45 kcal/kg/day during a 1-week weight-maintenance period (the abstract does not say whether per kg body mass or per kg fat-free mass)
findings.finding: In the trial protocol, resistance-trained men ate 45 kcal/kg/day for a one-week weight-maintenance period before restriction began. This is a protocol assumption, not a measured energy requirement, and the abstract does not state the reference mass.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 36114738); full text not accessible

findings.citation: Roth C, Schwiete C, Happ K, Rettenmaier L, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Resistance training volume does not influence lean mass preservation during energy restriction in trained males. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023;33(1):20-35. doi:10.1111/sms.14237
findings.parameter: energy-restriction prescription for trained males (kcal/kg/day) and resulting weight loss
findings.value: 30 kcal/kg/day for 6 weeks; body-mass change -1.69 ± 1.12 kg (high-volume) and -1.76 ± 1.76 kg (moderate-volume)
findings.finding: Cutting intake from 45 to 30 kcal/kg/day for six weeks led to about 1.7 kg of body-mass loss in both training arms. It is a worked example of a moderate deficit in trained lifters.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 36114738); full text not accessible

findings.citation: Roth C, Schwiete C, Happ K, Rettenmaier L, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Resistance training volume does not influence lean mass preservation during energy restriction in trained males. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023;33(1):20-35. doi:10.1111/sms.14237
findings.parameter: protein during energy restriction (g/kg FFM/day)
findings.value: 2.8 g/kg fat-free mass/day (fixed in both arms)
findings.finding: Both arms were held at 2.8 g of protein per kg of fat-free mass per day for the whole restriction period.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 36114738); full text not accessible

findings.citation: Roth C, Schwiete C, Happ K, Rettenmaier L, Schoenfeld BJ, Behringer M. Resistance training volume does not influence lean mass preservation during energy restriction in trained males. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023;33(1):20-35. doi:10.1111/sms.14237
findings.parameter: lean-mass change during 6-week moderate restriction in trained males
findings.value: lean mass -0.51 ± 2.30 kg (5 sets/exercise) vs -0.92 ± 1.59 kg (3 sets/exercise); significant fall over time in both (p = 0.022), no between-group difference (p = 0.966)
findings.finding: Lean mass fell significantly in both groups even with high protein and continued training. Doing 5 rather than 3 sets per exercise made no difference to lean mass or rectus femoris thickness.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 36114738); full text not accessible

findings.citation: Murphy C, Koehler K. Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: A meta-analysis and meta-regression. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022;32(1):125-137. doi:10.1111/sms.14075
findings.population: Adults in randomised controlled trials of resistance training with an energy deficit of at least 3 weeks
findings.parameter: maximum daily energy deficit that preserves lean mass during resistance training (kcal/day)
findings.value: avoid deficits above about 500 kcal/day (meta-regression: a deficit of about 500 kcal/day prevented lean-mass gains)
findings.finding: Pooling RCTs that combined resistance training with a deficit lasting at least 3 weeks, the meta-regression found that a deficit of roughly 500 kcal/day wiped out lean-mass gains. The authors advise lifters who want to keep lean mass to stay at or below about 500 kcal/day.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 34623696), meta-regression result and conclusion; full text not accessible, so study count and CI unverified

findings.citation: Murphy C, Koehler K. Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: A meta-analysis and meta-regression. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022;32(1):125-137. doi:10.1111/sms.14075
findings.population: Adults in randomised controlled trials of resistance training with an energy deficit of at least 3 weeks
findings.parameter: effect of an energy deficit on lean-mass gain from resistance training
findings.value: Analysis A: ES = -0.57 (p = 0.02) for RT+deficit vs RT+control; Analysis B: ES -0.11 (p = 0.03) in deficit vs +0.20 (p < 0.001) in energy balance
findings.finding: Compared with trials without a deficit, resistance training in a deficit gave smaller lean-mass gains, a moderate negative pooled effect. Matched comparisons showed slight lean loss in a deficit against gains in energy balance. Recomposition in a sustained deficit is therefore limited.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 34623696), Analyses A and B; full text not accessible

findings.citation: Murphy C, Koehler K. Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: A meta-analysis and meta-regression. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022;32(1):125-137. doi:10.1111/sms.14075
findings.population: Adults in randomised controlled trials of resistance training with an energy deficit of at least 3 weeks
findings.parameter: strength gain under an energy deficit
findings.value: Analysis A: ES = -0.31 (p = 0.28), not significant; Analysis B: ES 0.84 (deficit) vs 0.81 (control)
findings.finding: Strength gains did not differ significantly between training in a deficit and training without one. Strength progress alone therefore cannot confirm that lean mass is being kept.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 34623696); full text not accessible

findings.citation: Murphy C, Koehler K. Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: A meta-analysis and meta-regression. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022;32(1):125-137. doi:10.1111/sms.14075
findings.population: Adults in randomised controlled trials of resistance training with an energy deficit of at least 3 weeks
findings.parameter: energy-balance rule for the muscle-gain goal
findings.value: avoid a prolonged energy deficit (the trials lasted at least 3 weeks)
findings.finding: The authors conclude that people training to build lean mass should not stay in a prolonged energy deficit, because deficits reduced lean-mass gains.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 34623696), conclusion; full text not accessible

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.parameter: target weekly body-weight loss (% body mass/week)
findings.value: 0.5-1.0% of body weight per week; the lower the athlete's body fat, the more conservative the deficit
findings.finding: Set energy intake so that body weight falls by 0.5-1.0% per week, which helps keep fat-free mass. Leaner athletes should use smaller deficits. The authors note that direct research in resistance-trained athletes is very limited.
findings.locator: Abstract; Section 1 Introduction; Section 9 Conclusions and Practical Applications

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Physique-competition athletes in case studies cited by the review (individual case details not given in the review text)
findings.parameter: lean-mass share of weight lost at faster loss rates
findings.value: better FFM retention at 0.5%/week than at 0.7% or 1.0%/week; at 1%/week, FFM made up 42.8% of weight lost (case studies)
findings.finding: Case studies of competitors showed that fat-free mass was kept better at 0.5% body weight per week than at 0.7% or 1% per week. In the 1% case, fat-free mass was about 43% of the weight lost. Slower loss is favoured, especially late in preparation.
findings.locator: Section 3 Energy Intake

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Athletes, especially female aesthetic-sport competitors and male natural bodybuilders
findings.parameter: energy availability floor (kcal/kg FFM/day)
findings.value: about 45 kcal/kg FFM/day for optimal function (women); below 30 kcal/kg FFM/day hormonal disruption (women); below 25 kcal/kg FFM/day greater FFM loss and hormonal and psychological effects (men); pre-contest women observed at 18.2-31.1
findings.finding: Energy availability is intake minus exercise energy, divided by fat-free mass. Women function best near 45 and show hormonal disruption below 30 kcal/kg FFM/day. In men, below 25 is linked to fat-free mass loss and hormonal problems. Individual responses vary.
findings.locator: Section 3.1 Low Energy Availability

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Derived from adults with obesity (cited model); applied to athletes
findings.parameter: weight-change model (static 3500-kcal rule vs dynamic rule)
findings.value: the static 3500 kcal per 0.45 kg (1 lb) rule is questioned; a dynamic rule attributed to Hall et al. of about 55 kcal/day per lb: a 500 kcal/day intake reduction gives about 4 kg (9 lb) total loss, plateauing near 12 months as intake drifts up and expenditure adapts
findings.finding: The fixed 3500-kcal-per-pound rule overstates loss because it ignores adaptation. A dynamic rule attributed to Hall et al. predicts that a 500 kcal/day intake cut yields only about 4 kg total, plateauing near a year, partly because intake creeps up unnoticed. Intake must fall over time to keep losing.
findings.locator: Section 3 Energy Intake

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Inactive adults with obesity (MATADOR); resistance-trained athletes (Peos et al.)
findings.parameter: diet break (intermittent restriction) length
findings.value: 1-2 weeks at maintenance intake; MATADOR (2 weeks on / 2 weeks off, inactive adults with obesity): adjusted RMR fall -86 vs -179 kcal/day; strength athletes (3 weeks restriction plus 1 week maintenance): fat loss and FFM similar to continuous restriction; optimal length unknown
findings.finding: Diet breaks of 1-2 weeks at maintenance are proposed to blunt adaptation. In inactive adults with obesity they reduced the adjusted RMR decline. In strength athletes, results matched continuous dieting. The minimum length and frequency needed are unknown, and breaks lengthen the diet.
findings.locator: Section 3.2 Diet Break

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Bodybuilders (reported practice); the overfeeding study's population is not described in the review
findings.parameter: carbohydrate refeed protocol
findings.value: about 24 h, once or twice weekly (bodybuilding practice); raise mainly carbohydrate to at or above maintenance and offset on other days; 3 days at 40% overfeeding raised leptin 28% and energy expenditure 7%, transiently
findings.finding: Refeeds raise carbohydrate and calories to maintenance or above for about a day, once or twice a week, with the extra offset on other days to keep the weekly deficit. Metabolic effects are small and short-lived: expenditure rose only 7% despite 40% overfeeding.
findings.locator: Section 4.2 Carbohydrates

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Resistance-trained athletes in a caloric deficit
findings.parameter: protein g/kg body weight/day during a fat-loss phase
findings.value: 2.2-3.0 g/kg BW/day
findings.finding: Resistance-trained athletes losing fat should eat 2.2-3.0 g of protein per kg of body weight daily. This is above the roughly 1.6 g/kg that suffices in energy balance, because a sustained deficit increases the risk of fat-free mass loss.
findings.locator: Section 4.1 Protein; Section 6 Frequency; Section 9 Conclusions

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Resistance-trained athletes in a caloric deficit
findings.parameter: protein per meal and number of meals
findings.value: 0.40-0.55 g/kg BW per meal (at least 0.4 g/kg; about 0.60 g/kg in older adults); 3-6 meals/day; at least 2.5 g leucine per meal from high-quality sources; about 2-3 h between protein feedings (unconfirmed hypothesis)
findings.finding: Spread daily protein over 3-6 meals chosen for adherence, each with about 0.40-0.55 g/kg and at least 2.5 g leucine. Spacing feedings by 2-3 h is suggested by the muscle-full hypothesis, but the evidence conflicts.
findings.locator: Section 5 Nutritional Timing; Section 6 Frequency; Section 9 Conclusions

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.parameter: peri-training protein timing
findings.value: one protein feeding within 2-3 h before training and one within 2-3 h after
findings.finding: Place one protein-containing meal within 2-3 hours before training and another within 2-3 hours after. Pre- versus post-training timing makes no difference when the daily total is matched. Pre-sleep protein helps mainly when the daily target would otherwise be missed.
findings.locator: Section 5 Nutritional Timing; Section 6 Frequency; Section 9 Conclusions

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.parameter: meal frequency and feeding window effect
findings.value: 2-7 meals/day: no difference in thermogenesis (metabolic chamber studies); with matched intake, meal number or window does not change body composition; time-restricted feeding (about an 8-h window) gives mixed FFM results
findings.finding: Eating more often does not raise metabolism: 2 to 7 daily meals gave the same thermogenesis. When intake is equal, meal count and feeding window do not change body composition. Evidence on time-restricted eating and lean retention is mixed.
findings.locator: Section 6 Frequency

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Resistance-trained athletes in a caloric deficit
findings.parameter: carbohydrate g/kg BW/day during fat loss
findings.value: 2-5 g/kg BW/day, adjusted to activity level and food preference
findings.finding: During fat loss, carbohydrate can sit anywhere in a wide 2-5 g/kg range, set by training load, other physical activity and preference. The range is wide because a resistance session only partly depletes glycogen (24-40%).
findings.locator: Section 4.2 Carbohydrates; Section 9 Conclusions

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.parameter: very-low-carbohydrate caution (lower limit)
findings.value: ketogenic intake (<10% of energy or at most 50 g/day) may reduce FFM preservation while strength is kept; muscle glycogen threshold about 70 mmol/kg dry weight
findings.finding: Ketogenic diets, under 10% of energy or about 50 g/day or less, seem to keep strength but may keep less fat-free mass. The authors say minimum carbohydrate intake should keep muscle glycogen above about 70 mmol/kg dry weight.
findings.locator: Section 4.2 Carbohydrates; Section 9 Conclusions

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.parameter: dietary fibre (g/day)
findings.value: 25 g/day (EFSA reference, as cited by the review)
findings.finding: The review applies the EFSA fibre reference of 25 g/day to athletes. More fibre may help satiety during restriction, but very high intakes could impair absorption of some nutrients.
findings.locator: Section 4.2 Carbohydrates, final paragraph

findings.citation: Ruiz-Castellano C, Espinar S, Contreras C, Mata F, Aragon AA, Martinez-Sanz JM. Achieving an Optimal Fat Loss Phase in Resistance-Trained Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13(9):3255. doi:10.3390/nu13093255
findings.population: Resistance-trained athletes in a caloric deficit
findings.parameter: fat floor during a deficit
findings.value: 20-30% of energy where feasible; minimum at least 0.5 g/kg BW/day; fat at or below 20% of energy linked to lower testosterone
findings.finding: Set protein and carbohydrate first and give the remaining energy to fat. Aim for 20-30% of energy where possible, and never go below 0.5 g/kg/day. Diets at 20% fat or less have been linked to lower testosterone.
findings.locator: Section 4.3 Fats; Section 9 Conclusions

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: energy surplus (% above maintenance)
findings.value: about 10-20% above maintenance calories; advanced lifters at the lower end or below
findings.finding: For muscle gain, eat about 10-20% above maintenance. Advanced lifters should use the lower end or less, because their capacity to add muscle is limited and an aggressive surplus can add unnecessary fat.
findings.locator: Section 2 Energy, 'Positive Energy Balance'; Section 8 Summary; Abstract

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: weekly weight-gain target (% body mass/week)
findings.value: about 0.25-0.5% of body weight per week for novice and intermediate lifters; advanced lifters slower (other literature cites about 0.25-0.5 kg/week)
findings.finding: Target a gain of about 0.25-0.5% of body weight per week for novice and intermediate lifters, and a slower rate for advanced lifters. Energy intake should then be adjusted based on the observed rate and changes in body composition.
findings.locator: Section 2 Energy, 'Positive Energy Balance'; Section 8 Summary; Abstract

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: absolute daily surplus for highly trained athletes (kcal/day)
findings.value: 200-300 kcal/day may be preferable to 500 kcal/day (conclusion of the cited trial's researchers); a group eating about 600 kcal/day more than an ad libitum group gained LBM +1.7 vs +1.2 kg (not significant) but FM +1.1 vs +0.2 kg over 8-12 weeks
findings.finding: In a cited trial of elite athletes training four days a week, eating about 600 kcal/day more than an ad libitum group added non-significantly more lean mass but significantly more fat. The trial's researchers suggested 200-300 kcal/day for highly trained athletes; untrained people may gain muscle faster.
findings.locator: Section 2 Energy, 'Positive Energy Balance'

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: habitual off-season energy intake of bodybuilders (kcal/kg/day)
findings.value: about 45 kcal/kg/day on average (off-season); separately, male bodybuilders reported at about 3800 kcal/day off-season vs about 2400 kcal/day when dieting; the authors translate the recommended surplus to about 42-48 kcal/kg/day (arithmetic basis not explained)
findings.finding: Bodybuilders eat about 45 kcal/kg/day in the off-season on average; separately, male bodybuilders were reported at about 3800 kcal/day off-season versus 2400 when dieting. The authors equate their surplus to roughly 42-48 kcal/kg/day, but this does not follow clearly from a 10-20% surplus.
findings.locator: Section 2 Energy (intro and 'Positive Energy Balance')

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: weigh-in averaging for tracking the rate of change
findings.value: use the weekly average of daily (or several-times-weekly) weigh-ins; adjust intake to the rate of gain and body-composition change
findings.finding: Judge the rate of gain from weekly averages of daily or frequent weigh-ins rather than single readings, which fluctuate from day to day. Then adjust intake to hit the target weekly rate.
findings.locator: Section 2 Energy, 'Positive Energy Balance', final paragraph

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day during muscle gain
findings.value: 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day; minimum 1.6, target closer to 2.2
findings.finding: Eat at least 1.6 g/kg/day of protein during the off-season. Aiming nearer 2.2 g/kg more reliably covers individual variation, because 2.2 is the upper confidence limit in the cited meta-analysis and IAAO data.
findings.locator: Section 3.1 Daily Intake; Section 8 Summary

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: protein prescription unit
findings.value: prescribe per kg body weight, not as a % of energy (older guidance of 25-30% of energy is rejected)
findings.finding: Protein should be set in g/kg of body weight rather than as a share of calories. Percentage targets can push protein far above need in light people with high energy intake and can crowd out carbohydrate and fat.
findings.locator: Section 3.1 Daily Intake

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: plant-based protein adjustment
findings.value: quality matters mainly at the low end (1.6 g/kg) or with largely plant-based diets; use leucine- and EAA-rich sources (e.g., dairy, or pea protein if vegan); 48 g post-training rice vs whey protein: no body-composition difference over 8 weeks; 50 g/day pea vs whey: no significant difference in muscle-thickness gains over 12 weeks
findings.finding: Protein source matters little when total intake is adequate. Soy matched whey in a meta-analysis, and rice and pea protein matched whey in 8- and 12-week trials. At the low end of intake, or on a mostly plant diet, favour leucine-rich sources such as pea protein or dairy.
findings.locator: Section 3.2 Protein Quality

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: protein per meal, meal count and timing
findings.value: about 0.40-0.55 g/kg per meal; 3-6 meals/day; one meal within 1-2 h before or after training; one non-whey protein feeding 1-2 h before sleep
findings.finding: Split 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day into several meals of about 0.40-0.55 g/kg each. Include one meal within 1-2 hours of training and a slower, non-whey protein feeding 1-2 hours before bed. Long-term benefits of timing appear small.
findings.locator: Section 6.2 Nutrient Timing; Section 8 Summary

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: fat intake range during muscle gain
findings.value: 0.5-1.5 g/kg/day (about 20-35% of energy, in line with ACSM)
findings.finding: Keep dietary fat moderate, about 20-35% of energy or roughly 0.5-1.5 g/kg/day. Very low fat may lower testosterone, and high-fat ketogenic diets gave poorer muscle gains. Fat should not crowd out protein or carbohydrate.
findings.locator: Section 4 Fats; Section 8 Summary

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: carbohydrate allocation during muscle gain
findings.value: the remaining energy after protein and fat; aim for at least 3-5 g/kg/day; observed male off-season mean 5.3 g/kg/day
findings.finding: After setting protein and fat, give the remaining calories to carbohydrate, ideally at least 3-5 g/kg/day. Very low-carbohydrate diets may harm training, although an optimal intake for bodybuilders has not been established.
findings.locator: Section 5 Carbohydrates; Section 8 Summary

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: food-group exclusion rule and micronutrient safety net
findings.value: flexible approach with no food or food group eliminated; optional low-dose multivitamin/mineral at or below 100% RDA
findings.finding: Restrictive diets that drop food groups are linked to micronutrient shortfalls, and flexible approaches showed fewer deficiencies. Recommend a varied diet with no food group excluded, plus an optional low-dose multivitamin at or below the RDA as a safeguard.
findings.locator: Section 7.5 Multivitamin/Mineral

findings.citation: Iraki J, Fitschen P, Espinar S, Helms E. Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2019;7(7):154. doi:10.3390/sports7070154
findings.parameter: high-protein safety in lifters
findings.value: no apparent harm over 1-2-year trials in lifters eating at least 2.2 g/kg/day
findings.finding: The authors call a 2.2 g/kg target low-risk, citing 1-2-year trials in lifters that found no apparent harm at or above that intake. It is not a statement on clinical populations.
findings.locator: Section 3.1 Daily Intake

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: recommended daily energy surplus (conservative)
findings.value: about 1,500-2,000 kJ/day (about 359-478 kcal/day, converted at 4.184 kJ/kcal), with regular review of body composition and strength
findings.finding: Until the surplus is better defined, practitioners should use a conservative surplus of about 1,500-2,000 kJ/day to limit fat gain. Intake should be personalised from repeated body-composition and strength checks.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... How Much', final paragraph

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: validation status of the optimal surplus
findings.value: not established: no rigorously controlled trials of surplus size with resistance training; no single evidence-based energy estimate per kg of skeletal muscle; never validated in resistance-trained people
findings.finding: The ideal surplus for hypertrophy is unknown. No controlled long-term trials have titrated surplus size alongside resistance training, and textbook estimates have never been validated in trained people. Any surplus default should be flagged as uncertain.
findings.locator: Abstract; Section 'Energy Balance'; Section 'Energy Surplus... How Much'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: energy cost per kg of skeletal muscle gained
findings.value: stored energy about 5,000-5,200 kJ per kg muscle; estimated deposition cost 6,050-7,440 kJ/kg; textbook surplus 1,500-2,000 kJ/day (weight-stable athletes) up to about +4,000 kJ/day
findings.finding: A kilogram of muscle stores about 5,000-5,200 kJ, and estimated deposition costs run to 6,050-7,440 kJ/kg. These figures leave out training, protein-synthesis and adaptive costs, so the true cost of muscle gain remains unquantified.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... How Much'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: adaptive energy-expenditure response to overfeeding
findings.value: 60-70% of excess energy stored, 20-30% to lean accretion and movement cost, about 10% unexplained; NEAT +1,380 ± 1,080 kJ/day with +4,200 kJ/day for 56 days; DIT +1.1 kJ/h per 100 kJ extra; about 3.0 vs 1.0 g/kg protein may need about +500 kJ/day
findings.finding: A surplus is partly absorbed by rising expenditure, mainly NEAT and diet-induced thermogenesis, and responses vary widely between individuals. Most excess energy is still stored. Very high-protein diets may need a little extra energy to reach the same surplus.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... How Much'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: composition of weight gained in a surplus without resistance training
findings.value: about 2 kg fat per 1 kg lean (twins: +5.4 kg FM, +2.7 kg FFM after 353 MJ over 100 days); 33-40% of gain as FFM across overfeeding studies; about 40% surplus for 8 weeks: about 3.5 kg fat in all groups, about 3 kg LBM only at 15% and 25% protein
findings.finding: Overfeeding without training adds mostly fat, about two parts fat to one part lean. Lean gains in a surplus needed at least moderate protein. Resistance training is what directs surplus energy toward muscle.
findings.locator: Introduction; Section 'Energy Balance'; Section 'Energy Surplus... How Much'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.population: Overweight or obese resistance-training novices vs trained athletes
findings.parameter: feasibility of gaining muscle in a deficit, by training status
findings.value: shown in resistance-training-naive or overweight individuals (e.g., about 60% of estimated energy needs with 2.4 g/kg/day protein); less evident in highly trained people
findings.finding: Muscle can grow during an energy deficit, but mainly in untrained, overweight or obese people, and even at a large deficit when protein is high. Highly trained people show this far less, so recomposition expectations should depend on training history.
findings.locator: Introduction; Section 'Energy Balance'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.population: Adults performing resistance exercise in cited energy-cost studies (training status not specified in the review)
findings.parameter: net energy cost of a resistance training session
findings.value: net about 300 kJ (females) and about 600 kJ (males) for a ~30-min, 8-exercise, 2 x 8-10 rep hypertrophy program; the sex difference is not evident when normalised to lean mass; a separate upper-body protocol (5 exercises, 3 x 10 at 70% 1RM) cost 369.4 ± 174.1 kJ, about 0.10-0.12 kJ/kg LBM/min; post-exercise elevation up to about 20 min, considered negligible for shorter sessions
findings.finding: A typical 30-minute hypertrophy session costs only about 300-600 kJ net. The sex difference disappears when normalised to lean mass. A separate upper-body protocol cost about 0.10-0.12 kJ per kg lean mass per minute, and after-burn is minor for short sessions.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... How Much'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: rise in resting energy expenditure per kg of muscle gained
findings.value: skeletal muscle about 54 kJ/kg/day; a 1-2 kg muscle gain raises REE by about 100 kJ/day
findings.finding: Added muscle raises resting expenditure only slightly: a 1-2 kg gain adds about 100 kJ/day, which is within calorimetry measurement error. Maintenance estimates need little change for modest muscle gain.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... How Much'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.population: Adults undertaking resistance training (meta-regression of male and female participants)
findings.parameter: protein during a surplus (g/kg/day)
findings.value: 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day for athletes undertaking resistance training; cited meta-regression (49 studies, 1,863 male and female participants) found the greatest muscle gains at 1.6 g/kg/day; intakes beyond the guideline range, even up to double, gave no further hypertrophy or strength
findings.finding: Resistance-training athletes need about 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day of protein. The cited meta-regression linked the largest muscle gains to about 1.6 g/kg/day, and exceeding the guideline range, even greatly, gave no extra muscle or strength.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... Macronutrient Considerations'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: high-protein intake safety ceiling
findings.value: 1.8 g/kg/day: no adverse renal effect in healthy adults; 2.5-3.3 g/kg/day over one year: no deleterious effect on blood lipids, liver or renal function; long-term health implications above about 2.5 g/kg/day not yet validated
findings.finding: Healthy adults showed no kidney harm at 1.8 g/kg/day, and a year of 2.5-3.3 g/kg/day intake showed no lipid, liver or kidney effects. Longer-term safety above about 2.5 g/kg/day has not been confirmed, so very high intakes are hard to justify.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... Macronutrient Considerations'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: carbohydrate g/kg/day for strength-trained athletes
findings.value: 4-7 g/kg/day; the upper end when resistance training supplements sport-specific training; ketogenic diets consistently impaired muscle gains
findings.finding: Keep carbohydrate within 4-7 g/kg/day for strength-trained athletes, toward the top for those also doing sport training. Chronically restricted, ketogenic diets have consistently blunted muscle gain in trained lifters.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... Macronutrient Considerations'; Section 'Energy Surplus... Nutrient Timing'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: fat as % of energy during a surplus
findings.value: 20-35% of energy; discourage intakes below 15-20%; saturated fat at most 10% of energy; cutting fat from 33.3% to 13.9% modestly lowered resting testosterone
findings.finding: Follow general health guidance of 20-35% of energy from fat, and avoid dropping below about 15-20%. Low fat makes a surplus harder to reach and reduces fat-soluble vitamin intake. Keep saturated fat at or below 10% of energy.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... Macronutrient Considerations'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: macronutrient source of surplus energy
findings.value: no macronutrient shown to be superior; meet the macro minimums first; unsaturated fat preferred over saturated; whole-food proteins (whole milk, whole eggs) may favour anabolism
findings.finding: There is not enough evidence to favour any one macronutrient for the extra energy. Meet the protein, carbohydrate and fat minimums, then fill the surplus by preference and practicality. Leaning toward unsaturated fats and whole-food protein is reasonable but unproven in lifters.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... Macronutrient Considerations', concluding paragraphs

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: eating occasions during a surplus
findings.value: at least 3 main meals plus strategic snacks; 5-6 or more occasions advocated for GI tolerance; about 0.3 g/kg high-quality protein every 3-5 h; 4 vs 6 protein meals made no LBM difference (rugby players)
findings.finding: Eat at least three main meals plus snacks when trying to gain. More frequent, smaller occasions help people eat more without discomfort. Protein doses of about 0.3 g/kg every 3-5 hours are suggested, but going from four to six protein meals added nothing.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... Nutrient Timing'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: satiety management for reaching a surplus
findings.value: raise energy density (e.g., more fat); use energy-containing drinks (less satiating than solids); moderate protein servings; keep vegetable intake for health
findings.finding: When appetite limits intake, raise energy density and use nutritious drinks, which fill less than solid food. Keep protein servings moderate because protein is satiating. Do not cut vegetables below public-health guidance.
findings.locator: Section 'Managing Satiety'

findings.citation: Slater GJ, Dieter BP, Marsh DJ, Helms ER, Shaw G, Iraki J. Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training. Front Nutr. 2019;6:131. doi:10.3389/fnut.2019.00131
findings.parameter: surplus on training vs rest days
findings.value: unresolved; trials gave extra energy on training days only; muscle protein synthesis stays raised 24-48 h, suggesting a surplus on rest days too (untested)
findings.finding: Whether the surplus should apply only on training days or every day is unknown. Research has given extra energy on training days only, but raised muscle protein synthesis for 24-48 hours argues for a daily surplus. The question is untested.
findings.locator: Section 'Energy Surplus... Nutrient Timing'

findings.citation: Ribeiro AS, Nunes JP, Schoenfeld BJ, Aguiar AF, Cyrino ES. Effects of different dietary energy intake following resistance training on muscle mass and body fat in bodybuilders: a pilot study. J Hum Kinet. 2019;70:125-134. doi:10.2478/hukin-2019-0038
findings.population: Male competitive bodybuilders in the off-season, 26.8 ± 2.3 y, 90.1 kg, Brazil; supervised resistance training 6 d/wk; steroid abstention self-reported
findings.parameter: energy intake kcal/kg/day during a muscle-gain phase (trained lifters)
findings.value: Moderate 50.1 ± 0.51 vs high 67.5 ± 1.7 kcal/kg/d for 4 wk. Skeletal muscle mass +1.1% (36.1 to 36.5 kg) vs +2.7% (36.7 to 37.7 kg). Body fat % rose by a relative 0.8% (13.3 to 13.4%, ns) vs 7.4% (16.2 to 17.4%, P<0.05). Between-group ES 0.25 (muscle) and 0.30 (fat).
findings.finding: Higher intake gave slightly more estimated muscle gain but also a significant fat gain. Moderate intake showed no significant fat change. Muscle mass came from an anthropometric equation driven mainly by body weight and height, so the 'muscle' gains largely track weight gain. Very small 4-week pilot.
findings.locator: Abstract; Methods, Body composition (SMM equation); Results, Table 2 (energy kcal/kg), Table 3 (muscle mass, body fat), Table 4 (effect sizes)

findings.citation: Ribeiro AS, Nunes JP, Schoenfeld BJ, Aguiar AF, Cyrino ES. Effects of different dietary energy intake following resistance training on muscle mass and body fat in bodybuilders: a pilot study. J Hum Kinet. 2019;70:125-134. doi:10.2478/hukin-2019-0038
findings.parameter: RMR equation and intake above predicted RMR in a surplus
findings.value: RMR predicted with Harris-Benedict: 1989.9 ± 69.5 (moderate) and 2025.0 ± 218.1 kcal/d (high). Energy above RMR was 2511.6 ± 109.5 vs 4062.6 ± 635.6 kcal/d. Total intake was 4501.4 ± 177.9 vs 6087.6 ± 853.3 kcal/d.
findings.finding: Intake was set against a Harris-Benedict RMR prediction. TDEE was not measured, so the true surplus in each arm is unknown. Intake relative to RMR cannot be turned directly into a surplus target.
findings.locator: Methods, Design and Procedures (Harris-Benedict); Results, Table 1 (RMR, energy above RMR) and Table 2 (kcal)

findings.citation: Ribeiro AS, Nunes JP, Schoenfeld BJ, Aguiar AF, Cyrino ES. Effects of different dietary energy intake following resistance training on muscle mass and body fat in bodybuilders: a pilot study. J Hum Kinet. 2019;70:125-134. doi:10.2478/hukin-2019-0038
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day during an energy surplus
findings.value: 1.8 ± 0.15 g/kg/d (high-energy arm, 10.6% of energy) vs 2.0 ± 0.05 g/kg/d (moderate arm, 16.4% of energy)
findings.finding: Both arms met the usual 1.4–2.0 g/kg/d range. The arm eating slightly less protein but more non-protein energy gained more muscle. The authors read this as no added benefit from extra protein once needs are met, but the protein gap was narrow.
findings.locator: Results, Table 2 (Proteins); Discussion, protein paragraph

findings.citation: Ribeiro AS, Nunes JP, Schoenfeld BJ, Aguiar AF, Cyrino ES. Effects of different dietary energy intake following resistance training on muscle mass and body fat in bodybuilders: a pilot study. J Hum Kinet. 2019;70:125-134. doi:10.2478/hukin-2019-0038
findings.parameter: carbohydrate g/kg/day during an energy surplus
findings.value: 8.0 ± 0.05 g/kg/d (64.5% of energy, moderate arm) vs 12.9 ± 0.32 g/kg/d (76.9% of energy, high arm)
findings.finding: The energy gap between arms came mainly from carbohydrate. Training performance was not measured. The authors note that resistance training appears to need only moderate carbohydrate, so the very high intake mostly adds energy (and fat), not a proven performance benefit.
findings.locator: Results, Table 2 (Carbohydrates); Discussion, carbohydrate paragraph

findings.citation: Ribeiro AS, Nunes JP, Schoenfeld BJ, Aguiar AF, Cyrino ES. Effects of different dietary energy intake following resistance training on muscle mass and body fat in bodybuilders: a pilot study. J Hum Kinet. 2019;70:125-134. doi:10.2478/hukin-2019-0038
findings.parameter: fat g/kg/day during an energy surplus
findings.value: 1.06 ± 0.05 g/kg/d (19.0% of energy, moderate arm) vs 0.93 ± 0.05 g/kg/d (12.4% of energy, high arm)
findings.finding: Dietary fat was about 1 g/kg/d in both arms of this bulking protocol. Fat intake was not a tested variable, so this describes the protocol and is not evidence for an optimal fat target.
findings.locator: Results, Table 2 (Lipids)

findings.citation: Ribeiro AS, Nunes JP, Schoenfeld BJ, Aguiar AF, Cyrino ES. Effects of different dietary energy intake following resistance training on muscle mass and body fat in bodybuilders: a pilot study. J Hum Kinet. 2019;70:125-134. doi:10.2478/hukin-2019-0038
findings.parameter: diet readjustment cadence from body-weight change
findings.value: Prescribed plan readjusted weekly according to body-weight change (size of each adjustment not reported)
findings.finding: A nutritionist revised each individual plan every week based on scale-weight change during the 4-week gaining phase. This supports a weekly review cadence, but the paper gives no rule for how large each change should be.
findings.locator: Methods, Dietary control

findings.citation: Ribeiro AS, Nunes JP, Schoenfeld BJ, Aguiar AF, Cyrino ES. Effects of different dietary energy intake following resistance training on muscle mass and body fat in bodybuilders: a pilot study. J Hum Kinet. 2019;70:125-134. doi:10.2478/hukin-2019-0038
findings.parameter: meal spacing
findings.value: Meals every 3–4 h
findings.finding: Participants were told to space meals every 3–4 hours. This was part of the protocol in both arms and was not tested against other meal patterns.
findings.locator: Methods, Dietary control

findings.citation: Garthe I, Raastad T, Refsnes PE, Sundgot-Borgen J. Effect of nutritional intervention on body composition and performance in elite athletes. Eur J Sport Sci. 2013;13(3):295-303. doi:10.1080/17461391.2011.643923
findings.population: Elite athletes from several sports (men and women per MeSH), about 19 y, 71–75 kg, Norway; sport training plus 4 added strength sessions/wk
findings.parameter: counselled energy surplus vs ad libitum intake during a weight-gain phase
findings.value: Energy intake 3585 ± 601 vs 2964 ± 884 kcal/d (counselled vs ad libitum). Body weight +3.9 ± 0.6% vs +1.5 ± 0.4% over 8–12 wk (about 0.3–0.5%/wk for the counselled group if spread evenly; derived here, not reported). Fat mass +15 ± 4% vs +3 ± 3%. Lean-mass gain did not differ between groups. The abstract does not state the planned surplus size.
findings.finding: Athletes on a counselled surplus gained more weight than those eating freely. Much of the extra was fat, and lean-mass gain did not differ significantly. The authors caution against excess energy intake in weight-gain phases. Only the abstract was read, and it does not give the surplus size.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results, Conclusion)

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.population: Resistance-trained adults (review of trials and physique-athlete case studies)
findings.parameter: protein g/kg fat-free mass/day for recomposition
findings.value: 2.6–3.5 g/kg FFM/day
findings.finding: The authors suggest this intake may make recomposition more likely, or larger, in trained lifters. It is a practical suggestion drawn from mixed trials, not a pooled estimate, and it is expressed per kg of fat-free mass, not body mass.
findings.locator: Practical Applications, bullet 3

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.population: Resistance-trained men and women, athletes, aspiring physique competitors
findings.parameter: protein g/kg body mass/day in trained-population trials that showed recomposition
findings.value: A high-protein condition of >2.0 g/kg/d is highlighted. Table 3 trials used 1.6 (Rauch), 2.1–2.4 (Cribb, Kreipke, Haun, Slater), 2.3 vs 3.4 (Antonio 2015), 1.8 vs 4.4 (Antonio 2014) and 0.9 vs 2.5 g/kg/d (Campbell; only 2.5 lost FM significantly). About 70% of subjects improved composition on high protein (Antonio 2015).
findings.finding: Trained people recomposed across a wide range of protein intakes combined with progressive resistance training. Very low protein (0.9 g/kg) did not give significant fat loss. Individual responses varied widely.
findings.locator: Introduction (journal p. 8, >2.0 g/kg/d statement); Table 3; section 'Nutritional influence on body recomposition when coupled with resistance training', para 2

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.parameter: minimum resistance-training frequency for recomposition
findings.value: >= 3 progressive resistance-training sessions per week
findings.finding: The review recommends progressive resistance training at least three times weekly, with progress, performance and recovery tracked so training can be adjusted over time.
findings.locator: Practical Applications, bullets 1–2

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.population: Resistance-trained men and women; aspiring female physique athletes
findings.parameter: energy surplus supplied mainly as protein during recomposition
findings.value: Haun: ~500 kcal/d surplus in all groups, ~2.2–2.3 g/kg/d protein, 6 wk; FFM +1.22 to +2.93 kg; FM -0.65 and -1.0 kg in the whey groups (maltodextrin group FM +0.2, ns). Antonio 2015: high protein with ~495 kcal/d more energy gave FM -1.6 vs -0.3 kg, FFM +1.5 kg in both. Campbell: 2.5 g/kg, energy raised ~250 kcal from protein, and the high-protein group ate 423 kcal/d more than low protein (text and Table 3); FFM +2.1, FM -1.1 kg.
findings.finding: In several trials of trained people, extra energy eaten mainly as protein came with fat loss and lean gain, so a modest protein-driven surplus did not prevent recomposition. In Haun, the maltodextrin group was also in surplus and did not lose fat. Results are second-hand, and some changes are within measurement error.
findings.locator: Section 'Nutritional influence on body recomposition when coupled with resistance training', paras 2–4; Table 3

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.population: Mixed validation samples cited in the review
findings.parameter: body-composition measurement error
findings.value: DEXA vs MRI standard error for body fat about 1.6%. BodPod discrepancies of 1.8–3.6% body fat. In hockey players BodPod overestimated FFM by 2.93 ± 2.06 kg and underestimated FM by 3.27 ± 1.92 kg against DEXA. Test–retest ICC >0.99 for DEXA FFM and BodPod.
findings.finding: The review notes that some reported recomposition effects may fall within device error. The app should not change plans on small body-composition readings. Changes measured on the same standardised device are more trustworthy than absolute values.
findings.locator: Section 'Estimating body composition with different assessments', paras 3–4 (numbers); Table 1 (qualitative pros/cons)

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.population: Overweight adults (sleep restriction); untrained adults (sleep education)
findings.parameter: sleep restriction and composition of weight lost
findings.value: About 1 h less sleep on 5 nights/wk during a matched deficit: same weight loss (-3.2 kg), but FFM made up 84.8% of the loss vs 17.3% with normal sleep (Wang et al., overweight adults, no resistance training). Sleep-education plus RT, 10 wk: FM -1.8 kg vs no significant loss (untrained).
findings.finding: The review advises making sleep a priority, because short sleep during a deficit shifted losses toward lean mass. The evidence cited comes from untrained or non-training samples and is reported second-hand.
findings.locator: Section 'Nontraining/nutrition-related factors that may influence body recomposition', paras 2 and 5; Practical Applications bullet 5

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.parameter: recomposition feasibility in contest-prep deficits at very low body fat
findings.value: Male physique case studies: FFM -6.6 kg (FM -10.4 kg) over a 26-wk prep; FFM -2.8 kg over 24 wk (body fat 14.8 to 4.5%). Two female cases: FFM +0.7 kg (32 wk) and +1.3 kg (24 wk); a third female case maintained FFM.
findings.finding: In contest-prep case studies, both male bodybuilders with reported FFM lost fat-free mass while losing fat, whereas female cases kept or slightly gained it. The app should not promise recomposition during aggressive deficits at very low body fat. This rests on case studies only.
findings.locator: Table 4; section 'Training status', para 2

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.population: Trained men and women, elite rugby players
findings.parameter: expected recomposition magnitude by training status
findings.value: Recreationally trained: FFM +5.0 kg, FM -1.4 kg over 10 wk (Cribb, whey). Highly trained: FFM +1.9 kg, FM not significantly reduced over 8 wk (Antonio). After 4 wk of detraining, elite rugby: FFM +1.8 kg, FM -2.2 kg over 11 wk.
findings.finding: The more trained the person, the smaller and slower the recomposition. People returning after a layoff can recompose quickly. Expected-change messages in the app should be scaled to training history.
findings.locator: Section 'Training status', para 1

findings.citation: Barakat C, Pearson J, Escalante G, Campbell B, De Souza EO. Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7-21. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000584
findings.population: Resistance-trained men; female collegiate volleyball players
findings.parameter: post-exercise protein dose
findings.value: 25 g whey immediately after each session (Rauch); whey 25 g/d up to a graded 25–150 g/d (Haun)
findings.finding: Protein supplements, perhaps taken after exercise, are suggested as a convenient way to reach daily protein. The review says any timing benefit beyond total daily intake is unproven and needs more research.
findings.locator: Section 'Nutritional influence on body recomposition...', paras 3 and 5; Practical Applications bullet 4

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.population: Sedentary men with obesity, 25–54 y, BMI 30–45, about 110 kg, Australia; main meals and snacks provided, plus self-chosen discretionary items
findings.parameter: energy restriction as % of maintenance
findings.value: Intake at 67% of weight-maintenance energy (33% deficit), recalculated every 4 wk for measured REE change. Absolute deficit fell from about -4142/-4009 kJ/d (weeks 1–4) to -3810/-3740 kJ/d (weeks 13–16) in CON/INT (about -990 to -894 kcal/d; conversion mine).
findings.finding: The deficit was held as a fixed percentage of recalculated maintenance, so the absolute deficit shrank as REE fell. The trial was in sedentary men with obesity on provided food, so the 33% figure should not be carried over to lean trainees.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Energy restriction interventions'

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.population: Sedentary men with obesity (36 per-protocol completers: 19 CON, 17 INT)
findings.parameter: diet-break schedule (restriction : energy-balance block lengths)
findings.value: 2 wk restriction alternating with 2 wk energy balance (100% maintenance): 8 restriction and 7 balance blocks (30 wk) vs 16 wk continuous. Completers lost 14.1 ± 5.6 vs 9.1 ± 2.9 kg (P<0.001), FM 12.3 ± 4.8 vs 8.0 ± 4.2 kg, FFM 1.8 ± 1.6 vs 1.2 ± 2.5 kg (P=0.4).
