Weight change in balance blocks 0.0 ± 0.3 kg. 5% loss reached after 4 vs 8 wk of restriction.
findings.finding: With the same total restriction, the 2:2 schedule gave more weight and fat loss than continuous restriction without extra lean loss. It took nearly twice the calendar time, and the balance blocks were held at true maintenance with provided food.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results 'Intervention: completers' and time-course sections; Discussion paras 4 and 6

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.parameter: adaptive thermogenesis (REE adjusted for body composition)
findings.value: Adjusted REE change -360 ± 502 (INT) vs -749 ± 498 kJ/d (CON), P<0.05 (4 ± 6% vs 9 ± 6%). Absolute REE change -502 ± 481 vs -624 ± 557 kJ/d, P=0.5. CON about 377 kJ/d lower than INT at week 16.
findings.finding: Absolute resting expenditure fell by a similar amount in both groups. After adjusting for fat and lean mass, the fall was about half as large with intermittent restriction, which fits a blunted adaptive thermogenesis.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results 'Intervention: completers'; Discussion para 5

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity (prior studies cited by the authors)
findings.parameter: actual vs energetically predicted weight loss under continuous restriction
findings.value: In controlled 12–24 wk restriction, weight loss is about 60–70% of the energy-arithmetic prediction. For a 110 kg man at a 33% deficit over 16 wk: about 14 kg predicted vs about 9 kg expected (cited prior work).
findings.finding: The authors set expectations from earlier studies: sustained restriction loses less weight than energy arithmetic predicts, largely because REE falls. An adaptive app should not assume a fixed kcal-per-kg conversion over months.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Statistical analyses' (sample-size rationale); Introduction para 2

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.parameter: time course of the adaptive REE fall and its reversal
findings.value: Body-composition-adjusted REE drops about 400 kJ/d within 2 wk of moderate restriction. This drop is reported to reverse fully after 10–14 days back at energy balance (7–14 days in the Introduction; prior studies cited).
findings.finding: This was the rationale for 2-week blocks: an early adaptive fall in REE in about 2 weeks that reverses with 1–2 weeks at maintenance. It is background evidence cited by the authors and was not measured during the balance blocks in this trial.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Statistical analyses' (sample-size rationale, paragraph beginning on the uncertain degree of attenuation); Introduction paras 3–4; Discussion limitations

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.population: Sedentary men with obesity who completed the baseline phase
findings.parameter: maintenance energy estimation method
findings.value: Measured REE (ventilated hood, Weir equation) multiplied by a physical activity level from self-reported work and leisure activity. Over the 4-wk stabilisation phase, weight still changed by -1.6 ± 1.4 kg (-1.4 ± 1.2%). REE changed by -138 ± 511 kJ/d.
findings.finding: Even starting from measured REE, the maintenance estimate drifted and needed scale-based correction. The app should treat any starting maintenance estimate as provisional and correct it from weigh-ins.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Determination of weight maintenance energy requirements'; Results 'Baseline'

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.parameter: weight-drift rule for adjusting maintenance intake
findings.value: Home electronic scale, weighed at least weekly. Intake adjusted when weight rose or fell consistently over >= 3 days. INT balance blocks averaged 0.0 ± 0.3 kg weight change.
findings.finding: Home self-weighing, with intake adjusted after weight drifted consistently for at least 3 days, was how maintenance intake was set. It is described for setting requirements. The paper does not say it caused the stable balance blocks, which also used provided meals.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Determination of weight maintenance energy requirements' and 'Body height, weight and composition'; Results (energy balance blocks)

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.population: Sedentary men with obesity (analysis cohort not specified for this figure)
findings.parameter: fraction of weight lost as fat mass
findings.value: Fat mass made up about 87 ± 21% of weight lost (air-displacement plethysmography); proportion did not differ between groups
findings.finding: In men with obesity on a 33% deficit, most of the weight lost was fat. This can inform the energy density an adaptive model assigns to weight change. The paper does not address leaner or resistance-trained people, who may lose a larger lean fraction.
findings.locator: Results, 'Intervention: completers', para 2

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.population: Sedentary men with obesity available at follow-up (CON 13, INT 15)
findings.parameter: weight regain 6 months after the diet
findings.value: Regain INT 3.5 ± 5.9 vs CON 5.9 ± 4.7 kg (P=0.24). Net loss from end of baseline -11.1 ± 7.4 vs -3.0 ± 4.4 kg (P=0.001). CON regained 0.6 ± 1.3 kg (wk 4) and 1.2 ± 2.1 kg (wk 8) during the 8-wk post-diet balance phase.
findings.finding: Both groups regained weight once free-living. The intermittent group kept more of its loss at 6 months, but the difference in regain itself was not significant, and follow-up covered only a subset.
findings.locator: Results, 'Intervention: post-weight loss and follow-up'

findings.citation: Byrne NM, Sainsbury A, King NA, Hills AP, Wood RE. Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2018;42(2):129-138. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
findings.parameter: macronutrient distribution (% energy) used in the restriction and balance diets
findings.value: Planned 25–30% of energy from fat, 15–20% from protein, 50–60% from carbohydrate
findings.finding: This was the protocol mix for both arms and was not tested against other mixes. A protein share of 15–20% of energy is lower than typical sports recommendations, so it should not be copied as a target for resistance-trained users.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Provision of diet'

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Ong J, Hall C, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. Continuous versus intermittent dieting for fat loss and fat-free mass retention in resistance-trained adults: the ICECAP trial. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(8):1685-1698. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002636
findings.population: Resistance-trained adults (32 women), 28.7 ± 6.5 y, 77.2 kg, 25.5% body fat, Australia (University of Western Australia)
findings.parameter: 1-wk diet breaks (3 wk restriction : 1 wk balance) vs continuous restriction: body composition and REE
findings.value: mIER (4 x 3 wk restriction + 3 x 1 wk balance, 15 wk) vs 12 wk mCER. FM 15.3 (97.5% CI 12.5–18.0) vs 18.0 (14.3–21.7) kg, P=0.321. FFM 56.7 (51.5–61.9) vs 56.7 (51.4–62.0) kg, P=0.309. BW 72.1 (95% CI 66.4–77.9) vs 74.6 (69.3–80.0) kg, P=0.283. No differences in REE, strength, endurance, leptin, testosterone, IGF-1, fT3, ghrelin, sleep or eating-disorder measures.
findings.finding: In resistance-trained men and women, diet breaks did not improve fat loss, lean retention or resting expenditure compared with continuous moderate restriction, and they made the diet 3 weeks longer. This conflicts with MATADOR in men with obesity. Only the abstract was read.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed), Results and Conclusions

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Ong J, Hall C, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. Continuous versus intermittent dieting for fat loss and fat-free mass retention in resistance-trained adults: the ICECAP trial. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(8):1685-1698. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002636
findings.parameter: diet-break effect on appetite (between groups)
findings.value: mIER vs mCER: lower hunger (P=0.002) and desire to eat (P=0.014); greater satisfaction (P=0.016) and peptide YY (P=0.034)
findings.finding: The only between-group benefit of diet breaks was lower appetite at the end of restriction. The app could offer diet breaks as an optional adherence tool rather than as a metabolic need. Effect sizes were not available because only the abstract was read.
findings.locator: Abstract, Results and Conclusions

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.population: Resistance-trained adults (15 men, 11 women), 29.3 ± 6.4 y, 72.7 kg, 21.3% body fat, from the ICECAP intermittent arm
findings.parameter: target weekly weight loss (% body mass) during restriction, resistance-trained
findings.value: Designed for about 0.7% of body weight lost per week during restriction blocks. Reported loss about 4.2 kg body weight and 3.6% body fat over 12 wk of restriction (spread over 15 wk). If this applies to the 26-person cohort (~76.9 kg start), that is about 0.45%/wk during restriction (derived here, approximate).
findings.finding: ICECAP's moderate restriction targeted about 0.7% body-weight loss weekly in resistance-trained adults. The reported loss suggests a slower achieved rate. The rate was a design choice and was not compared with other rates.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Dietary intervention'; Results para 1

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day during restriction and diet breaks
findings.value: 2.3 g per kg absolute body weight per day, in all phases including diet breaks
findings.finding: Protein was held at 2.3 g/kg body weight daily throughout restriction and breaks, and lean mass was retained similarly in both ICECAP arms. The dose was a fixed prescription, not a tested variable.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Dietary intervention'

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.parameter: fat % of energy during restriction and diet breaks
findings.value: About 20% of energy from fat. During diet breaks the amount of fat eaten stayed the same, so all extra energy came from carbohydrate (implying fat's share of energy fell during breaks).
findings.finding: Fat was set at about a fifth of energy, with carbohydrate filling the remainder after protein. In breaks, fat intake stayed the same and only carbohydrate rose. This was a protocol choice, not a tested variable.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Dietary intervention'

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.parameter: diet-break prescription (duration, energy level, macronutrient used)
findings.value: 7 days at about 100% of predicted maintenance (estimated from age, sex, body size and activity). Extra energy entirely from carbohydrate. Self-reported intake 6950 (95% CI 6310–7590) to 8720 (7900–9540) kJ/d, about +1770 kJ/d.
findings.finding: The diet break raised intake to predicted maintenance for one week by adding carbohydrate only, with protein and fat unchanged. The final break was taken after the last restriction block.
findings.locator: Materials and methods, 'Dietary intervention'; Results para 1 and Table 1 (self-reported energy intake)

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.parameter: expected scale-weight change during a 1-week diet break
findings.finding: The roughly 0.6 kg weight rise over a carbohydrate diet break showed up as DXA fat-free mass, not fat. The authors suggest temporary glycogen replenishment. The app should not read a post-break jump as fat regain or cut targets because of it. Uncontrolled pre-post data.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, Table 1 and Fig 1; Discussion para 1

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.parameter: REE change across a 1-week diet break
findings.value: REE 7000 (95% CI 6420–7580) to 7200 (6620–7780) kJ/d, P=0.026. Leptin, IGF-1, testosterone and fT3 unchanged (n=13).
findings.finding: Resting expenditure rose a little during the break. The authors think this is probably transient, from diet-induced thermogenesis and glycogen, because the main trial found no lasting REE benefit of breaks. There was no parallel control group.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, Table 1 and Fig 1; Discussion para 1

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.population: Resistance-trained adults (ICECAP intermittent arm, appetite subset)
findings.parameter: appetite and mood change across a 1-week diet break (0–100 VAS, fasted)
findings.value: Hunger 34.8 to 19.2 (P=0.017). Prospective consumption 54.3 to 41.0 (P=0.020). Irritability 21.6 to 10.7 (P=0.041). Fullness 41.5 to 56.1 (P=0.002). Satisfaction 53.5 to 69.6 (P=0.002). Alertness 47.1 to 66.6 (P=0.003). Desire to eat 41.8 to 31.0 (P=0.069, ns).
findings.finding: A week at maintenance cut hunger and irritability and raised alertness. The authors suggest placing breaks in the later part of a diet, when appetite threatens adherence, or around demanding training.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, Table 1 and Fig 2; Discussion para 5

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.parameter: effect of a carbohydrate-based diet break on muscle performance
findings.value: 25-rep total work, quadriceps 2530 to 2660 J and hamstrings 1280 to 1380 J (both P=0.018). Arm endurance and all strength measures (peak torque, power) unchanged.
findings.finding: Restoring energy with carbohydrate improved leg muscular endurance but not strength or arm performance. This may reflect glycogen repletion, but glycogen was not measured and the design was uncontrolled.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results 'Muscle performance', Table 1, Figs 3–4; Discussion paras 2–4

findings.citation: Peos JJ, Helms ER, Fournier PA, Krieger J, Sainsbury A. A 1-week diet break improves muscle endurance during an intermittent dieting regime in adult athletes: a pre-specified secondary analysis of the ICECAP trial. PLoS One. 2021;16(2):e0247292. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0247292
findings.parameter: dropout with diet breaks vs continuous restriction
findings.value: Dropout in the intermittent arm was about half that of the continuous arm in ICECAP (not statistically significant; few dropouts). 4 of 30 dropped out of the intermittent arm.
findings.finding: Diet breaks may help people stick with a diet, but the difference in dropout was not significant. Diet breaks also made the diet 25% longer without extra fat loss.
findings.locator: Introduction paras 2–3; Materials and methods, 'Eligibility criteria for participants'; Results para 1

findings.citation: Campbell BI, Aguilar D, Colenso-Semple LM, Hartke K, Fleming AR, Fox CD, et al. Intermittent energy restriction attenuates the loss of fat free mass in resistance trained individuals. A randomized controlled trial. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2020;5(1):19. doi:10.3390/jfmk5010019. PMID: 33467235; PMCID: PMC7739314.
findings.population: 27 resistance-trained men and women completing the trial (25 +/- 6.1 y, 80 +/- 15.6 kg); 4 d/wk supervised resistance training
findings.parameter: weekly carbohydrate refeed protocol (2 consecutive maintenance days) vs continuous deficit
findings.value: Refeed arm: 5 d/wk at -35% of maintenance + 2 consecutive d at maintenance, with the extra energy from carbohydrate only (refeed days averaged ~19 kcal above maintenance); continuous arm: -25% daily; 7 wk. Reported change refeed vs continuous: FFM -0.4 vs -1.3 kg; dry FFM -0.2 vs -1.9 kg; RMR -38 vs -78 kcal/d
findings.finding: Authors concluded a weekly 2-day carbohydrate refeed preserved FFM, dry FFM and RMR, but this rested on within-group significance. The published between-group reanalysis (Peos 2020) found only dry FFM differed. Refeeds should not be treated as proven FFM or RMR protection.
findings.locator: Methods 2.1 and 2.3 (diet prescription); Abstract (outcome values; Tables 2-3 not rendered in PMC text); Discussion para 7 (refeed-day energy); weighed against Peos et al. 2020 comment

findings.citation: Campbell BI, Aguilar D, Colenso-Semple LM, Hartke K, Fleming AR, Fox CD, et al. Intermittent energy restriction attenuates the loss of fat free mass in resistance trained individuals. A randomized controlled trial. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2020;5(1):19. doi:10.3390/jfmk5010019. PMID: 33467235; PMCID: PMC7739314.
findings.population: 27 resistance-trained men and women (completers); 50% of those baseline-tested did not complete
findings.parameter: energy deficit % below maintenance in lean resistance-trained adults
findings.value: Prescribed 25% below maintenance (achieved 26% refeed arm, 21% continuous arm) for 7 wk, with protein 1.8 g/kg body mass/d and remaining energy split equally between fat and carbohydrate; body mass -3.2 kg (76.4 to 73.2) and -3.6 kg (83.1 to 79.5); fat mass -2.8 and -2.3 kg
findings.finding: A roughly 21-26% deficit over 7 weeks with high protein and supervised lifting produced about 3-3.6 kg weight loss, mostly fat, with no between-group difference in body or fat mass. These are protocol values, not a tested dose-response for deficit size.
findings.locator: Methods 2.3; Results para 1; Abstract

findings.citation: Campbell BI, Aguilar D, Colenso-Semple LM, Hartke K, Fleming AR, Fox CD, et al. Intermittent energy restriction attenuates the loss of fat free mass in resistance trained individuals. A randomized controlled trial. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2020;5(1):19. doi:10.3390/jfmk5010019. PMID: 33467235; PMCID: PMC7739314.
findings.parameter: maintenance-energy estimation method before prescribing a deficit
findings.value: 2 weeks of tracked habitual food intake before the diet, taken as the weight-stable maintenance intake; deficit then prescribed as % of that value
findings.finding: Each participant's maintenance calories came from a 2-week food log recorded before dieting, and deficits were set as a percentage of it. This is a method used in the trial; its accuracy against measured expenditure was not tested.
findings.locator: Methods 2.1 (study design) and 2.3

findings.citation: Campbell BI, Aguilar D, Colenso-Semple LM, Hartke K, Fleming AR, Fox CD, et al. Intermittent energy restriction attenuates the loss of fat free mass in resistance trained individuals. A randomized controlled trial. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2020;5(1):19. doi:10.3390/jfmk5010019. PMID: 33467235; PMCID: PMC7739314.
findings.parameter: measurement timing after high-carbohydrate days
findings.value: Post-diet testing scheduled at least 2 days after the last refeed day; testing after overnight fast and 48 h without exercise; total body water measured by multi-frequency BIA
findings.finding: Investigators delayed post-diet measurement by at least 2 days after the last carbohydrate refeed to limit glycogen-linked water retention inflating mass or FFM. This is a design precaution, not a validated threshold, but it bears on interpreting weigh-ins after high-carbohydrate days.
findings.locator: Methods 2.4 and 2.5; Discussion (limitations/strengths paragraph)

findings.citation: Peos J, Brown AW, Vorland CJ, Allison DB, Sainsbury A. Contrary to the conclusions stated in the paper, only dry fat-free mass was different between groups upon reanalysis. Comment on: Intermittent energy restriction attenuates the loss of fat-free mass in resistance trained individuals. A randomized controlled trial. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2020;5(4):85. doi:10.3390/jfmk5040085. PMID: 33467300; PMCID: PMC7739336.
findings.population: Reanalysis of Campbell et al. 2020 data: 54 resistance-trained adults baseline-tested, 27 completers
findings.parameter: refeed vs continuous restriction: between-group effect on FFM, dry FFM and RMR
findings.value: No between-group difference in FFM (Welch p = 0.1795 completers; 0.1656 ITT-BOCF) or RMR (p = 0.4916; 0.4452). Dry FFM favoured refeed by 1.7 kg (95% CI 0.86-2.57; p = 0.0004) in completers and 0.9 kg (95% CI 0.33-1.46; p = 0.0028) under ITT-BOCF; 27 of 54 baseline-tested completed
findings.finding: Reanalysis of the trial's shared data shows the FFM and RMR claims came from comparing within-group significance. Directly compared, only dry FFM (FFM minus BIA total body water) differed, and intention-to-treat halved that effect. A 2-day weekly refeed has no demonstrated FFM or RMR benefit.
findings.locator: Full comment, paragraphs 3-4 (ANCOVA and Welch reanalysis; BOCF ITT)

findings.citation: Henselmans M, Bjornsen T, Hedderman R, Varvik FT. The effect of carbohydrate intake on strength and resistance training performance: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2022;14(4):856. doi:10.3390/nu14040856. PMID: 35215506; PMCID: PMC8878406.
findings.population: 49 trials; adults under 60 y, mostly strength-trained young men (some women, untrained or recreationally active)
findings.parameter: daily carbohydrate minimum (g/kg/day) for strength trainees
findings.value: No minimum identified: 15 of 17 long-term studies (3 wk-3 mo) found no between-group strength effect, including all 8 isocaloric and isonitrogenous comparisons; low arms 15-347 g/d (median 44 g) vs high 82-758 g/d (median 275 g). Authors state conventional 4-10 g/kg/d may be excessive for strength trainees
findings.finding: Across 49 trials, 39 found no strength benefit from more carbohydrate, including all 16 isocaloric comparisons. Possible benefits were confined to otherwise-fasted training, workouts over 10 sets per muscle group, or twice-daily sessions. Trials were small, mostly young men, and not meta-analysed.
findings.locator: Results 3.4 (Main Findings); Discussion 4 opening paragraph; Discussion 4.4; 4.5 Conclusions and Practical Applications

findings.citation: Henselmans M, Bjornsen T, Hedderman R, Varvik FT. The effect of carbohydrate intake on strength and resistance training performance: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2022;14(4):856. doi:10.3390/nu14040856. PMID: 35215506; PMCID: PMC8878406.
findings.parameter: pre-workout carbohydrate and protein
findings.value: >= 15 g carbohydrate and 0.3 g/kg protein within 3 h before a strength session
findings.finding: Given uncertain evidence with potential benefit and no expected harm, the authors advise at least 15 g carbohydrate plus 0.3 g/kg protein in the 3 hours before training. Acute carbohydrate benefits appeared mainly against overnight-fasted or non-caloric controls; no dose-response was found.
findings.locator: Discussion 4.1 (final paragraph); 4.5; Results 3.1.2 (no dose-response)

findings.citation: Henselmans M, Bjornsen T, Hedderman R, Varvik FT. The effect of carbohydrate intake on strength and resistance training performance: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2022;14(4):856. doi:10.3390/nu14040856. PMID: 35215506; PMCID: PMC8878406.
findings.population: Strength trainees; acute crossover trials averaging about 11 participants
findings.parameter: training-volume threshold for higher carbohydrate intake
findings.value: > 10 sets per muscle group per session (studies used 11-17 sets), or a second session for the same muscles on the same day
findings.finding: Carbohydrate benefits were more consistent above 10 sets per muscle group: two significant results plus one trend among four studies. At 10 or fewer sets in a fed state, glycogen is unlikely to limit performance. No positive study used an isocaloric control.
findings.locator: Results 3.1.2; Discussion 4.1 (paragraphs on >10 sets); 4.5

findings.citation: Henselmans M, Bjornsen T, Hedderman R, Varvik FT. The effect of carbohydrate intake on strength and resistance training performance: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2022;14(4):856. doi:10.3390/nu14040856. PMID: 35215506; PMCID: PMC8878406.
findings.population: Strength trainees; 6 glycogen-depletion crossover trials (mean n about 9)
findings.parameter: carbohydrate refuelling rate between same-day sessions (g/kg/h)
findings.value: up to 1.2 g/kg/h between sessions when another glycogen-demanding workout for the same muscles follows within hours
findings.finding: Carbohydrate helped after glycogen depletion mainly when recovery before the next session was 4 hours or less. The authors suggest up to 1.2 g/kg/h between same-day sessions to maximise glycogen resynthesis. They flag this dose as unvalidated for strength training.
findings.locator: Discussion 4.2 (conclusion paragraph); 4.5

findings.citation: Henselmans M, Bjornsen T, Hedderman R, Varvik FT. The effect of carbohydrate intake on strength and resistance training performance: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2022;14(4):856. doi:10.3390/nu14040856. PMID: 35215506; PMCID: PMC8878406.
findings.population: Long-term trials, 3 wk-3 mo, strength-trained and other adults
findings.parameter: interpreting body-mass/FFM change after a carbohydrate intake change
findings.value: Of 15 long-term studies estimating or measuring FFM or muscle thickness, 5 favoured higher carbohydrate: lower-carbohydrate arms lost 0.7-1.7 kg FFM (vs +0.5-0.8 kg) or gained less (1.4 vs 3.4 kg; 0.6 vs 2.2 kg); authors attribute this largely to lower energy intake and glycogen/water loss. A cited trial found 1 wk of carbohydrate reintroduction after a 10-wk ketogenic diet raised measured FFM by 4.8%
findings.finding: Apparent lean-mass deficits on low-carbohydrate diets were mostly explained by lower energy intake and glycogen-bound water, not contractile tissue loss. Body mass and FFM readings move when carbohydrate intake changes, independent of true tissue change.
findings.locator: Discussion 4.4 (paragraph on FFM and muscle thickness)

findings.citation: Escobar KA, VanDusseldorp TA, Kerksick CM. Carbohydrate intake and resistance-based exercise: are current recommendations reflective of actual need? Br J Nutr. 2016;116(12):2053-65. doi:10.1017/S0007114516003949. PMID: 27993175.
findings.population: Resistance-trained adults (narrative review of human and some animal data)
findings.parameter: daily carbohydrate for resistance training (current recommendations and their basis)
findings.value: Commonly advised 3-7 g/kg/d: 3-5 g/kg/d for strength and power athletes and 4-7 g/kg/d for bodybuilders (per Slater & Phillips); 5-6 g/kg/d or 55-60% of energy for bodybuilders (per Lambert et al.); a resistance bout lowers muscle glycogen by about 25-40%
findings.finding: The review argues these ranges come largely from endurance data. Resistance sessions deplete glycogen only partly, and low glycogen did not blunt mTORC1 signalling or myofibrillar protein synthesis. Still, the authors judge it premature to change the recommendations, and they propose no alternative number.
findings.locator: Sections 'Current recommendations for carbohydrate intake' (all values incl. 25-40% glycogen), 'Low carbohydrate intake, muscle glycogen concentrations and cell signalling in response to resistance exercise', Discussion final paragraph (premature to amend); full text read directly from the Cambridge Core article page

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: daily carbohydrate g/kg/day by training load
findings.value: Light (low-intensity or skill-based) 3-5 g/kg/d; Moderate (~1 h/d) 5-7 g/kg/d; High (1-3 h/d moderate-high intensity endurance) 6-10 g/kg/d; Very high (>4-5 h/d moderate-high intensity) 8-12 g/kg/d
findings.finding: These targets provide high carbohydrate availability when session quality matters. When quality matters less, intake can follow energy goals, preferences and food availability, and low availability may be used deliberately for adaptation. Targets are per kg body mass and should be periodized day to day.
findings.locator: MSSE p.550, Table 2 'Daily needs for fuel and recovery' (table adapted from Burke et al. 2011, ref 36); p.562 summary. Read from the publisher PDF of the MSSE co-publication (JAND 2016;116:501-28 is the same statement). Some symbols garbled in extraction ('<' as G, '>' as 9). The statement lists itself in effect until 31 Dec 2019

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: carbohydrate during exercise (g/h) by session duration
findings.value: <45 min: not needed; 45-75 min sustained high intensity: small amounts incl. mouth rinse; 1-2.5 h endurance or stop-start sports: 30-60 g/h; >2.5-3 h ultra-endurance: up to 90 g/h, using multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose:fructose)
findings.finding: Intake during exercise scales with duration. Higher intakes in very long events are associated with better performance, but the Evidence Analysis Library rated evidence for choosing special carbohydrate blends as limited (Grade III). Plans should be practised for gut comfort.
findings.locator: MSSE p.550 Table 2 (Acute fuelling strategies); p.557 (exercise fuelling text); p.551 (blends premature); p.562 summary; Table 1 EAL Q9 p.544

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: pre-event carbohydrate (g/kg) and timing
findings.value: 1-4 g/kg consumed 1-4 h before exercise lasting >60 min; at least 1 g/kg in the pre-event meal to offset raised carbohydrate oxidation in individuals prone to premature fatigue
findings.finding: Low-fat, low-fibre, low-to-moderate-protein foods are preferred to limit gut problems. Choosing low-glycaemic-index foods has shown no universal performance benefit, and carbohydrate intake during exercise dampens any pre-exercise effects.
findings.locator: MSSE p.550 Table 2 (Pre-event fuelling); p.557 'Achieving adequate muscle glycogen stores'

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: carbohydrate loading / fuelling-up before events (g/kg per 24 h)
findings.value: Events <90 min: 7-12 g/kg per 24 h (as daily fuel needs); events >90 min sustained or intermittent: 36-48 h of 10-12 g/kg per 24 h with training taper
findings.finding: About 24 hours of reduced training plus adequate fuel normalises muscle glycogen. Extending a carbohydrate-rich diet and taper to 48 hours achieves supercompensation for events over 90 minutes. Low-fibre, easily eaten sources can help meet targets and gut-comfort goals.
findings.locator: MSSE p.550 Table 2 (General fuelling up; Carbohydrate loading); p.557; p.562 summary

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: rapid post-exercise carbohydrate refuelling (g/kg/h)
findings.value: <8 h between two fuel-demanding sessions: 1-1.2 g/kg/h for the first 4 h (text: 4-6 h), then resume daily needs; 0.8 g/kg carbohydrate + 0.4 g/kg protein gave glycogen repletion and performance recovery similar to 1.2 g/kg carbohydrate alone
findings.finding: Glycogen resynthesis runs at only about 5% per hour, so early carbohydrate lengthens the effective refuelling window. Co-ingested protein can replace part of the carbohydrate when intake is suboptimal, and small regular snacks may help.
findings.locator: MSSE p.550 Table 2 (Speedy refuelling); p.557-558; p.563 summary

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day
findings.value: 1.2-2.0 g/kg/d generally; >= 2.0 g/kg/d, spread over the day, may help prevent FFM loss during energy restriction or sudden inactivity; a trial of 2.3 vs 1.0 g/kg/d over 2 wk of energy restriction retained muscle mass
findings.finding: Needs vary with training status (experienced athletes need less), session frequency, intensity and novelty, carbohydrate availability and above all energy availability. Adequate energy, especially from carbohydrate, spares amino acids for synthesis. Daily goals should come from regular moderate doses of high-quality protein.
findings.locator: MSSE p.551 'Protein needs'; p.548 (weight loss paragraph); p.562 summary

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: protein per dose (g/kg) and spacing
findings.value: 0.25-0.3 g/kg body weight (~15-25 g; ~10 g essential amino acids) in the 0-2 h after key sessions and every 3-5 h across multiple meals; doses >40 g not yet shown to raise MPS further
findings.finding: Per-dose targets translate laboratory muscle protein synthesis data. The EAL graded evidence that about 20-30 g protein after exercise raises MPS and nitrogen balance as Good (Grade I). Larger doses may suit only the largest athletes or periods of weight loss.
findings.locator: MSSE p.551-552 'Protein timing as a trigger for metabolic adaptation'; Table 1 EAL Q8 p.544; p.562 summary

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: fat % of energy (range and floor)
findings.value: Typically 20-35% of total energy; chronic intakes below 20% of energy discouraged; saturated fat <10% of energy (per US 2015-2020 and Canadian guidelines)
findings.finding: Fat intakes of 20% of energy or less give no performance benefit and risk low fat-soluble vitamin and essential/n-3 fatty acid intake. Tight restriction should be limited to acute pre-event or carbohydrate-loading periods. Very high-fat, carbohydrate-restricted diets impair high-intensity performance.
findings.locator: MSSE p.552 'Fat'; p.562 summary

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: energy availability floor kcal/kg FFM/day
findings.value: EA = (energy intake - exercise energy expenditure) / FFM; ~45 kcal/kg FFM/d associated with energy balance and optimal health; chronic reduction, particularly <30 kcal/kg FFM/d, associated with impaired body functions; raising EA to ~40 kcal/kg FFM/d restored menses in all subjects (mean 2.6 mo). Worked example: 60 kg, 48.0 kg FFM, EI 2400, EEE 500 kcal/d gives 39.6
findings.finding: Thresholds come mainly from research in women. Harm accrues along a continuum rather than at a single cut-off. Low EA can coexist with stable weight if RMR falls, so weight stability does not rule it out.
findings.locator: MSSE p.546 (Energy availability paragraphs and example calculation)

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: weekly loss % body mass
findings.value: < 1% of body mass per week; EAL Q1 (Grade II Fair): a slower loss rate (0.7% body mass reduction) benefited performance more than a faster one (1.4%)
findings.finding: To preserve FFM and performance, loss should be slow (under 1% body mass weekly), with a slight deficit and higher protein, and scheduled in base training or well before competition. In three of six EAL studies negative energy balance did not reduce performance.
findings.locator: MSSE p.548 'Principles of altering body composition and weight'; Table 1 EAL Q1 p.544

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: daily energy deficit kcal/day
findings.value: reduce intake by ~250-500 kcal/d below periodized energy needs while maintaining or slightly raising expenditure; progress toward short-term goals over ~3-6 wk
findings.finding: This is the practical starting deficit for most athletes. Moderate added aerobic training with close monitoring may augment it without hurting recovery, and the prescription should be individualised by goals, current practice, history and trial and error.
findings.locator: MSSE p.548 'Principles of altering body composition and weight'

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: maintaining or gaining lean mass during an energy deficit
findings.value: EAL Q2 (Grade III Limited): over 4-12 wk, increasing protein under hypocaloric conditions maintained lean body mass in resistance-trained men and women; lean mass gains may occur when energy is adequate or weight loss is gradual
findings.finding: Evidence is too limited in amount and range for definitive timing, energy or macronutrient rules for gaining FFM in a deficit, but it supports raising protein intake.
findings.locator: Table 1 EAL Q2 p.544; p.548 text on EAL Question #2

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: RMR/BMR equation and TEE model
findings.value: TEE = BMR + TEF + TEA (TEA = planned exercise + spontaneous activity + NEAT); BMR estimated with Cunningham or Harris-Benedict equations times an activity factor; RMR may be ~10% higher than BMR; RMR is 60-80% of TEE in sedentary people vs 38-47% in elite endurance athletes
findings.finding: Population-specific regression equations are preferred where available. DRI and dietary-guideline estimates typically underestimate athletes' needs. Requirements vary day to day with training volume and intensity, and rise with heat, cold, altitude, stress and gains in FFM.
findings.locator: MSSE p.545-546 'Energy requirements, energy balance and energy availability'

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: food-intake logging method and bias
findings.value: 3-7 day weighed/measured food records, multi-pass 24-h recall or food frequency questionnaire; all methods biased toward under-reporting
findings.finding: Every intake-assessment method has limits, and all tend to under-report. Educating people on the purpose and protocol of recording may improve compliance and the accuracy of self-reported intake.
findings.locator: MSSE p.545 (opening paragraph of 'Energy requirements, energy balance and energy availability')

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: morning weigh-in protocol
findings.value: body weight measured early morning after waking and voiding; when in energy balance, acute changes mainly reflect body water; 1 kg of exercise body-mass loss is about 1 L of sweat
findings.finding: Day-to-day weight shifts largely reflect hydration. Body-composition tracking should use the same calibrated equipment and a standard protocol, with consistent training, fasting and hydration state, and should report results as ranges tracked over time.
findings.locator: MSSE p.555 (hydration assessment); p.556 (sweat-loss estimation); p.547 'Methodologies for body composition assessment'

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: pre-exercise fluid (mL/kg)
findings.value: 5-10 mL/kg body weight (~2-4 mL/lb) in the 2-4 h before exercise, aiming for pale-yellow urine
findings.finding: Drinking this volume a few hours before exercise leaves time to void any excess. Sodium in pre-exercise food or fluid may aid retention. Glycerol and other plasma expanders for hyperhydration are prohibited by WADA.
findings.locator: MSSE p.555 'Before exercise'

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: during-exercise fluid deficit limit and drinking rate
findings.value: limit total fluid deficit to < 2% body weight; typical intake 0.4-0.8 L/h; sweat rates 0.3-2.4 L/h; deficits > 2% can impair cognition and aerobic performance, particularly in hot weather; losses of 3-5% more commonly impair anaerobic/high-intensity, skill and cool-weather aerobic performance; hyponatremia defined as blood sodium < 135 mmol/L
findings.finding: Drinking should replace as much sweat loss as practical, neither exceeding sweat rate nor letting dehydration become problematic. Over-drinking is the main cause of hyponatremia, and recreational athletes and women face higher risk.
findings.locator: MSSE p.555 (opening paragraphs of 'Hydration Guidelines': >2% and 3-5% thresholds); p.556 'During exercise'; p.562 summary

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: post-exercise rehydration volume
findings.value: ~125-150% of the remaining fluid deficit (1.25-1.5 L per 1 kg body weight lost)
findings.finding: Because sweat and urine losses continue after exercise, rehydration needs more fluid than the measured deficit, taken with sodium at a modest rate to limit urine loss. Heavy alcohol intake is discouraged. Habitual moderate caffeine (under about 180 mg) is not a meaningful diuretic.
findings.locator: MSSE p.556 'After exercise'; p.562 summary

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: sodium intake during and after exercise
findings.value: ingest sodium during exercise when sweat rate > 1.2 L/h, sweat is salty, or exercise lasts > 2 h; average sweat sodium ~50 mmol/L (~1 g/L); do not restrict sodium after exercise when losses are large
findings.finding: Sodium replacement is advised for heavy or salty sweaters and long sessions. Post-exercise sodium from food or drink helps retain ingested fluid, including plasma volume, so it should not be restricted after large losses.
findings.locator: MSSE p.556 'During exercise' and 'After exercise'

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: vegetarian/vegan nutrient risk flags
findings.value: at-risk nutrients: energy, protein, fat, creatine, carnosine, n-3 fatty acids, iron, calcium, riboflavin, zinc, vitamin B-12
findings.finding: A vegetarian diet can be nutritionally adequate, but long-term performance research is lacking and bone mineral density and stress-fracture risk may be higher. Vegetarian athletes may benefit from comprehensive dietary assessment and screening for disordered eating.
findings.locator: MSSE p.559 'Vegetarian athlete'; p.563 summary

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.population: Athletes at risk of iron deficiency
findings.parameter: iron intake target for at-risk groups (incl. vegetarians)
findings.value: iron intake above the RDA: > 18 mg/d for women and > 8 mg/d for men, for distance runners, vegetarians and regular blood donors; female athletes' requirement may be up to 70% above the EAR; diets supply ~6 mg iron per ~1000 kcal
findings.finding: Well-absorbed food iron (heme, or non-heme with vitamin C foods) is the first line. Routine unmonitored supplements are not recommended, and supplements should not be taken right after strenuous exercise because of hepcidin. At-risk athletes should be screened regularly.
findings.locator: MSSE p.553 'Micronutrients of key interest: Iron'

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: train-low (training with low carbohydrate availability)
findings.value: EAL Q10 (Grade II Fair): some metabolic adaptations but no performance improvement; training intensity and duration were impaired
findings.finding: Low-carbohydrate-availability training upregulates endurance-adaptation signalling in theory, but performance benefits are unclear, possibly because poorly periodized use reduced training quality. It needs deliberate integration into the training plan.
findings.locator: Table 1 EAL Q10 p.544; MSSE p.549 (carbohydrate and adaptation); p.551

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: glycaemic index/load of carbohydrate foods
findings.value: EAL Q11 (Grade I Good): neither glycaemic index nor glycaemic load affected endurance performance or metabolic responses when carbohydrate and energy were matched
findings.finding: Once carbohydrate and energy totals are met, glycaemic index need not steer food choice for training. Nutrient-rich carbohydrate sources are advised so overall nutrient needs are covered.
findings.locator: Table 1 EAL Q11 p.544; MSSE p.550-551 text; Table 2 comments p.550

findings.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and athletic performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-68. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852. PMID: 26891166.
findings.parameter: micronutrient floor
findings.value: diet should provide at least the RDA/AI for all micronutrients; a multivitamin/mineral may be appropriate during energy restriction or with limited dietary variety
findings.finding: Those who restrict energy, use severe weight-loss practices or cut whole food groups are at greatest risk of micronutrient deficiency, most often calcium, vitamin D, iron and some antioxidants. Single-nutrient supplements suit only clinically defined needs.
findings.locator: MSSE p.553 'Micronutrients'; p.562-563 summary

findings.citation: Burke LM, Hawley JA, Wong SH, Jeukendrup AE. Carbohydrates for training and competition. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S17-27. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.585473. PMID: 21660838.
findings.population: Athletes in endurance and high-intensity sports
findings.parameter: carbohydrate during exercise (g/h) by event duration
findings.value: ~1 h sustained high-intensity: small amounts, even mouth-rinsing; longer events: 30-60 g/h; events > 2.5 h: up to 90 g/h, with multiple-carbohydrate blends to maximise absorption
findings.finding: Intake during exercise should scale with the event. Short high-intensity efforts benefit through central nervous system effects, while long events benefit from higher intakes of mixed carbohydrate sources. These are IOC consensus-review targets and were verified from the abstract only.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (full text not opened); the same values appear in ACSM 2016 Table 2, which cites this paper as ref 36

findings.citation: Burke LM, Hawley JA, Wong SH, Jeukendrup AE. Carbohydrates for training and competition. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S17-27. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.585473. PMID: 21660838.
findings.parameter: train-low strategies and carbohydrate availability
findings.value: no numeric value; performance benefit of added train-low strategies in well-trained athletes is unclear
findings.finding: Carbohydrate availability, meaning intake in the hours and days before, during and after sessions relative to fuel demand, should be high for competition and high-intensity training. Whether deliberately training low improves performance in well-trained athletes remains unresolved.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (full text not opened)

findings.citation: International Olympic Committee. IOC consensus statement on sports nutrition 2010. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S3-4. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.619349
findings.parameter: intra-exercise carbohydrate rate by event duration
findings.value: Small amounts help in ~1 h events; amount rises with duration; up to 90 g/h for events longer than ~3 h, using sports foods/drinks with carbohydrate combinations that maximise gut absorption
findings.finding: Even small carbohydrate intakes help performance in events of about an hour. Needs rise with duration, reaching up to 90 g/h beyond about 3 h. At that rate athletes should rehearse in training and use carbohydrate blends that absorb well and limit gut upset.
findings.locator: Statement paragraph 4 (IOC-hosted official PDF dated Lausanne, 27 Oct 2010; the typeset journal version was not opened)

findings.citation: International Olympic Committee. IOC consensus statement on sports nutrition 2010. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S3-4. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.619349
findings.parameter: post-session protein dose (g)
findings.value: 15-25 g high-quality protein after each training session
findings.finding: Eat high-quality protein regularly through the day, and especially soon after exercise. The statement says 15-25 g after each session maximises protein synthesis for keeping or gaining muscle and bone and for tissue repair.
findings.locator: Statement paragraph 3 (IOC-hosted PDF)

findings.citation: International Olympic Committee. IOC consensus statement on sports nutrition 2010. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S3-4. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.619349
findings.parameter: daily protein relative to general-population recommendation
findings.value: Above general-population recommended amounts; no g/kg/day figure given
findings.finding: Athletes need more daily protein than the general-population recommendation. A varied diet that meets energy needs usually supplies more protein than required. The statement gives no numeric daily target.
findings.locator: Statement paragraph 3 (IOC-hosted PDF)

findings.citation: International Olympic Committee. IOC consensus statement on sports nutrition 2010. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S3-4. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.619349
findings.parameter: fluid-loss limit during exercise (% body mass)
findings.value: Limit dehydration to less than ~2% of body mass; do not gain weight during exercise; add sodium when sweat losses are high, especially if exercise lasts more than ~2 h
findings.finding: Start exercise well hydrated and drink enough to keep losses under about 2% of body mass, without drinking so much that weight rises. Include sodium when sweating heavily, particularly beyond about 2 h. Recovery drinks should replace both water and salt.
findings.locator: Statement paragraph 4 (IOC-hosted PDF)

findings.citation: International Olympic Committee. IOC consensus statement on sports nutrition 2010. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S3-4. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.619349
findings.parameter: low energy availability rule
findings.value: Avoid low energy availability (no numeric threshold given); refer people at risk of disordered eating or reproductive disorders to a qualified health professional
findings.finding: Low energy availability can impair performance and training adaptation and may harm brain, reproductive, metabolic, immune and bone health, so it should be avoided. People at risk of disordered eating should be referred promptly. No kcal threshold is given.
findings.locator: Statement paragraph 5 (IOC-hosted PDF)

findings.citation: International Olympic Committee. IOC consensus statement on sports nutrition 2010. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S3-4. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.619349
findings.parameter: food-first and nutrient-density rule
findings.value: A varied diet of commonly available foods with adequate energy meets needs; favour nutrient-rich foods when restricting energy; supplements do not make up for poor food choices
findings.finding: A varied diet of ordinary foods with enough energy can cover carbohydrate, protein, fat and micronutrient needs. Choosing nutrient-rich foods matters most when intake is cut to lose fat. Calcium, iron and vitamin D need particular attention.
findings.locator: Statement paragraphs 2, 5 and 6 (IOC-hosted PDF)

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: daily carbohydrate g/kg/day by training load
findings.value: 5-12 g/kg/day general range; upper end 8-10 g/kg/day for athletes training at ≥70% VO2max for upwards of (i.e., more than) ~12 h/week (body text); 8-12 g/kg/day for ≥8 h/week (practical applications); ≥8 g/kg/day restored maximal glycogen within 24 h in elite high-volume athletes with only moderate muscle damage
findings.finding: Daily carbohydrate should scale with training volume and intensity. The top of the range is for high-volume athletes. The body text and the practical applications give different bands and volume cut-offs, so this inconsistency needs owner review. Evidence is mostly from male endurance athletes.
findings.locator: Carbohydrate section, paras 1-2; Carbohydrate > Endurance training section, last para; Practical applications bullet 6

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: carbohydrate prescription unit
findings.value: Prescribe as g/kg/day; percentage-of-energy targets (60-70% of energy) are no longer favoured
findings.finding: Setting carbohydrate as a percentage of energy (such as 60-70%) prescribes the wrong amount for people eating very large or restricted energy intakes, so body-mass-relative (g/kg) targets are preferred.
findings.locator: Carbohydrate section, para 1

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: intra-exercise carbohydrate rate and solution
findings.value: ~30-60 g/h as a 6-8% carbohydrate-electrolyte solution, 6-12 fl oz every 10-15 min, for bouts >60 min at >70% VO2max, especially beyond 70 min (abstract). The paper gives different volumes elsewhere: 230-350 mL every 10-12 min (body text) and 12-16 fl oz of a 6-8% solution (practical bullet 3)
findings.finding: In long, hard sessions, take about 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour as a 6-8% drink sipped every 10-15 minutes. The benefit is clearest beyond 70-90 minutes and uncertain in shorter efforts. This ceiling is lower than the newer 90 g/h guidance.
findings.locator: Abstract; Endurance training section, paras 4-5; Practical applications bullet 3

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: rapid post-exercise glycogen refuelling rate
findings.value: ≥1.2 g/kg/h for 4-6 h after exhausting exercise; alternative 0.6-1.0 g/kg within 30 min then every 2 h for 4-6 h; prefer high-GI (>70) sources when recovery is <4 h
findings.finding: When the next session is under 4 hours away, aggressive carbohydrate feeding (around 1.2 g/kg per hour, high-glycaemic sources) speeds glycogen recovery. With a full day to recover and adequate daily carbohydrate, timing matters much less.
findings.locator: Abstract; Endurance training section, paras 7-8; Practical applications bullet 4

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: protein added to recovery carbohydrate (g/kg/h)
findings.value: 0.2-0.5 g/kg/h protein with carbohydrate helps only when carbohydrate is <1.2 g/kg/h (e.g., 0.8 g/kg/h CHO + 0.2-0.4 g/kg/h protein)
findings.finding: Adding protein to recovery carbohydrate speeds glycogen resynthesis only when the carbohydrate dose is below about 1.2 g/kg/h. With optimal carbohydrate, the extra protein gave little or no further glycogen or performance benefit.
findings.locator: Abstract; Carbohydrate + protein, Endurance training section, para 3; Practical applications bullet 5

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: daily protein g/kg/day
findings.value: 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day
findings.finding: The ISSN ranks reaching a daily protein intake of 1.4-2.0 g/kg above precise timing. Timing effects are small once daily needs are met.
findings.locator: Practical applications bullet 10; Protein > Resistance training section, para 7 (the Aragon and Schoenfeld reviews paragraph)

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.population: Young adults after resistance exercise (mostly acute MPS studies using whey isolate)
findings.parameter: protein dose per meal and interval
findings.value: 20-40 g (0.25-0.40 g/kg) high-quality protein containing ~10-12 g essential amino acids, every 3-4 h
findings.finding: Spreading medium-sized, high-quality protein doses of about 20-40 g every 3-4 hours best supports muscle protein synthesis across the day. The main evidence is short-term acute studies with whey alone, so it may not carry over to mixed meals.
findings.locator: Abstract; Timing and distribution of protein feeding section; Practical applications bullets 7 and 12

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.population: Young and older men; resistance-trained adults
findings.parameter: pre-sleep protein dose
findings.value: 30-40 g casein within ~30 min before sleep
findings.finding: About 30-40 g of casein before sleep can raise overnight muscle protein synthesis without blunting fat breakdown. It is also a practical way to reach daily protein. Long-term trials are few and partly confounded by higher total protein.
findings.locator: Pre-sleep protein intake section; Practical applications bullet 13

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: meal frequency rule
findings.value: No required meal count; with energy intake controlled, meal frequency has limited effect on weight or body-composition change
findings.finding: Under equal energy restriction, eating 2, 3 or 6 meals a day produced similar weight and body-composition outcomes. A cited meta-analysis's apparent advantage for more meals depended on one short exercise study. More frequent meals may help appetite control.
findings.locator: Meal frequency section; Practical applications bullet 11

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: daily energy distribution across meals
findings.value: Example reported: 50%/35%/15% of 1400 kcal/day at breakfast/lunch/dinner gave ~2.5x more weight loss than the reverse over 12 weeks
findings.finding: Studies report that eating more of the day's energy earlier gave more weight loss. However, one such study also lost more fat-free mass, and the evidence comes from sedentary, overweight people without exercise, so relevance to training users is uncertain.
findings.locator: Timing and distribution of meals section, paras 1-2; Practical applications bullet 14

findings.citation: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, Stout JR, Campbell B, Wilborn CD, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017;14:33. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4
findings.parameter: pre-exercise carbohydrate amount
findings.value: 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate in meals or snacks in the hours before >90 min at ≥70% VO2max (the paper prints the unit as 'g/kg/day')
findings.finding: Carbohydrate-rich meals or snacks in the hours before long, hard exercise help top up glycogen. The paper prints the unit as g/kg/day, which does not fit a pre-exercise meal. Treat it as unverified and prefer the IAAF 1-4 g/kg in 1-4 h wording.
findings.locator: Endurance training section, para 2; carbohydrate summary para

findings.citation: Jeukendrup A. A step towards personalized sports nutrition: carbohydrate intake during exercise. Sports Med. 2014;44 Suppl 1:S25-33. doi:10.1007/s40279-014-0148-z
findings.parameter: intra-exercise carbohydrate rate by duration
findings.value: ~30 min-1 h: mouth rinse or small amounts; 2-3 h: up to ~60 g/h (single source is sufficient; glucose absorption saturates near 60 g/h); ultra-endurance: ~90 g/h, requiring multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose:fructose)
findings.finding: Carbohydrate targets rise with duration: a rinse or small amount for about an hour, up to about 60 g/h for 2-3 hours, and about 90 g/h for ultra events. Rates above 60 g/h need glucose-fructose blends. The author was a Gatorade Sports Science Institute employee, a possible conflict of interest.
findings.locator: Abstract; sections 'Prolonged Exercise and Multiple Transportable Carbohydrates' and 'Recommendations for Carbohydrate Intake During Different Endurance Events'; Fig. 1 caption (the figure's band graphic is an image and could not be read)

findings.citation: Jeukendrup A. A step towards personalized sports nutrition: carbohydrate intake during exercise. Sports Med. 2014;44 Suppl 1:S25-33. doi:10.1007/s40279-014-0148-z
findings.parameter: intra-exercise carbohydrate scaling rule
findings.value: Express as absolute g/h, not g/kg body mass; independent of training status; adjust downward at low absolute intensity
findings.finding: Uptake of carbohydrate eaten during exercise is limited by gut absorption, not body size or fitness, so targets should be grams per hour. Slow, low-intensity exercisers (for example a 5-hour marathoner) may need less than 90 g/h. The guidance may not apply to sedentary people.
findings.locator: Sections 'Training Status', 'The Effect of Exercise Intensity' and 'Effect of Body Weight'

findings.citation: Jeukendrup A. A step towards personalized sports nutrition: carbohydrate intake during exercise. Sports Med. 2014;44 Suppl 1:S25-33. doi:10.1007/s40279-014-0148-z
findings.parameter: dose-response optimum for intra-exercise carbohydrate
findings.value: 60-80 g/h gave the greatest time-trial improvement (multicentre study, n=51, 12 glucose:fructose doses from 10-120 g/h during a 2 h ride followed by a 20 km time trial)
findings.finding: A cited multicentre dose-response trial found performance improved with dose, with the biggest gain at 60-80 g/h. A cited meta-analysis reportedly agrees. This review reports these results second-hand.
findings.locator: Section 'Carbohydrate during Exercise and Performance: Dose Response', para 3

findings.citation: Jeukendrup A. A step towards personalized sports nutrition: carbohydrate intake during exercise. Sports Med. 2014;44 Suppl 1:S25-33. doi:10.1007/s40279-014-0148-z
findings.population: Humans in a single cited study (Cox et al.); the review does not describe the participants
findings.parameter: gut-training carbohydrate intake
findings.value: 28 days at 6.5 g/kg/day carbohydrate (1.5 g/kg of it taken during training) raised exogenous carbohydrate oxidation versus a 5 g/kg/day control diet
findings.finding: The gut appears trainable. A higher daily carbohydrate diet with carbohydrate taken during training increased how much ingested carbohydrate was used during exercise. Athletes should rehearse race fuelling in training to reduce gut discomfort.
findings.locator: Section 'Training the Gut'

findings.citation: Jeukendrup A. A step towards personalized sports nutrition: carbohydrate intake during exercise. Sports Med. 2014;44 Suppl 1:S25-33. doi:10.1007/s40279-014-0148-z
findings.parameter: intra-exercise carbohydrate food forms
findings.value: Drinks, gels, or low-fat, low-protein, low-fibre solid bars, chosen by preference and mixed as needed; solid foods and concentrated solutions reduce fluid absorption
findings.finding: Hourly carbohydrate targets can be met with drinks, gels or low-fat, low-protein, low-fibre bars in any combination the athlete likes. Pair them with a fluid plan, because solids and concentrated drinks slow fluid absorption.
findings.locator: Section 'Recommendations for Carbohydrate Intake During Different Endurance Events' bullets 3-5; Conclusion

findings.citation: Stellingwerff T, Cox GR. Systematic review: carbohydrate supplementation on exercise performance or capacity of varying durations. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2014;39(9):998-1011. doi:10.1139/apnm-2014-0027
findings.population: Adults in all-out or endurance performance protocols
findings.parameter: intra-exercise carbohydrate for exercise >2 h
findings.value: High delivery rates (>90 g/h) with multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose:fructose), tailored to individual tolerance; benefit rises with duration (correlation p=0.0036); 82% of 61 randomised placebo-controlled studies (n=679) showed benefit
findings.finding: Across 61 randomised placebo-controlled studies, most showed carbohydrate improved performance, and the gain grew with exercise duration. Beyond 2 hours the benefit comes mainly from high delivery and oxidation rates using glucose-fructose blends, adjusted to individual tolerance. The abstract reports only a vote count, not a pooled effect.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only (full text not accessible)

findings.citation: Stellingwerff T, Cox GR. Systematic review: carbohydrate supplementation on exercise performance or capacity of varying durations. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2014;39(9):998-1011. doi:10.1139/apnm-2014-0027
findings.parameter: carbohydrate for ~1 h exercise
findings.value: Oral exposure (mouth rinse or ingestion with enough mouth contact) is sufficient; carbohydrate type and amount appear irrelevant
findings.finding: In efforts of about an hour, the benefit seems to come from carbohydrate sensed in the mouth acting on the brain, so a rinse or small intake is enough. The type or amount absorbed does not appear to matter.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only (full text not accessible)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.population: Younger and older adults doing resistance training
findings.parameter: daily protein g/kg/day for lean-mass gain
findings.value: 1.6 g/kg/day optimal; up to 2.2 g/kg/day with no adverse effects (with progressive resistance exercise)
findings.finding: With resistance training, about 1.6 g/kg/day of protein is described as optimal for lean-mass gain, and up to 2.2 g/kg/day showed no harm. The statement cites meta-analyses showing real but modest gains; those meta-analyses were not opened here.
findings.locator: Table 6 (Gaining LBM, Protein row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: protein dose per meal and meals per day
findings.value: 0.3-0.5 g/kg per meal, 3-4 times per day, including close to exercise (post-exercise consistently effective)
findings.finding: Split protein into 3-4 meals of about 0.3-0.5 g/kg each, with one near training. Eating protein after exercise has consistently been effective.
findings.locator: Table 6 (Gaining LBM, Protein row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: protein during energy deficit (direction of effect)
findings.value: Higher dietary protein during an exercise- or diet-induced deficit: small but significant extra fat loss and lean-mass retention; no g/kg value given in this row
findings.finding: During an energy deficit, eating more protein slightly improves fat loss and helps keep lean mass, according to meta-analyses the statement cites (not opened here). This row gives no numeric target.
findings.locator: Table 6 (Losing fat mass, Protein row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: fat-loss supplement efficacy
findings.value: Pyruvate, green tea catechins/caffeine, alpha-lipoic acid, conjugated linolenic acid (as printed), glucomannan, omega-3 and chitosan: small to trivial effect; chromium: no effect
findings.finding: Evidence for 'fat-burning' supplements is weak or absent. Most products have no supporting evidence, and many sold as fat burners are banned in sport. The app should not recommend them for fat loss.
findings.locator: Section 'Supplements that improve performance indirectly', para 2; Table 6 (Losing fat mass rows)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: supplement contamination and harm risk
findings.value: ~15% of >600 products in the original survey held undeclared prohormones; 2.5 µg of 19-norandrostenedione contamination can push urinary 19-norandrosterone past the 2 ng/mL violation threshold; ~23,000 US emergency visits a year linked to supplements (2015)
findings.finding: Supplements are loosely regulated, may contain undeclared banned or harmful substances, and cause many emergency visits. Use only products with strong evidence of safety and effect, preferably third-party tested, after a nutrition assessment.
findings.locator: Section 'Adverse effects', paras 2-8; 'Practical implications and decision tree'

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: caffeine dose and upper threshold
findings.value: 3-6 mg/kg body mass ~60 min before exercise, or lower doses (<3 mg/kg, ~200 mg) before and during exercise with carbohydrate; ≥9 mg/kg gives no extra benefit and more side effects
findings.finding: Performance benefits usually peak at 3-6 mg/kg. At 9 mg/kg or more there is no added benefit but more nausea, anxiety, fast heart rate and insomnia. Dosing errors in lab studies caused serious harm.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Caffeine row); Section 'Adverse effects', para 1

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: creatine-related body-mass change (weigh-in confounder)
findings.value: Loading ~20 g/day (4 doses) for 5-7 days, then 3-5 g/day; loading may add 1-2 kg body mass, mainly water
findings.finding: Creatine loading can raise body mass by 1-2 kg, mostly water. A weight-trend algorithm should not read that jump as fat gain or a surplus. No health harm was seen with up to 4 years of appropriate use.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Creatine row, protocol and side effects); Table 5 (Creatine row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: iron supplementation rule
findings.value: RDA reference: 18 mg/day women, 8 mg/day men; supplement above the RDA only if status is inadequate; high-dose iron only when deficiency is diagnosed
findings.finding: Do not supplement iron at high doses without a diagnosed deficiency. Iron taken when stores are already adequate can cause GI symptoms and, over time, iron overload and liver failure. Deficiency needs clinical follow-up.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Iron row); Section 'Adverse effects', para 1

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.population: Athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction
findings.parameter: calcium and vitamin D with low energy availability
findings.value: Calcium 1500 mg/day plus vitamin D 1500-2000 IU/day to optimise bone health in athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction
findings.finding: When energy availability is low or periods are disrupted, higher calcium (1500 mg/day) with vitamin D (1500-2000 IU/day) is advised for bone health. Avoiding dairy and restricting energy raise the risk of low calcium status.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Calcium row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: vitamin D maintenance intake
