findings.value: 800 to 1000-2000 IU/day to maintain status in the general population (1000 IU/day autumn to spring suggested for immune support); no athlete-specific guideline; high-dose repletion only under monitoring
findings.finding: Vitamin D needs depend on sun exposure and skin type. General-population maintenance doses are 800-2000 IU/day. High-dose correction of deficiency needs monitoring because of toxicity risk.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Vitamin D row); Table 4 (Vitamin D row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.population: General population following vegan or near-vegan diets
findings.parameter: vegan diet micronutrient supplementation
findings.value: Vitamin B12 supplementation may be warranted on vegan or near-vegan diets (no dose given); iodine where foods are low in iodine or iodised salt is not used
findings.finding: People on vegan or near-vegan diets may need a vitamin B12 supplement, and those without iodised salt or iodine-rich foods may need iodine. These apply to the general population, not only athletes, and no doses are given.
findings.locator: Section 'Supplements used to prevent or treat nutrient deficiencies', para 3

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: sports drink composition
findings.value: 5-8% carbohydrate, 10-35 mmol/L sodium, 3-5 mmol/L potassium
findings.finding: A typical sports drink gives fluid and carbohydrate together during exercise and helps rehydration and refuelling afterwards. Its usual composition is 5-8% carbohydrate with modest sodium and potassium.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Sports drink row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: gel and sports confectionery carbohydrate per unit
findings.value: Gel: 30-40 g sachet with ~25 g carbohydrate; jelly confectionery: ~5 g carbohydrate per piece (pouches ~40-50 g)
findings.finding: Gels and jelly sweets are compact carbohydrate sources for use during exercise. Some also contain caffeine or electrolytes.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Sports gel or sports confectionery row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: sports bar composition
findings.value: 40-50 g carbohydrate, 5-10 g protein, usually low in fat and fibre; 50-100% of RDA/RDI for vitamins/minerals
findings.finding: Sports bars give carbohydrate during exercise and carbohydrate plus some protein for recovery, and are portable. They may contain unproven ingredients that raise contamination risk.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Sports bar row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: liquid meal supplement composition for high-energy diets
findings.value: 1-1.5 kcal/mL; 15-20% protein, 50-70% carbohydrate, low to moderate fat; 500-1000 mL supplies RDI/RDA for vitamins and minerals
findings.finding: Liquid meals are an easy, low-bulk way to add energy for weight gain or heavy training. They also serve as a pre-event meal or recovery drink. No surplus size is specified.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Liquid meal supplement row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: protein supplement and protein-enhanced food serving
findings.value: Protein supplement: 20-50 g protein per serve from whey, casein, milk, egg or soy; protein-enhanced foods (milk, yoghurt, cereal bars): ~20 g protein per normal portion
findings.finding: Protein powders and protein-enriched everyday foods offer a portable, dose-controlled protein source for recovery or lean-mass goals. Supplements may contain unproven ingredients that raise contamination risk.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Protein supplement and Protein-enhanced food rows)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: omega-3 source preference
findings.value: Supplement dose studied ~2 g/day; prefer fatty fish in the diet over supplements
findings.finding: Low omega-3 intake has not been shown to impair performance. High-dose supplements can cause bleeding, digestive problems, higher LDL or heavy-metal exposure, so fatty fish in the diet is suggested as the better source.
findings.locator: Table 5 (Omega-3 fatty acids row)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: high-dose antioxidant supplements
findings.value: High doses of single antioxidants (vitamins C and E) may blunt training adaptations; vitamin E showed no immune benefit in young healthy people (and possibly more upper respiratory symptoms under heavy exertion)
findings.finding: High-dose vitamin C or E supplements may reduce the adaptive response to training. The app should not suggest them as routine.
findings.locator: Section 'Supplements that improve performance indirectly', para 1; Table 4 (Vitamin C and Vitamin E rows)

findings.citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(7):439-55. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027
findings.parameter: dietary nitrate food sources and dose
findings.value: Leafy green and root vegetables (spinach, rocket, celery, beetroot); acute bolus 5-9 mmol (310-560 mg) nitrate, benefit ~2-3 h later; no added benefit at 16.8 mmol vs 8.4 mmol
findings.finding: Nitrate-rich vegetables can supply the nitrate linked to endurance gains. Benefits are harder to get in highly trained athletes. Try it in training first because it may upset the gut.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Nitrate row)

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: daily protein g/kg/day for weight-stable or weight-gaining athletes
findings.value: 1.3-1.7 g/kg/day (the general-adult RDA of 0.8-1.0 g/kg/day is below athlete needs)
findings.finding: Athletes aiming to hold or gain weight do best at about 1.3-1.7 g/kg/day, above the general-adult allowance. Whole foods are preferred for cost, safety and nutrients; supplements are for when eating is impractical.
findings.locator: Theme 3 text; Table 2 items 1-2 (read from the World Athletics-hosted PDF of the published article)

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: daily protein g/kg/day during weight loss
findings.value: More than 1.6 and up to 2.4 g/kg/day, combined with resistance exercise
findings.finding: For losing fat while keeping or even adding lean mass, the statement advises resistance training plus 1.6-2.4 g/kg/day of protein.
findings.locator: Theme 3 text; Table 2 item 5

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: daily protein upper useful limit
findings.value: >2.5 g/kg/day offers no adaptive advantage
findings.finding: Protein above about 2.5 g/kg/day gives no additional training-adaptation benefit, which gives the app a sensible ceiling for protein targets.
findings.locator: Table 2 item 4

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: high-protein diet safety during weight loss
findings.value: 2.4 g/kg/day during weight loss is not associated with increased risk of kidney problems or poor bone health
findings.finding: The statement says athletes eating a high-protein diet (about 2.4 g/kg/day) while losing weight are not at higher risk of kidney or bone problems. The population is healthy athletes, not people with kidney disease.
findings.locator: Table 2 item 6

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: protein per eating occasion and number of occasions
findings.value: ~0.3-0.4 g/kg rapidly digested high-quality protein at 4-5 eating occasions per day; raise to 0.4-0.5 g/kg for mixed meals or during energy deficit/weight loss
findings.finding: Leucine-rich, high-quality protein at about 0.3-0.4 g/kg per occasion, 4-5 times a day, optimises training adaptation when energy availability is adequate. Raise the dose to 0.4-0.5 g/kg for mixed meals or when dieting.
findings.locator: Theme 3 text; Table 2 item 3

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.population: Distance and ultra-distance runners and race walkers
findings.parameter: pre-race carbohydrate g/kg/day (glycogen normalisation and loading)
findings.value: Glycogen normalisation: 7-12 g/kg/day for 24 h; carbohydrate loading: 10-12 g/kg/day for 36-48 h (for marathon, 50 km walk and ultra events, ideally low-residue)
findings.finding: Before distance races, eat 7-12 g/kg of carbohydrate over the prior 24 h to restore glycogen. For marathon and longer events, load at 10-12 g/kg/day for 36-48 h, choosing low-residue foods to limit gut issues.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Pre-race refueling row); Theme 5

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: pre-event meal carbohydrate
findings.value: 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate eaten 1-4 h before the race; reduce fat, fibre and protein according to gut-upset risk
findings.finding: A familiar pre-race meal of 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate, 1-4 hours out, restores liver glycogen after the overnight fast. Susceptible people should keep fat, fibre, protein and fructose low, and may add carbohydrate after the warm-up.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Pre-race meal row); Table 4 (runner's diarrhoea strategies); Theme 5

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: in-race carbohydrate rate by duration
findings.value: 45-75 min: mouth rinse or small amount; 1-2.5 h: 30-60 g/h; >2.5 h: up to 90 g/h (Table 3; Theme 5 text says races >2 h, from mixed CHO sources); ultramarathon: 30-90 g/h depending on pace and tolerance
findings.finding: In-race carbohydrate targets rise with duration, from a rinse or small amount up to 90 g/h beyond 2.5 hours. In the longest, slowest events the useful rate may fall, and gut tolerance becomes the main constraint. Rehearse every plan in training.
findings.locator: Table 3 (In-race fueling goals row); Theme 5 text

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: in-race net fluid deficit limit (% body mass)
findings.value: Keep net fluid deficit below 2-3% body mass, especially in hot weather; losses above 2-3% impair performance in warm-hot conditions; slower competitors should not drink beyond thirst
findings.finding: Aim to keep fluid losses under 2-3% of body mass, especially in the heat. Slower, low-sweat runners risk low blood sodium from overdrinking, so they should drink to thirst rather than to a schedule.
findings.locator: Theme 4 text; Table 3 (In-race hydration and nonelite rows)

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: energy availability / RED-S rule
findings.value: Energy availability = dietary intake minus exercise energy expenditure (described conceptually; no fat-free-mass normalisation or numeric threshold given in this statement); low energy availability to be screened for and treated primarily by raising energy availability
findings.finding: An energy shortfall relative to training makes the body cut spending on other functions, harming hormones, bone, immunity, the gut and performance in both sexes. Risk is highest in weight-sensitive endurance and jumping events. Screening and early correction are advised.
findings.locator: Theme 2 (Energy availability, Melin et al. 2019 summary)

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet for endurance
findings.value: Fat adaptation impairs performance at intensities above ~80-85% VO2peak; utility probably limited to selected individuals, events or scenarios (discussed for ultra-endurance events >4 h)
findings.finding: Adapting to a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet raises fat use but increases the oxygen cost of exercise and reduces carbohydrate-burning capacity. This harms higher-intensity race segments, so the statement limits the approach to selected individuals, events or scenarios, mainly ultra-endurance.
findings.locator: Theme 5, final para

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: vegetarian diet adequacy rule
findings.value: Vegetarian diets can theoretically support athletic demands with planning for energy and nutrients less abundant or less well absorbed from plants (e.g., iron); vegetarians are a high-risk group for low iron status
findings.finding: The statement says vegetarian eating can in theory meet training needs, but it needs deliberate planning for energy and for nutrients that plants supply less of or that are absorbed less well, especially iron. Vegetarians should have iron checked regularly.
findings.locator: Theme 12 text; Table 4 (maintain adequate iron status)

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.population: Athletes, particularly females, endurance athletes and vegetarians
findings.parameter: iron-rich food selection and bioavailability pairing
findings.value: Include red meats, nuts, seeds, fortified cereals, leafy green vegetables and legumes; pair plant iron with vitamin C or animal iron sources
findings.finding: To keep iron adequate, choose iron-rich foods from animal and plant sources and boost plant-iron absorption by pairing it with vitamin C or animal protein. Females, endurance athletes and vegetarians should be screened.
findings.locator: Table 4 (Nutritional strategies: maintain adequate iron status); Theme 6

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: gluten-free and low-FODMAP diet rule
findings.value: No direct benefit of gluten avoidance in clinically healthy athletes; low-FODMAP eating may reduce exercise-related gut symptoms in susceptible individuals (emerging evidence; Table 4 frames a trial of FODMAP avoidance for irritable bowel syndrome)
findings.finding: Healthy athletes gain nothing directly from cutting gluten. Reducing fermentable carbohydrates may ease exercise-related gut symptoms in those prone to them. Unnecessary restriction can do more harm than good.
findings.locator: Theme 12 text; Table 4 (runner's diarrhoea strategies)

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: food-first and sports-food use rule
findings.value: Food-first; sports foods (drinks, electrolyte supplements, gels/confectionery, protein supplements, liquid meals) when eating food is impractical; five evidence-based performance supplements (caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine, bicarbonate) only when safe, legal, effective and trialled
findings.finding: Base the plan on whole foods. Use sports foods only when real food is impractical. Most performance products lack evidence; only a few may help depending on the event, and banned-substance contamination is a risk.
findings.locator: Theme 8 text; Table 5

findings.citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
findings.parameter: periodisation of energy and carbohydrate to training load
findings.value: Daily energy and carbohydrate vary with session, cycle and season training load (no numeric rule); deliberate low-carbohydrate-availability sessions may amplify adaptation signalling
findings.finding: Energy and carbohydrate intake should change with the day's and phase's training load rather than stay fixed. High carbohydrate availability supports performance sessions. Some sessions deliberately done with low glycogen may boost adaptation but need expert individualisation.
findings.locator: Theme 1 text and Figure 1 caption; Table 1 (Distance row)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.population: Ultra-marathon runners training for single-stage races up to 245 km
findings.parameter: daily energy intake for ultra-endurance training (kcal/kg/day)
findings.value: Evidence statement: ~38-63 kcal/kg/day across sexes, body masses, durations and paces. The stand's own Table 2 (1 h or 3 h/day at 8.4, 10.7 or 13.8 km/h) works out to ~34.8-68.5 kcal/kg/day. Examples: 50 kg female (15% BF), 1 h/day at 8.4 km/h = ~2004 kcal/day (40.1 kcal/kg, Table 3); same runner, 3 h at 13.8 km/h = ~3423 kcal/day; 85 kg male (20% BF), 3 h at 13.8 km/h = ~5372 kcal/day
findings.finding: Estimated daily energy needs in ultra-marathon training vary widely with sex, body and lean mass, session length and pace. The stand advises individualised, periodised intake aimed at energy balance unless the athlete wants to change weight. Its summary range does not exactly match its own tables.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Energy and macronutrient demands; Evidence statement (category B/C); Table 2 and Table 3 (energy intake rows)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: energy cost of running (kcal/km)
findings.value: 200-300 kJ/km (47-71 kcal/km in the training section; 47.8-71.7 kcal/km in the racing section). Race examples: 80 km at 8.0 km/h (~10 h) = ~3460 kcal (50 kg) vs ~4845 kcal (70 kg), i.e. ~346-484 kcal/h; 161 km at 6.5 km/h (~25 h) = ~6922 kcal (50 kg) vs ~9891 kcal (70 kg), i.e. ~277-395 kcal/h
findings.finding: The stand puts the energy cost of running at about 200-300 kJ (roughly 47-72 kcal) per kilometre, with heavier runners at the upper end in its examples. It uses these figures to show that race-day expenditure far exceeds what runners can realistically eat, so some deficit during a race is expected.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Energy and macronutrient demands; Considerations for racing > Energy and macronutrient demands > Energy expenditure

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: daily carbohydrate intake for endurance training (g/kg/day)
findings.value: ~5-8 g/kg/day for frequent intense training (2-3 h/day, 5-6 days/week); 7-10 g/kg/day for greater mileage and/or pace; about 60% of energy. Table 3 examples range 5.2-8.2 g/kg/day
findings.finding: To avoid chronic glycogen depletion, ultra-runners are advised to eat a moderate-to-high carbohydrate diet. About 5-8 g/kg/day suits frequent 2-3 h sessions, rising to 7-10 g/kg/day for greater volume or pace, adjusted for the athlete's capacity to burn fat.
findings.locator: Abstract (Recommendations for Training iii); Considerations for training > Energy and macronutrient demands; Evidence statement (category B/C); Table 3

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day (endurance training)
findings.value: ~1.6-2.1 g/kg/day; up to 2.5 g/kg/day during demanding training or when carbohydrate/energy intake is insufficient. Intakes <1.6 g/kg/day may produce negative nitrogen balance in high-volume endurance athletes; >2.1 g/kg/day unlikely to add further to muscle protein synthesis. General endurance guidelines cited: 1.2-2.1 g/kg/day
findings.finding: Protein intakes around 1.6-2.1 g/kg/day are considered sufficient to maximise muscle protein synthesis and support recovery. Up to 2.5 g/kg/day may be justified in very heavy training or when carbohydrate or total energy is low. Below 1.6 g/kg/day, nitrogen balance may turn negative.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Protein and muscle damage > Protein dose and timing; Evidence statement (category B/C)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: fat g/kg/day (endurance training)
findings.value: 1.0-1.5 g/kg/day; up to ~2.0 g/kg/day for heavier or faster runners; Table 3 examples 1.0-1.5 g/kg/day
findings.finding: Unless a ketogenic approach is deliberately chosen, 1.0-1.5 g/kg/day of fat is likely enough for ultra-runners. Heavier or faster athletes may need close to 2.0 g/kg/day to meet their energy needs.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Energy and macronutrient demands; Evidence statement (category B/C); Table 3

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: macronutrient energy distribution (% of energy)
findings.value: 60% carbohydrate / 15% protein / 25% fat (evidence statement pairs these with 7-10 g/kg/day CHO, 1.3-2.1 g/kg/day protein, 1.0-1.5 g/kg/day fat)
findings.finding: For repeated bouts of endurance training, the stand endorses an energy split of about 60% carbohydrate, 15% protein and 25% fat. It pairs each percentage with a gram-per-kilogram range and notes that duration, pace and body mass change the actual requirement.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Energy and macronutrient demands; Evidence statement (category B/C)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.population: Endurance / ultra-marathon runners (evidence partly from resistance-exercise studies)
findings.parameter: protein dose per feeding and feeding interval
findings.value: ~20 g protein every 3 waking hours (better than ~10 g every 1.5 h or ~40 g every 6 h); 20 g whey maximises post-resistance-exercise synthesis rate, up to 30 g for athletes >85 kg; pre-sleep protein supports overnight synthesis. Racing section: ~20-30 g every 3 h where possible
findings.finding: Spreading protein as roughly 20 g every three waking hours stimulated muscle protein synthesis better than smaller frequent doses or large infrequent ones. About 20 g appears enough after exercise, or around 30 g for athletes over 85 kg. Protein before sleep is also supported.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Protein dose and timing; Evidence statement (category B); Considerations for racing > Protein intake

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: in-race energy intake (kcal/h)
findings.value: 150-400 kcal/h overall; ~150-300 kcal/h for races up to 50 miles (~81 km); ~200-400 kcal/h for longer races; avoid persistent intakes <200 kcal/h in longer races. Field data: finishers 4.6 +/- 1.7 vs non-finishers 2.5 +/- 1.3 kcal/kg/h (161 km)
findings.finding: During ultra-races, runners should aim for 150-400 kcal/h: the lower end for races up to about 81 km and 200-400 kcal/h for longer events. Brief dips for gut distress are acceptable, but sustained intake below 200 kcal/h is discouraged in long races.
findings.locator: Considerations for racing > Energy and macronutrient demands > Energy intake; Evidence statements (category C) under Savory vs. sweet and Strategies to minimize GI distress

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: in-race carbohydrate and protein intake (g/h)
findings.value: Carbohydrate 30-50 g/h; protein 5-10 g/h; plus fat (Table 4 footnote target 1.1-17.7 g/h). The ~90 g/h multiple-transportable-carbohydrate target advocated for events >120 min is judged likely unrealistic for races >6 h
findings.finding: In-race calories should come from a mix of carbohydrate (30-50 g/h), protein (5-10 g/h) and fat, and fattier foods are often preferred in longer races. The authors consider the roughly 90 g/h carbohydrate rate used for shorter events impractical beyond six hours.
findings.locator: Considerations for racing > Carbohydrate versus fat intake; Protein intake; Evidence statement (category C); Table 4 footnote

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: in-race fluid volume (mL/h)
findings.value: 450-750 mL/h (~150-250 mL every 20 min), adjusted for environment, duration, work rate, body mass, tolerance and gut training; individual sweat rate estimated from pre/post nude body mass
findings.finding: The stand recommends drinking about 450-750 mL per hour during races, taken as 150-250 mL every 20 minutes. Volumes should be tuned to heat, pace, body size and gut tolerance, ideally using sweat rates measured by weighing before and after exercise in race-like conditions.
findings.locator: Considerations for racing > Offsetting dehydration; Evidence statement (category C)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: sodium intake to limit exercise-associated hyponatraemia
findings.value: 500-700 mg sodium per L of fluid (abstract states >575 mg/L); ~300-600 mg sodium/h (stated as 1000-2000 mg NaCl) in heat >25 C and/or humidity >60%; avoid drink concentrations above ~1000 mg/L (stated as 50 mmol/L) for palatability. Hyponatraemia defined as serum sodium <135 mmol/L
findings.finding: To reduce hyponatraemia risk in long races, runners should take in 500-700 mg sodium per litre of fluid, or 300-600 mg per hour in hot or humid conditions. Most commercial drinks fall short, and sodium alone cannot offset excessive drinking.
findings.locator: Considerations for racing > Exercise-associated hyponatraemia (EAH); Evidence statement (category C); Abstract (Recommendations for Racing vii)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: pre-race carbohydrate loading (g/kg/day)
findings.value: ~10 g/kg/day for the 48 h before the race; pre-race meal familiar, low-GI carbohydrate, low in fat and fibre
findings.finding: To start races with full glycogen stores, runners should load at about 10 g carbohydrate per kg per day over the final 48 hours while avoiding gut upset. The race-day meal should be familiar, easy to digest and low in fat and fibre.
findings.locator: Considerations for racing > Energy and macronutrient demands > Energy expenditure; Evidence statement (category C)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.population: Endurance athletes after training (evidence from small rehydration trials)
findings.parameter: post-exercise rehydration volume and sodium
findings.value: Drink ~150% of exercise-induced body-mass loss with at least 460 mg/L sodium; volumes up to 200% only help with higher sodium (~61 mmol/L, ~1403 mg/L), and larger volumes are not recommended; commercial sports drinks (~20-25 mmol/L, 460-575 mg/L) are a conservative target
findings.finding: After key sessions, athletes should replace about 150% of the body mass lost as fluid, with at least 460 mg sodium per litre from drinks, food or supplements. Plain water restores balance poorly, and drinking slowly over several hours works best.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Daily hydration guidelines > Post-exercise fluid intake; Evidence statement (category A/B)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: day-to-day body-water fluctuation (weigh-in noise) and pre/post-exercise weighing
findings.value: Daily total body water fluctuates up to ~+/-1% of body weight (0.6-0.9 kg in a 60-90 kg adult), cited second-hand from Cheuvront et al.; pre- to post-exercise body-mass change used to estimate sweat loss
findings.finding: Day-to-day shifts in body water can reach about 1% of body weight, so a single weigh-in can carry hydration noise of that size. Weighing before and after exercise is recommended for estimating fluid loss and planning rehydration.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Daily hydration guidelines > Day-to-day fluid intake; Hydration monitoring strategies; Evidence statement (category A/B)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: daily (non-exercise) hydration rule
findings.value: Drink to thirst (ad libitum) for general daily hydration; similar plasma osmolality seen in ~1.2 L/day and 2-4 L/day drinkers; avoid excessive low-electrolyte fluid (risk of dilutional hyponatraemia)
findings.finding: For ordinary daily hydration, drinking to thirst is usually adequate, and people reach similar hydration with widely varying fluid volumes. Runners are warned against drinking large amounts of water or hypotonic drinks because of myths about flushing the kidneys.
findings.locator: Considerations for training > Daily hydration guidelines > Day-to-day fluid intake; Evidence statement (category B/C)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: carbohydrate drink concentration/osmolality ceiling (GI tolerance)
findings.value: Avoid hyperosmolar solutions >500 mOsm/L and >8% carbohydrate concentration; multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose, fructose and/or maltodextrin) improve absorption and gut comfort; gut-train in advance
findings.finding: High carbohydrate intake, especially drinks above about 8% carbohydrate or 500 mOsm/L, is named as the main nutritional trigger of gut distress in ultra-racing. Mixing carbohydrate sources and practising race nutrition in training are advised to improve tolerance.
findings.locator: Gastrointestinal (GI) distress > Strategies to minimize GI distress; Evidence statements (category C and category B)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: ketogenic / high-fat diet for endurance training
findings.value: Insufficient evidence to support use for ultra-marathon training or performance; caution urged. Definitions cited: classic ketogenic ~4:1 fat:protein or fat:carbohydrate, early CHO cap 50 g/day (80 g/day in Volek et al.); modified ketogenic ~70% of energy from fat; nutritional ketosis ~0.5-3.0 mmol/L
findings.finding: Ketogenic diets raise fat oxidation but have no proven performance benefit for ultra-running and may impair high-intensity work. They are linked to fatigue, gut upset and lower fibre and micronutrient intake. The stand urges caution rather than recommending them.
findings.locator: Nutrition to maximize fuel efficiency > High-fat, ketogenic diets; Evidence statement (category B/C)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: pre-training carbohydrate timing (fat-adaptation sessions)
findings.value: Avoid carbohydrate, especially high-glycaemic foods, within 90 min before sessions aimed at fat oxidation; start euglycaemic. Periodic 'train-low' (e.g. fasted low-to-moderate runs) preferred over chronic restriction
findings.finding: For training aimed at improving fat use, the stand advises against high-glycaemic carbohydrate in the 90 minutes before a session. Occasional low-glycogen sessions are acceptable, but chronic depletion, especially around hard or repeated training, risks low energy availability.
findings.locator: Nutrition to maximize fuel efficiency > Carbohydrate ingestion before training; Train-low, compete-high; Consequences of carbohydrate restriction; Evidence statement (category B)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: in-race caffeine dose
findings.value: Repeated doses of 1-2 mg/kg (70-140 mg for 70 kg) or ~50 mg/h, reserved for latter stages or night running; frequent 4-6 mg/kg boluses not recommended. Elite 161 km runners reported ~912 +/- 322 mg over 15-19 h
findings.finding: Caffeine can help late in long races, especially overnight, but frequent large doses are discouraged. Smaller repeated amounts of about 1-2 mg/kg, or roughly 50 mg per hour, are suggested as safer across many hours, with individual sensitivity considered.
findings.locator: Supplements and drugs > Caffeine; Evidence statement (category A, for efficacy only)

findings.citation: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, Smith L, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2019;16(1):50. doi:10.1186/s12970-019-0312-9
findings.parameter: in-race food options (energy, macronutrients, sodium)
findings.value: Table 4 example serves, e.g. banana 150 g: 135 kcal, 30 g CHO; peanut-butter sandwich: 342 kcal, 38 g CHO, 12 g protein, 17 g fat, 568 mg Na; beef jerky 25 g: 103 kcal, 8 g protein, 520 mg Na; foods with >250 mg Na flagged as sodium-rich. Examples come from a survey of 12 runners and typical commercial serves
findings.finding: In longer races, runners increasingly prefer savoury, fattier and saltier foods over sweet gels and drinks, so varied, calorie-dense options are suggested. Table 4 lists indicative values for example foods; they are brand-based illustrations and should not be treated as food-composition data.
findings.locator: Considerations for racing > Savory vs. sweet; Evidence statement (category D); Table 4

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.population: Female and male athletes (developing to world-class, Tiers 2-5)
findings.parameter: energy availability (EA) equation
findings.value: EA (kcal/kg FFM/day) = [dietary energy intake (kcal) - exercise energy expenditure (kcal)] / fat-free mass (kg), per day
findings.finding: Energy availability is the dietary energy remaining for body functions after exercise costs are subtracted, scaled to fat-free mass. Low energy availability means intake falls short of what the body needs once exercise is paid for, and it spans a continuum from benign to harmful.
findings.locator: Introduction and Box 1 'Definitions: Low Energy Availability' (pp.1073-1074). Read via the BJSM typeset PDF hosted by CASEM (header '2024;57:1073-1098')

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.population: Derived from habitually sedentary females; applied to athletes
findings.parameter: energy availability zones (kcal/kg FFM/day)
findings.value: >=45 high EA (mass gain and growth); ~45 adequate (weight maintenance, body function); 30-45 reduced (body mass/fat loss); <=30 LEA with health implications. Derived from short-term lab studies in small samples of sedentary females; intended as a guide, not a diagnostic endpoint
findings.finding: Early lab work in sedentary women produced EA zones: about 45 for maintenance, 30-45 for fat loss, and 30 or below for health risk. The consensus warns that these came from small, short studies and that thresholds differ widely by individual, sex and body system, so no firm clinical cut-off should be set.
findings.locator: Clinical applications > Assessment of EA (pp.1078 and 1080)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.parameter: sex-specific low-EA threshold
findings.value: Universal 30 kcal/kg FFM/day cut-off in females is debated; in males the level at which REDs symptoms appear is less understood but appears lower (~9-25 kcal/kg FFM/day)
findings.finding: A single 30 kcal/kg FFM/day threshold is contested even for women. Men seem to tolerate lower energy availability, roughly 9-25 kcal/kg FFM/day, before disturbances appear, yet problematic LEA still harms their hormones, bone, immunity and performance. The updated models prefer qualitative judgement to universal numeric thresholds.
findings.locator: Key scientific advances > REDs in male athletes (p.1077); REDs Conceptual Models (p.1077); Assessment of EA (p.1080)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.population: Male endurance athletes; young females; elite endurance athletes
findings.parameter: low carbohydrate availability (LCA) as defined in cited studies (g/kg/day)
findings.value: LCHF arms in the cited <=6-day studies of male endurance athletes used <3 g CHO/kg body mass/day; these raised bone-resorption markers, post-exercise IL-6 and hepcidin, sometimes without LEA. LEA intervention studies typically cut CHO by 25-60%. 3-day study in young females: hepcidin +264% (low energy, low CHO) vs +69% (low energy, higher CHO). ~3.5 weeks LCHF in elite endurance athletes impaired bone-remodelling markers
findings.finding: In short studies, carbohydrate intake below about 3 g/kg/day worsened bone, immune and iron markers, either on its own or on top of low energy availability. The consensus counts six such studies since 2019. It does not set a carbohydrate floor; it asks that future LEA studies control carbohydrate intake.
findings.locator: Key scientific advances > The magnifying impact of LCA in the context of REDs (p.1076)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.parameter: LEA exposure duration categories
findings.value: Short-term LEA: a few days to weeks; medium-term: weeks to months; long-term: months to years. Cut-offs need validation and may differ by sex and LEA severity/duration
findings.finding: Emerging definitions class LEA exposure as short-term (days to weeks), medium-term (weeks to months) or long-term (months to years). The consensus stresses that these boundaries are unvalidated. Brief mild LEA does not always cause harm, whereas problematic exposure leads to REDs.
findings.locator: Key scientific advances > Time-course of LEA resulting in REDs (p.1076)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.parameter: adaptable vs problematic LEA classification
findings.value: Adaptable LEA: short-term, benign, mild and quickly reversible biomarker changes (e.g. monitored, mindful body-composition manipulation or a scheduled intensified-training block). Problematic LEA: prolonged and/or severe, with persistent disruption and signs/symptoms
findings.finding: The consensus treats LEA as a continuum. Brief, monitored reductions such as a supervised body-composition phase can be benign and reversible, while prolonged or severe deficits are problematic and cause REDs. Body-composition work can be periodised safely only with expert guidance, readiness, recovery and maintained health.
findings.locator: Box 1 Definitions (Adaptable LEA; Problematic LEA) (p.1074); What is REDs? (p.1075)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.population: Premenopausal/andropausal adult athletes (thresholds mostly from adults)
findings.parameter: REDs CAT2 indicators (referral triggers)
findings.value: Severe primary (count double): primary amenorrhoea; secondary amenorrhoea >=12 missed cycles; clinically low testosterone (males). Primary: secondary amenorrhoea 3-11 missed cycles; testosterone or T3 in lowest quartile of reference range; >=1 high-risk or >=2 low-risk bone stress injuries in 2 y (or >=6 months out); BMD Z-score <-1; EDE-Q global >2.30 (F) / >1.68 (M) or diagnosed ED. Secondary: oligomenorrhoea >35 days between periods (<=8/yr); 1 low-risk BSI; elevated LDL/total cholesterol; diagnosed depression/anxiety. Potential (unscored): RMR <30 kcal/kg FFM/day or RMR ratio <0.90; adult HR <40 bpm; BP <90/60 mmHg; low libido; low BMI
findings.finding: The CAT2 tool weights self-reportable and clinical signs such as missed periods, low hormones, bone stress injuries and eating-disorder scores. An app could use some of these as prompts to seek clinical assessment, but the tool is not diagnostic without a physician and a differential diagnosis.
findings.locator: IOC REDs CAT2 section (p.1083); Table 4 IOC REDs CAT2 Severity/Risk Assessment tool (p.1085)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.population: Athletes (adapted from eating-disorder and cardiovascular guidance)
findings.parameter: serious medical red flags requiring immediate care
findings.value: <=75% of median BMI for age and sex; electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypophosphataemia); prolonged QTc or severe bradycardia (adult HR <=30 bpm; adolescent <=45 bpm); BP <=90/45 mmHg; orthostatic drop >20 mmHg systolic and >10 mmHg diastolic; syncope, seizures, cardiac failure, pancreatitis; failed outpatient eating-disorder treatment
findings.finding: These findings call for immediate medical attention, possible hospitalisation and removal from training and competition. An app that detects related user-entered values, such as a very low BMI, should stop giving targets and direct the user to urgent care.
findings.locator: Table 5 Serious medical indicators of REDs and/or EDs (p.1085)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.parameter: CAT2 traffic-light participation levels
findings.value: Four levels: green (full training and competition), yellow (continued monitoring), orange (intensive medical intervention and monitoring), red (full medical support; consider removal from training and competition). Replaces the 2015 three-colour system
findings.finding: The 2023 tool sorts athletes into four severity/risk colours, each tied to participation guidance from full participation to possible removal. The authors stress that it is less reliable when indicators cannot be measured and must not be used alone for diagnosis.
findings.locator: IOC REDs CAT2 section (pp.1083-1084); Figure 6 caption (p.1084); Box 2 (p.1086)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.parameter: body-composition assessment method and handling
findings.value: Proposed methods: skinfolds, DXA, B-mode ultrasound; 'doubly indirect' regression-based methods judged invalid and presentation/hydration-sensitive; assessment under 18 y only for medical purposes; results are confidential health data requiring informed consent
findings.finding: Only skinfolds, DXA and B-mode ultrasound are proposed for athlete body composition; easy regression-based estimates are judged unreliable. Trained staff should run assessments with eating-behaviour prescreening, and results are confidential health data shared only with consent.
findings.locator: Clinical applications > Body composition assessment and management (pp.1080, 1082-1083)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, Burke LM, Constantini N, Hackney AC, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994
findings.population: Exercising females with REDs biomarkers; athletes generally
findings.parameter: remediation rule when LEA is suspected
findings.value: Primary treatment: restore optimal EA non-pharmacologically via diet and exercise changes with adequate macro- and micronutrients; poor intake explains more perturbation than excess exercise; the one 12-month intention-to-treat RCT had 57% drop-out, with menses resuming in some but bone loss not halted
findings.finding: Treating REDs starts with restoring energy availability by eating more and adjusting training, since low intake drives most of the harm. Recovery evidence is thin: the only year-long trial lost over half its participants and improved some outcomes but not others. A multidisciplinary team is recommended.
findings.locator: Prevention and treatment of REDs > Treatment (tertiary prevention) principles of REDs (p.1084)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: EA operational definition (exercise energy expenditure component)
findings.value: EA = [EI (kcal) - EEE (kcal)] / FFM (kg); EEE is only the extra energy the exercise bout costs beyond what normal daily living would have used in that time; FFM chosen as the most metabolically active tissue
findings.finding: In the EA equation, exercise energy expenditure should count only the extra energy the workout costs beyond normal daily living, not the gross energy of the session. The result is expressed per kilogram of fat-free mass.
findings.locator: Low Energy Availability section (IJSNEM p.317). Full text read in the IJSNEM co-publication (PMID 29771168); BJSM version itself was not opened

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.population: Women in laboratory trials; applied to athletes
findings.parameter: optimal energy availability
findings.value: ~45 kcal/kg FFM/day (188 kJ/kg FFM/day) typically achieves healthy physiological function, based on controlled laboratory trials in women (Loucks & Heath 1994; Loucks & Thuma 2003)
findings.finding: Tightly controlled lab studies in women found that an energy availability of about 45 kcal per kg fat-free mass per day usually supports healthy physiological function. The consensus presents this as the typical optimum.
findings.locator: Low Energy Availability section (IJSNEM p.317)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: low energy availability threshold
findings.value: <30 kcal/kg FFM/day (125 kJ/kg FFM/day) substantially perturbs many body systems (historical LEA threshold); ~equal to average RMR; does not predict amenorrhoea in all women; cross-sectional mean EA 30.9 (amenorrhoeic) vs 36.9 (eumenorrhoeic) kcal/kg FFM/day (Reed et al. 2015)
findings.finding: Many body systems are markedly disturbed below 30 kcal/kg FFM/day, roughly average resting metabolic rate, so this became the traditional cut-off. Newer studies show it does not predict loss of periods in every woman, and no precise threshold for menstrual disturbance was found.
findings.locator: Low Energy Availability (IJSNEM p.317); Health Effects > Menstrual Function (p.319)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: reliability of EA estimated from self-reported logs
findings.value: No standardised EA protocol (collection days, intake method, EEE method, FFM method); self-reported energy intake is the largest error source; EEE and lifestyle activity hard to capture; EA not recommended as a stand-alone diagnostic
findings.finding: Calculating energy availability outside a lab is unreliable: there is no standard method, self-reported intake is the biggest source of error, and exercise expenditure is hard to measure. Expert bodies therefore do not endorse EA as a stand-alone diagnostic, so an app's EA estimate should be treated as approximate.
findings.locator: Measurement of EA (IJSNEM pp.317-318)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: rapid weight-loss LEA indicator (% body mass per month)
findings.value: >=10% body-weight loss within one month is a proposed LEA indicator (cited second-hand from De Souza et al. 2014, Female Athlete Triad Coalition)
findings.finding: Losing 10% or more of body weight within a month is listed as a proposed marker of low energy availability, alongside low BMI. It can serve as a hard alarm on loss rate, but it is a warning sign, not a safe-rate guideline, and the value comes second-hand from the Triad Coalition statement.
findings.locator: Health Effects > Bone Health (IJSNEM pp.319-320)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: BMI floor indicating LEA
findings.value: BMI <=17.5 kg/m2 (adults); <85% of expected body weight (adolescents); both associated with higher risk of low BMD in both sexes (cited from De Souza et al. 2014)
findings.finding: Low BMI is an imperfect proxy for low energy availability, but a BMI of 17.5 kg/m2 or less is a proposed warning sign and is linked to higher risk of low bone density in men and women.
findings.locator: Health Effects > Bone Health (IJSNEM pp.319-320)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.population: Elite male and female rowers; normal-weight women
findings.parameter: metabolic adaptation to energy deficit
findings.value: Elite rowers: 4 weeks with training load +21% and unchanged energy intake significantly reduced RMR and altered pacing/reduced 5 km time-trial performance (Woods et al. 2017); normal-weight women with induced deficits lost less weight over 3 months than predicted; moderate deficit lowered RMR, severe deficit lowered leptin, T3 and IGF-1 and raised ghrelin (Koehler et al. 2017)
findings.finding: Sustained deficits trigger energy-saving adaptations: resting metabolic rate fell when training rose without extra food, and weight loss over months fell short of predictions. An adaptive app should therefore expect observed loss to lag the calculated deficit.
findings.locator: Health Effects > Metabolic (IJSNEM p.320); Performance Consequences of LEA (p.321)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: male endocrine response to short-term LEA
findings.value: Koehler et al. 2016 (6 male habitual exercisers, four 4-day conditions): 15 vs 40 kcal/kg FFM/day, each with and without exercise; LEA reduced leptin -53% to -56% and insulin -34% to -38% vs baseline; no significant change in ghrelin, T3, testosterone or IGF-1. EA threshold and duration inducing RED-S in men unknown
findings.finding: In a tiny short-term study, four days at 15 kcal/kg FFM/day cut leptin by about half and insulin by about a third in men, without changing testosterone or thyroid hormone. The consensus says the threshold and duration that cause RED-S in men remain unknown.
findings.locator: Low Energy Availability in Male Athletes (IJSNEM p.318); Health Effects > Endocrine (p.319)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: EA during physique contest preparation
findings.value: Prolonged EA ~20-25 kcal/kg FFM/day in the final stage of male bodybuilding contest diets may be pathological; ~4% total body fat accompanied by endocrine dysfunction, mood disturbance, loss of muscle mass and strength (Fagerberg 2017)
findings.finding: Male bodybuilders held at about 20-25 kcal/kg FFM/day late in contest diets showed signs that may be pathological. Those reaching around 4% body fat lost muscle and strength and had hormonal and mood problems, which argues against deep, prolonged cuts.
findings.locator: Health Effects > Psychological (IJSNEM pp.320-321)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: dietary features that may compound LEA
findings.value: High fibre intake, stimulants, artificial sweeteners, low-energy-density foods, high dietary restraint, and poor spread of energy across the day
findings.finding: Several diet traits that often accompany low energy availability may worsen it: very high fibre, stimulants, artificial sweeteners, low-energy-density foods, strong dietary restraint and uneven energy spread through the day. Food suggestions for active users in a deficit should avoid stacking these.
findings.locator: Measurement of EA (IJSNEM p.318)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.parameter: calcium and vitamin D intake targets (bone health)
findings.value: Calcium 1000 mg/day (men and women 19-50 y), 1300 mg/day (9-18 y) (citing US DHHS 2015); vitamin D 600-800 IU/day (citing USDA 2011); serum 25(OH)D goal >30 ng/mL, levels <30 ng/mL associated with more bone stress injury
findings.finding: For bone health in LEA, the consensus restates US intake recommendations for calcium and vitamin D and a serum vitamin D goal above 30 ng/mL. These are secondary citations, so the app should cite the primary NASEM/USDA documents for these values.
findings.locator: Treatment of RED-S > Non-pharmacologic Management (IJSNEM pp.322-323)

findings.citation: Mountjoy M, Sundgot-Borgen J, Burke L, Ackerman KE, Blauwet C, Constantini N, et al. IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(11):687-97. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099193. Co-published as: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(4):316-31. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0136
findings.population: Female and male athletes with RED-S
findings.parameter: LEA treatment approach and recovery time course
findings.value: Increase food intake and adjust food choices and energy spread, individualised and periodised to expenditure; reduce or stop exercise if deficit is severe; education may suffice for unintentional undereating; menstrual function may recover over months, bone more slowly and possibly incompletely; combined oral contraceptives not recommended to restore menses/BMD
findings.finding: Correcting LEA mainly means eating more and changing food choices and timing, cutting training if needed. Menstrual function can take months to return, and bone recovers more slowly, sometimes incompletely. Early input from a sports dietitian is advised.
findings.locator: Treatment of RED-S > Non-pharmacologic Management; Pharmacologic Interventions (IJSNEM pp.322-323)

findings.citation: Loucks AB, Thuma JR. Luteinizing hormone pulsatility is disrupted at a threshold of energy availability in regularly menstruating women. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2003;88(1):297-311. doi:10.1210/jc.2002-020369
findings.population: 29 regularly menstruating, habitually sedentary young women of normal body composition
findings.parameter: EA threshold for LH pulsatility disruption (females, kcal/kg LBM/day)
findings.value: LH pulsatility unaffected at 30 kcal/kg LBM/day (P>0.3); below 30, LH pulse frequency fell and amplitude rose (all P<0.04). Protocol: 5 days, early follicular phase; supervised exercise 15 kcal/kg LBM/day at 70% aerobic capacity; EA 45 vs 10, 20 or 30 kcal/kg LBM/day in two randomised trials >=2 months apart
findings.finding: In a small within-subject trial of sedentary young women, five days at 30 kcal/kg lean body mass per day left LH pulsatility intact, while lower levels disrupted it, more so in women with short luteal phases. This underpins the often-cited threshold of 30, but it is short-term, female-only and expressed per kg LBM.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 12519869) only; full text not accessed

findings.citation: Loucks AB, Kiens B, Wright HH. Energy availability in athletes. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S7-15. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.588958
findings.parameter: diet-management metric: energy availability vs energy balance
findings.value: Rule (no number in abstract): manage athletes' diets using energy availability (intake minus exercise expenditure) rather than energy balance
findings.finding: This review, which updates the 2003 IOC consensus-conference review, argues that energy availability is more useful than energy balance for managing athletes' diets. It also summarises the existence, causes and clinical consequences of low energy availability. The abstract gives no thresholds.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 21793767) only; full text not accessed

findings.citation: Loucks AB, Kiens B, Wright HH. Energy availability in athletes. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S7-15. doi:10.1080/02640414.2011.588958
findings.parameter: appetite compensation for exercise energy expenditure
findings.value: Rule (no number in abstract): appetite fails to raise ad libitum energy intake enough to compensate for exercise energy expenditure
findings.finding: The review summarises research showing that appetite often does not raise spontaneous intake enough to cover the energy spent in exercise. An app should therefore not assume hunger will correct a training-induced deficit, and should prompt deliberate intake increases on heavy training days.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 21793767) only; full text not accessed

findings.citation: Stellingwerff T, Mountjoy M, McCluskey WT, Ackerman KE, Verhagen E, Heikura IA. Review of the scientific rationale, development and validation of the International Olympic Committee Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Clinical Assessment Tool: V.2 (IOC REDs CAT2)-by a subgroup of the IOC consensus on REDs. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1109-18. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106914
findings.population: Athletes; intended for qualified clinical professionals
findings.parameter: REDs screening and escalation process
findings.value: Three steps: (1) initial screening with validated questionnaires/clinical interview; (2) severity/risk stratification from weighted primary and secondary indicators into four traffic-light levels (green, yellow, orange, red) with sport-participation guidance; (3) physician-led diagnosis and treatment plan. No single validated diagnostic test exists
findings.finding: Because REDs has many signs and no single validated test, CAT2 moves from screening to a four-colour severity rating from weighted indicators, then to physician diagnosis. Experts validated the indicators by voting. A consumer app can at most screen and refer; diagnosis belongs to clinicians.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 37752002) only; full text blocked (BMJ HTTP 403)

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad: 1st International Conference held in San Francisco, California, May 2012 and 2nd International Conference held in Indianapolis, Indiana, May 2013. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119. doi:10.1097/JSM.0000000000000085.
findings.population: Physically active girls and women; female athletes
findings.parameter: energy availability floor kcal/kg FFM/day
findings.value: 30 kcal/kg FFM/day (threshold below which reproductive, metabolic and bone disruption occurs in short-term lab studies of women)
findings.finding: The panel cites short controlled experiments in women. Below about 30 kcal per kg fat-free mass per day, reproductive hormones, metabolism and bone turnover get worse. Outside the lab this index is imprecise, because intake, exercise expenditure and body composition are all hard to measure.
findings.locator: 'How is Low EA Diagnosed?' section (read in the Clin J Sport Med 24(2):96-119 co-publication, full text)

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: energy availability target kcal/kg FFM/day
findings.value: >=45 kcal/kg FFM/day (adequacy target; also the treatment target when EA can be estimated reliably)
findings.finding: Physically active women should aim for energy availability of at least 45 kcal per kg fat-free mass per day to cover all physiological functions. The same figure is the treatment target once EA can be estimated reliably.
findings.locator: 'How is Low EA Diagnosed?' (final sentence) and 'Treatment Targets for Low EA' sections, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: energy availability equation
findings.value: EA = (energy intake kcal - exercise energy expenditure kcal) / kg FFM; exercise kcal = MET x body mass (kg) x duration (h), per the 2011 Compendium of Physical Activities
findings.finding: Daily EA is energy intake minus exercise energy expenditure, divided by fat-free mass. The panel recommends estimating exercise expenditure with the 2011 Compendium (MET x kg x hours). All inputs carry error, including self-reported intake, expenditure estimates and body-fat estimates.
findings.locator: 'How is Low EA Diagnosed?' section, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: body-weight stability as evidence of adequate energy availability
findings.value: Not valid: a stable weight can coexist with low EA because physiological suppression restores energy balance
findings.finding: Low EA cannot be diagnosed from energy balance or a weight trend. Athletes in a chronic deficit can suppress physiological functions until their weight stabilises. A flat weigh-in trend therefore must not be read as adequate energy availability.
findings.locator: 'How is Low EA Diagnosed?' section, first paragraph, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: low-energy-store BMI flag
findings.value: Adults: BMI <17.5 kg/m2; adolescents: <85% of expected body weight (absolute BMI cut-offs not used for adolescents)
findings.finding: Overt low energy availability is suggested by low energy stores: a BMI under 17.5 kg/m2, or under 85% of expected weight in adolescents. When weight is not especially low, detailed intake and expenditure data are needed to diagnose low EA.
findings.locator: 'How is Low EA Diagnosed?' section, second paragraph, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: measured/predicted RMR ratio indicating chronic energy deficiency
findings.value: <0.90 (other markers: reduced RMR and low T3)
findings.finding: In people without disordered eating or recent weight loss, physiological adaptation to chronic energy deficiency can still show. The markers are a reduced resting metabolic rate, low triiodothyronine, and a measured-to-predicted RMR ratio below 0.90.
findings.locator: 'How is Low EA Diagnosed?' section, second paragraph, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: rate of recent weight loss risk flag (% body mass per month)
findings.value: Moderate risk (1 point): 5 to <10% in 1 month, BMI 17.5 to <18.5, or <90% expected weight; high risk (2 points): >=10% in 1 month, BMI <=17.5, or <85% expected weight
findings.finding: The cumulative risk worksheet scores low BMI or rapid weight loss. Losing 5 to under 10% of body weight in a month is moderate risk. Losing 10% or more in a month is high risk and, on its own, a reason for a bone-density (DXA) scan.
findings.locator: Figure 4 (Cumulative Risk Assessment) and 'Who Should Get DXA Scans for BMD Testing?' list, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: Triad cumulative risk score and clearance bands
findings.value: Six factors each scored 0/1/2 (low EA/DE, low BMI, delayed menarche, oligo/amenorrhoea, low BMD, stress reaction/fracture); total 0-1 = full clearance; 2-5 = provisional/limited clearance; >=6 = restricted/disqualified
findings.finding: Six risk factors are each scored 0, 1 or 2 points and then summed. A total of 0-1 points means low risk (full clearance), 2-5 means moderate risk (provisional or limited clearance), and 6 or more means high risk (restricted from training and competition).
findings.locator: Figure 4 (Cumulative Risk Assessment) and Figure 5 (Clearance/RTP by risk stratification), CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: menstrual frequency risk cut-points (menses per 12 months)
findings.value: >9 menses/12 mo = low risk; 6-9 = moderate risk (the DXA-indication text says 6 to 8); <6 = high risk; the paper says evaluation of secondary amenorrhoea in girls can begin after >=3 months of missed menses
findings.finding: Menstrual frequency is scored for risk. More than 9 cycles a year is low risk, 6-9 is moderate (the body text says 6-8) and fewer than 6 is high. The paper says secondary amenorrhoea in girls can be evaluated after 3 or more months of missed periods.
findings.locator: Figure 4; 'Who Should Get DXA Scans' list; 'What are the Most Important Risk Factors to Screen for?', CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.population: Female athletes with low EA or functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea
findings.parameter: energy intake increase to restore energy availability
findings.value: +20-30% over baseline energy needs, or enough to gain ~0.5 kg every 7-10 days; e.g. +200-600 kcal/d, reached over several months, from a 2000 kcal/d baseline
