findings.finding: To restore body weight, energy intake should rise gradually. Start with roughly 20-30% above baseline needs, or enough to gain about 0.5 kg every 7-10 days. For someone eating 2000 kcal/d, that is 200-600 kcal/d more, built up over several months.
findings.locator: 'Treatment Targets for Low EA' section, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: minimum energy intake during low-EA treatment kcal/day
findings.value: >=2000 kcal/d; more is likely needed depending on exercise energy expenditure
findings.finding: One treatment target for low energy availability sets energy intake at no less than 2000 kcal per day. The panel adds that more is usually required, depending on how much energy the athlete spends in exercise.
findings.locator: 'Treatment Targets for Low EA' bullet list, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.population: Underweight or amenorrhoeic female athletes; case studies and retrospective data
findings.parameter: weight-restoration targets for low EA
findings.value: BMI >=18.5 kg/m2 or >=90% of predicted weight; reverse recent weight loss; weight gain seen before menses returned ~5-10% of body weight (1-4 kg)
findings.finding: Treatment targets include reversing recent weight loss, reaching a weight associated with normal menses, and a BMI of at least 18.5 or at least 90% of predicted weight. In studies, menses returned after gains of about 5-10% of body weight (1-4 kg). Individuals vary.
findings.locator: 'Specific Nonpharmacologic Recommendations' and 'Treatment Targets for Low EA' sections, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: weigh-in frequency during low-EA treatment
findings.value: Weekly when starting treatment; same scale, minimal clothing (shorts and t-shirt)
findings.finding: Successful treatment needs standardised, periodic weight checks on the same scale in minimal clothing. How often depends on how much weight governs health and eligibility to compete. Weekly is reasonable when a treatment programme begins.
findings.locator: 'Steps in a Plan to Increase EA', paragraph after Step 2, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: clinician referral triggers
findings.value: Any one Triad component prompts evaluation for the others. Referral depends on cause: inadvertent undereating or intentional weight loss without DE = nutrition education; DE = physician plus sports dietitian; clinical ED = physician, sports dietitian and mental-health professional. Anorexia nervosa with BMI <16 kg/m2, or bulimia with purging >4 times/week = categorical restriction from training and competition; return depends on ED treatment including BMI >18.5 kg/m2, cessation of bingeing/purging and close follow-up
findings.finding: Finding any one Triad component should trigger a check for the others. An inadvertent energy shortfall may need only nutrition education. A clinical eating disorder needs physician, dietitian and psychological care. Very low BMI or frequent purging rules out training until treatment milestones are met.
findings.locator: 'What are the Best Tools to Screen for the Triad?'; 'Specific Nonpharmacologic Recommendations' pathways 1-4; Figure 5 legend, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: calcium intake mg/day
findings.value: 1000-1300 mg/d, from calcium-rich foods
findings.finding: For athletes with Triad components, the panel recommends calcium-rich foods to reach an optimal calcium intake of 1000-1300 mg per day. It cites the Institute of Medicine for this range.
findings.locator: 'What Therapy can We Offer?' > 'Calcium and vitamin D', CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: vitamin D intake and serum status
findings.value: 600 IU/d intake (IOM, adolescents and adults up to age 70); serum 25(OH)D kept at 32-50 ng/mL; higher doses if deficient
findings.finding: Vitamin D status should be optimised. The panel cites the IOM intake of 600 IU per day for ages up to 70 and recommends keeping serum vitamin D between 32 and 50 ng/mL. Higher doses may be needed when levels are deficient or insufficient.
findings.locator: 'What Therapy can We Offer?' > 'Calcium and vitamin D', CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: food choices to raise energy availability
findings.value: Prefer real foods over supplements; energy- and nutrient-dense options such as fortified milk drinks, fish, healthy oils, nuts, avocados and dried fruit; attend to calcium, vitamin D, iron, zinc and vitamin K
findings.finding: Meal plans to raise EA should favour real foods over meal supplements. They should include energy- and nutrient-dense items such as fortified milk drinks, fish, oils, nuts, avocado and dried fruit, while keeping variety, macronutrient balance and key micronutrients in view.
findings.locator: 'Steps in a Plan to Increase EA', Step 2, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: De Souza MJ, Nattiv A, Joy E, Misra M, Williams NI, Mallinson RJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play of the Female Athlete Triad. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48(4):289. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218. Co-published: Clin J Sport Med. 2014;24(2):96-119.
findings.parameter: meal frequency when raising energy intake
findings.value: Small, frequent meals through the day if large caloric loads cause GI discomfort; timed around practice and competition; target times of day when intake is low (no numeric frequency given)
findings.finding: If high-calorie meals cause stomach discomfort, eat small, frequent meals across the day, timed around training and competition. Look for periods of the day when intake is particularly low, and adjust the plan across the competitive season.
findings.locator: 'Steps in a Plan to Increase EA', Step 2, CJSM co-publication

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: maximum body-mass loss during exercise (% body mass)
findings.value: Prevent >2% body-weight loss from water deficit (Evidence A: >2% can impair aerobic performance, especially in warm or hot weather; Evidence B: can impair cognitive performance)
findings.finding: Drinking during exercise aims to prevent water-deficit losses above 2% of body weight, and large electrolyte shifts. Losses above 2% can reduce aerobic and mental performance in temperate to hot conditions. Goulet's 2013 meta-analysis disputes this threshold for self-paced time trials.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract; 'Durante el ejercicio' and Table 6 (Effects of Hydration), pp. 9-10 and 15-18 of the ACSM-hosted Spanish translation (English full text paywalled)

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: pre-exercise fluid volume mL/kg
findings.value: ~5-7 mL/kg body weight, drunk slowly >=4 h before; if no urine or dark urine, another ~3-5 mL/kg ~2 h before; drinks with 20-50 mEq/L sodium, or salty snacks, help retain fluid
findings.finding: When pre-exercise hydration is needed, sip about 5-7 mL/kg at least 4 hours beforehand. Add 3-5 mL/kg about 2 hours before if urine is absent or dark. Sodium-containing drinks or salty snacks help retention. Hyperhydrating with glycerol is not advantageous.
findings.locator: 'Reposición de líquidos > Antes del ejercicio', pp. 14-15 of the ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: sweat-rate estimation from body-mass change
findings.value: Sweat loss = pre-exercise body mass - post-exercise body mass, corrected for urine and fluid drunk; 1 g lost = 1 mL sweat; ignoring respiratory and carbon-exchange losses overestimates by ~5-15%, which needs no correction for exercise <3 h
findings.finding: Changes in body mass across a session estimate sweat loss, assuming 1 g equals 1 mL of sweat and correcting for fluid drunk and urine passed. Weigh nude where possible. For sessions under 3 hours, respiratory and metabolic mass losses can be ignored.
findings.locator: 'Evaluación de la hidratación', p. 7 of the ACSM-hosted Spanish translation; Table 6 (Evidence A)

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.population: Active adults (baseline data from active men; note on women)
findings.parameter: euhydrated baseline body-mass protocol and day-to-day noise
findings.value: Nude, after voiding, on waking; >=3 consecutive mornings; fluctuation <1% when euhydrated and in energy balance; women may need more readings (luteal phase can add >2 kg)
findings.finding: Morning nude weight after voiding stays within about 1% in well-hydrated people in energy balance. Establish a baseline from at least three consecutive mornings. Women may need more readings, because the luteal phase can add over 2 kg. Changes in eating and bowel habits also shift it.
findings.locator: 'Evaluación de la hidratación', p. 7 and Table 3 (p. 8), ACSM-hosted Spanish translation; Evidence B

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: urine and biomarker euhydration cut-offs
findings.value: First-morning urine specific gravity <=1.020 or urine osmolality <=700 mOsmol/kg (Evidence B); Table 3: plasma osmolality <290 mOsmol, body-mass change <1%, total body water change <2%
findings.finding: A person whose first-morning urine has a specific gravity of 1.020 or less, or an osmolality of 700 mOsmol/kg or less, can be considered euhydrated. Urine collected during rapid rehydration is misleading. Use first-morning samples or samples taken after hydration has been stable.
findings.locator: 'Evaluación de la hidratación', pp. 6-8 and Table 3, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.population: Athletes in prolonged exercise in hot weather
findings.parameter: sports-drink electrolyte and carbohydrate composition
findings.value: ~20-30 mEq/L sodium (chloride as anion), ~2-5 mEq/L potassium, ~5-10% carbohydrate (citing IOM guidance for prolonged activity in heat)
findings.finding: For prolonged activity in the heat, a fluid-replacement drink may contain about 20-30 mEq/L sodium, 2-5 mEq/L potassium and 5-10% carbohydrate. Whether each is needed depends on intensity, duration and climate. Gels, bars and foods can supply the same components.
findings.locator: 'Durante el ejercicio', p. 17, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: carbohydrate intake during exercise g/h
findings.value: ~30-60 g/h for high-intensity exercise of ~1 h or more, or longer lower-intensity exercise; a single fluid-plus-carbohydrate drink should be <=8% carbohydrate (0.5-1 L/h of a 6-8% drink gives 30-80 g/h)
findings.finding: About 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour maintains blood glucose and performance in hard sessions of about an hour or more. Drink mixes should stay at or below 8% carbohydrate to avoid slowing gastric emptying. Mixed sugars give higher delivery rates.
findings.locator: 'Durante el ejercicio', p. 17, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: in-race drinking starting point L/h (marathon)
findings.value: 0.4-0.8 L/h ad libitum (higher for faster, heavier runners in warm weather; lower for slower, lighter runners in the cool); predicted running sweat rates ~0.4-1.8 L/h (Table 4)
findings.finding: A suggested starting point for euhydrated marathoners is 0.4-0.8 L/h, adjusted for body size, pace and weather. Modelling (Table 5) shows that one rate for all runners leads small runners to overdrink and large runners to over-dehydrate. Measure your own weight change instead.
findings.locator: 'Durante el ejercicio', pp. 15-17, Tables 4-5, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: post-exercise rehydration volume L per kg lost
findings.value: ~1.5 L of fluid per kg of body mass lost for rapid, complete recovery (aggressive rehydration when recovery is <12 h); IV only for >7% loss, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea, or inability to drink
findings.finding: With enough time, normal meals and drinks restore euhydration. For fast, complete recovery, drink about 1.5 L per kg lost, spread over time and with sodium, to offset extra urine output. Intravenous fluids are rarely better than drinking.
findings.locator: 'Después del ejercicio', pp. 19-20, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: sweat electrolyte concentrations mEq/L
findings.value: Sodium ~35 (range 10-70); potassium ~5 (3-15); calcium ~1 (0.3-2); magnesium ~0.8 (0.2-1.5); chloride ~30 (5-60) mEq/L; heat acclimatisation can lower sweat sodium by >50%
findings.finding: Average sweat sodium is about 35 mEq/L, but it varies widely with genetics, diet, sweat rate and acclimatisation. Sweat sodium concentration rises with sweat rate. Heat-acclimatised people usually have much lower sweat sodium for a given sweat rate.
findings.locator: 'Requerimientos de líquidos y electrolitos', p. 5, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: exercise-associated hyponatraemia thresholds and cause
findings.value: Symptoms possible when plasma sodium falls rapidly to ~130 mmol/L or lower; <125 mmol/L more severe; <120 mmol/L raises the risk of cerebral oedema; drinking beyond sweat rate is the main cause (Evidence A)
findings.finding: Symptomatic hyponatraemia can occur in endurance events, mainly from drinking more than is sweated. Smaller, slower runners who drink heavily are most at risk. In events under 4 hours it usually reflects overdrinking. Women appear to be at higher risk (Evidence C).
findings.locator: 'Salud > Hiponatremia asociada al ejercicio', pp. 11-12, and 'Sexo', pp. 12-13, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: dehydration level affecting strength and anaerobic performance
findings.value: 3-5% body-mass loss probably does not reduce muscle strength or anaerobic performance (Evidence A and B); a 3% loss has little effect on aerobic performance in the cold (Evidence B)
findings.finding: ACSM concludes that dehydration of 3-5% of body mass probably does not impair strength or anaerobic performance. NATA 2017 disagrees and reports decrements above 2%. Treat strength-related hydration thresholds as uncertain.
findings.locator: 'Efectos de la hidratación > Fisiología y rendimiento', pp. 9-10, and Table 6, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-90. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597.
findings.parameter: caffeine and alcohol effect on daily hydration
findings.value: Caffeine <180 mg/day is unlikely to raise daily urine output or cause dehydration (Evidence B); alcohol can raise urine output and delay rehydration and should be moderated after exercise (Evidence B)
findings.finding: Relatively small caffeine doses, under 180 mg per day, probably do not increase daily urine output or dehydrate. Caffeine during exercise is unlikely to cause dehydration. Alcohol can act as a diuretic, so it should be limited when rehydration is the goal.
findings.locator: 'Factores modificantes > Dieta', p. 14, ACSM-hosted Spanish translation

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: fluid intake cap during exercise
findings.value: Fluid intake must not exceed exercise-related body-mass loss; no body-mass gain from pre- to post-exercise unless a deficit existed at the start (SOR A)
findings.finding: Hyponatraemia comes from drinking too much hypotonic fluid, sports drinks included, so that weight is kept or gained in sessions of 1 hour or more. Active people should drink no more than they lose and should weigh themselves before and after exercise to check.
findings.locator: Recommendations 5 and 6 (SOR A), 'Importance of Maintaining Euhydration'

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: hydration target band around exercise (% body mass)
findings.value: Before exercise: euhydration within +1% to -1% of baseline; end of exercise: body-mass loss <2% (SOR A)
findings.finding: Athletic trainers should promote euhydration within 1% either side of baseline before exercise, and a body-mass loss under 2% by the end. Safety and performance are best when losses stay at 2% or less with no fluid gain.
findings.locator: Recommendations 7-8; Summary

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: sweat-rate equation
findings.value: Sweat loss (L) = pre-exercise body mass (kg) - post-exercise body mass (kg) + fluid consumed (L) - urine volume (L); sweat rate (L/h) = sweat loss / exercise duration (h)
findings.finding: Sweat rate comes from body mass before and after exercise, adjusted for fluid drunk and urine passed, divided by duration. Assess it several times in realistic conditions, clothing and intensities to build an individual plan. Table 3 gives worked examples of 1.3-3.2 L/h.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Sweat-Rate Equation), Table 3; 'Fluid Replacement' literature review

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: body-mass baseline for hydration assessment
findings.value: Average of >=3 consecutive days of euhydrated body mass, measured at the same time each morning; calibrated scale +/-0.1 kg (0.2 lb)
findings.finding: Body-mass change tracks hydration over 24 hours only when compared with a baseline averaged over at least 3 consecutive euhydrated days. Baseline mass is subject to daily variation from diet, digestion, fluid intake and bowel habits, so weigh at the same time each morning.
findings.locator: Recommendation 22 (SOR B); 'Hydration Assessment > Body Mass'; Weight-Certification item 3

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: post-exercise fluid replacement (% of loss)
findings.value: 100-150% of the calculated fluid loss when recovery is <4 h; with >12 h recovery, ad libitum food and fluid restores balance
findings.finding: When recovery time is short (under 4 hours), replace 100-150% of the measured fluid loss, because a large fluid load increases urine output. With more than 12 hours, normal eating and drinking restores balance. Meal sodium and water aid retention.
findings.locator: 'Fluid Replacement' literature-review opening paragraphs (after Table 2) for 100-150% and >12 h; 'Rehydration After Exercise' for up to 150% within <4 h and meal contribution

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: adult sweat-rate range L/h
findings.value: 0.5-4.0 L/h (adults >18 y); worked examples: 0.4 L/h (first-time 50-year-old marathoner) vs >2 L/h (elite runner)
findings.finding: Adult sweat rates during exercise range from 0.5 to 4.0 L/h. Population estimates should be used only when individual measurement is impossible. Fluid plans should rest on the person's own data, experience and goals.
findings.locator: 'Fluid Replacement > Sweat-Rate Variability', literature review

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: sweat sodium losses and sodium supplementation trigger
findings.value: Sodium losses 0.2-7.3 g/h; sweat sodium 10-100 mEq/L; people with sweat sodium >60 mEq/L and sweat rate >2.5 L/h may benefit from sodium in fluids during activity; no evidence of benefit beyond individual losses; assess sweat electrolytes before supplementing
findings.finding: Sodium lost in sweat varies widely. People with high sweat sodium and high sweat rates may benefit from sodium in their drinks. There is no evidence for supplementing beyond individual losses, and sodium tablets have little support. Test sweat electrolytes before supplementing.
findings.locator: 'Sweat-Rate Variability' and 'Beverage Additives' (first paragraph), literature review; sodium-tablet paragraph in the opening 'Fluid Replacement' section; Recommendations 17-18

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: beverage additives by session duration
findings.value: <1 h: water only; >1 h or with intense intervals: carbohydrate and/or electrolytes may help, especially in extreme environments
findings.finding: Most active people on a balanced diet need nothing added to water. Sessions under an hour need only water. Longer sessions, sessions with intense intervals, and endurance events may benefit from carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks.
findings.locator: 'Beverage Additives', literature review

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: drink carbohydrate concentration and drinking cadence
findings.value: 3-8% carbohydrate optimal for fluid absorption (>5-8% may slow it); ~200 mL every 15-20 min; 400-600 mL of fluid in the stomach optimises emptying; hypohydration >4% slows emptying
findings.finding: Gastric emptying depends mostly on stomach volume. Carbohydrate concentrations of 3-8% suit absorption, while stronger drinks may slow it. About 200 mL every 15-20 minutes may be ideal. Exercise above 80% VO2max, or dehydration above 4%, slows emptying.
findings.locator: 'Beverage Additives', second paragraph, literature review

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.population: Physically active individuals, especially distance athletes
findings.parameter: exercise-associated hyponatraemia definition and incidence
findings.value: Serum sodium <135 mmol/L during or within 24 h of activity; usually symptomatic <130 mmol/L; found in 10-20% of sampled distance-race/marathon finishers, though clinically significant cases are relatively uncommon; more common in women and after >4 h of activity
findings.finding: Exercise-associated hyponatraemia is a potential emergency. It is defined by serum sodium under 135 mmol/L, with symptoms usually below 130. Early signs overlap with dehydration, so weight gain, overdrinking and swelling help tell them apart. A blood sodium test is needed before giving fluids.
findings.locator: 'Definitions > Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia'; 'Physiological Implications of Hyperhydration'; 'Recognition of Hypohydration and Fluid Overload'

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: in-exercise drinking rule when sweat rate is unknown
findings.value: Drink to thirst (thirst typically rises near 2% hypohydration); competitive athletes chasing performance should use a measured sweat-rate plan instead
findings.finding: If someone does not know their sweat rate, drinking to thirst is most likely a safe way to avoid overdrinking. Thirst may lag in competition, so performance-focused athletes should know their sweat rate and plan to replace losses.
findings.locator: 'Rehydration During Exercise' (after Table 3); 'Fluid Replacement' paragraph on thirst

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: hypohydration severity bands (% body-mass deficit)
findings.value: Athletic: mild-moderate 2-5%, severe >5%; clinical: mild 1-5%, moderate 5-10%, severe >10%; thermoregulation compromised >1%; exertional heat-illness risk rises >3% (SOR B)
findings.finding: Losses above 5% consistently impair performance and cause marked symptoms. Thermoregulation suffers above 1% and heat-illness risk climbs above 3%. For 2-5% or greater deficits, oral fluids come first, and intravenous fluids only if oral intake is not tolerated.
findings.locator: 'Definitions > Hypohydration'; Recommendations 4 and 26

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: post-exercise refuelling window
findings.value: Eat and drink within 2 h after activity to replace fluid, electrolytes, carbohydrate and protein (SOR B); optimal amounts not determined
findings.finding: Active people should refuel within 2 hours after activity. Taking carbohydrate and protein together recovers muscle glycogen and blood glucose better than fluid alone. The optimal carbohydrate and protein amounts have not been determined.
findings.locator: Recommendation 15 (SOR B); 'Beverage Additives', third paragraph

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: caffeine and alcohol in rehydration beverages
findings.value: Caffeine ~3 mg/kg before and every 30 min during exercise need not be discouraged for diuretic reasons (SOR A); up to 3 mg/kg does not impair rehydration; beverages <=4% alcohol do not dehydrate, >4% should be discouraged (SOR B)
findings.finding: Moderate caffeine does not cause diuresis during exercise and does not hinder recovery rehydration at small doses. Low-alcohol drinks (4% or less) did not increase urine output. Stronger alcoholic drinks promote excess urine loss and should not be used for rehydration.
findings.locator: Recommendations 19 and 21; 'Beverage Additives' paragraphs on caffeine and alcohol

findings.citation: McDermott BP, Anderson SA, Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Cheuvront SN, Cooper L, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active. J Athl Train. 2017;52(9):877-95. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-52.9.02.
findings.parameter: daily hydration self-check markers
findings.value: Three simultaneous measures: first-morning urine colour (or specific gravity), thirst sensation, and morning body mass; urine reagent strips are unreliable
findings.finding: For the best field estimate of hydration, combine first-morning urine colour, thirst and morning body mass. Spot urine at other times is confounded by food, fluid and exercise. Thirst, void frequency and urine colour work as personal daily cues.
findings.locator: Recommendations 23-24; 'Hydration Assessment > Other Techniques' final paragraph (three measures); 'Hydration Assessment > Urine Concentration' (reagent strips)

findings.citation: Goulet EDB. Effect of exercise-induced dehydration on endurance performance: evaluating the impact of exercise protocols on outcomes using a meta-analytic procedure. Br J Sports Med. 2013;47(11):679-86. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2012-090958.
findings.parameter: body-mass loss threshold for endurance performance impairment
findings.value: Time-trial protocols: dehydration <=4% body mass very unlikely to impair (pooled change in power output +0.09 +/- 2.60%, p=0.9); fixed-intensity protocols: -1.91 +/- 1.53% (p<0.05), with impairment only at >=2% (p=0.03). 15 articles, 28 effect estimates, 122 subjects
findings.finding: In self-paced time trials, dehydration of up to about 4% of body mass did not measurably reduce endurance performance. Fixed-intensity lab protocols showed impairment at 2% or more. The author argues the 2% rule comes from non-ecological protocols.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only (Results and Conclusions); full text not accessible

findings.citation: Goulet EDB. Effect of exercise-induced dehydration on endurance performance: evaluating the impact of exercise protocols on outcomes using a meta-analytic procedure. Br J Sports Med. 2013;47(11):679-86. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2012-090958.
findings.parameter: in-exercise drinking strategy
findings.value: Drink according to thirst during exercise
findings.finding: The author concludes that athletes should drink to thirst during exercise, because the 2% body-weight rule does not hold under outdoor, real-world conditions. It may still apply to fixed-intensity military or occupational work.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only (Conclusions)

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate. Washington (DC): The National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10925.
findings.parameter: total water Adequate Intake L/day
findings.value: Adults >=19 y: men 3.7 L/d total water (~3.0 L from beverages incl. drinking water, ~0.7 L from food); women 2.7 L/d (~2.2 L beverages, ~0.5 L food); ~81% from beverages, ~19% from food
findings.finding: The total-water AI equals median US intake (NHANES III), since serum osmolality stays constant across a wide range of intakes. It is not a strict requirement. Intake below it may be fine, and active people or those in heat need more.
findings.locator: Summary chapter, 'Water' section and Tables S-1/S-2, pp. 5-7 (read online at NAP; the full 618-page report was not read)

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate. Washington (DC): The National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10925.
findings.population: Healthy people with normal kidney function
findings.parameter: maximal renal water excretion (fluid-rate ceiling)
findings.value: ~0.7 L/h (Table S-2 footnote); 0.7-1.0 L/h (UL section); no UL set for water
findings.finding: No upper limit was set for water because healthy people self-regulate intake. Acute water intoxication has been reported when large volumes were drunk much faster than the kidneys' maximal excretion rate of about 0.7-1.0 L/h.
findings.locator: Summary, Table S-2 footnote a (p. 6); 'Criteria and Proposed Values for ULs > Water', p. 14

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate. Washington (DC): The National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10925.
findings.parameter: sodium Adequate Intake g/day
findings.value: 2005: 1.5 g (65 mmol)/d at 19-50 y; 1.3 g/d at 51-70 y; 1.2 g/d at >70 y. Updated by NASEM 2019 (doi:10.17226/25353): 1,500 mg/d for all adults >=19 y
findings.finding: The sodium AI covers other nutrients and ordinary sweat losses. It does not apply to people with heavy sweat sodium losses, such as competitive athletes or heat-stressed workers, who may need more. NASEM 2019 reaffirmed 1,500 mg/d and extended it to older adults.
findings.locator: Summary, 'Sodium Chloride' section, p. 11, and Table S-4, pp. 12-13; NASEM 2019 Summary Table S-2 checked for the update

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate. Washington (DC): The National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10925.
findings.parameter: sodium upper intake g/day
findings.value: 2005 UL: 2.3 g (100 mmol)/d = 5.8 g NaCl, based on blood pressure. Superseded by NASEM 2019 (doi:10.17226/25353): no UL; Chronic Disease Risk Reduction Intake = reduce intake if above 2,300 mg/d for adults
findings.finding: Dose-response trials show blood pressure rising progressively with sodium intake, which set the adult UL of 2.3 g/day. People unacclimatised to prolonged activity in heat may need more because of sweat losses. NASEM 2019 moved this 2,300 mg figure into a chronic-disease risk-reduction category.
findings.locator: Summary, 'ULs > Sodium Chloride', pp. 15-16, and Table S-4 (p. 13); NASEM 2019 Summary Box S-3 and Table S-2

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate. Washington (DC): The National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10925.
findings.parameter: chloride Adequate Intake and upper limit g/day
findings.value: AI 2.3 g (65 mmol)/d at 19-50 y; 2.0 g/d at 51-70 y; 1.8 g/d at >70 y; UL 3.6 g/d in Table S-4 (Summary text says 3.5 g); set equimolar to sodium
findings.finding: Chloride values match sodium on a molar basis, because nearly all dietary chloride comes with added sodium. The AI for younger adults is 2.3 g per day, equal to 3.8 g of salt. The table and the text disagree slightly on the UL.
findings.locator: Summary, p. 12 (chloride AI text), p. 13 (Table S-4 values) and p. 16 (UL text)

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate. Washington (DC): The National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10925.
findings.parameter: potassium Adequate Intake g/day
findings.value: 2005: 4.7 g (120 mmol)/d for adults; no UL from food; supplements only under medical supervision. Updated by NASEM 2019 (doi:10.17226/25353): AI 3,400 mg/d men, 2,600 mg/d women (>=19 y)
findings.finding: Potassium benefits come mainly from foods, such as fruit and vegetables, that supply bicarbonate precursors. No food UL exists for healthy people. Supplements carry toxicity risk, and people with kidney disease or on certain drugs may need less. NASEM 2019 lowered and sex-split the adult AI.
findings.locator: Summary, 'Potassium' section, pp. 8-9; Table S-3, p. 10; ULs > Potassium, pp. 14-15; NASEM 2019 Summary Table S-1 checked

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate. Washington (DC): The National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10925.
findings.parameter: beverages counted toward total water intake
findings.value: All beverages, including caffeinated and alcoholic ones, count toward total water (diuretic effects appear transient); ~80% of total water comes from beverages; no single source is essential
findings.finding: Caffeinated and alcoholic beverages can be counted toward total water intake, because their diuretic effects seem transient. Drinking water, other beverages and food moisture all contribute, and none of them is essential by itself.
findings.locator: Summary, 'Water' section, after Table S-2 (pp. 7-8)

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate. Washington (DC): The National Academies Press; 2005. doi:10.17226/10925.
findings.parameter: exercise duration linked to symptomatic hyponatraemia
findings.value: Typically >6 h of prolonged stressful exercise; does not occur in healthy people eating a typical North American diet
findings.finding: Symptomatic exercise hyponatraemia, from excess fluid, too little sodium replacement, or both, is typically associated with more than 6 hours of prolonged, stressful exercise. Rapid drinking beyond the kidneys' excretion capacity can cause acute water toxicity.
findings.locator: Summary, 'ULs > Water', p. 14

findings.citation: Hall KD. What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss? Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(3):573-6. doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720.
findings.population: Modelling; Forbes parameterisation from 166 women; checked against obese and lean weight-loss data
findings.parameter: energy density of weight change equation
findings.value: dE/dBW = rhoF + (rhoL - rhoF) x dL/dBW, where rhoF = 39.5 MJ/kg and rhoL = 7.6 MJ/kg (protein hydration h = 1.6 g water/g protein); dL/dBW from the modified Forbes equation (Lambert W function, constant 10.4 kg) with inputs initial body fat Fi and weight loss dBW
findings.finding: The energy content of lost weight depends on how much comes from fat versus lean tissue. That split is predicted from initial body fat and the amount lost. Using other hydration assumptions changes the estimate only modestly (for example 24.7 vs 23.1 MJ/kg).
findings.locator: Main text, the two displayed (unnumbered) equations and the paragraphs on protein hydration; Figure 1 (PMC author manuscript)

findings.citation: Hall KD. What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss? Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(3):573-6. doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720.
findings.population: Obese (bariatric and non-surgical) and lean (Keys men, three lean studies) weight-loss groups
findings.parameter: validity of the fixed 3500 kcal/lb (32.2 MJ/kg) rule
findings.value: Roughly valid only when initial body fat is >30 kg; overestimates the required deficit when initial fat is lower (significantly lower below 25 kg); example: 15 kg lost from 20 kg initial fat = ~24.7 MJ/kg
findings.finding: Leaner people need a smaller cumulative deficit per kg lost than the 32.2 MJ/kg rule assumes, because more of their loss is low-energy lean tissue. Data from lean groups (Keys semistarvation, three other studies) confirm this. Obese groups fit the rule reasonably well.
findings.locator: Abstract; main text on Figure 1A and the sensitivity example

findings.citation: Hall KD. What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss? Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(3):573-6. doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720.
findings.parameter: validity of a static deficit-to-target calculation
findings.value: Inappropriate. Worked example: 65 kg woman with 20 kg fat aiming to lose 5 kg in 6 months; 28 MJ/kg x 5 kg = 140 MJ, i.e. a 780 kJ/d cut, which falls short because energy expenditure adapts
findings.finding: The energy density of lost tissue must not be used alone to set a fixed daily intake cut for a target loss by a date. Expenditure falls as weight drops, so the goal would be missed. The size of that adaptation was not modelled.
findings.locator: Main text, paragraph after Figure 1B discussion (the 163 cm woman example)

findings.citation: Hall KD. What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss? Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(3):573-6. doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720.
findings.parameter: metabolizable energy density of body stores
findings.value: Glycogen 17.6 MJ/kg; protein 19.7 MJ/kg; fat 39.5 MJ/kg; body water contributes mass but 0 energy
findings.finding: A deficit is met by burning stored fat, protein and glycogen, so the energy of lost tissue equals the deficit that produced it. Water loss changes mass but supplies no energy. The fat-mass change is endogenous fat oxidised, not adipose tissue.
findings.locator: Main text, paragraphs 2-4 (citing Livesey and Elia 1988)

findings.citation: Hall KD. What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss? Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(3):573-6. doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720.
findings.population: Modelling interpretation of published diet studies
findings.parameter: interpreting slowing weight loss on a constant prescribed intake
findings.value: The model alone predicts faster loss over time (lower energy density as the lean share grows); observed slowing implies falling energy expenditure, relaxed adherence, or both
findings.finding: Because later losses contain more lean tissue, a constant deficit should in theory speed weight loss. Real diets usually slow down, which the author attributes to falling energy expenditure, relaxed adherence, or both. The paper does not quantify either.
findings.locator: Main text, penultimate paragraph

findings.citation: Hall KD. What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss? Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(3):573-6. doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720.
findings.parameter: glycogen-related early weight-change window
findings.value: Glycogen (with its associated water) affects weight change mainly within the first week (modelling assumption)
findings.finding: Glycogen is a small fraction of lean mass and its effect on weight change typically appears within about the first week. The model therefore treats longer-term lean-mass change as protein plus associated water. This is a stated assumption, not something the paper tests.
findings.locator: Main text, paragraph on the energy density of lean-mass change

findings.citation: Hall KD. What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss? Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(3):573-6. doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720.
findings.population: Modelling; Forbes female dataset with inferred male shift
findings.parameter: sex difference in energy density of weight loss
findings.value: Hypothesis only: men (more lean mass for the same fat) would sit on right-shifted Figure 1B curves, so at the same body weight they may need a smaller cumulative deficit per kg lost than women; no numeric sex offset given
findings.finding: At similar body weight, women typically carry more fat than men. The model predicts a higher energy density for their weight loss, which may explain why men lose more weight than women for the same deficit. No numeric sex offset is given.
findings.locator: Abstract; main text on Figure 1B

findings.citation: Hall KD. What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss? Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(3):573-6. doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720.
findings.parameter: effect of resistance training or high protein on the composition of weight loss
findings.value: May shift the fat:lean proportion of weight lost; not captured by the modified Forbes model (no number given)
findings.finding: Resistance exercise or high-protein diets may change how much lost weight is fat versus lean tissue. The Forbes-based model does not account for this. A fuller macronutrient and body-composition model would be needed for people who train.
findings.locator: Main text, final paragraph

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.parameter: steady-state weight change per sustained change in daily energy intake
findings.value: About 1 kg eventual body-weight change per 100 kJ/d (about 24 kcal/d) of permanent intake change; stated equivalently as 10 kcal/d per lb
findings.finding: The validated dynamic model gives a population-average rule of thumb: each permanent 100 kJ/d change in intake eventually shifts body weight by about 1 kg. It is good for setting expectations, not for precise individual prediction.
findings.locator: Section 'Modelling average weight change in a population', final paragraph (rule of thumb)

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.population: Adults; model simulations (e.g., 100 kg sedentary man)
findings.parameter: time course to new steady-state weight after a sustained intake change
findings.value: About 1 year to reach half of the total weight change; about 3 years to reach 95%; longer with greater initial body fat
findings.finding: Weight responds slowly to a sustained intake change. Half the eventual change takes about a year and nearly all of it about three years. People with more initial body fat end up changing more and take longer to reach steady state.
findings.locator: Abstract; 'Modelling the dynamics of weight change' paragraphs 3 and 5 (100 kg vs 80 kg man); 'Modelling average weight change in a population', final paragraph

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.population: US adults (population average; DLW cross-sectional sample)
findings.parameter: change in total energy expenditure per kg body-weight change
findings.value: Dynamic model slope 100 kJ/kg/d; cross-sectional doubly labelled water regression 94 ± 6 kJ/kg/d
findings.finding: Total energy expenditure changes by roughly 100 kJ/d per kg of body-weight change. A cross-sectional doubly labelled water regression gave a similar slope, which supports lowering maintenance estimates as weight falls.
findings.locator: 'Modelling average weight change in a population', paragraph comparing model-predicted expenditure with doubly labelled water data

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.parameter: energy content of body fat vs lean tissue change
findings.value: Body fat 39.5 MJ/kg; lean tissue 7.6 MJ/kg (about 5-fold difference)
findings.finding: Losing a kilogram of fat takes about five times the net deficit of losing a kilogram of lean tissue. The energy per kg of weight change therefore depends on its fat-to-lean mix and is not one fixed constant.
findings.locator: 'Quantitative physiology of weight change in adults', paragraph 1

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.parameter: uncertainty of baseline maintenance energy estimate in free-living adults
findings.value: Best achievable precision about 5% (the paper implies this needs doubly labelled water); without doubly labelled water the uncertainty is typically much greater than 5%
findings.finding: A free-living adult's baseline maintenance requirement cannot be pinned down more precisely than about 5%, and typical estimates without doubly labelled water are far worse. This alone spreads weight-loss outcomes between people, even with perfect adherence.
findings.locator: 'Modelling the dynamics of weight change', paragraph 2

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.parameter: weight-loss projection method (static 3500 kcal/lb rule vs dynamic model)
findings.value: For a 2 MJ/d (480 kcal/d) intake cut in a 100 kg sedentary man, the static rule predicts 22 kg lost in year 1, about 100% more than the dynamic model. The model plateaus near 75 kg (10-year simulation), with about ±4 kg individual spread after several years.
findings.finding: The static 3500 kcal/lb rule roughly doubles first-year weight-loss predictions because it ignores falling expenditure. Projections should use a dynamic model that shows the slowing trajectory and its uncertainty range.
findings.locator: 'Modelling the dynamics of weight change', paragraphs 3-4

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.parameter: adherence / deviation flag from weigh-ins
findings.value: Rule (qualitative, no numeric threshold): a weight course lying well outside the model's predicted trajectory band may indicate non-adherence or atypical physiology. The gap between measured and model-predicted weight change can quantify compensation in intake or activity.
findings.finding: The authors suggest checking each person's weigh-ins against the model's expected range. A large departure points to non-adherence or unusual physiology, and the measured-versus-predicted gap can estimate compensatory changes in eating or activity.
findings.locator: 'Setting goals for weight loss and weight-loss maintenance', paragraph 3; 'Modelling the dynamics of weight change', paragraph 8 (the paragraph after the exercise-vs-diet comparison), final sentence

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.parameter: interpretation of the 6-8 month weight-loss plateau
findings.value: Controlled feeding shows near-linear loss over 6 months. Outpatient programmes plateau at 6-8 months, then regain. The modelled metabolic plateau takes several years. The typical regain curve is reproduced by an initial cut of about 3.3 MJ/d (800 kcal/d) that relaxes back to baseline within the first year.
findings.finding: The model plateaus only after years, so metabolic adaptation alone cannot explain the common 6-8 month plateau, and waning adherence is the likelier cause. App inference, not stated by the authors: a stall could prompt an adherence check before any further calorie cut.
findings.locator: 'Assessment of obesity interventions and patients' adherence', paragraphs 1-4

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.parameter: two-phase loss-then-maintenance intake plan (worked example)
findings.value: 100 kg sedentary man with baseline 12.7 MJ/d (3000 kcal/d): cut by 5 MJ/d (1200 kcal/d) to lose 20 kg in 6 months, then hold a permanent intake of 10.9 MJ/d (2600 kcal/d) to keep the loss
findings.finding: A worked two-stage plan: a larger temporary deficit reaches the goal weight in a set time, then intake rises to a new maintenance level still below the old baseline. This is an illustrative simulation, not a tested prescription.
findings.locator: 'Setting goals for weight loss and weight-loss maintenance', paragraph 2

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.population: Adults (computational macronutrient-balance model and inpatient studies)
findings.parameter: expenditure effect of isocaloric carbohydrate-fat exchange
findings.value: Expenditure changes by less than 400 kJ/d (about 10 g body fat/d); detection would need a sustained change of more than 100 days (protein held constant)
findings.finding: With protein unchanged, even large carbohydrate-for-fat swaps shift expenditure only slightly in the authors' macronutrient model. Treating calories as equivalent across carbohydrate and fat is a reasonable short-term first estimate. Long-term effects remain untested.
findings.locator: Panel 'Does diet composition matter?', paragraphs 4-5 (numbers in paragraph 5)

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.population: Adults (model; 100 kg vs 80 kg simulated men)
findings.parameter: partitioning of weight change into fat vs lean by initial adiposity
findings.value: Qualitative rule: higher initial fat mass means a larger fat share of both gains and losses, a larger eventual change and a longer time to steady state. The numeric (Forbes-type) equation is in the web appendix, which was not accessed. The model does not include exercise (including resistance training) effects on body composition.
findings.finding: How a surplus or deficit splits between fat and lean tissue depends non-linearly on starting fat mass, with leaner people partitioning more to lean tissue. The model excludes training effects on composition, so it cannot set muscle-gain partitioning for lifters.
findings.locator: 'Quantitative physiology of weight change in adults', paragraph 1; 'Modelling the dynamics of weight change', paragraphs 5-6 and 8

findings.citation: Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, Chow CC, Wang YC, Gortmaker SL, Swinburn BA. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826-37. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X
findings.parameter: added exercise vs energy-equivalent intake reduction
findings.value: About 20 km/week of extra moderate running (initial cost about 1.2 MJ/d) gave slightly faster and greater modelled loss than an equal intake cut. Larger interventions favoured diet. The model assumes no compensatory intake.
findings.finding: In simulation, a modest added exercise dose produced slightly more loss than an energy-equal food cut, because activity cost scales with body weight. Real compensatory eating and activity changes vary widely between people and are not modelled.
findings.locator: 'Modelling the dynamics of weight change', physical-activity paragraphs (paragraphs 7-8)

findings.citation: Thomas DM, Martin CK, Lettieri S, Bredlau C, Kaiser K, Church T, Bouchard C, Heymsfield SB. Can a weight loss of one pound a week be achieved with a 3500-kcal deficit? Commentary on a commonly accepted rule. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(12):1611-3. doi:10.1038/ijo.2013.51
findings.population: 103 adults (71 men, 32 women), baseline 82.1 ± 22.0 kg, baseline intake 2876 ± 484 kcal/d, in 7 confinement or objectively monitored weight-loss studies
findings.parameter: accuracy of the 3500 kcal/lb rule
findings.value: Observed loss 20.1 ± 11.3 lb vs rule-predicted 27.6 ± 16.0 lb (overestimate 7.4 ± 12.6 lb). Mean prescribed deficit was 1439 ± 784 kcal/d over 64.8 ± 23.6 d (range 31-93 d).
findings.finding: Across seven tightly supervised experiments, most participants lost markedly less than the 3500 kcal/lb rule predicted, even within one to three months. The app should not project weight change with this static rule.
findings.locator: 'Results and Discussion: How well does the 3500 kcal rule predict weight loss?'; Methods, paragraph 3

findings.citation: Thomas DM, Martin CK, Lettieri S, Bredlau C, Kaiser K, Church T, Bouchard C, Heymsfield SB. Can a weight loss of one pound a week be achieved with a 3500-kcal deficit? Commentary on a commonly accepted rule. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(12):1611-3. doi:10.1038/ijo.2013.51
findings.population: Subset of the 103 adults (5 of 7 studies meeting model input requirements)
findings.parameter: accuracy of dynamic weight-change model (short-term supervised data)
findings.value: 5 studies: observed 17.0 ± 11.0 lb vs dynamic-model 18.4 ± 13.8 lb. Single CALERIE case: 13 lb observed vs 14 lb predicted, with the energy-balance plateau predicted at 1.4 years.
findings.finding: A validated dynamic model tracked supervised weight loss much more closely than the static rule. It predicts a curving trajectory that reaches a plateau after more than a year.
findings.locator: 'Results and Discussion', paragraph 2

findings.citation: Thomas DM, Martin CK, Lettieri S, Bredlau C, Kaiser K, Church T, Bouchard C, Heymsfield SB. Can a weight loss of one pound a week be achieved with a 3500-kcal deficit? Commentary on a commonly accepted rule. Int J Obes (Lond). 2013;37(12):1611-3. doi:10.1038/ijo.2013.51
findings.parameter: required inputs for dynamic weight-change model
findings.value: Baseline age, height, sex and weight (weight-stable), intervention duration, and either target total intake or change from baseline
findings.finding: The dynamic model tools need only a few baseline demographics plus planned intake, all fields an app can collect at onboarding. The model is meant for weight-stable starting points and calorie-restriction or low-dose exercise scenarios.
findings.locator: Methods, paragraph 2; 'Downloadable weight change predictor'

findings.citation: Heymsfield SB, Thomas D, Martin CK, Redman LM, Strauss B, Bosy-Westphal A, Müller MJ, Shen W, Martin Nguyen A. Energy content of weight loss: kinetic features during voluntary caloric restriction. Metabolism. 2012;61(7):937-43. doi:10.1016/j.metabol.2011.11.012
findings.population: CALERIE Phase I overweight adults (n=23; 10 men, 13 women; about 39 y; BMI about 28, range 21-31) on 25% CR or VLCD (890 kcal/d)
findings.parameter: energy content of weight change by week of dieting
findings.value: Cumulative from baseline: week 4 4858 ± 388 kcal/kg; week 6 6041 ± 376 kcal/kg (mean ± SEM). No significant change from week 6 to week 24. About 7700 kcal/kg (3500 kcal/lb) is approached only in the later phase.
findings.finding: Early weight loss carries little energy (glycogen, protein, water). Energy per kg rose significantly from week 4 to week 6, then stabilised. App inference, not stated by the authors: early weigh-ins overstate fat loss and deserve less weight when estimating energy balance.
findings.locator: Results 'Compartmental Kinetics', paragraph 1; Discussion, paragraphs 1-2

findings.citation: Heymsfield SB, Thomas D, Martin CK, Redman LM, Strauss B, Bosy-Westphal A, Müller MJ, Shen W, Martin Nguyen A. Energy content of weight loss: kinetic features during voluntary caloric restriction. Metabolism. 2012;61(7):937-43. doi:10.1016/j.metabol.2011.11.012
findings.population: Kiel obese adults (n=75; 15 men, 60 women; BMI about 35) on 800-1000 kcal/d liquid VLCD for about 13 weeks
findings.parameter: energy content of weight loss by sex
findings.value: Kiel 13-week VLCD: women 6804 ± 226 vs men 6119 ± 240 kcal/kg (P<0.05). Earlier cohorts cited as about 20-25% higher in women.
findings.finding: Each kilogram lost carries more energy in women, because men lose relatively more lean tissue. In CALERIE, sex stopped predicting it at week 12 once baseline fat mass was controlled. In Kiel, however, baseline fat mass was not significantly associated, so the driver remains unsettled.
findings.locator: Results 'Compartmental Kinetics', paragraphs 3-4; Discussion, paragraph 5

findings.citation: Heymsfield SB, Thomas D, Martin CK, Redman LM, Strauss B, Bosy-Westphal A, Müller MJ, Shen W, Martin Nguyen A. Energy content of weight loss: kinetic features during voluntary caloric restriction. Metabolism. 2012;61(7):937-43. doi:10.1016/j.metabol.2011.11.012
findings.parameter: fraction of weight loss as fat-free mass over time
findings.value: ΔFFM/ΔW at week 4: 0.60 ± 0.06 (men), 0.50 ± 0.07 (women); at week 24: about 0.35 ± 0.05 (men), 0.24 ± 0.03 (women)
findings.finding: The lean share of weight lost falls steeply over the first months of dieting, from half or more at week 4 to roughly a quarter to a third by week 24. Men lose proportionally more lean tissue.
findings.locator: Results 'Compartmental Kinetics', paragraph 2

findings.citation: Heymsfield SB, Thomas D, Martin CK, Redman LM, Strauss B, Bosy-Westphal A, Müller MJ, Shen W, Martin Nguyen A. Energy content of weight loss: kinetic features during voluntary caloric restriction. Metabolism. 2012;61(7):937-43. doi:10.1016/j.metabol.2011.11.012
findings.parameter: energy densities of fat and fat-free mass for converting body-composition change to energy
findings.value: Fat 9.3 kcal/g; FFM 1.1 kcal/g (published FFM range 1.1-1.8 kcal/g)
findings.finding: Energy content of weight change was computed from DXA fat and fat-free mass changes with these densities. The authors state that choosing other values within the published FFM range would not change their conclusions.
findings.locator: Methods 'Statistical Methods', paragraph 1

findings.citation: Heymsfield SB, Thomas D, Martin CK, Redman LM, Strauss B, Bosy-Westphal A, Müller MJ, Shen W, Martin Nguyen A. Energy content of weight loss: kinetic features during voluntary caloric restriction. Metabolism. 2012;61(7):937-43. doi:10.1016/j.metabol.2011.11.012
findings.population: Obese women (Dole); overweight men and women (de Jonge); overweight men (Kiel-II)
findings.parameter: energy content of very early (under 4 weeks) weight change (cited studies)
findings.value: About 2500 kcal/kg over 4-day gain and loss periods (Dole 1955); 3-week CR: 3810 ± 858 (men) and 5507 ± 1221 (women) kcal/kg (de Jonge); 7-day overfeeding and CR intervals: 4720 kcal/kg pooled (Kiel-II)
findings.finding: Short studies cited in the discussion agree that the first days to weeks of weight change carry far less energy per kg than 7700 kcal/kg, which fits a two-phase model. App inference: converting the first 2-4 weeks of weigh-ins at 7700 kcal/kg would overstate the deficit.
findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph 3

findings.citation: Sanghvi A, Redman LM, Martin CK, Ravussin E, Hall KD. Validation of an inexpensive and accurate mathematical method to measure long-term changes in free-living energy intake. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(2):353-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.111070
findings.population: 140 non-obese adults 21-51 y, BMI 21-29 kg/m², 2 y of prescribed 25% caloric restriction (CALERIE)
findings.parameter: equation to infer intake change from repeated weigh-ins
findings.value: ΔEI_i = ε(BW_i − BW_0) + ρ·dBW_i/dt, with ρ = 8840 ± 450 kcal/kg and ε = 25.8 ± 1.0 kcal/kg/d (mean ± SD across subjects; assumed PAL about 1.6). dBW/dt comes from a moving average of weights; interval length t = (N − 1)·T.
findings.finding: A linearised model estimates intake change from baseline using only weight change from baseline and the smoothed rate of weight change. Parameters came from age, sex, height and an assumed activity level and were not fitted to the validation data.
findings.locator: Methods 'Mathematical modeling to calculate ΔEI by using repeated body weight measurements', Equation 3 (equation image on PMC)

findings.citation: Sanghvi A, Redman LM, Martin CK, Ravussin E, Hall KD. Validation of an inexpensive and accurate mathematical method to measure long-term changes in free-living energy intake. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(2):353-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.111070
findings.parameter: precision of weight-derived intake-change estimate
findings.value: Mean bias under 40 kcal/d (model slightly underestimated reductions). Individual RMS deviation 215 kcal/d overall: 191, 199, 227 and 246 kcal/d for weeks 0-26, 26-52, 52-78 and 78-104. Most estimates were within 132 kcal/d and 75% within 250 kcal/d. Limits of agreement span about 800-1000 kcal/d.
findings.finding: Group-average intake changes from weigh-ins matched doubly labelled water/DXA closely. Individual estimates were imprecise, and agreement weakened over time, so single-person adjustments should be coarse and shown with uncertainty.
findings.locator: Results, paragraphs 2-3 and Table 1; Discussion, paragraph 6

findings.citation: Sanghvi A, Redman LM, Martin CK, Ravussin E, Hall KD. Validation of an inexpensive and accurate mathematical method to measure long-term changes in free-living energy intake. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(2):353-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.111070
findings.parameter: absolute intake vs change-from-baseline estimation
findings.value: Rule: the model yields only the change from baseline. Absolute intake needs a baseline requirement estimate, whose uncertainty adds in quadrature to the change uncertainty.
findings.finding: Weigh-ins show how intake has changed, not what it is. Turning that into an absolute calorie target needs a baseline maintenance estimate, and that estimate's error greatly widens the total uncertainty.
findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph 7

findings.citation: Sanghvi A, Redman LM, Martin CK, Ravussin E, Hall KD. Validation of an inexpensive and accurate mathematical method to measure long-term changes in free-living energy intake. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(2):353-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.111070
findings.parameter: validated population range for weight-based intake model
findings.value: Validated in non-obese adults aged 21-51 y with BMI 21-29 kg/m² over 2 years. The authors limit current use to young and middle-aged adults. It is not validated with repeated DLW in obesity.
findings.finding: The weight-based intake estimate was validated only in young to middle-aged adults without obesity, and the authors say it is currently limited to such adults. The underlying model was originally built on controlled-feeding data from people with obesity.
findings.locator: Methods 'Description of the data'; Discussion, paragraphs 7 and 9

findings.citation: Sanghvi A, Redman LM, Martin CK, Ravussin E, Hall KD. Validation of an inexpensive and accurate mathematical method to measure long-term changes in free-living energy intake. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(2):353-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.111070
findings.parameter: weigh-in frequency
findings.value: Rule: more frequent body weights improve precision (no optimal frequency given). The study weighed at months 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 24. Adding activity monitoring was hypothesised (not tested) to improve estimates.
findings.finding: Even sparse clinic weigh-ins gave unbiased group estimates. The authors state that more frequent weighing improves the individual estimate, and they propose frequent remote weights for ongoing adherence feedback, bearing in mind the method's limited precision.
findings.locator: Methods 'Description of the data'; Discussion, paragraphs 3, 5 and 8

findings.citation: Sanghvi A, Redman LM, Martin CK, Ravussin E, Hall KD. Validation of an inexpensive and accurate mathematical method to measure long-term changes in free-living energy intake. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(2):353-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.111070
findings.parameter: body energy-store change equation (intake-balance reference method)
findings.value: ΔES = ΔFM × 9300 kcal/kg + ΔFFM × 1100 kcal/kg
findings.finding: The reference method valued body-energy change from DXA fat and fat-free mass changes using these densities, matching Heymsfield 2012 (9.3 and 1.1 kcal/g) and differing from the 7.6 MJ/kg lean value in Hall 2011.
findings.locator: Methods 'Calculating ΔEI by using the intake-balance method', Equation 2 (equation image on PMC)

findings.citation: Sanghvi A, Redman LM, Martin CK, Ravussin E, Hall KD. Validation of an inexpensive and accurate mathematical method to measure long-term changes in free-living energy intake. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(2):353-8. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.111070
findings.parameter: self-reported intake bias (cited)
findings.value: Self-report often underestimates actual intake by several hundred kcal/d (no single figure given)
findings.finding: Food logs commonly under-report intake by several hundred kcal/d, far more than the weight-based model's mean bias under 40 kcal/d. This supports inferring intake from weigh-ins rather than trusting logged intake alone.
findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph 2; Introduction, paragraph 1

findings.citation: Müller MJ, Bosy-Westphal A. Adaptive thermogenesis with weight loss in humans. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2013;21(2):218-28. doi:10.1002/oby.20027
findings.parameter: magnitude of adaptive thermogenesis
findings.value: Average about 0.5 MJ (about 120 kcal), with considerable between-subject variance (no CI given; the abstract gives no time unit, though per day is the evident context)
findings.finding: During weight loss, expenditure falls on average by roughly 120 kcal (per day implied) more than weight and body-composition changes predict, with wide individual variation. This is abstract-level only, with no pooled estimate or interval.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results)

findings.citation: Müller MJ, Bosy-Westphal A. Adaptive thermogenesis with weight loss in humans. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2013;21(2):218-28. doi:10.1002/oby.20027
findings.parameter: onset of adaptive thermogenesis
findings.value: Develops only after more than 2 weeks of controlled underfeeding
findings.finding: Adaptive thermogenesis takes more than two weeks of controlled underfeeding to appear, so it should not be modelled as starting immediately with a deficit. This is abstract-level only.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results)

findings.citation: Müller MJ, Bosy-Westphal A. Adaptive thermogenesis with weight loss in humans. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2013;21(2):218-28. doi:10.1002/oby.20027
findings.parameter: definition and measurement of adaptive thermogenesis
findings.value: Definition: an underfeeding-related fall in resting and non-resting expenditure beyond what changes in body weight and composition explain. Assess using individual expenditure components, detailed body composition and mathematical modelling.
findings.finding: Conflicting results come mainly from differing definitions, non-standard protocols and imprecise expenditure methods. The authors recommend assessing adaptation component by component with detailed body composition and modelling. This is abstract-level only.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Objective, Results, Conclusion)

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.population: Narrative review; cited Minnesota semi-starvation men
findings.parameter: magnitude of adaptive thermogenesis (cited Minnesota data)
findings.value: About 70-100 kcal/d (cited, reference 150)
findings.finding: The review cites an adaptive thermogenesis of roughly 70-100 kcal/d and warns that fat-free mass composition and methods affect the estimate. Cited later work suggests adaptation seen during restriction does not explain long-term regain.
findings.locator: 'Evolutionary Origins and Models to Metabolic Adaptation', adaptive thermogenesis passage (publisher full text; journals.lww.com now redirects to ovid.com)

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.parameter: main source of expenditure decline during weight loss
findings.value: Rule: mostly involuntary reductions in non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). A cited review with high risk of bias found no significant NEAT reduction.
findings.finding: The review concludes that expenditure falls during weight loss mostly through involuntary drops in non-exercise activity, while acknowledging a conflicting, high-risk-of-bias review that found no significant NEAT reduction.
findings.locator: 'Components of Energy Expenditure', paragraph 5 (NEAT); 'Practical Applications'

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.parameter: share of total daily energy expenditure by component
findings.value: REE about 70%; TEF about 10%; exercise (EAT) 5-10%; NEAT about 15% (sedentary) up to 50% (highly active)
findings.finding: Resting expenditure makes up most of daily expenditure. Non-exercise activity is the most variable component and drives most of the variation between and within people.
findings.locator: 'Components of Energy Expenditure', paragraphs 1-5 and Figure 1

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day during energy deficit (overweight/obese adults)
findings.value: 1.2-1.5 g/kg/d (citing several meta-analyses)
findings.finding: For adults with overweight or obesity who are losing weight, the review cites meta-analyses supporting 1.2-1.5 g/kg/d protein and notes the RDA is a minimum, not an optimum. This is a secondary citation, so check it against the primary meta-analyses.
findings.locator: 'Protein', paragraph 1 (final sentence; meta-analyses refs 107, 112, 208) and paragraph 3 (RDA as minimum); 'Practical Applications'

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.population: Athletes and lean adults (cited trials); ~2 g/kg advice applies to non-athletes seeking fat loss
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day during energy deficit (lean adults/athletes)
findings.value: 1.2-2.0 g/kg/d. About 2 g/kg/d is suggested for non-athletes losing fat when FFM is unknown. In the cited Mettler study, 2.3 g/kg/d retained more lean mass than 1.0 g/kg/d.
findings.finding: Leaner, trained people may need more protein while dieting, up to about 2 g/kg/d. Resistance training combined with high protein protected fat-free mass better than protein alone.
findings.locator: 'Protein', paragraphs 2-3 (publisher HTML)

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
