findings.population: Resistance-trained adults (cited Antonio et al. studies)
findings.parameter: very high protein intake: tolerance and adherence
findings.value: 3.4-4.4 g/kg/d studied in resistance-trained adults with no reported harm; dropout 77 to 48 and 40 to 30 participants
findings.finding: The review reports very high protein intakes studied in trained people without reported harm, but adherence was poor. Dropouts cited difficulty eating that much and gastrointestinal upset, and the review advises caution.
findings.locator: 'Protein', end of paragraph 2 and start of paragraph 3 (publisher HTML)

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.population: Obese adults after 5-10% loss in 3 months (48 g trial); overweight adults over 7 months (30 g trial) (cited trials)
findings.parameter: added protein after weight loss to limit regain
findings.value: +48 g/d or +30 g/d above usual intake (two trials from one research group)
findings.finding: Two trials from one group found that adding about 30-48 g/d protein above usual intake after weight loss reduced regain. The review says replication is needed.
findings.locator: 'Protein', paragraph 1 (publisher HTML)

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.population: Athletes/leaner adults in energy restriction (cited sources)
findings.parameter: fat % of energy during deficit (athletes/lean)
findings.value: 10-25% of energy from fat, with the remainder biased toward carbohydrate
findings.finding: For athletes or lean dieters in energy restriction, the review suggests fat at 10-25% of energy, with the rest weighted toward carbohydrate to support training performance. This comes from cited sources, not primary trials.
findings.locator: 'Carbohydrate and Fat', final paragraph (last sentence)

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.parameter: carbohydrate-to-fat ratio for limiting adaptation and regain
findings.value: Rule: of little relevance in overweight adults. Low-carbohydrate diets show larger early loss, attributed to glycogen and water depletion.
findings.finding: The carbohydrate-to-fat split seems to matter little for limiting adaptation or regain in overweight adults, so either pattern can be allowed. Extra early loss on low-carbohydrate diets is mostly glycogen and water.
findings.locator: 'Carbohydrate and Fat', paragraphs 1-2

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.parameter: rate of weight loss
findings.value: Rule: gradual rates are linked with greater fat-mass loss and better REE maintenance (cited systematic review). No agreed numeric weekly threshold.
findings.finding: A cited systematic review linked slower loss with more fat lost and better-preserved resting expenditure. The review notes that definitions of gradual versus aggressive are inconsistent and gives no numeric weekly rate.
findings.locator: 'Rate of Body Mass Loss'

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.population: Overweight/obese adults and resistance-trained adults (cited trials)
findings.parameter: diet refeeds and diet breaks
findings.value: Refeed: 1-2 days at or slightly above maintenance (mainly carbohydrate) within a weekly deficit. Diet break: days to weeks at maintenance. Cited meta-analyses found no significant weight-loss difference between intermittent and continuous restriction.
findings.finding: Evidence for refeeds and diet breaks is mixed and scarce, and cited pooled analyses found no weight-loss advantage over continuous restriction. The review suggests some athletes and overweight people might still benefit within a periodised plan.
findings.locator: 'Diet Refeeds and Diet Breaks'; 'Practical Applications'

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.parameter: meal frequency and thermic effect of food
findings.value: Rule: more frequent meals do not increase the thermic effect of food (cited)
findings.finding: Eating more often does not raise diet-induced thermogenesis, so meal count need not be set for metabolic reasons. Larger meals and higher protein or carbohydrate content raise the thermic effect.
findings.locator: 'Components of Energy Expenditure', thermic-effect-of-food paragraph (paragraph 3)

findings.citation: Martínez-Gómez MG, Roberts BM. Metabolic adaptations to weight loss: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(10):2970-81. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003991
findings.parameter: fibre-rich food selection during energy deficit
findings.value: Rule: favour whole grains, fruit and vegetables for satiation and food volume. A cited acute-satiety meta-analysis found no clear effect of fibre.
findings.finding: The review recommends high-fibre whole foods to lower energy density and allow larger portions while dieting. Interventional satiety evidence is inconsistent and methodologically weak.
findings.locator: 'Fiber'; 'Practical Applications'

findings.citation: Schwartz A, Doucet E. Relative changes in resting energy expenditure during weight loss: a systematic review. Obes Rev. 2010;11(7):531-47. doi:10.1111/j.1467-789X.2009.00654.x
findings.population: Participants in weight-loss interventions of several types including pharmacological (other types and age range not stated in abstract), 90 publications
findings.parameter: resting energy expenditure decline per kg of weight lost
findings.value: -15.4 ± 8.7 kcal per kg lost (mean ± SD; abstract units kcal·kg⁻¹, REE being a daily rate); 90 publications, 2977 subjects (erratum-corrected figure). This is the total REE fall relative to weight lost, not an adaptive term beyond body composition
findings.finding: Across 90 publications (2977 people), resting expenditure fell by about 15 kcal/d for each kg lost, with wide spread between studies. This is the total fall (tissue loss plus any adaptation), so it should not be added on top of a mass-based RMR equation. Low certainty.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed PMID 19761507); full text subscription-only (Europe PMC, Wiley)

findings.citation: Schwartz A, Doucet E. Relative changes in resting energy expenditure during weight loss: a systematic review. Obes Rev. 2010;11(7):531-47. doi:10.1111/j.1467-789X.2009.00654.x
findings.parameter: REE decline per kg by intervention duration
findings.value: Short interventions (>2 to <6 wk): -27.7 ± 6.7 kcal/kg; long interventions: -12.8 ± 7.1 kcal/kg (P < 0.001). The abstract labels the long group '<6 weeks', apparently a typo for 6 weeks or longer (not verifiable without full text)
findings.finding: The per-kg drop in resting expenditure was about twice as large in short interventions (2 to 6 weeks) as in longer ones. So early readings likely overstate the lasting decline, and a per-kg adjustment should use the longer-duration figure after the first weeks.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed PMID 19761507)

findings.citation: Schwartz A, Doucet E. Relative changes in resting energy expenditure during weight loss: a systematic review. Obes Rev. 2010;11(7):531-47. doi:10.1111/j.1467-789X.2009.00654.x
findings.parameter: sex-specific coefficient for REE decline
findings.value: No overall sex difference; greater decline in men than women only with pharmacological interventions (P < 0.05); magnitudes not reported in abstract
findings.finding: Men and women showed a similar per-kg fall in resting expenditure overall. A larger fall in men appeared only with drug-based interventions, so a sex-specific adaptation coefficient is not indicated for diet-and-exercise users.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed PMID 19761507)

findings.citation: Martins C, Roekenes J, Salamati S, Gower BA, Hunter GR. Metabolic adaptation is an illusion, only present when participants are in negative energy balance. Am J Clin Nutr. 2020;112(5):1212-8. doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqaa220
findings.population: Adults with obesity (BMI 34.6 ± 3.4, age 45.4 ± 8.2 y, 33 men), Norway
findings.parameter: adaptive RMR shortfall during deficit vs after weight stabilisation
findings.value: Week 9 (right after 8 wk at 1000 kcal/d, -14.1 kg, 13.2%): -92 ± 110 kcal/d (P < 0.001); week 13 (after 4 wk stabilisation): -38 ± 124 kcal/d (P = 0.011); reduction between them -53 ± 101 kcal/d (P < 0.001)
findings.finding: Right after an 8-week 1000 kcal/d diet, measured RMR was about 92 kcal/d below the value predicted from body composition. After 4 weeks of stable weight the shortfall had roughly halved, so any adaptive term should shrink once the deficit ends.
findings.locator: Results para 2; Table 2 (PMC7657334)

findings.citation: Martins C, Roekenes J, Salamati S, Gower BA, Hunter GR. Metabolic adaptation is an illusion, only present when participants are in negative energy balance. Am J Clin Nutr. 2020;112(5):1212-8. doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqaa220
findings.population: Adults with obesity: complete-data subgroup (n = 45; paper prints 33 males) and a separate subgroup of the full 71 who gained weight between weeks 9 and 13 (n = 33)
findings.parameter: persistence of adaptive RMR term after the deficit ends
findings.value: 1 y (subgroup with data at all time points, n = 45): -7 ± 129 kcal/d (P = 0.701, not significant), measured after a mean regain of 4.1 kg between week 13 and 1 y. Week 13 in a separate subgroup of the full cohort who gained weight during stabilisation (n = 33): -26.8 ± 121.5 kcal/d (P = 0.214, not significant)
findings.finding: The RMR shortfall was not significant at one year, when people were regaining weight, nor at week 13 in those who gained slightly during stabilisation. The adaptive part seems tied to ongoing negative energy balance, but strictly weight-stable maintenance at one year was not tested.
findings.locator: Results paras 2-3; Table 3 (PMC7657334)

findings.citation: Martins C, Roekenes J, Salamati S, Gower BA, Hunter GR. Metabolic adaptation is an illusion, only present when participants are in negative energy balance. Am J Clin Nutr. 2020;112(5):1212-8. doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqaa220
findings.population: Adults with obesity after diet-induced weight loss
findings.parameter: metabolic adaptation as a predictor of weight regain
findings.value: No correlation with % of lost weight regained at 1 y: week 9 r = 0.034 (P = 0.824); week 13 r = 0.106 (P = 0.488); n = 45. Mean regain 29.1 ± 52.1% of loss
findings.finding: The size of the RMR shortfall at week 9 or week 13 did not correlate with how much lost weight people regained by one year. An app should not treat measured or estimated adaptation as a regain-risk signal.
findings.locator: Results, correlation paragraph (PMC7657334)

findings.citation: Martins C, Roekenes J, Salamati S, Gower BA, Hunter GR. Metabolic adaptation is an illusion, only present when participants are in negative energy balance. Am J Clin Nutr. 2020;112(5):1212-8. doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqaa220
findings.population: Adults with obesity, BMI 30-43, age 26-62 y, Norway
findings.parameter: RMR prediction equation (sample-derived)
findings.value: RMRp (kcal/d) = 505.945 + 110.894 × sex (1 = female, 2 = male) + 0.402 × age (y) + 5.616 × FM (kg) + 15.213 × FFM (kg); derived from this cohort's baseline data only
findings.finding: The authors fitted an RMR equation to their own baseline data using sex, age, fat mass and fat-free mass. It comes from 71 adults with obesity and was not externally validated, so it is a reference point, not a general default.
findings.locator: Methods, Statistical analysis (PMC7657334)

findings.citation: Martins C, Roekenes J, Salamati S, Gower BA, Hunter GR. Metabolic adaptation is an illusion, only present when participants are in negative energy balance. Am J Clin Nutr. 2020;112(5):1212-8. doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqaa220
findings.population: Adults with obesity after an 8-week low-energy diet
findings.parameter: post-deficit maintenance energy prescription method
findings.value: Energy needs = measured RMR × physical activity level from armband monitor; macronutrients 15-20% protein, 20-30% fat, 50-60% carbohydrate (Nordic Nutrition Recommendations); recalculated after 4 wk using new RMR and PAL
findings.finding: To hold weight steady after the diet, the study set energy needs as measured RMR multiplied by monitor-derived activity level, used Nordic macronutrient ranges, and recalculated after four weeks. This describes the protocol; it was not tested against alternatives.
findings.locator: Methods, Study design (PMC7657334)

findings.citation: Martins C, Roekenes J, Salamati S, Gower BA, Hunter GR. Metabolic adaptation is an illusion, only present when participants are in negative energy balance. Am J Clin Nutr. 2020;112(5):1212-8. doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqaa220
findings.population: Adults with obesity after a 1000 kcal/d diet with 70-130 g/d carbohydrate
findings.parameter: expected water-weight rebound after leaving a ketogenic low-energy diet
findings.value: Authors' estimate about 1.6-2.5 kg (400-500 g glycogen × 3-4 g bound water per g; the range includes the glycogen mass itself; inputs taken from cited earlier studies). Not observed as scale gain here: mean weight changed +0.09 kg from week 9 to 13 on a weight-stabilisation diet. Bioimpedance intracellular water fell by week 9 and returned to baseline by week 13
findings.finding: The authors estimate that leaving ketosis refills glycogen and its bound water, worth roughly 1.6-2.5 kg of non-fat weight. The estimate is theoretical and drawn from earlier studies. A jump of this size after a very-low-carbohydrate phase should not automatically be read as a calorie surplus.
findings.locator: Discussion para 3; Results para 2; Table 2 (PMC7657334); estimate draws on cited prior work

findings.citation: Thomas DM, Martin CK, Redman LM, Heymsfield SB, Lettieri S, Levine JA, et al. Effect of dietary adherence on the body weight plateau: a mathematical model incorporating intermittent compliance with energy intake prescription. Am J Clin Nutr. 2014;100(3):787-95. doi:10.3945/ajcn.113.079822
findings.population: Simulated average US man and woman (NHANES 1999-2004 inputs)
findings.parameter: effect of extra metabolic adaptation on weight-plateau timing
findings.value: Extra 5% or 10% reduction in expenditure beyond the model's built-in adaptation: plateau at a higher weight (10% gives about 11% higher predicted stabilised weight) but timing unchanged, 365-730 d, assuming 100% adherence to a 25% deficit
findings.finding: In simulations, cutting expenditure by an extra 5% or 10% made weight settle higher but did not bring the plateau earlier. With full adherence it still arrived at one to two years, so adaptation cannot explain a plateau at around six months.
findings.locator: Results, 'Reduced EE does not induce an earlier weight plateau'; Figure 2 (PMC4135489)

findings.citation: Thomas DM, Martin CK, Redman LM, Heymsfield SB, Lettieri S, Levine JA, et al. Effect of dietary adherence on the body weight plateau: a mathematical model incorporating intermittent compliance with energy intake prescription. Am J Clin Nutr. 2014;100(3):787-95. doi:10.3945/ajcn.113.079822
findings.population: CALERIE phase 1, 25% calorie restriction group (6 men, 6 women, overweight)
findings.parameter: realistic adherence fraction for an adaptive intake model
findings.value: Back-calculated from CALERIE 25% restriction group: women 80% of days adherent (month 1), 60% (month 2), 50% (month 3), 40% (after month 3); men 80% (months 1-5), 70% thereafter. With these inputs the model plateaus at about 24 wk
findings.finding: Fitting the model to real weight curves under 25% restriction needed adherence falling from 80% to 40% of days in women and from 80% to 70% in men. With those inputs the model reproduced a plateau near 24 weeks.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Adherence model'; Results, 'Intermittent loss of dietary adherence...'; Figure 3 (PMC4135489)

findings.citation: Thomas DM, Martin CK, Redman LM, Heymsfield SB, Lettieri S, Levine JA, et al. Effect of dietary adherence on the body weight plateau: a mathematical model incorporating intermittent compliance with energy intake prescription. Am J Clin Nutr. 2014;100(3):787-95. doi:10.3945/ajcn.113.079822
findings.population: Minnesota Starvation Experiment men (n = 13) vs CALERIE free-living adults (n = 12)
findings.parameter: rule for interpreting a weight plateau
findings.value: Supervised in-residence restriction (Minnesota, n = 13 men, 10 wk of constant restriction): all weight curves fall monotonically. Free-living 25% restriction (CALERIE, n = 12, 24 wk): curves oscillate with periodic gains. The authors conclude intermittent non-adherence, not metabolic adaptation, is a major contributor to the ~6-month plateau
findings.finding: Supervised dieters lost weight smoothly, while free-living dieters showed repeated small regains. The authors judge intermittent lapses a major contributor to the common 6-month plateau, so a stalled trend should prompt a check on adherence and logging before assuming adaptation.
findings.locator: Results, 'Weight graphs from confined weight-loss studies are monotonically decreasing'; Figure 4; Discussion (PMC4135489)

findings.citation: Thomas DM, Martin CK, Redman LM, Heymsfield SB, Lettieri S, Levine JA, et al. Effect of dietary adherence on the body weight plateau: a mathematical model incorporating intermittent compliance with energy intake prescription. Am J Clin Nutr. 2014;100(3):787-95. doi:10.3945/ajcn.113.079822
findings.population: CALERIE overweight adults (n = 23) and male monozygotic twins overfed 840 kcal/d for 100 d (n = 24)
findings.parameter: prediction error of a dynamic energy-balance weight model
findings.value: CALERIE restriction (n = 23): bias 0.4 kg (reported 95% CI -2.4, 3.2) at 3 mo, R² = 0.99; bias 2.2 kg (95% CI -2.4, 6.8) at 6 mo, R² = 0.96; significant error trend at 3 mo (R² = 0.22, P = 0.02). Bouchard overfeeding (n = 24): bias 0.9 kg (95% CI -3.7, 5.5), R² = 0.93. Validation intake was derived objectively (DLW plus body-composition change)
findings.finding: The dynamic energy-balance model tracked measured weights under restriction and overfeeding, with mean bias up to about 2.2 kg by six months. The reported 95% intervals spanned several kilograms, and validation used objectively derived intake, so projections from logged intake need correcting with real weigh-ins.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Dynamic energy balance model validation'; Results, 'Model validation'; Figure 1 legend (PMC4135489)

findings.citation: Thomas DM, Martin CK, Redman LM, Heymsfield SB, Lettieri S, Levine JA, et al. Effect of dietary adherence on the body weight plateau: a mathematical model incorporating intermittent compliance with energy intake prescription. Am J Clin Nutr. 2014;100(3):787-95. doi:10.3945/ajcn.113.079822
findings.parameter: tissue energy densities and Forbes slope in a linearised weight-change model
findings.value: Equation 2: 1020 × dFFM/dt + 9500 × dFM/dt = EI − PAL × RMR, so energy densities are 1020 kcal/kg fat-free mass and 9500 kcal/kg fat mass (the text's 'kcal/d' is a unit typo). Forbes curve slope 10.4. Half-life = −ln[1 − ½·FM0/Constant]/λ, with λ = −PAL × (10.4/FM0 + 1)·c1 / (9500 + 10.4 × 1020/FM0), where c1 = Mifflin-St Jeor weight coefficient
findings.finding: The linearised model converts an energy gap into tissue change at 9500 kcal per kg of fat and 1020 kcal per kg of fat-free mass, with a Forbes slope of 10.4. Time to plateau depends on activity level, these constants, the Mifflin-St Jeor weight coefficient and starting fat mass.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Linearized model to calculate weight-loss half-life', Equation 2; Results, 'Calculation of half-life', Equations 5-6 (equation images read from PMC4135489)

findings.citation: Turicchi J, O'Driscoll R, Horgan G, Duarte C, Palmeira AL, Larsen SC, et al. Weekly, seasonal and holiday body weight fluctuation patterns among individuals engaged in a European multi-centre behavioural weight loss maintenance intervention. PLoS One. 2020;15(4):e0232152. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0232152
findings.population: Adults ≥18 y with ≥5% weight loss in the prior 12 months and pre-loss BMI ≥25 (NoHoW trial; UK, Denmark, Portugal; 69% women)
findings.parameter: systematic day-of-week weight cycle (mean detrended pattern)
findings.value: Mean day-of-week cycle about 0.35% of body weight (about 0.3 kg); peak Monday, low Friday. Men 0.41% vs women 0.29%; by BMI 0.39% (healthy) to 0.26% (class 2-3 obesity); by age 0.24% (>60 y) to 0.43% (30-45 y). Individual detrended readings spread about 1.0-1.2% per day (Table 2 parentheses, labelled SE in the header but SD in the caption)
findings.finding: After removing each person's trend, average weight peaked on Monday and bottomed on Friday, a cycle of about 0.35% (0.3 kg). This is the systematic weekly pattern. Single readings scatter more widely around the trend, so smoothing weigh-ins beats reacting to any one reading.
findings.locator: Results, 'Weekly patterns of body weight'; Table 2; Discussion para 2 (PMC7192384)

findings.citation: Turicchi J, O'Driscoll R, Horgan G, Duarte C, Palmeira AL, Larsen SC, et al. Weekly, seasonal and holiday body weight fluctuation patterns among individuals engaged in a European multi-centre behavioural weight loss maintenance intervention. PLoS One. 2020;15(4):e0232152. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0232152
findings.parameter: holiday (Christmas) weight excursion
findings.value: +1.35% (SD 1.74) of body weight (about 1.1 kg), computed as the highest detrended weight in the month after Christmas minus the lowest in the month before (peak-to-trough). Lowest in the first week of December, highest on 2 January; still at least 0.35% above the pre-Christmas level through March. UK 1.52% vs Portugal 1.13% (p = 0.011)
findings.finding: Over Christmas, detrended weight rose by 1.35% on average (about 1.1 kg) and was still at least 0.35% above the pre-holiday level in March. Holiday gains partly persist, so they should not be discarded as pure noise.
findings.locator: Results, 'Christmas patterns of body weight'; Methods, 'Statistical analysis'; Table 3; Discussion (PMC7192384)

findings.citation: Turicchi J, O'Driscoll R, Horgan G, Duarte C, Palmeira AL, Larsen SC, et al. Weekly, seasonal and holiday body weight fluctuation patterns among individuals engaged in a European multi-centre behavioural weight loss maintenance intervention. PLoS One. 2020;15(4):e0232152. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0232152
findings.parameter: seasonal weight fluctuation
findings.value: About 0.8% per year after linear detrending, mostly the Christmas effect; other seasonal differences small and inconsistent (e.g. summer: men 0.23% vs women 0.40% above trend, p = 0.034)
findings.finding: Across the year, detrended weight varied by about 0.8%, mostly because of the Christmas rise. Other seasonal patterns were small and inconsistent, so seasonal adjustment of targets is not supported.
findings.locator: Results, 'Seasonal patterns of body weight'; Table 4 (PMC7192384)

findings.citation: Turicchi J, O'Driscoll R, Horgan G, Duarte C, Palmeira AL, Larsen SC, et al. Weekly, seasonal and holiday body weight fluctuation patterns among individuals engaged in a European multi-centre behavioural weight loss maintenance intervention. PLoS One. 2020;15(4):e0232152. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0232152
findings.parameter: weight-series smoothing and gap-filling method
findings.value: LOESS detrending, span 0.5 (weekly) and 0.7 (Christmas), chosen by visual inspection; linear trend for the seasonal analysis. Gaps imputed with an exponentially weighted moving average, 3 days either side (1-week window), for the Christmas and seasonal analyses only (not weekly). First weight of the day kept; at least 20 weights per year required, plus analysis-specific minimums
findings.finding: The researchers removed trends with LOESS regression, filled gaps with a one-week exponentially weighted moving average for longer-period analyses only, and kept the first weigh-in of each day. These were research choices (spans picked by eye), not a validated smoothing rule for an app.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Participants', 'Fitbit Aria scale' and 'Statistical analysis' (PMC7192384); outlier criteria are in supplementary S1 Table, which was not accessed

findings.citation: Turicchi J, O'Driscoll R, Horgan G, Duarte C, Palmeira AL, Larsen SC, et al. Weekly, seasonal and holiday body weight fluctuation patterns among individuals engaged in a European multi-centre behavioural weight loss maintenance intervention. PLoS One. 2020;15(4):e0232152. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0232152
findings.population: NoHoW weight-loss-maintenance participants with smart scales
findings.parameter: weigh-in protocol and achievable frequency
findings.value: Instruction: at least 2 weigh-ins per week, on waking after voiding, in light or no clothing. Achieved: about 4 per week at the start, falling to about 2.5 per week over 2 years; data sparsest on weekends and in December
findings.finding: Participants asked to weigh at least twice a week, first thing in the morning after voiding, managed about four weigh-ins a week at first, falling to about 2.5 a week over two years. Weekend and December data were the most often missing.
findings.locator: Methods, 'Study design' and 'Fitbit Aria scale'; Results para 1; Figures 2-3 (PMC7192384)

findings.citation: Madigan CD, Daley AJ, Lewis AL, Aveyard P, Jolly K. Is self-weighing an effective tool for weight loss: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2015;12:104. doi:10.1186/s12966-015-0267-4
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in a weight-loss RCT
findings.parameter: effect of self-weighing as a stand-alone feature
findings.finding: The only trial testing advice to self-weigh with no other support found no clear weight benefit. Weigh-in prompts on their own should not be presented as a weight-loss intervention.
findings.locator: Results, 'Synthesis of results'; Table 3 (PMC4546162)

findings.citation: Madigan CD, Daley AJ, Lewis AL, Aveyard P, Jolly K. Is self-weighing an effective tool for weight loss: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2015;12:104. doi:10.1186/s12966-015-0267-4
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: added effect of self-weighing within a behavioural programme
findings.value: -1.7 kg (95% CI -2.6 to -0.8); 4 trials, n = 274; I² = 0%; 95% prediction interval -7.5 to 4.1; all but one instructed daily weighing
findings.finding: Adding self-weighing or self-regulation tools to the same behavioural programme gave about 1.7 kg more weight loss across four trials. The prediction interval included possible gain, and other self-regulation parts were mixed in, so the effect of weighing alone is unclear.
findings.locator: Results, 'Synthesis of results'; Table 3 (PMC4546162)

findings.citation: Madigan CD, Daley AJ, Lewis AL, Aveyard P, Jolly K. Is self-weighing an effective tool for weight loss: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2015;12:104. doi:10.1186/s12966-015-0267-4
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in weight-loss RCTs (mostly USA; median 75% women)
findings.parameter: effect of multi-component programmes that include self-weighing
findings.value: -3.4 kg (95% CI -4.2 to -2.6) vs no or minimal control; 15 trials, n = 2490; I² = 82%; 95% prediction interval -6.9 to 0.1. All 19 pooled trials (n = 2843): -3.0 kg (95% CI -3.7 to -2.3)
findings.finding: Multi-component programmes that included self-weighing beat no or minimal intervention by about 3.4 kg across 15 trials, with high heterogeneity. So weigh-ins belong inside a wider programme of feedback and goals.
findings.locator: Results, 'Synthesis of results'; Table 3 (PMC4546162)

findings.citation: Madigan CD, Daley AJ, Lewis AL, Aveyard P, Jolly K. Is self-weighing an effective tool for weight loss: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2015;12:104. doi:10.1186/s12966-015-0267-4
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in multi-component weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: minimum weigh-in frequency
findings.value: Daily weighing: -3.6 kg (95% CI -5.4 to -1.8), 7 trials, n = 795, I² = 91%. Less than daily: -3.3 kg (95% CI -4.0 to -2.5), 8 trials, n = 1695, I² = 65%. Subgroup difference P = 0.57
findings.finding: Programmes asking for daily weighing and those asking for less frequent (mostly weekly) weighing gave similar net losses, with no significant difference between them. A weekly minimum looks adequate and daily can be optional, but this comparison is across trials, not randomised.
findings.locator: Results, 'Theoretical concepts'; Table 3 (PMC4546162)

findings.citation: Madigan CD, Daley AJ, Lewis AL, Aveyard P, Jolly K. Is self-weighing an effective tool for weight loss: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2015;12:104. doi:10.1186/s12966-015-0267-4
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in multi-component weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: accountability for weigh-ins
findings.value: With accountability: -3.6 kg (95% CI -4.6 to -2.7), 14 trials, n = 2073. Without: -2.3 kg (95% CI -3.2 to -1.5 in Table 3; text gives -3.1 to -1.5), 2 trials, n = 313. P = 0.03
findings.finding: Trials where participants knew a therapist or researcher was checking their weigh-ins showed larger losses than trials without this. The comparison rests on only two trials without accountability. For a local-only app, the nearest option is self-set review prompts, which are untested.
findings.locator: Results, 'Theoretical concepts'; Table 3 (PMC4546162)

findings.citation: Madigan CD, Daley AJ, Lewis AL, Aveyard P, Jolly K. Is self-weighing an effective tool for weight loss: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2015;12:104. doi:10.1186/s12966-015-0267-4
findings.population: Adults in weight-loss RCTs instructed to weigh daily
findings.parameter: expected adherence to a daily weigh-in instruction
findings.value: 44%, 50% and 95% adherence in the 3 trials that measured it (all instructed daily weighing). A fourth trial instructed daily weighing with weekly log submission and reported 76.8% (SD 23.7%); the paper leaves unclear whether this counts weighing days or logs returned
findings.finding: In the three trials that measured it, people followed a daily-weighing instruction 44%, 50% and 95% of the time. A fourth trial reported 76.8% compliance with daily weighing plus weekly logs. The app should expect incomplete weigh-in series and handle gaps.
findings.locator: Results, 'Theoretical concepts' (PMC4546162)

findings.citation: Madigan CD, Daley AJ, Lewis AL, Aveyard P, Jolly K. Is self-weighing an effective tool for weight loss: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2015;12:104. doi:10.1186/s12966-015-0267-4
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: psychological harm from self-weighing
findings.value: No significant between-group differences in 3 trials measuring body dissatisfaction, depressive symptoms, dietary restraint, disinhibition or binge eating; one trial's non-randomised sensitivity analysis found no difference in body dissatisfaction or depressive symptoms between daily weighers who did and did not lose weight; most trials did not report adverse effects
findings.finding: Three trials that measured psychological outcomes found no significant harm from self-weighing versus control. One trial's non-randomised analysis also found no extra body dissatisfaction or depressive symptoms in daily weighers who did not lose weight. Most trials did not report adverse effects, so the evidence is thin.
findings.locator: Results, 'Adverse events' (PMC4546162)

findings.citation: Zheng Y, Klem ML, Sereika SM, Danford CA, Ewing LJ, Burke LE. Self-weighing in weight management: a systematic literature review. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2015;23(2):256-65. doi:10.1002/oby.20946
findings.population: Adults seeking weight-loss treatment; 17 prospective longitudinal studies from the prior 25 years
findings.parameter: self-weighing frequency
findings.value: Regular self-weighing (defined by the review as weighing regularly over time, e.g. daily or weekly) associated with more weight loss across 17 prospective longitudinal studies; effect sizes and reported frequencies varied; no optimal frequency or pooled estimate in abstract
findings.finding: Across 17 prospective longitudinal studies of adults seeking weight-loss treatment, regular self-weighing was associated with greater weight loss. These are associations, not randomised effects, and both effect sizes and weighing frequencies varied too much to set an optimal frequency.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed PMID 25521523); full text subscription-only (Europe PMC, Wiley returned 403)

findings.citation: Zheng Y, Klem ML, Sereika SM, Danford CA, Ewing LJ, Burke LE. Self-weighing in weight management: a systematic literature review. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2015;23(2):256-65. doi:10.1002/oby.20946
findings.population: Adults seeking weight-loss treatment; subset of 17 prospective longitudinal studies (size of subset unknown)
findings.parameter: psychological safety of regular self-weighing
findings.value: Regular self-weighing not associated with adverse psychological outcomes (e.g. depression, anxiety); the abstract does not say how many of the 17 studies assessed these outcomes and gives no effect sizes
findings.finding: Regular self-weighing was not linked to adverse psychological outcomes such as depression or anxiety in the studies that assessed them (number not stated in the abstract). This supports offering routine weigh-in prompts, at low certainty.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed PMID 25521523)

findings.citation: Burke LE, Wang J, Sevick MA. Self-monitoring in weight loss: a systematic review of the literature. J Am Diet Assoc. 2011;111(1):92-102. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2010.10.008
findings.population: US adults in behavioural weight-loss or weight-gain-prevention studies (1993-2009), mostly white women with overweight or obesity
findings.parameter: self-weighing frequency
findings.value: at least weekly; weighing daily to weekly beat weighing less often. No firm optimal dose
findings.finding: Across six self-weighing studies, weighing daily to weekly went with more weight loss than weighing less often. The authors judged dose evidence limited but suggested at least weekly weighing may help. Mostly correlational: one 20-week RCT of daily versus delayed weekly weighing found no between-group difference.
findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph 2 (daily-to-weekly vs less often) and paragraph 9 (dose); Results, 'Self-Monitoring Weight' (Linde, Wing, Gokee-LaRose, VanWormer). Paragraph numbers follow the PMC author manuscript

findings.citation: Burke LE, Wang J, Sevick MA. Self-monitoring in weight loss: a systematic review of the literature. J Am Diet Assoc. 2011;111(1):92-102. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2010.10.008
findings.population: 15 dietary self-monitoring studies (of 22 reviewed) of US adults in behavioural weight-loss programmes, mostly white women
findings.parameter: dietary logging dose (frequency)
findings.value: No evidence-based minimum. 15 of 15 dietary self-monitoring studies linked more frequent or complete logging with more weight loss
findings.finding: All 15 dietary self-monitoring studies linked more complete or more frequent food recording with greater weight loss. Measurement varied too much to recommend a specific logging frequency, so the review supports logging as much as feasible.
findings.locator: Results, 'Self-Monitoring Dietary Intake', paragraph 1; Discussion, paragraphs 2 and 9 (PMC author manuscript numbering). The published abstract (PubMed) and body say 15 dietary studies; the PMC manuscript abstract says 14

findings.citation: Burke LE, Wang J, Sevick MA. Self-monitoring in weight loss: a systematic review of the literature. J Am Diet Assoc. 2011;111(1):92-102. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2010.10.008
findings.population: Adults in a behavioural weight-loss clinical trial (US)
findings.parameter: complete food-log day threshold
findings.value: A diary counted as adherent when it recorded at least 50% of the day's energy goal (one trial's definition)
findings.finding: One weight-loss trial scored a food diary as adherent only if it captured at least half of the day's energy goal; a week with an incomplete or absent diary counted as non-adherent. Apart from early therapist-rated completeness scores, this was the only stated completeness criterion the review found.
findings.locator: Results, 'Self-Monitoring Dietary Intake', paragraph 1 (adherence definition); Discussion, paragraphs 4-5 (PMC author manuscript numbering)

findings.citation: Burke LE, Wang J, Sevick MA. Self-monitoring in weight loss: a systematic review of the literature. J Am Diet Assoc. 2011;111(1):92-102. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2010.10.008
findings.population: Adults in US behavioural weight-loss and regain-prevention trials
findings.parameter: expected decline in logging adherence
findings.value: Only 25% of one trial's sample were still self-monitoring at the end; self-weighing adherence also fell over 18 months
findings.finding: Self-monitoring adherence fell gradually and dropped further as treatment contact became less frequent. In one trial only a quarter of participants were still recording at the end. Self-weighing adherence also declined over an 18-month regain-prevention trial.
findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph 5 (PMC author manuscript numbering); Results, 'Self-Monitoring Weight' (Wing et al.)

findings.citation: Burke LE, Wang J, Sevick MA. Self-monitoring in weight loss: a systematic review of the literature. J Am Diet Assoc. 2011;111(1):92-102. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2010.10.008
findings.population: Adults in an ancillary study of a US behavioural weight-loss trial
findings.parameter: logging adherence measure (timestamps)
findings.value: Rule: measure adherence from date- and time-stamped electronic entries. Self-reported diary completion agreed poorly with electronic records ('backfilling')
findings.finding: An instrumented diary binder showed little agreement between self-reported and electronically recorded diary use, including diaries filled in for days the binder stayed shut. Timing of entries relative to meals was also significantly related to weight loss. Date- and time-stamped electronic logs gave objective adherence data.
findings.locator: Results, 'Adherence to Self-Monitoring', paragraph 2 (instrumented binder study); Discussion, paragraph 4 (PMC author manuscript numbering)

findings.citation: Burke LE, Wang J, Sevick MA. Self-monitoring in weight loss: a systematic review of the literature. J Am Diet Assoc. 2011;111(1):92-102. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2010.10.008
findings.population: New users of dietary self-monitoring software (US adults)
findings.parameter: time burden per meal entry
findings.value: 8-10 minutes per meal for new users of dietary software
findings.finding: New users of a dietary software program took about 8 to 10 minutes to enter one meal, the same as or less than paper recording. The authors expected saved meals and large food databases to cut this burden, but time savings were unproven.
findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph 6 (Beasley et al.)

findings.citation: Burke LE, Wang J, Sevick MA. Self-monitoring in weight loss: a systematic review of the literature. J Am Diet Assoc. 2011;111(1):92-102. doi:10.1016/j.jada.2010.10.008
findings.population: 22 US studies, predominantly white women with overweight or obesity
findings.parameter: evidence grade for logging features
findings.value: Diet logging: Class IIa, Level A. Self-weighing: Class IIa, Level A. Exercise logging: Class IIb, Level B (AHA/ACC scheme). Overall evidence rated weak
findings.finding: Using AHA/ACC grading, the authors rated dietary self-monitoring and self-weighing Class IIa, Level A, and exercise self-monitoring Class IIb, Level B. They still called the overall evidence weak because of descriptive designs, homogeneous samples and reliance on self-report.
findings.locator: Results, 'Weight of the Evidence' and Table 2; Abstract

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in 39 behavioural weight-loss RCTs (2009-2019); mean BMI 28.3-37.0 kg/m2; 68% female; mostly US and White
findings.parameter: expected share of days logged (daily prescription)
findings.value: Mean logging reached at least 50% of intervention days in 33/57 (58%) occasions and at least 75% in 5/57 (9%)
findings.finding: When trials asked for daily digital self-monitoring, average engagement reached half of intervention days in 58% of occasions but three-quarters of days in only 9%. Many days therefore go unlogged even when daily tracking is prescribed.
findings.locator: Results, 'Secondary aim 2: overview of self-monitoring engagement' - 'Days over the length of the intervention'

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in digital behavioural weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: decline in logging engagement with programme length
findings.value: At least 50% of days: 14/15 (93%) over the first 3 months, 15/33 (45%) over 6 months, 3/8 (38%) over 12 months or more. At least 75% of days: 3/15 (20%), 2/33 (6%), 0/8 (0%)
findings.finding: Engagement fell as the reporting window grew. Nearly all interventions reached half of days logged over the first 3 months, fewer than half did over 6 months, and none reached three-quarters of days over 12 months or longer.
findings.locator: Results, 'Days over the length of the intervention' (stratified by reporting interval)

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in digital behavioural weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: weigh-in vs food-log engagement (daily prescription)
findings.value: Weight: 11/17 (65%) reached at least 50% of days and 1/17 (6%) at least 75%. Diet: 11/19 (58%) and 2/19 (11%). Activity: 8/16 (50%) and 2/16 (13%)
findings.finding: Under daily prescriptions, weight, diet and activity tracking had broadly similar engagement: 50-65% of interventions reached half of days and 6-13% reached three-quarters. Engagement was highest for weight, then diet, then activity, though the authors note differing prescribed frequencies likely confound this ordering.
findings.locator: Results, 'Days over the length of the intervention' (by behaviour); Discussion, 'Key findings' paragraph 4

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in digital behavioural weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: average days logged per week
findings.value: 10/20 (50%) daily-tracking interventions averaged at least 4 days/week; 3/20 (15%) averaged at least 6 days/week
findings.finding: Of 20 daily-tracking interventions reporting days per week, half averaged at least 4 logged days a week and 15% at least 6. Design inference, not the authors': a weekly adaptive update should expect roughly four or fewer logged days.
findings.locator: Results, 'Secondary aim 2' - 'Days per week'

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in 39 behavioural weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: link between self-monitoring and weight loss
findings.value: Positive in 50/68 (74%) occasions. Weight 13/18 (72%), diet 16/20 (80%), activity 8/11 (73%). Interventions under 12 months 41/49 (84%); 12 months or longer 9/19 (47%)
findings.finding: More frequent digital self-monitoring went with greater weight loss in about three-quarters of reported associations, with similar results for weight, diet and activity tracking. The link weakened in programmes of 12 months or longer. The associations are correlational because participants chose how much to engage. Burke 2011 agrees.
findings.locator: Results, 'Primary aim: the relationship between self-monitoring engagement and weight change'; Discussion, 'Strengths and limitations' (selection bias)

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in 9 RCTs comparing digital and paper tracking
findings.parameter: digital vs paper logging engagement
findings.value: Results text: digital better in 19/34 (56%), worse in 4/34 (12%), no different in 11/34 (32%); for diet, better in 10/13. The abstract instead says 21/34 better and 2 worse
findings.finding: In nine trials comparing digital and paper self-monitoring, digital engagement was higher on most occasions, especially for diet. The abstract and the results text give different counts, so the exact split is uncertain.
findings.locator: Results, 'Secondary aim 2: Comparison of digital versus paper-based self-monitoring' versus Abstract, Results (discrepant counts)

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in 12 digital weight-loss interventions
findings.parameter: passive vs manual capture engagement
findings.value: The passively captured behaviour had higher engagement in 10/12 interventions (7 wearables, 3 transmitting e-scales); not significance-tested
findings.finding: When one behaviour was captured automatically (wearable or transmitting scale) and another entered by hand, the automatic one usually had higher engagement (10 of 12). A cited commercial-platform study found that only manually entered weights were associated with weight loss.
findings.locator: Results, 'Comparison of tracked behaviors' - 'Passive versus active'; Discussion, 'Key findings' paragraph 6

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in digital behavioural weight-loss RCTs
findings.parameter: prescribed logging frequency
findings.value: Weight: daily in 23/48 (48%), weekly in 18/48 (38%). Diet: daily in 37/54 (69%). No trial randomised participants to different logging frequencies
findings.finding: Trials most often prescribed daily food logging and daily or weekly weighing. No digital weight-loss trial randomised participants to different self-monitoring frequencies, so the optimal frequency is untested.
findings.locator: Results, 'Secondary aim 1' - 'Prescribed frequency of self-monitoring'; Discussion, 'Key findings' paragraph 2

findings.citation: Patel ML, Wakayama LN, Bennett GG. Self-monitoring via digital health in weight loss interventions: a systematic review among adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2021;29(3):478-499. doi:10.1002/oby.23088
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in 5 RCTs with counselling and stand-alone digital arms
findings.parameter: stand-alone app vs counselling engagement
findings.value: Counselling arm better on 5/18 (28%) occasions, worse on 7/18 (39%), no different on 6/18 (33%)
findings.finding: In five trials with both counselling and stand-alone digital arms, counselling did not consistently raise self-monitoring engagement. Stand-alone arms that did better often used incentives or prompts.
findings.locator: Results, 'Secondary aim 2: Comparison of intervention type' - 'Stand-alone versus counseling'; Discussion, 'Key findings' paragraph 5

findings.citation: Lichtman SW, Pisarska K, Berman ER, Pestone M, Dowling H, Offenbacher E, et al. Discrepancy between self-reported and actual caloric intake and exercise in obese subjects. N Engl J Med. 1992;327(27):1893-8. doi:10.1056/NEJM199212313272701
findings.population: US adults with obesity presenting for treatment: 10 with self-reported diet resistance (9 women, 1 man), compared with 80 controls, from 224 consecutive patients
findings.parameter: intake under-reporting in users who report diet resistance
findings.value: Reported intake was 47 +/- 16% (mean +/- SD) below measured intake
findings.finding: People with obesity who said they could not lose weight on under 1200 kcal/day actually ate far more than they reported. Over a 14-day measured period they under-reported intake by about 47% on average.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract, Methods and Results (full text not accessible)

findings.citation: Lichtman SW, Pisarska K, Berman ER, Pestone M, Dowling H, Offenbacher E, et al. Discrepancy between self-reported and actual caloric intake and exercise in obese subjects. N Engl J Med. 1992;327(27):1893-8. doi:10.1056/NEJM199212313272701
findings.population: US adults with obesity and self-reported diet resistance
findings.parameter: over-reporting of physical activity
findings.value: Self-reported physical activity was 51 +/- 75% (mean +/- SD) above measured
findings.finding: The same diet-resistant group over-reported physical activity by about 51% on average, with very wide individual variation (SD 75%). In this small, selected sample self-reported exercise was unreliable, which argues against raising energy targets on reported exercise alone.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract, Results (full text not accessible)

findings.citation: Lichtman SW, Pisarska K, Berman ER, Pestone M, Dowling H, Offenbacher E, et al. Discrepancy between self-reported and actual caloric intake and exercise in obese subjects. N Engl J Med. 1992;327(27):1893-8. doi:10.1056/NEJM199212313272701
findings.population: US adults with obesity: 10 diet-resistant patients (9 women, 1 man); controls were subgroups of 80 non-diet-resistant patients (size per comparison not given in the abstract)
findings.parameter: metabolic-rate deviation in apparent weight-loss resistance
findings.value: Total energy expenditure and RMR within 5% of values predicted from body composition; thermic effects of food and exercise not different from controls
findings.finding: In ten self-described diet-resistant patients, measured total expenditure and resting metabolic rate were within 5% of predictions from body composition, and thermic effects of food and exercise matched controls. Failure to lose weight reflected under-reported intake and over-reported activity, not low metabolism.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract, Results and Conclusions (full text not accessible)

findings.citation: Subar AF, Freedman LS, Tooze JA, Kirkpatrick SI, Boushey C, Neuhouser ML, et al. Addressing current criticism regarding the value of self-report dietary data. J Nutr. 2015;145(12):2639-45. doi:10.3945/jn.115.219634
findings.population: Adults in general (dietary surveillance and epidemiology context)
findings.parameter: source of the energy-balance signal
findings.value: Rule: never treat self-reported energy intake as true intake; body-weight change is the best available measure of energy balance
findings.finding: The expert authors advise against using self-reported energy intake as a measure of actual intake or to judge energy balance. They name weight change as the best indicator of energy balance, while self-report stays valuable for showing which foods are eaten.
findings.locator: Section 'EI Is Inaccurately Measured by Self-Report Data'; 'Implications for dietary surveillance', paragraph 2; 'The Future...' - 'Dietary surveillance'; Conclusions, recommendation 2

findings.citation: Subar AF, Freedman LS, Tooze JA, Kirkpatrick SI, Boushey C, Neuhouser ML, et al. Addressing current criticism regarding the value of self-report dietary data. J Nutr. 2015;145(12):2639-45. doi:10.3945/jn.115.219634
findings.population: Healthy US adults in 5 pooled recovery-biomarker studies
findings.parameter: 24-h recall energy under-reporting vs DLW
findings.value: Middle-aged men 12-13%; young and middle-aged women 6-16%; elderly women 25% (pooled from 5 US recovery-biomarker studies)
findings.finding: As summarised here, pooled data from five large US biomarker studies showed that 24-hour recalls under-reported energy by about 6-16% in younger and middle-aged adults and about 25% in elderly women. The primary pooling study was not read.
findings.locator: Section 'Magnitude of the Measurement Error in Dietary Self-Report Data', paragraph 1

findings.citation: Subar AF, Freedman LS, Tooze JA, Kirkpatrick SI, Boushey C, Neuhouser ML, et al. Addressing current criticism regarding the value of self-report dietary data. J Nutr. 2015;145(12):2639-45. doi:10.3945/jn.115.219634
findings.population: Healthy US adults in 5 pooled recovery-biomarker studies
findings.parameter: FFQ energy under-reporting vs DLW
findings.value: 24-33% in both men and women
findings.finding: In the same pooled biomarker data, food-frequency questionnaires, which are not designed to measure energy, under-reported energy intake by 24-33% against doubly labelled water in both sexes.
findings.locator: Section 'Magnitude of the Measurement Error in Dietary Self-Report Data', paragraph 1

findings.citation: Subar AF, Freedman LS, Tooze JA, Kirkpatrick SI, Boushey C, Neuhouser ML, et al. Addressing current criticism regarding the value of self-report dietary data. J Nutr. 2015;145(12):2639-45. doi:10.3945/jn.115.219634
findings.population: Healthy US adults in pooled recovery-biomarker studies
findings.parameter: protein vs energy logging accuracy
findings.value: 24-h recall under-reporting against recovery biomarkers: protein 5%, potassium 3%, versus 6-25% for energy
findings.finding: On 24-hour recalls, absolute protein and potassium intakes were under-reported far less than energy (about 5% and 3%). This suggests logged protein may be less biased than logged calories, though it was shown for interviewer recalls, not app food logs.
findings.locator: Section 'Magnitude of the Measurement Error in Dietary Self-Report Data', paragraph 1

findings.citation: Subar AF, Freedman LS, Tooze JA, Kirkpatrick SI, Boushey C, Neuhouser ML, et al. Addressing current criticism regarding the value of self-report dietary data. J Nutr. 2015;145(12):2639-45. doi:10.3945/jn.115.219634
findings.population: US adults (NHANES III; DLW validation cohorts)
findings.parameter: expected share of implausible energy reporters
findings.value: 21-24% on 24-h recalls in large DLW studies; NHANES III, individual-level Goldberg cutoff 2: 27.7% of women, 18.1% of men
findings.finding: With appropriate individual-level methods, about one in five 24-hour-recall respondents report implausible energy intakes: 21-24% in DLW studies, and 18% of men and 28% of women in NHANES III. That is far below the 59-67% claimed with a misapplied cutoff.
findings.locator: Section 'Magnitude of the Measurement Error in Dietary Self-Report Data', paragraph 2

findings.citation: Subar AF, Freedman LS, Tooze JA, Kirkpatrick SI, Boushey C, Neuhouser ML, et al. Addressing current criticism regarding the value of self-report dietary data. J Nutr. 2015;145(12):2639-45. doi:10.3945/jn.115.219634
findings.parameter: Goldberg EI:BMR plausibility cutoff
findings.value: Drop the fixed cutoff 1 (EI:BMR 1.35). Use cutoff 2 per individual, calculated from days recorded, within-person CV of intake, estimated BMR, activity level and sample size
findings.finding: The fixed EI:BMR ratio of 1.35 assumes a measured BMR and habitual intake, and it should not be used. The recommended alternative calculates each person's cutoff from recording days, day-to-day variation, estimated BMR and activity level.
findings.locator: Section 'Magnitude of the Measurement Error in Dietary Self-Report Data', paragraph 2 (Goldberg/Black cutoffs)

findings.citation: Subar AF, Freedman LS, Tooze JA, Kirkpatrick SI, Boushey C, Neuhouser ML, et al. Addressing current criticism regarding the value of self-report dietary data. J Nutr. 2015;145(12):2639-45. doi:10.3945/jn.115.219634
findings.parameter: foods most likely to be under-logged
findings.value: Low-energy reporters report fewer high-fat and sweet foods. Expect more under-reporting of added sugars and saturated fat, and less of fruit, vegetables and whole grains
findings.finding: People who under-report energy tend to report fewer foods high in fat and sugar. The authors expect social desirability to cause less under-reporting of fruit, vegetables and whole grains than of added sugars and saturated fat, so logged diet quality probably looks better than reality.
findings.locator: Section 'Implications for dietary surveillance', paragraphs 3-4

findings.citation: Subar AF, Freedman LS, Tooze JA, Kirkpatrick SI, Boushey C, Neuhouser ML, et al. Addressing current criticism regarding the value of self-report dietary data. J Nutr. 2015;145(12):2639-45. doi:10.3945/jn.115.219634
findings.parameter: food-record reactivity
findings.value: Rule: keeping a food record can change intake itself, including eating less on recording days; entries made at the end of the day act like a recall
findings.finding: Real-time food records can be accurate but are reactive: people may eat differently or less on recording days, which is why behavioural programmes use them to drive change. Records completed at the end of the day share the memory limits of recalls.
findings.locator: Section 'EI Is Inaccurately Measured by Self-Report Data', paragraph 2

findings.citation: Burrows TL, Ho YY, Rollo ME, Collins CE. Validity of dietary assessment methods when compared to the method of doubly labeled water: a systematic review in adults. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:850. doi:10.3389/fendo.2019.00850
findings.population: Free-living adults aged 18-96 in DLW validation studies (59 studies overall, 1973-Feb 2019, mostly US and Caucasian); 23 food-record studies reported group-level accuracy
findings.parameter: food-record energy under-reporting vs DLW
findings.value: 11-41% under-reporting in 19 studies; over-reporting (8%) in 1 study; no significant difference in 3
findings.finding: Most food-record validation studies found energy intake significantly under-reported, by 11-41%, against doubly labelled water; only one found over-reporting. Food records are the closest analogue to app meal logging.
findings.locator: Results, 'Outcomes by Dietary Assessment Category' - 'Food Record'; Discussion, paragraph 1

findings.citation: Burrows TL, Ho YY, Rollo ME, Collins CE. Validity of dietary assessment methods when compared to the method of doubly labeled water: a systematic review in adults. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:850. doi:10.3389/fendo.2019.00850
findings.population: Adults in DLW validation studies of technology-assisted food records
findings.parameter: under-reporting in image- or technology-assisted food records
findings.value: Digital-camera records: 6%, 17% and 24% (3 studies; 1 showed no difference). Smartphone image-based: 20-37%. Adding a wearable camera to a food record: 34% to 30%
findings.finding: Technology did not remove under-reporting. Camera-assisted records under-reported energy by 6-24%, smartphone image-based methods by 20-37%, and a wearable camera cut food-record under-reporting only from 34% to 30%. The evidence rests on a few small studies.
findings.locator: Results, 'Food Record with technology component'; Discussion, paragraph 2

findings.citation: Burrows TL, Ho YY, Rollo ME, Collins CE. Validity of dietary assessment methods when compared to the method of doubly labeled water: a systematic review in adults. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:850. doi:10.3389/fendo.2019.00850
findings.population: Free-living adults in DLW validation studies
findings.parameter: 24-h recall energy under-reporting vs DLW
findings.value: 8-30% under-reporting; the lowest and least variable of all methods
findings.finding: Twenty-four-hour recalls under-reported energy by 8-30%, the smallest and least variable error among the methods reviewed. In every recall study that reported by sex, women tended to under-report more than men.
findings.locator: Results, '24-Hour Recall'; Discussion, paragraph 1; Conclusion

findings.citation: Burrows TL, Ho YY, Rollo ME, Collins CE. Validity of dietary assessment methods when compared to the method of doubly labeled water: a systematic review in adults. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:850. doi:10.3389/fendo.2019.00850
findings.population: Adults in one New Zealand DLW validation study (n=40)
findings.parameter: under-reporting in camera-assisted 24-h recall
findings.value: Women 13% to 7%, men 17% to 9% (24-h multiple-pass recall vs the same recall plus a wearable camera; one study)
findings.finding: In one study, adding a neck-worn sensor camera to multiple-pass 24-hour recalls roughly halved energy under-reporting, from 13% to 7% in women and 17% to 9% in men, although some under-reporting remained.
findings.locator: Results, '24 h MPR with technology component'

findings.citation: Burrows TL, Ho YY, Rollo ME, Collins CE. Validity of dietary assessment methods when compared to the method of doubly labeled water: a systematic review in adults. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:850. doi:10.3389/fendo.2019.00850
findings.population: Free-living adults in DLW validation studies
findings.parameter: FFQ energy under-reporting vs DLW
findings.value: 4.6-42% under-reporting; significant at group level in all but one FFQ study
findings.finding: All but one FFQ study showed significant group-level energy under-reporting, ranging from 4.6% to 42%; one adapted FFQ in low-income Brazilian women showed no group-level difference, though individual misreporting remained. The wide spread makes FFQ energy unreliable, consistent with Subar 2015's pooled 24-33%.
findings.locator: Results, 'Food Frequency Questionnaire', paragraph 1; Discussion, paragraph 5

findings.citation: Burrows TL, Ho YY, Rollo ME, Collins CE. Validity of dietary assessment methods when compared to the method of doubly labeled water: a systematic review in adults. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:850. doi:10.3389/fendo.2019.00850
findings.population: Adults in 5 DLW validation studies using diet history
findings.parameter: diet-history energy under-reporting vs DLW
findings.value: 1.3-47% under-reporting in 4 of 5 studies; in one study women under-reported by 47% and men by 1.3%
findings.finding: Four of five diet-history studies found energy under-reported by 1.3-47%. One found a large sex gap, with women under-reporting far more than men.
findings.locator: Results, 'Diet History'

findings.citation: Burrows TL, Ho YY, Rollo ME, Collins CE. Validity of dietary assessment methods when compared to the method of doubly labeled water: a systematic review in adults. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:850. doi:10.3389/fendo.2019.00850
findings.population: Free-living adults in DLW validation studies
findings.parameter: subgroups with greater under-reporting
findings.value: Adults with overweight or obesity (recalls, diet history, food records) and women using recall-based methods; in one FFQ study the EI-TEE gap correlated with BMI (r = 0.50)
findings.finding: Under-reporting was greater in adults with overweight or obesity and in women using recall-based methods. Sex differences for food records and FFQs were inconsistent. One study found the FFQ-DLW gap correlated with BMI (r = 0.50).
findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph 3; Results, 'Food Record' and 'Food Frequency Questionnaire' (BMI associations)

findings.citation: Burrows TL, Ho YY, Rollo ME, Collins CE. Validity of dietary assessment methods when compared to the method of doubly labeled water: a systematic review in adults. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:850. doi:10.3389/fendo.2019.00850
findings.parameter: weight-stability condition for reconciling intake with expenditure
findings.value: Rule: DLW expenditure equals intake only in roughly weight-stable people; DLW urine collection lasts 7-14 days
findings.finding: Doubly labelled water is a valid reference for intake only in roughly weight-stable people, because expenditure differs from intake while weight is changing. Measurement runs over 7-14 days, and a mismatch with the dietary-reporting period can distort apparent misreporting.
findings.locator: Introduction, paragraph 5; Discussion, final paragraph

findings.citation: Hevia-Larraín V, Gualano B, Longobardi I, Gil S, Fernandes AL, Costa LAR, et al. High-protein plant-based diet versus a protein-matched omnivorous diet to support resistance training adaptations: a comparison between habitual vegans and omnivores. Sports Med. 2021;51(6):1317-30. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01434-9
findings.population: Healthy untrained young men: 19 habitual vegans and 19 omnivores (mean age 26 y, about 73 kg, BMI about 23 kg/m2), Brazil
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day (vegan or omnivore, resistance training)
findings.value: About 1.6 g/kg/day, topped up with soy isolate (vegans) or whey (omnivores)
findings.finding: Habitual protein intake was topped up to about 1.6 g/kg/day. Vegans and omnivores both gained leg lean mass (about 1.2 kg each), muscle cross-sectional area and leg-press strength over 12 weeks of twice-weekly supervised training.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract, Methods and Results; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03907059 arm descriptions (1.6 g/kg/day)

findings.citation: Hevia-Larraín V, Gualano B, Longobardi I, Gil S, Fernandes AL, Costa LAR, et al. High-protein plant-based diet versus a protein-matched omnivorous diet to support resistance training adaptations: a comparison between habitual vegans and omnivores. Sports Med. 2021;51(6):1317-30. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01434-9
findings.population: Healthy untrained young men, habitual vegans vs omnivores
findings.parameter: protein-target adjustment for vegans
findings.value: None needed at a matched ~1.6 g/kg/day. Leg lean mass +1.2 +/- 1.0 kg (vegan) vs +1.2 +/- 0.8 kg (omnivore); leg-press 1RM +97 +/- 38 vs +117 +/- 35 kg; all between-group p > 0.05
findings.finding: With protein matched at about 1.6 g/kg/day, a plant-based diet with soy isolate supplementation produced muscle and strength gains not significantly different from a mixed diet with whey. Vegans may need no higher target at this intake, but this rests on one small non-randomised trial in untrained men.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract, Results and Conclusions; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03907059 design module (allocation: non-randomised)

findings.citation: Hevia-Larraín V, Gualano B, Longobardi I, Gil S, Fernandes AL, Costa LAR, et al. High-protein plant-based diet versus a protein-matched omnivorous diet to support resistance training adaptations: a comparison between habitual vegans and omnivores. Sports Med. 2021;51(6):1317-30. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01434-9
findings.population: Healthy untrained young men, habitual vegans vs omnivores
findings.parameter: supplemental protein source for vegan users
findings.value: Soy protein isolate (vegans) or whey (omnivores), dosed per person to reach 1.6 g/kg/day; intake monitored every 4 weeks
findings.finding: Vegans took soy protein isolate and omnivores took whey, each dosed individually to close the gap between habitual intake and 1.6 g/kg/day, with diet checked every four weeks. That gives soy isolate direct trial support as a plant protein supplement.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract, Methods; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03907059 interventions

findings.citation: Messina M, Lynch H, Dickinson JM, Reed KE. No difference between the effects of supplementing with soy protein versus animal protein on gains in muscle mass and strength in response to resistance exercise. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(6):674-85. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0071
findings.population: Adults 18-70 y (mostly untrained men) in 9 randomised trials with resistance training of at least 6 wk (range 6-36, mean 13.6 +/- 8.6 wk) and at least 2 sessions/wk; supplements 12 g (+7 g IAA) to ~86 g/day
findings.parameter: protein source (soy vs animal) effect on lean body mass gain
findings.value: Within-arm LBM change SMD: soy 0.37 (95% CI -0.00 to 0.73; I2=0%) vs whey/beef/dairy 0.43 (0.06 to 0.81; I2=23%); between-subgroup chi2=0.06, p=0.80; 9 trials, 266 participants
findings.finding: Lean-mass gains with soy supplements did not differ significantly from those with whey, beef or dairy protein. The analysis compares within-arm pre-post changes (fixed effect) rather than direct between-arm contrasts, trials were small, and the first author directs an institute partly funded by the soy industry.
findings.locator: Results, 'Other Proteins Versus Soy Protein'; Figure 7; Table 1; Acknowledgments (conflict statement)

findings.citation: Messina M, Lynch H, Dickinson JM, Reed KE. No difference between the effects of supplementing with soy protein versus animal protein on gains in muscle mass and strength in response to resistance exercise. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(6):674-85. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0071
findings.population: Adults 18-70 y in resistance-training RCTs (5 trials bench, 6 trials squat/leg press)
findings.parameter: protein source (soy vs animal) effect on 1RM strength gain
findings.value: Bench press SMD: soy 1.43 (0.81-2.05) vs other 1.50 (0.83-2.16), chi2=0.02, p=0.88; squat/leg press SMD: soy 1.57 (1.00-2.13) vs other 1.22 (0.70-1.75), chi2=0.78, p=0.38, I2=88% in both arms
findings.finding: Strength rose to a similar extent whether trainees took soy or animal protein; neither upper- nor lower-body one-repetition-maximum gains differed by protein source. The lower-body pooled estimates were highly heterogeneous.
findings.locator: Results, 'Other Proteins Versus Soy Protein'; Figures 5 and 6

findings.citation: Messina M, Lynch H, Dickinson JM, Reed KE. No difference between the effects of supplementing with soy protein versus animal protein on gains in muscle mass and strength in response to resistance exercise. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(6):674-85. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0071
findings.population: Adults 18-50 y in 5 trials comparing whey with soy (strength outcomes from only 3 of them)
findings.parameter: soy vs whey supplement substitution
findings.value: No between-group difference: bench press chi2=0.02, p=0.90 and squat chi2=0.22, p=0.64 (each pooled from 3 trials: Candow, Denysschen, Volek); LBM chi2=0.00, p=0.96 (5 trials); LBM did not rise significantly within either arm (whey SMD 0.41, -0.15 to 0.98; soy 0.39, -0.15 to 0.94)
findings.finding: When soy was compared only with whey, strength gains did not differ significantly, though the strength analyses rest on just three trials. Neither supplement significantly raised lean mass in this subset, so it cannot show whether whey's larger acute synthesis response leads to long-term differences.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Whey Versus Soy Protein'; Figures 2-4

findings.citation: Messina M, Lynch H, Dickinson JM, Reed KE. No difference between the effects of supplementing with soy protein versus animal protein on gains in muscle mass and strength in response to resistance exercise. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(6):674-85. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0071
findings.parameter: soy protein amount supplying 3 g leucine
findings.value: ~38 g soy protein provides ~3 g leucine; only 3 of 9 trials (Candow, Haub, Kalman) gave that much soy per day, and 3 of the 5 whey-comparison trials (Brown, Denysschen, Volek) gave less than 38 g/day
findings.finding: The authors estimate about 38 g of soy protein supplies the 3 g leucine per-dose level ISSN cites. Because soy and whey did not differ even in trials giving less, they suggest that level is unnecessary; note they compared daily totals, sometimes split into several servings, with a per-dose threshold.
findings.locator: Discussion, leucine paragraph; Table 1 (daily doses and timing)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.population: All life stages including athletes; professional-body position (authors: consultant, Andrews University, Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine)
findings.parameter: adequacy of vegetarian and vegan patterns
findings.value: Appropriately planned vegetarian, including vegan, diets judged nutritionally adequate for all life stages and athletes; patterns defined as lacto-ovo, lacto, ovo, vegan, raw vegan (Figure 1); position stated to be in effect until 31 Dec 2021
findings.finding: The Academy holds that well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets meet nutrient needs, athletes included, with deficiencies avoidable through planning. The paper says the position was valid only until the end of 2021, so a newer confirmation is needed. Authors reported no conflicts and no funding.
findings.locator: Abstract; Position Statement; Figure 1 (p.1971); end matter (effective date, conflict and funding statements). Read from the Academy-hosted PDF of the published article because the journal page returned 403

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.population: Adult vegetarians and vegans including athletes
findings.parameter: vegetarian/vegan adult protein adjustment
findings.value: No adult protein multiplier given: needs are met when energy intake is adequate and plant proteins are varied across the day. Increases of 15-35% are suggested only for vegan children (30-35% at 1-2 y, 20-30% at 2-6 y, 15-20% over 6 y), which does not apply to adults
findings.finding: For adults, including athletes, the position says varied plant proteins eaten over a day supply all indispensable amino acids when calories are sufficient, with regular legumes and soy helping. It sets no higher adult protein target.
findings.locator: Nutrition Considerations for Vegetarians: Protein (pp.1970-1971); Infants, Children, and Adolescents (p.1975)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: ALA intake target
findings.value: Dietary Reference Intake for ALA: 1.6 g/day (men), 1.1 g/day (women); somewhat higher ALA may be prudent for vegetarians/vegans
findings.finding: Vegetarians' ALA intake resembles omnivores', but EPA and DHA are lower, and typically absent in vegan diets. The paper cites the ALA reference intakes and suggests plant eaters aim a little above them, using flax, chia, camelina, canola or hemp seeds, walnuts and their oils.
findings.locator: n-3 Fatty Acids (p.1971)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: linoleic acid to ALA ratio; long-chain omega-3 source
findings.value: LA:ALA ratio no higher than 4:1 suggested for optimal ALA conversion; low-dose microalgae DHA supplements for those with raised needs (e.g., pregnancy, lactation) or reduced conversion (e.g., hypertension, diabetes)
findings.finding: A high linoleic acid intake may suppress conversion of ALA to EPA and DHA, so a ratio of at most 4:1 has been suggested. Microalgae DHA is the plant-based option for people with higher needs. The clinical relevance of low EPA/DHA status in vegetarians is unknown.
findings.locator: n-3 Fatty Acids (p.1971)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: vitamin B12 source rule
findings.value: Vegans must regularly use B12-fortified foods or B12 supplements; 1 cup milk plus 1 egg per day gives only about two-thirds of the RDA; tempeh, nori, spirulina, chlorella and unfortified nutritional yeast are not reliable sources
findings.finding: Plant foods provide no usable B12, so vegans need fortified foods or supplements, and most vegetarians should also use them because modest dairy and egg intake falls short. Fermented foods and algae should not be counted toward B12.
findings.locator: Vitamin B-12 (p.1972)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: vitamin B12 dosing pattern
findings.value: Intrinsic-factor uptake saturates at about half the RDA and needs 4-6 h before further absorption, so fortified foods are best eaten twice a day; passive diffusion (~1%) allows large doses, e.g. 500-1,000 ug cyanocobalamin several times per week; cyanocobalamin preferred for stability
findings.finding: Spread fortified B12 foods over two eating occasions, or use less frequent high-dose cyanocobalamin, which relies on passive absorption. Methyl- and adenosylcobalamin supplements appear no more effective and may need higher doses. Units verified as micrograms on the rendered page.
findings.locator: Vitamin B-12 (pp.1972-1973)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: iron requirement multiplier for vegetarians
findings.value: IOM 2001 iron DRI for vegetarians is 80% higher (x1.8), assuming 10% vs 18% bioavailability; non-heme absorption varies 1-23%; up to 10x higher when iron-deficient; absorption rose by almost 40% after 10 wk on a low-bioavailability diet
