findings.finding: The official vegetarian iron allowance is 1.8 times the omnivore value. The authors argue it rests on limited single-meal data and that absorption adapts over time. Vitamin C and organic acids enhance non-heme iron absorption, while phytates and polyphenols inhibit it.

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.population: Vegan women of child-bearing age; vegans generally
findings.parameter: iodine supplementation for vegans
findings.value: Vegan women of child-bearing age should take 150 ug/day iodine; sea salt, kosher salt and tamari are generally not iodized; iodized salt is not used in processed foods
findings.finding: Vegans who use neither iodized salt nor sea vegetables risk iodine deficiency, and the position recommends a daily supplement for vegan women who could become pregnant. Units verified as micrograms on the rendered page; the PDF text layer shows the symbol as 'm'.
findings.locator: Iodine (p.1972)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: iodine tolerable upper intake level
findings.value: Tolerable Upper Intake Level 1,100 ug/day for adults (IOM value cited)
findings.finding: The iodine content of sea vegetables varies widely and some are very rich, so total iodine from seaweed and supplements should stay below the adult upper level. This is an IOM value restated in the position, not derived in it.
findings.locator: Iodine (p.1972)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: calcium fractional absorption by plant food
findings.value: High-oxalate greens (spinach, beet greens, Swiss chard) as low as ~5%; low-oxalate greens (kale, turnip greens, Chinese cabbage, bok choy) ~50%; calcium-set tofu and most fortified plant milks ~30% (similar to cow's milk); white beans, almonds, tahini, figs, oranges ~20%; calcium citrate malate at least 36%, other fortificants ~30%
findings.finding: Spinach-type greens should not count as good calcium sources despite high content. Low-oxalate brassica greens, calcium-set tofu and fortified plant milks are dependable choices.
findings.locator: Calcium (p.1972)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: vegan calcium intake floor related to fracture risk
findings.value: Calcium intake above 525 mg/day: EPIC-Oxford vegans had 30% higher fracture risk overall, and the excess disappeared when only vegans above this intake were analysed
findings.finding: Low calcium intake appears to explain vegans' higher fracture risk in one cohort. The position advises vegetarians and vegans to meet the RDA for calcium, vitamin D, B12 and protein for bone health.
findings.locator: Osteoporosis (p.1974)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.population: Vegetarians and vegans, especially older adults and those at high latitudes
findings.parameter: vitamin D supplementation
findings.value: Supplements recommended when sun exposure and fortified foods are insufficient; some experts recommend 1,000-2,000 IU/day or more; D2 and D3 appear equivalent at low doses, but D2 is less effective at higher doses
findings.finding: Sunlight synthesis varies with season, latitude, skin pigmentation and age, so fortified foods or supplements are often needed. The 1,000-2,000 IU figure is attributed to some experts rather than set as the Academy's own target.
findings.locator: Vitamin D (p.1972)

findings.citation: Melina V, Craig W, Levin S. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(12):1970-80. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025
findings.parameter: zinc sources and bioavailability rule
findings.value: Sources: soy products, legumes, grains, cheese, seeds, nuts; soaking and sprouting beans, grains, nuts and seeds, and leavening bread reduce phytate binding; citric acid modestly enhances absorption
findings.finding: Adult vegetarians' serum zinc is lower but within the normal range, with no adverse effects shown. Food preparation that breaks down phytate is the recommended way to improve zinc uptake. No numeric intake target is given.
findings.locator: Zinc (p.1972)

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.population: Composition analyses of flours, protein concentrates/isolates and freeze-dried raw products; authors report dairy and food-industry research funding and a GSSI honorarium
findings.parameter: leucine content of protein sources (% of protein)
findings.value: Reference requirement 5.9% (WHO/FAO/UNU). Quinoa 3.8, hemp 5.1, lupin 5.2, oat 5.9, spirulina 6.0, wheat 6.1, soy 6.9, canola 6.9, pea 7.2, brown rice 7.4, potato 8.3, corn 13.5; egg 7.0, casein 8.0, whey 11.0
findings.finding: Leucine share varies widely among plant proteins. Several meet or exceed the reference and corn exceeds whey, while quinoa, hemp and lupin fall short. The values come from the authors' own analyses of flours, concentrates or isolates and freeze-dried products, not cooked whole foods.
findings.locator: Section 'Amino Acid Composition of Protein', paragraphs 2-3 (Fig. 1b)

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.population: Theoretical calculation based on acute whey studies
findings.parameter: per-meal plant protein dose providing ~2.7 g leucine
findings.value: 20-25 g whey provides 2.2-2.7 g leucine; matching 2.7 g needs ~20 g corn, ~33 g potato, ~37 g brown rice, ~38 g pea, ~40 g canola, ~40 g soy, ~45 g wheat or ~71 g quinoa protein
findings.finding: If about 2.7 g of leucine maximally triggers muscle protein synthesis, most plant proteins need larger servings than whey to match it. This is arithmetic, not an outcome trial, and whole-food volume and calories make large plant servings harder.
findings.locator: Section 'Amino Acid Composition of Protein', paragraph 3

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.population: Composition analyses of plant and animal protein sources
findings.parameter: lysine and methionine limiting-amino-acid flags
findings.value: Requirements: lysine 4.5%, methionine 1.6% of protein. Lysine below requirement: wheat 1.4, corn 1.5, oat 2.1, brown rice 2.4, pumpkin seed 2.7, sunflower seed 2.8, hemp 2.8, quinoa 3.3, spirulina 3.5, lupin 3.5 (soy 4.6, canola 5.9, pea 5.9, potato 6.0). Methionine below requirement: oat 0.2, field bean 0.2, brown bean 0.3, lentil 0.3, chickpea 0.3, marrowfat pea 0.3, lupin 0.3, pea 0.4, soy 0.4, quinoa 0.6, wheat 0.9 (potato 1.6 through brown rice 2.5 meet it). Animal proteins: lysine 5.3-9.0%, methionine 2.2-2.8%
findings.finding: Cereals and seeds tend to be short in lysine, while legumes are short in methionine. This is the basis for pairing grains with legumes in plant-based meal suggestions.
findings.locator: Section 'Amino Acid Composition of Protein', paragraph 4 (Fig. 1c,d)

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.parameter: protein blend compensation factor
findings.value: Corn, hemp, brown rice, soy or pea protein alone needs 2-4x more to cover its lysine/methionine deficit; a 1:1 blend of corn, hemp or brown rice with soy or pea needs 1.1-1.9x; oat, lupin, quinoa or wheat alone needs 3-8x, and blended 1:1 with animal protein needs 1.05-1.4x; omnivorous diets derive ~40-50% of protein from plants
findings.finding: Combining grain-type with legume-type proteins, or plant with animal protein, largely closes the amino acid gap, so much less extra protein is needed than when one plant source is relied on. These multipliers are modelled, not trial-tested.
findings.locator: Section 'Improving the Anabolic Properties of Plant-Based Proteins', paragraph 4 (text cites Fig. 2)

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.population: Composition analyses of plant and animal protein sources
findings.parameter: essential amino acid content of protein sources
findings.value: EAA as % of protein (sum excludes tryptophan, which was not measured): canola 29, pea 30, corn 32, potato 37; casein 34, egg 32
findings.finding: Some plant protein sources, such as potato, pea and corn, have essential amino acid contents comparable to or above egg and casein, meeting WHO/FAO/UNU requirements. The generalisation that plant proteins are low in essential amino acids therefore does not hold for every source.
findings.locator: Section 'Amino Acid Composition of Protein', paragraph 1 (Fig. 1a)

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.parameter: protein absorbability of whole foods
findings.value: ~85-95% of protein absorbed from egg whites, whole eggs and chicken vs ~50-75% from chickpeas, mung beans and yellow peas; dehulling mung beans raises absorbability by ~10%; plant isolates or concentrates approach animal-protein levels
findings.finding: Whole plant foods deliver less absorbable protein, mainly because of fibre and tannins in the food matrix rather than the protein itself. Processing, dehulling, heating and extraction narrow the gap.
findings.locator: Section 'Protein Digestion and Amino Acid Absorption', paragraph 1

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.parameter: plant-based protein intake multiplier
findings.value: None established; whether plant-based diets require higher protein intake is stated as unresolved. Context: well-trained athletes habitually eat ~1.5 g/kg/day; 1.6 g/kg/day has been argued to maximise resistance-training gains; WHO RDA 0.8 g/kg/day; a vegan vs omnivore training trial at ~1.6 g/kg/day found no difference
findings.finding: The review offers no multiplier for plant-based eaters. At high habitual intakes, small quality differences likely matter little. The authors speculate that quality may matter more during calorie restriction for fat loss, but this is untested.
findings.locator: Section 'Plant-Based Proteins in Sports Nutrition', paragraphs 2-4; Conclusions

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.population: Acute muscle protein synthesis studies in young and older adults
findings.parameter: plant protein dose increase and leucine fortification
findings.value: 60 g (not 35 g) wheat protein hydrolysate raised MPS in healthy older men; 40 g soy did not match 20 g whey; 20 g soy + 2.5 g free leucine gave no greater post-exercise MPS than 20 g soy or 20 g whey in young adults; no human studies of lysine or methionine fortification
findings.finding: Evidence on fixing plant proteins by eating more or adding leucine is sparse and mixed. A larger wheat dose worked, a larger soy dose did not, and no human studies have tested lysine or methionine fortification.
findings.locator: Section 'Amino Acid Composition of Protein', paragraph 5; 'Improving the Anabolic Properties of Plant-Based Proteins', paragraphs 3 and 5

findings.citation: Pinckaers PJM, Trommelen J, Snijders T, van Loon LJC. The anabolic response to plant-based protein ingestion. Sports Med. 2021;51(Suppl 1):59-74. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01540-8
findings.parameter: mycoprotein and insect protein as alternative sources
findings.value: Mycoprotein is ~45% protein; 70 g mycoprotein (31.5 g protein) raised resting and post-exercise MPS more than a leucine-matched 31 g milk protein (26.2 g protein); lesser mealworm protein MPS did not differ from an equal amount of milk protein
findings.finding: Fungal mycoprotein and insect protein performed at least as well as milk protein in single acute studies. They are candidate non-animal or alternative high-quality sources, with limited evidence.
findings.locator: Section 'Alternative Protein Sources', paragraphs 2-3

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: protein quality metric (DIAAS formula)
findings.value: DIAAS (%) = 100 x lowest value, across indispensable amino acids, of [mg digestible IAA in 1 g dietary protein / mg of the same IAA in 1 g reference protein]; digestible IAA = IAA content x true ileal digestibility coefficient (humans preferred, else growing pig, else growing rat); replaces PDCAAS
findings.finding: FAO recommends replacing PDCAAS with DIAAS, treating each amino acid as a separate nutrient with its own ileal digestibility. The lowest amino acid ratio sets the score.
findings.locator: Chapter 2, section 2.1 Key findings (pp.3-4); section 4.2 Calculation of DIAAS (pp.22-23)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: amino acid reference scoring pattern (older child, adolescent, adult)
findings.value: mg/g protein: His 16, Ile 30, Leu 61, Lys 48, SAA 23, AAA 41, Thr 25, Trp 6.6, Val 40 (3-10 y child pattern applied to adults)
findings.finding: This is the reference pattern for dietary assessment of adults. The values derive from the 2007 WHO/FAO/UNU requirement report, based on nitrogen-balance and isotope studies, which FAO acknowledges have limitations.
findings.locator: Table 5 (p.29); section 2.1 (p.4); section 4.10 Strength of evidence (pp.46-49)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.population: All foods except infant formula (regulatory use)
findings.parameter: regulatory amino acid scoring pattern
findings.value: Child 6 mo-3 y pattern, mg/g protein: His 20, Ile 32, Leu 66, Lys 57, SAA 27, AAA 52, Thr 31, Trp 8.5, Val 43; infant formula uses the human-milk pattern
findings.finding: For labelling and regulating foods other than infant formula, FAO recommends scoring against the young-child pattern. It is stricter than the adult pattern and gives lower scores, so the app should record which pattern produced any DIAAS it shows.
findings.locator: Section 2.1 (p.4); section 4.1 (p.21); Table 5 (p.29)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: DIAAS protein-quality claim bands
findings.value: Excellent/high: 100 or more; good/source: 75-99; no source/high protein claim below a cut-off, e.g. 75 (all given as examples)
findings.finding: FAO proposes illustrative DIAAS bands for protein quality claims and says the exact cut-offs need further consideration, including local dietary patterns. It stresses that quality cannot replace quantity.
findings.locator: Section 4.8 DIAAS - regulatory issues (pp.42-43); Table 6 (p.44)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: DIAAS truncation and diet-level protein adjustment
findings.value: Single foods or ingredients: do not truncate values above 100; mixed diets and sole-source foods: truncate at 100; quality-adjusted protein = measured protein x DIAAS, used only when DIAAS is 100 or less; safe intake of a diet = safe protein requirement / diet DIAAS; DIAAS must never inflate apparent protein content
findings.finding: A diet's DIAAS can scale down, but never up, the protein credited toward requirements. Scores above 100 for individual foods indicate potential to complement lower-quality proteins.
findings.locator: Section 4.1, 'Practical application of the DIAAS' (pp.21-22)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: interim digestibility data source for DIAAS
findings.value: Until an agreed true ileal amino acid digestibility dataset for human foods exists, compute DIAAS using faecal crude protein digestibility applied to amino acid contents; available ileal data judged insufficient for practical use
findings.finding: In 2013 FAO judged human ileal digestibility data too sparse for routine DIAAS calculation. Any app-computed DIAAS therefore rests on interim or animal-derived digestibility values and should be labelled accordingly.
findings.locator: Section 2.1 Key findings (pp.4-5)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: example DIAAS values for foods and a mixed meal
findings.value: Child pattern: wheat 40, peas 64, whole milk powder 122 (Table 6); whole milk powder 143 (SAA) with adult pattern (Table 1); 400 g wheat + 100 g pea + 35 g milk powder: 82 (Lys) adult pattern, 68 child pattern (Table 2)
findings.finding: The worked examples show cereals and legumes scoring low alone and milk high, with a mixed wheat-pea-milk combination landing in between, which illustrates complementation. The report presents them as illustrations, not reference values.
findings.locator: Tables 1 and 2 (pp.24-25); Table 6 (p.44)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: protein content claim thresholds
findings.value: Protein NRV 50 g; 'source' = 10% NRV per 100 g (solids), 5% NRV per 100 ml (liquids), 5% NRV per 100 kcal (12% per MJ), or 10% NRV per serving; 'high' = twice the 'source' values; quality (DIAAS) applied after the quantity criteria are met
findings.finding: Quantity thresholds for calling a food a protein source or high in protein come first, with DIAAS then used as a quality gate. This could define 'protein-rich' food suggestions.
findings.locator: Section 4.8 DIAAS - regulatory issues (p.43)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: adult mean protein requirement (research note, not adopted)
findings.value: The research agenda refers to 0.66 g protein/kg/day (worded in the report as the current mean protein intake, in the context of subjects adapted to lower-than-usual intakes) and cites one recent study estimating the mean adult requirement at 0.91 g/kg/day, which it says needs careful assessment
findings.finding: The consultation did not re-examine protein requirements. It listed evaluating the higher recent estimate as a research priority, so the app should not treat 0.91 g/kg/day as an official value.
findings.locator: Section 4.9 Recommendations for further research, item 1 (p.44); section 4.10 Preamble (pp.46-47)

findings.citation: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition: report of an FAO Expert Consultation, 31 March-2 April 2011, Auckland, New Zealand. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92. Rome: FAO; 2013. ISBN 978-92-5-107417-6.
findings.parameter: dataset licence
findings.value: All rights reserved (copyright FAO 2013); non-commercial uses authorized free of charge upon request; commercial reproduction may incur fees; permissions via copyright@fao.org
findings.finding: The report carries no open licence. Reproducing its tables or text needs FAO permission, so it is not among the licence types the project accepts for bundled data. Citing its values needs owner review.
findings.locator: Copyright page (PDF page 4, verso of title page)

findings.citation: Mathai JK, Liu Y, Stein HH. Values for digestible indispensable amino acid scores (DIAAS) for some dairy and plant proteins may better describe protein quality than values calculated using the concept for protein digestibility-corrected amino acid scores (PDCAAS). Br J Nutr. 2017;117(4):490-9. doi:10.1017/S0007114517000125
findings.population: 9 ileal-cannulated growing barrows (animal model), raw unprocessed ingredients; funded by the National Dairy Institute (no role in design/analysis), authors declare no conflicts
findings.parameter: DIAAS of dairy and plant protein ingredients (older child/adolescent/adult pattern)
findings.value: DIAAS: whey isolate 125 (His), whey concentrate 133 (His), milk protein concentrate 141 (SAA), skim milk powder 123 (SAA), pea protein concentrate 73 (SAA), soy protein isolate 98 (SAA), soy flour 105 (SAA), whole-grain wheat 54 (Lys); PDCAAS-like: 122, 134, 142, 132, 84, 102, 109, 51
findings.finding: Using the adult pattern, dairy proteins scored well above 100, soy near 100, and pea and wheat below 75. The Discussion calls soy flour 'good' (below 100) even though Table 7 lists 105. The results come from pigs fed raw ingredients.
findings.locator: Table 7 (lower panel, 3 years and above); Discussion, paragraph 4

findings.citation: Mathai JK, Liu Y, Stein HH. Values for digestible indispensable amino acid scores (DIAAS) for some dairy and plant proteins may better describe protein quality than values calculated using the concept for protein digestibility-corrected amino acid scores (PDCAAS). Br J Nutr. 2017;117(4):490-9. doi:10.1017/S0007114517000125
findings.parameter: DIAAS of dairy and plant protein ingredients (child 6 mo-3 y regulatory pattern)
findings.value: DIAAS: whey isolate 100 (His), whey concentrate 107 (His), milk protein concentrate 120 (SAA), skim milk powder 105 (SAA), pea protein concentrate 62 (SAA), soy protein isolate 84 (SAA), soy flour 89 (SAA), whole-grain wheat 45 (Lys); PDCAAS-like (same pattern): 97, 107, 121, 112, 71, 86, 93, 51
findings.finding: Under the stricter regulatory pattern, soy products fall in the 75-99 band and pea and wheat below 75. The table footnote gives child-pattern valine as 40 mg/g, whereas FAO Table 5 gives 43.
findings.locator: Table 6 (DIAAS and PDCAAS 2013 columns) and footnote section-sign

findings.citation: Mathai JK, Liu Y, Stein HH. Values for digestible indispensable amino acid scores (DIAAS) for some dairy and plant proteins may better describe protein quality than values calculated using the concept for protein digestibility-corrected amino acid scores (PDCAAS). Br J Nutr. 2017;117(4):490-9. doi:10.1017/S0007114517000125
findings.parameter: PDCAAS vs DIAAS for ranking plant proteins
findings.value: With the same scoring pattern, PDCAAS-like values exceeded DIAAS (P<0.05) for skim milk powder, pea protein concentrate, soy isolate, soy flour and wheat (e.g., pea 71 vs 62; wheat 51 vs 45, child pattern)
findings.finding: Scores based on whole-tract crude protein digestibility overstated the quality of the less digestible proteins, which supports amino-acid-specific ileal digestibility for ranking plant proteins. The authors note that FAO's claim cut-offs were chosen arbitrarily.
findings.locator: Results (Tables 6-7); Discussion, paragraphs 4 and 8-9

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.population: Generally healthy adults 18 y and older; 141 observational or baseline studies from 2000 to Jan 2020, mostly Europe, South/East Asia and North America; pregnant/lactating women, disease populations and athletes excluded; both authors Unilever employees
findings.parameter: dietary pattern classification rule
findings.value: Vegan: no meat, fish, dairy or eggs (or at most once/month, or self-defined); vegetarian: no meat or fish (at most once/month); pesco-vegetarian: no meat (at most once/month); semi-vegetarian: meat/fish at most once/week but more than once/month; meat-eater: meat more than once/week
findings.finding: The review provides operational frequency cut-offs, applied uniformly across 141 studies, that could classify a user's self-reported pattern.
findings.locator: Section 2.4 Data Handling

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: protein intake by pattern (% energy)
findings.value: Vegetarians 13.4%E, vegans 12.9%E, meat-eaters 16.0%E; all above the AMDR lower limit of 10%E; no study reported intake below 10%E
findings.finding: Plant-based eaters consumed less protein than meat-eaters but stayed within the acceptable range in every study. Protein adequacy is not a typical problem for general-population vegetarians, though percent-energy figures say nothing about g/kg targets for training goals.
findings.locator: Section 3.1.2; Figure 2a

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: plant-based protein requirement adjustment
findings.value: Some authors propose ~20% higher protein needs (diet protein quality estimated ~80% for vegan and ~90% for vegetarian diets vs omnivore), e.g. 12%E instead of 10%E; WHO and IOM specify no increase
findings.finding: Official bodies do not raise protein requirements for vegetarians, because varied plant proteins complement each other and processing improves digestibility. Observed intakes would meet even a 20% uplift. Older adults may find plant-only protein targets harder to reach.
findings.locator: Section 4.3 Findings on Energy and Macronutrients, paragraph 2

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: vitamin B12 risk by pattern
findings.value: Mean intake: meat-eaters 5.6, vegetarians 2.1, vegans 1.5 ug/d (EAR 2.0 ug/d); 10/13 food-only vegan studies below EAR; serum B12 309/220/226 pmol/L (meat/vegetarian/vegan); deficiency (<150 pmol/L, 13 studies) mean prevalence 44% vegans, 32% vegetarians; 0-16% in meat-eaters
findings.finding: Without supplements or fortified foods, most studies found vegan and half found vegetarian B12 intakes below the requirement, and deficiency is common. Studies counting supplements found mean intakes above the EAR, though vegan medians stayed below it, supporting a supplement or fortified-food prompt for plant-based users.
findings.locator: Section 3.2.7; section 4.4, paragraph 2

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: vitamin D intake gap (all patterns)
findings.value: Mean intake below EAR of 10 ug/d in every group: pesco-vegetarians 5.25, meat-eaters 4.17, vegetarians 2.67, vegans 1.52 ug/d; 25(OH)D <10 ug/L deficiency 0-6% meat-eaters/pesco, 0-33% vegetarians, 3-67% vegans; insufficiency (<20 ug/L) 15% meat-eaters vs 25% vegetarians and vegans (4 studies each)
findings.finding: Vitamin D intake is inadequate across all patterns and lowest in vegans. Skin synthesis may not suffice in winter above about 40 degrees north, so fortified foods or supplements are generally advised.
findings.locator: Section 3.2.9; section 4.4, paragraph 3

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: iron: bioavailability-adjusted requirement and status
findings.value: Plant-based intakes compared with EAR x1.8 (14.6 mg/d women, 10.8 mg/d men); ferritin 55.5 (meat), 33.8 (vegetarian), 31.3 (vegan) ug/L, vegetarian women 24.3; iron deficiency (ferritin <15 ug/L, 4 studies) 7%/11%/15%; anaemia 5%/11%/17%; heme absorbed 15-40% vs non-heme 1-15%
findings.finding: Although vegetarians and vegans eat as much or more iron, their stores are lower and deficiency and anaemia are more frequent, especially in women. Vitamin C-rich foods with meals can improve absorption.
findings.locator: Section 2.5 Data Analysis; section 3.3.3; section 4.4, paragraph 5

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: zinc: bioavailability-adjusted requirement
findings.value: Plant-based intakes divided by 1.5 (requirement up to 50% higher on high-phytate diets); adjusted EAR 10.3 mg/d women, 14.3 mg/d men; deficiency prevalence vegans 30%, vegetarians 14%, meat-eaters 13% (3 studies)
findings.finding: Mean zinc intakes were similar across patterns but fell short of the phytate-adjusted requirement for plant-based men, and deficiency was most common in vegans. No adult health consequences of lower zinc status have been reported.
findings.locator: Section 2.5; section 3.3.6; section 4.4, paragraph 6

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: iodine risk by pattern
findings.value: EAR 95 ug/d; mean intake vegans 111, vegetarians 146, meat-eaters 170 ug/d; 3 of 4 studies reported vegan intake below EAR; urinary iodine <100 ug/L in 92% vegans, 37% vegetarians, 51% meat-eaters
findings.finding: Iodine deficiency appears very common in vegans and frequent in all groups, though few studies exist. WHO advises iodized salt regardless of diet. Seaweed iodine varies and can be excessive.
findings.locator: Section 3.3.2; section 4.4, paragraph 7

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.population: Adults; 40 calcium intake studies, few bone-marker studies
findings.parameter: calcium intake and bone markers by pattern
findings.value: EAR 800 mg/d; mean intake vegetarians 895, vegans 838, meat-eaters 858 mg/d; about one third of studies below EAR in every group (vegans 7/17); PTH 5.21 (vegan), 4.91 (vegetarian), 4.04 (meat) pmol/L; lower lumbar spine BMD in vegans in 2/3 studies
findings.finding: Average calcium intake only slightly exceeds requirements in all patterns. Vegans show signs of higher bone turnover, so calcium-rich plant foods and fortified products deserve emphasis.
findings.locator: Section 3.3.1; section 4.4, paragraph 4

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.population: Adults; 8 EPA/DHA intake and 13 status studies
findings.parameter: EPA+DHA intake by pattern
findings.value: Lower AMDR 250 mg/d EPA+DHA; vegans 27 + 4 mg/d, vegetarians 16 + 31 mg/d, meat-eaters 94 + 172 mg/d; ALA-to-EPA/DHA conversion generally <10%
findings.finding: Vegetarians and vegans eat far below the long-chain omega-3 range and consistently show lower EPA/DHA status. Conversion from ALA is limited, so the authors suggest supplements or fortified foods may be needed; algae are the only direct plant source of EPA/DHA.
findings.locator: Section 3.1.5; section 4.3, paragraph 3

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: PUFA and ALA intake by pattern
findings.value: PUFA %E: vegans 8.84, pesco-vegetarians 7.77, semi-vegetarians 7.67, vegetarians 6.79, meat-eaters 5.95 (lower AMDR 6%E); ALA: vegans 2.01, vegetarians 1.78, meat-eaters 1.38 g/d (plant groups above AI; meat-eater men below AI)
findings.finding: Meat-eaters' polyunsaturated fat intake falls just under the acceptable range and men miss the ALA adequate intake, whereas plant-based eaters exceed both.
findings.locator: Sections 3.1.4-3.1.5; Figure 2c,d

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: dietary fibre intake by pattern
findings.value: Vegans 44 g/d, vegetarians 28 g/d, meat-eaters 21 g/d; adequate intake met in 74% of vegan studies (14/19), 29% of vegetarian studies (10/35), 6% of meat-eater studies (2/33)
findings.finding: Meat-eaters most often fall short of the fibre adequate intake, though many vegetarian studies also do. Whole grains, pulses, nuts and seeds are the suggested remedy.
findings.locator: Section 3.1.3; section 4.3, paragraph 3

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: energy intake by pattern
findings.value: Mean (min-max) kcal/d: meat-eaters 2101 (1374-2985), vegetarians 2098 (1495-2820), vegans 1947 (1130-2757)
findings.finding: Reported energy intakes were broadly similar across patterns. This review gives no basis for pattern-specific calorie adjustments, but the figures are self-reported intakes, not requirements.
findings.locator: Section 3.1.1; section 4.3, paragraph 1

findings.citation: Neufingerl N, Eilander A. Nutrient intake and status in adults consuming plant-based diets compared to meat-eaters: a systematic review. Nutrients. 2021;14(1):29. doi:10.3390/nu14010029
findings.parameter: omnivore nutrient-gap flags
findings.value: Meat-eaters at risk of inadequate fibre, PUFA, ALA, folate (EAR 320 ug/d; 9/24 studies below), vitamin D, vitamin E (EAR 12 mg/d; 9/14 studies below), calcium and magnesium (11/19 studies below EAR); folate deficiency prevalence 11%
findings.finding: Every pattern has gaps. Omnivore users should get prompts for plant-food nutrients, just as plant-based users get prompts for B12, iodine, iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin D and EPA/DHA.
findings.locator: Sections 3.2.6, 3.2.10, 3.3.4; section 5 Conclusions

findings.citation: Haider LM, Schwingshackl L, Hoffmann G, Ekmekcioglu C. The effect of vegetarian diets on iron status in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr. 2018;58(8):1359-74. doi:10.1080/10408398.2016.1259210
findings.population: Adult vegetarians vs non-vegetarian controls (27 cross-sectional + 3 interventional studies reviewed; 24 pooled)
findings.parameter: serum ferritin difference, adult vegetarians vs non-vegetarians
findings.value: -29.71 µg/L (95% CI -39.69 to -19.73; p<0.01), pooled from 24 cross-sectional studies; with semi-vegetarians included -23.27 µg/L (95% CI -29.77 to -16.76)
findings.finding: Random-effects pooling of 24 cross-sectional studies showed adult vegetarians have clearly lower iron stores (serum ferritin) than non-vegetarians. Adding semi-vegetarians barely changed this. Supports flagging iron for vegetarian and vegan patterns. The data are observational, and heterogeneity and risk of bias cannot be seen in the abstract.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 27880062), Results paragraph; full text not accessible (publisher returned HTTP 403)

findings.citation: Haider LM, Schwingshackl L, Hoffmann G, Ekmekcioglu C. The effect of vegetarian diets on iron status in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr. 2018;58(8):1359-74. doi:10.1080/10408398.2016.1259210
findings.population: Adult vegetarians vs non-vegetarians, stratified by sex/menopausal status
findings.parameter: serum ferritin difference by sex (vegetarian vs non-vegetarian)
findings.value: Men -61.88 µg/L (95% CI -85.59 to -38.17); premenopausal women -17.70 µg/L (95% CI -29.80 to -5.60); all women -13.50 µg/L (95% CI -22.96 to -4.04)
findings.finding: In a sex subgroup analysis, the ferritin gap was several times larger in vegetarian men than in women, premenopausal or all. This matters for sex-specific iron messaging, but the subgroup numbers come only from the abstract.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 27880062), Results paragraph (subgroup analysis by gender)

findings.citation: Haider LM, Schwingshackl L, Hoffmann G, Ekmekcioglu C. The effect of vegetarian diets on iron status in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr. 2018;58(8):1359-74. doi:10.1080/10408398.2016.1259210
findings.parameter: iron status monitoring rule
findings.value: No numeric threshold. The authors advise regular iron-status checks for both vegetarians and non-vegetarians, noting that high iron stores are a risk factor for some non-communicable diseases (e.g., type 2 diabetes)
findings.finding: High iron stores are also a risk factor for some non-communicable diseases such as type 2 diabetes, so the authors advise vegetarians and non-vegetarians alike to check iron status regularly and improve dietary iron content and bioavailability, framed as eating more plants and less meat. Author opinion, not pooled.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (PMID 27880062), Conclusions paragraph

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Standing Committee on the Scientific Evaluation of Dietary Reference Intakes. Dietary Reference Intakes for Thiamin, Riboflavin, Niacin, Vitamin B6, Folate, Vitamin B12, Pantothenic Acid, Biotin, and Choline. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 1998. Chapter 9, Vitamin B12; p. 306-56. doi:10.17226/6015
findings.parameter: vitamin B12 EAR and RDA, adults
findings.value: EAR 2 µg/day; RDA 2.4 µg/day for men and women 19-30, 31-50, 51-70 and >70 y; RDA = EAR + 2 CV (CV 10%) = 120% of EAR; 50% absorption from food assumed
findings.finding: The adult B12 average requirement is 2 µg/day and the recommended allowance is 2.4 µg/day, the same for both sexes at all adult ages. These are the reference targets for any B12 adequacy check, which matters most for the vegan pattern.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Vitamin B12: 'B12 EAR and RDA Summary, Ages 19 through 50 Years' pp. 337-338; 'Adults Ages 51 Years and Older' pp. 338-339; absorption assumption in chapter Summary p. 306 (also p. 309) (NAP online reader)

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Standing Committee on the Scientific Evaluation of Dietary Reference Intakes. Dietary Reference Intakes for Thiamin, Riboflavin, Niacin, Vitamin B6, Folate, Vitamin B12, Pantothenic Acid, Biotin, and Choline. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 1998. Chapter 9, Vitamin B12; p. 306-56. doi:10.17226/6015
findings.parameter: B12 source rule for adults >50 y
findings.value: Get most of the 2.4 µg/day RDA as crystalline B12 from fortified foods or supplements. An estimated 10-30% of adults >50 y have atrophic gastritis, which impairs absorption of food-bound B12
findings.finding: For users over 50, most B12 should come from fortified foods or supplements, because many older adults absorb protein-bound B12 from food poorly. Crystalline B12 in fortified foods and supplements is absorbed normally.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Vitamin B12: chapter Summary p. 306; 'Adults Ages 51 Years and Older' p. 338 and RDA footnote p. 339; atrophic gastritis prevalence also pp. 318-319

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Standing Committee on the Scientific Evaluation of Dietary Reference Intakes. Dietary Reference Intakes for Thiamin, Riboflavin, Niacin, Vitamin B6, Folate, Vitamin B12, Pantothenic Acid, Biotin, and Choline. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 1998. Chapter 9, Vitamin B12; p. 306-56. doi:10.17226/6015
findings.parameter: vitamin B12 UL
findings.value: No UL established (insufficient evidence of adverse effects)
findings.finding: The committee found too little evidence of harm to set an upper limit for B12. The app should not invent a B12 ceiling. Unknown stays unknown.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Vitamin B12: chapter Summary p. 306; 'Tolerable Upper Intake Levels' section p. 346

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Standing Committee on the Scientific Evaluation of Dietary Reference Intakes. Dietary Reference Intakes for Thiamin, Riboflavin, Niacin, Vitamin B6, Folate, Vitamin B12, Pantothenic Acid, Biotin, and Choline. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 1998. Chapter 9, Vitamin B12; p. 306-56. doi:10.17226/6015
findings.parameter: B12 food sources for vegan pattern
findings.value: Plant foods are not a normal B12 source (certain algae excepted); commonly eaten plant foods supply B12 only if fortified (e.g., fortified ready-to-eat cereals, meal-replacement formulas), bacterially exposed or contaminated; dietary deficiency is listed as occurring in complete vegetarians
findings.finding: B12 normally comes only from animal foods. For a vegan pattern, B12 suggestions must be fortified foods or supplements, not ordinary plant foods. Insufficient intake in complete vegetarians is a recognised cause of deficiency.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Vitamin B12: 'Intake of Vitamin B12 - Food Sources' p. 342; Table 9-4 'Conditions That May Result in Vitamin B12 Deficiency' p. 317

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 9, Iron; p. 290-393. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: iron EAR and RDA, adults
findings.value: Men 19-30, 31-50, 51-70, >70 y: EAR 6 mg/day, RDA 8 mg/day; women 19-30 and 31-50 y: EAR 8.1 mg/day, RDA 18 mg/day; women 51-70 and >70 y: EAR 5 mg/day, RDA 8 mg/day; derived by factorial modelling with an 18% upper absorption limit
findings.finding: The adult iron allowance is 8 mg/day for men and for women over 50, and 18 mg/day for women aged 19-50. These values assume a mixed diet with about 18% iron absorption.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Iron: chapter Summary p. 290; 'Iron EAR and RDA Summary, Ages 19 Years and Older' pp. 343-344

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 9, Iron; p. 290-393. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: iron UL, adults
findings.value: 45 mg/day (adults ≥19 y, including pregnancy/lactation); critical effect gastrointestinal distress; LOAEL 70 mg/day total iron (60 mg/day supplemental ferrous fumarate + ~11 mg/day from food) ÷ uncertainty factor 1.5
findings.finding: Total iron intake for adults should not routinely exceed 45 mg/day. The limit rests on gastrointestinal side effects from supplemental iron salts. The report says ordinary food, including fortified food, does not cause this distress.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Iron: chapter Summary p. 290; 'Dose-Response Assessment' pp. 373-374; 'Iron UL Summary, Ages 19 Years and Older' p. 375; 'Risk Characterization' p. 377

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 9, Iron; p. 290-393. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: vegetarian iron requirement multiplier
findings.value: Vegetarian iron requirement set at 1.8x the standard values, because iron bioavailability from vegetarian diets is estimated at ~10% vs 18% for a mixed Western diet; overall absorption may approach 5% with very strict vegetarianism
findings.finding: Because non-haem iron is absorbed less well, the report sets vegetarian iron needs at 1.8 times the standard values. Absorption may be even lower on very strict vegetarian diets. The factor rests on a bioavailability estimate from one comparison of meals with 2-week diets.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Iron: 'Special Considerations - Vegetarianism' p. 351; bioavailability algorithms pp. 314-316

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 9, Iron; p. 290-393. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.population: Adults engaged in regular intense or endurance exercise
findings.parameter: iron EAR adjustment for regular intense exercise
findings.value: EAR conservatively 30% greater for those doing regular intense exercise; may be up to 70% greater in athletes (Weaver & Rajaram estimate); estimated losses with prolonged training 1.75 mg/day (male athletes) and 2.3 mg/day (female athletes) vs about 1.08 mg/day (post-pubertal males) and 1.45 mg/day (menstruating females) generally
findings.finding: People who train intensely, especially endurance runners, lose more iron. The report raises their average requirement by at least 30%, and by up to 70% under one estimate. The evidence is a small number of iron-loss studies.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Iron: 'Special Considerations - Increased Iron Losses in Exercise and Intense Endurance Training' pp. 352-353

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 9, Iron; p. 290-393. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: extra iron need from blood donation
findings.value: Annual 0.5 L donation = 200-250 mg iron, about 0.6-0.7 mg/day; more frequent donation may require supplemental iron, especially in women
findings.finding: Regular blood donors lose extra iron, averaging roughly 0.6-0.7 mg a day per annual donation, and have lower ferritin. Frequent donors, particularly women, may need supplemental iron. This could be an optional user flag.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Iron: 'Special Considerations - Blood Donation' p. 352

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 9, Iron; p. 290-393. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: iron requirement for premenopausal women using oral contraceptives
findings.value: 50th percentile requirement 6.4 mg/day; 97.5th percentile 10.9 mg/day (based on an estimated 60% reduction in menstrual loss)
findings.finding: Oral contraceptives reduce menstrual blood loss, so the modelled iron requirement for premenopausal users is lower than the standard 18 mg/day allowance. Women on hormone replacement therapy who still menstruate may need more than other postmenopausal women.
findings.locator: Ch. 9 Iron: 'Special Considerations - Use of Oral Contraceptives and Hormone Replacement Therapy' pp. 350-351; Appendix Table I-4

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 12, Zinc; p. 442-501. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: zinc EAR and RDA, adults
findings.value: Men ≥19 y: EAR 9.4 mg/day, RDA 11 mg/day; women ≥19 y: EAR 6.8 mg/day, RDA 8 mg/day; RDA = 120% of EAR (CV 10%), rounded to nearest 1 mg
findings.finding: The adult zinc allowance is 11 mg/day for men and 8 mg/day for women at every adult age. These are the reference targets for zinc adequacy checks.
findings.locator: Ch. 12 Zinc: chapter Summary p. 442; 'Zinc EAR and RDA Summary, Ages 19 Years and Older' p. 475

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 12, Zinc; p. 442-501. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: zinc UL, adults
findings.value: 40 mg/day total zinc (food, water and supplements); LOAEL 60 mg/day (50 mg/day supplemental + ~10 mg/day dietary) ÷ uncertainty factor 1.5; critical effect reduced copper status (erythrocyte Cu-Zn superoxide dismutase activity)
findings.finding: Adults should not routinely exceed 40 mg of zinc per day from all sources. The limit protects copper status, which matters if the app ever suggests zinc-fortified foods or supplements to plant-based users.
findings.locator: Ch. 12 Zinc: chapter Summary p. 442; LOAEL identification pp. 485-486; 'Derivation of a UL' and 'Zinc UL Summary, Ages 19 Years and Older' p. 486

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 12, Zinc; p. 442-501. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: vegetarian zinc requirement adjustment
findings.value: Zinc requirement possibly up to 50% higher for vegetarians. This applies most to strict vegetarians who rely mainly on grains and legumes and whose diet has a phytate:zinc molar ratio above 15:1. The report found the data insufficient to set an adjustment algorithm
findings.finding: High-phytate plant diets lower zinc absorption, so vegetarian and especially vegan users may need up to half again the standard zinc allowance. The report presents 50% as a possible maximum and declines to set an adjustment formula.
findings.locator: Ch. 12 Zinc: 'Special Considerations - Vegetarianism' pp. 479-480

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 8, Iodine; p. 258-289. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: iodine EAR and RDA, adults
findings.value: EAR 95 µg/day; RDA 150 µg/day for men and women ≥19 y; CV 20%, RDA = 140% of EAR, rounded to nearest 50 µg
findings.finding: The adult iodine allowance is 150 µg/day for both sexes. The iodine chapter contains no vegetarian- or vegan-specific adjustment.
findings.locator: Ch. 8 Iodine: chapter Summary p. 258; 'Iodine EAR and RDA Summary, Ages 19 Years and Older' pp. 274-275

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients. Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2001. Chapter 8, Iodine; p. 258-289. doi:10.17226/10026
findings.parameter: iodine UL, adults
findings.value: 1,100 µg/day (LOAEL 1,700 µg/day ÷ uncertainty factor 1.5 = 1,133, rounded down)
findings.finding: Adults should not routinely exceed 1,100 µg of iodine per day. This is relevant if the app suggests seaweed or iodised products to plant-based users.
findings.locator: Ch. 8 Iodine: LOAEL identification p. 281; 'Derivation of a UL' and 'Iodine UL Summary, Ages 19 Years and Older' p. 282; seaweed noted p. 283

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Committee to Review Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin D and Calcium. Dietary Reference Intakes for Calcium and Vitamin D. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2011. doi:10.17226/13050
findings.parameter: calcium EAR and RDA, adults
findings.value: Men 19-50 and 51-70 y: EAR 800 mg, RDA 1,000 mg/day; men >70 y: EAR 1,000 mg, RDA 1,200 mg/day; women 19-50 y: EAR 800 mg, RDA 1,000 mg/day; women 51-70 and >70 y: EAR 1,000 mg, RDA 1,200 mg/day
findings.finding: The adult calcium allowance is 1,000 mg/day. It rises to 1,200 mg/day for women from 51 and men from 71, mainly on the basis of calcium-balance and bone data. These are the targets for checking calcium adequacy in dairy-free patterns.
findings.locator: Summary, Table S-1 'Calcium Dietary Reference Intakes by Life Stage' p. 7; basis described p. 8

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Committee to Review Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin D and Calcium. Dietary Reference Intakes for Calcium and Vitamin D. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2011. doi:10.17226/13050
findings.parameter: calcium UL, adults
findings.value: 2,500 mg/day for ages 19-50 y; 2,000 mg/day for ages ≥51 y (both sexes; pregnancy/lactation 19-50 y: 2,500 mg/day)
findings.finding: Total calcium intake should stay below 2,500 mg/day up to age 50 and below 2,000 mg/day from 51. This caps any calcium-rich food or fortified-food suggestion.
findings.locator: Summary, Table S-1 'Calcium Dietary Reference Intakes by Life Stage' p. 7; basis p. 8

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Committee to Review Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin D and Calcium. Dietary Reference Intakes for Calcium and Vitamin D. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2011. doi:10.17226/13050
findings.parameter: vitamin D EAR and RDA, adults
findings.value: EAR 400 IU (10 µg)/day; RDA 600 IU (15 µg)/day for ages 19-70 y; RDA 800 IU (20 µg)/day for >70 y; values assume minimal sun exposure
findings.finding: The adult vitamin D allowance is 600 IU (15 µg) a day, and 800 IU for people over 70. The values assume almost no skin synthesis from sun and target serum 25OHD of about 40 nmol/L (median requirement) and 50 nmol/L (RDA).
findings.locator: Summary, 'Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin D' p. 8 and Table S-2 'Vitamin D Dietary Reference Intakes by Life Stage' p. 9; minimal-sun assumption p. 6 and Ch. 5 p. 370

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Committee to Review Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin D and Calcium. Dietary Reference Intakes for Calcium and Vitamin D. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2011. doi:10.17226/13050
findings.parameter: vitamin D UL, adults
findings.value: 4,000 IU (100 µg)/day for adults ≥19 y, including pregnancy and lactation; starting NOAEL 10,000 IU/day (hypercalcaemia), with the UL set 20% below the 5,000 IU/day studied by Heaney et al. 2003
findings.finding: Adults should not routinely exceed 4,000 IU of vitamin D per day. The committee's regression suggests this intake gives a mean serum 25OHD of about 91 nmol/L, although it warns the model was not built for such high intakes.
findings.locator: Summary, Table S-2 p. 9; Ch. 6 'Tolerable Upper Intake Levels: Calcium and Vitamin D', adult UL derivation pp. 443-445 and footnote 7 p. 445

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Committee to Review Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin D and Calcium. Dietary Reference Intakes for Calcium and Vitamin D. Washington (DC): National Academies Press; 2011. doi:10.17226/13050
findings.parameter: serum 25OHD reference thresholds
findings.value: <30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) risk of deficiency; 30-50 nmol/L some at risk of inadequacy; ≥50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) sufficient for practically all; >75 nmol/L (30 ng/mL) not consistently more beneficial; possible concern >125 nmol/L (50 ng/mL); Ch. 6 advises avoiding >about 125-150 nmol/L
findings.finding: The report gives serum vitamin D bands. Sufficiency is reached at 50 nmol/L, there is no consistent extra benefit above 75, and levels above about 125 may be a concern. The app collects no lab values, so this is context only, never an input.
findings.locator: Summary pp. 8, 13-14; Ch. 6 p. 443

findings.citation: Dansinger ML, Gleason JA, Griffith JL, Selker HP, Schaefer EJ. Comparison of the Atkins, Ornish, Weight Watchers, and Zone diets for weight loss and heart disease risk reduction: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2005;293(1):43-53. doi:10.1001/jama.293.1.43
findings.population: Adults 22-72 y with overweight/obesity (BMI 27-42) and hypertension, dyslipidaemia or fasting hyperglycaemia; single centre, Boston
findings.parameter: effect of diet type (macronutrient pattern) on 1-year weight loss
findings.value: Diet type not associated with weight loss (r = 0.07, P = .40); intention-to-treat 1-year loss: Atkins 2.1 (SD 4.8) kg, Zone 3.2 (6.0) kg, Weight Watchers 3.0 (4.9) kg, Ornish 3.3 (7.3) kg; no significant between-diet difference
findings.finding: Four very different popular diets (very-low-carb, 40-30-30 balance, points-based calorie restriction, very-low-fat) produced similar modest weight loss at one year. This supports letting users choose their dietary pattern rather than imposing one macronutrient split.
findings.locator: Abstract Results; Results 'Weight Loss' and 'Cardiac Risk Factors' (JAMA full text, jamanetwork.com fullarticle/200094)

findings.citation: Dansinger ML, Gleason JA, Griffith JL, Selker HP, Schaefer EJ. Comparison of the Atkins, Ornish, Weight Watchers, and Zone diets for weight loss and heart disease risk reduction: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2005;293(1):43-53. doi:10.1001/jama.293.1.43
findings.population: Adults with overweight/obesity and cardiometabolic risk factors
findings.parameter: self-rated adherence score and its association with weight loss
findings.value: Adherence self-rated on a 10-point scale for the previous 30 days (10 = perfect, 1 = baseline diet); correlation with weight loss r = 0.60 (P<.001); top adherence tertile lost about 7% of body weight on average
findings.finding: A simple 1-10 self-rating of adherence over the past month tracked weight loss strongly and curvilinearly, far better than diet type did. An app could log a similar adherence rating alongside weigh-ins. The ratings are self-reported.
findings.locator: Methods 'Dietary Adherence'; Results 'Weight Loss'; Figure 3 (JAMA full text)

findings.citation: Dansinger ML, Gleason JA, Griffith JL, Selker HP, Schaefer EJ. Comparison of the Atkins, Ornish, Weight Watchers, and Zone diets for weight loss and heart disease risk reduction: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2005;293(1):43-53. doi:10.1001/jama.293.1.43
findings.population: Adults with overweight/obesity and cardiometabolic risk factors
findings.parameter: adherence decay and attrition over 1 year
findings.value: Non-completion 34 (21%) at 2 mo, 61 (38%) at 6 mo, 67 (42%) at 12 mo; about 25% in each diet group sustained mean adherence ≥6/10; about 25% per group sustained >5% and about 10% sustained >10% weight loss at 1 year (intention-to-treat)
findings.finding: Self-rated adherence declined gradually through the year, similarly on every diet. About two in five participants had dropped out by one year, and only about a quarter per diet kept more than 5% weight loss. An adaptive app should expect adherence to drift and re-plan.
findings.locator: Results 'Attrition and Adverse Effects', 'Dietary Intake and Adherence', 'Weight Loss'; Figure 2 (JAMA full text)

findings.citation: Dansinger ML, Gleason JA, Griffith JL, Selker HP, Schaefer EJ. Comparison of the Atkins, Ornish, Weight Watchers, and Zone diets for weight loss and heart disease risk reduction: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2005;293(1):43-53. doi:10.1001/jama.293.1.43
findings.population: Adults with overweight/obesity and cardiometabolic risk factors
findings.parameter: realised (self-reported) energy reduction at 1 year
findings.value: Mean reduction from baseline at 12 months (3-day diet records): Atkins 138 kcal/day, Zone 251, Weight Watchers 244, Ornish 192 (all P<.05; between-diet P = .70)
findings.finding: At one year, energy intake from 3-day food records was only about 140-250 kcal/day below baseline on every diet, with no between-diet difference. Intake was self-reported, so this is imprecise, but it supports adapting targets from observed weight change rather than intended intake.
findings.locator: Results 'Dietary Intake and Adherence' (text); 3-day diet record intake data in Table 2 (JAMA full text)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.population: Healthy resistance-trained men (10) and women (13), 18-39 y, ≥1 y training, 75.4 ± 10.3 kg
findings.parameter: flexible (macro targets, free food choice) vs rigid (set meal plan) diet
findings.value: 10-wk diet phase: FLEX -2.6 kg body weight, -2.3 kg fat mass, -2.4% body fat; RIGID -3.0 kg, -3.2 kg, -3.3%; no significant between-group difference on any variable
findings.finding: Giving resistance-trained dieters daily macronutrient targets and free food choice worked as well for weight and fat loss as a dietitian-set fixed meal plan. This supports user-chosen foods within targets. It was a small trial with about 40% attrition, and adherence superiority was not shown.
findings.locator: Abstract Results; Results paragraphs 1-2; Methods 'Dietary and Exercise Intervention' (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: energy deficit % of maintenance
findings.value: Prescribed 25% below estimated maintenance; achieved about 20% (FLEX 20%, RIGID 17.7%) for 10 weeks
findings.finding: A moderate deficit, prescribed at 25% and achieved at about 18-20% below habitual intake, was chosen for adherence and effectiveness. It produced fat loss while fat-free mass was preserved in trained lifters.
findings.locator: Methods 'Dietary and Exercise Intervention'; Results paragraph 1 (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: weekly loss % body mass
findings.value: About 0.4% of body mass per week (both groups combined) over 10 weeks
findings.finding: The achieved loss rate was about 0.4% of body weight per week. The authors credit this slow rate, together with high protein and continued resistance training, for the favourable body-composition result.
findings.locator: Discussion paragraph 2 (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: proportion of weight lost as fat mass
findings.value: About 98% of body mass lost came from fat mass (groups combined); fat-free mass maintained during the diet phase
findings.finding: With about a 20% deficit, 2 g/kg protein and ongoing resistance training, nearly all the weight lost by lean trained adults was fat. The authors expected a larger lean-mass share in lean people. Body composition was measured by A-mode ultrasound, a two-compartment model.
findings.locator: Discussion paragraph 3; Results paragraph 2 (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: protein g/kg/day during energy deficit
findings.value: 2 g protein per kg body mass per day (both arms, isonitrogenous)
findings.finding: Both diet arms were prescribed 2 g/kg/day of protein during the deficit, and fat-free mass was preserved. The trial did not test protein dose, so this is the protocol value, not a dose-response result.
findings.locator: Methods 'Dietary and Exercise Intervention' (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: non-protein energy split between carbohydrate and fat
findings.value: Remaining energy after protein split approximately evenly between carbohydrate and fat
findings.finding: After setting protein, the protocol divided the remaining calories roughly half and half between carbohydrate and fat. Weight and fat loss were comparable in both arms, but the split itself was not tested against alternatives.
findings.locator: Methods 'Dietary and Exercise Intervention' (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: minimum prescribed energy intake floor
findings.value: 1,200 kcal/day floor; when reported maintenance intake was below measured RMR, the higher of a 15% reduction or 1,200 kcal/day was prescribed (4 participants per group)
findings.finding: The protocol never prescribed below 1,200 kcal/day. When food-record intake fell below measured resting metabolic rate, suggesting under-reporting, it used a smaller 15% cut or 1,200 kcal, whichever was higher. This is a trial safeguard, not a validated threshold.
findings.locator: Methods 'Dietary and Exercise Intervention' (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: baseline maintenance energy estimation method
findings.value: Mean of a 3-day food record (including 1 weekend day) of habitual intake; when reported intake fell below measured RMR, the prescription was adjusted (15% cut or 1,200 kcal/day, whichever higher)
findings.finding: Maintenance calories were estimated from three days of habitual food records. Some records fell below measured RMR, and the authors say a longer tracking period would have estimated maintenance more accurately. This supports calibrating maintenance over a longer logging period rather than from a short food record.
findings.locator: Methods 'Dietary and Exercise Intervention'; Discussion limitations paragraph (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: resting metabolic rate response to moderate deficit
findings.value: No significant between-group difference in RMR (measured at weeks 0, 5, 10, 16, 20); numeric RMR values are in a table not rendered in the retrieved text
findings.finding: Resting metabolic rate did not differ between flexible and rigid dieters. The authors suggest that a non-severe deficit with high protein and resistance training limits adverse metabolic adaptation. Within-group RMR changes could not be extracted.
findings.locator: Discussion paragraph 6; Results paragraph 2 (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Conlin LA, Aguilar DT, Rogers GE, Campbell BI. Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals seeking to optimize their physiques: a randomized controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021;18(1):52. doi:10.1186/s12970-021-00452-2
findings.parameter: post-diet ad libitum fat-free mass change
findings.value: 10-wk post-diet phase: FLEX +1.7 kg FFM vs RIGID -0.7 kg (diet x time p<0.001); 10 of 11 FLEX vs 3 of 12 RIGID gained FFM
findings.finding: After the diet ended, the flexible group gained more fat-free mass. The authors explicitly decline to attribute this to diet assignment, because post-diet intake and training time did not differ and training intensity was not measured. Do not use it as evidence that flexible dieting builds muscle.
findings.locator: Abstract Results/Conclusions; Discussion paragraph 4 (PMC8243453)

findings.citation: Yancy WS Jr, Mayer SB, Coffman CJ, Smith VA, Kolotkin RL, Geiselman PJ, et al. Effect of allowing choice of diet on weight loss: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2015;162(12):805-14. doi:10.7326/M14-2358
findings.population: US veterans with BMI >=30 kg/m2, mean age 55 y, 27% women, 23% type 2 diabetes; Durham VA outpatient clinic
findings.parameter: effect of letting the user choose the diet pattern (low-carb vs low-fat) on 48-week weight loss
findings.value: Choice 5.7 kg (95% CI 4.3 to 7.0) vs randomly assigned 6.7 kg (95% CI 5.4 to 8.0); difference -1.1 kg (95% CI -2.9 to 0.8), p=0.26; 5.6% vs 6.2% of baseline weight; multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis -1.3 kg (95% CI -3.1 to 0.6)
findings.finding: Letting participants pick between two diet patterns did not increase weight loss at 48 weeks, and the confidence interval rules out a clinically meaningful benefit of choice. The app should not claim that choosing a pattern improves results.
findings.locator: PMC author manuscript: Abstract; Results > Weight outcomes; Table 2 (body weight rows)

findings.citation: Yancy WS Jr, Mayer SB, Coffman CJ, Smith VA, Kolotkin RL, Geiselman PJ, et al. Effect of allowing choice of diet on weight loss: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2015;162(12):805-14. doi:10.7326/M14-2358
findings.population: US veterans with obesity, mean age 55 y, mostly men
findings.parameter: effect of diet-pattern choice on dietary adherence and weight-related quality of life
findings.value: 48-wk adherence (% deviation from macronutrient goal; lower = better) 9.4 choice vs 10.3 assigned; difference -0.9 (95% CI -4.9 to 3.1), p=0.66. IWQOL-Lite total difference -0.8 (95% CI -4.1 to 2.6), p=0.65
findings.finding: Being allowed to choose a diet pattern did not improve how closely people kept to their macronutrient goal, or their weight-related quality of life, at 48 weeks. Only 5 of 105 switched diets at week 12. This one trial gives no support for choice as a way to improve adherence.
findings.locator: Results > Dietary adherence, physical activity, and quality of life outcomes; Table 2 (diet adherence and IWQOL-Lite total rows); Results > Participants, retention and attendance (switching)

findings.citation: Yancy WS Jr, Mayer SB, Coffman CJ, Smith VA, Kolotkin RL, Geiselman PJ, et al. Effect of allowing choice of diet on weight loss: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2015;162(12):805-14. doi:10.7326/M14-2358
findings.parameter: energy deficit prescribed in the low-fat arm (trial protocol, not a tested dose)
findings.value: Low-fat diet: 500 kcal/day subtracted from the daily maintenance energy requirement (the paper cites the IOM 2002 DRI report); total fat <30% of energy, saturated fat <10%, cholesterol <300 mg/day. Low-carb diet: ~20 g/day carbohydrate at first, no calorie limit. Randomised-arm results (choice vs assigned, each arm mixing both diets): 5.6% vs 6.2% of baseline weight lost at 48 wk
findings.finding: The trial's low-fat diet used a fixed 500 kcal/day cut below estimated maintenance. The roughly 6% losses at 48 weeks belong to the choice and assigned arms, each mixing both diets, not to the low-fat diet alone. The trial did not compare deficit sizes.
findings.locator: Methods > Interventions > Dietary interventions; Results > Weight outcomes

findings.citation: Yancy WS Jr, Mayer SB, Coffman CJ, Smith VA, Kolotkin RL, Geiselman PJ, et al. Effect of allowing choice of diet on weight loss: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2015;162(12):805-14. doi:10.7326/M14-2358
findings.parameter: timing of the weight-loss plateau
findings.value: Linear mixed-model estimated mean weight 108.4 kg at baseline; 104.2/103.9 kg at 12 wk; 102.0/101.3 kg at 24 wk; 102.2/101.6 kg at 36 wk; 102.7/101.7 kg at 48 wk (choice/assigned)
findings.finding: Nearly all the weight was lost by week 24. Weight was then flat or crept up to week 48, consistent with the authors' uncited remark that loss plateaus at 4-6 months. Counselling dropped from fortnightly to monthly at week 24, so reduced contact may explain part of the plateau.
findings.locator: Table 2 (body weight rows); Methods > Procedures common to all participants (session schedule); Discussion (4-6 month plateau remark)

findings.citation: Yancy WS Jr, Mayer SB, Coffman CJ, Smith VA, Kolotkin RL, Geiselman PJ, et al. Effect of allowing choice of diet on weight loss: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2015;162(12):805-14. doi:10.7326/M14-2358
findings.parameter: programme engagement (session attendance) vs weight loss
findings.value: Attended >=15 of 19 sessions: 7.6 kg (choice) and 8.2 kg (assigned) lost at 48 wk; attended <15 sessions: 2.7 kg and 2.8 kg. Exploratory, non-randomised subgroup
findings.finding: People who attended at least about 80% of counselling sessions lost roughly three times as much weight as people who attended fewer. This split was exploratory and not randomised, so it shows an association with engagement, not a causal effect.
findings.locator: Methods > Statistical analysis (subgroup definition); Results > Weight outcomes (exploratory subgroup analysis)

findings.citation: Westenhoefer J, Engel D, Holst C, Lorenz J, Peacock M, Stubbs J, et al. Cognitive and weight-related correlates of flexible and rigid restrained eating behaviour. Eat Behav. 2013;14(1):69-72. doi:10.1016/j.eatbeh.2012.10.015
findings.population: Women in a commercial slimming organisation for >=6 months (mean 15.7 months), trying to maintain weight loss
findings.parameter: style of dietary control (flexible vs rigid restraint) and weight-loss maintenance
findings.value: Multiple regression over the 6-month study: higher flexible-restraint scores predicted greater weight loss and better maintenance; higher rigid-restraint scores predicted smaller loss (coefficients not given in abstract). Participants had lost 10.1 +/- 9.7 kg before the study
findings.finding: In women keeping off weight they had lost, flexible control of eating predicted better maintenance and rigid control predicted less loss. This supports flexible targets over rigid meal rules. It is an observational association, and only the abstract was read.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results; Conclusions); full text not accessible

findings.citation: Westenhoefer J, Engel D, Holst C, Lorenz J, Peacock M, Stubbs J, et al. Cognitive and weight-related correlates of flexible and rigid restrained eating behaviour. Eat Behav. 2013;14(1):69-72. doi:10.1016/j.eatbeh.2012.10.015
findings.population: Women in a commercial slimming programme maintaining weight loss
findings.parameter: rigid restraint and preoccupation with food and body shape
findings.value: Rigid restraint correlated with attentional bias to food stimuli r=0.43 (p<0.001) and to body-shape stimuli r=0.49 (p<0.001); flexible restraint correlated with poorer working memory r=-0.25 (p<0.05)
findings.finding: Rigid restraint went with stronger attentional bias toward food and body-shape cues on a modified Stroop test, a correlational warning against pushing rigid rules. Flexible restraint went with poorer working-memory scores; the abstract gives no explanation for this. Abstract only.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results)

findings.citation: Kutz AM, Marsh AG, Gunderson CG, Maguen S, Masheb RM. Eating disorder screening: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test characteristics of the SCOFF. J Gen Intern Med. 2020;35(3):885-93. doi:10.1007/s11606-019-05478-6
findings.population: 25 validation studies in 13 countries, ages 10-95, mostly female samples
findings.parameter: SCOFF eating-disorder screen: pooled diagnostic accuracy
findings.value: Sensitivity 0.86 (95% CI 0.78-0.91); specificity 0.83 (95% CI 0.77-0.88); AUC 0.91 (0.88-0.93); LR+ 5.0 (3.6-6.8); LR- 0.17 (0.11-0.27); I2 97.6% (sensitivity) and 98.2% (specificity); no significant threshold effect (r=-0.21, p=0.32)
findings.finding: Across 25 validation studies, the SCOFF showed good overall accuracy. Heterogeneity was extreme, and only two studies were rated low on every risk-of-bias and applicability domain. The SCOFF suits a first-pass flag, not a diagnosis.
findings.locator: Results > Study characteristics; Diagnostic accuracy (pooled estimates, AUC, I2, likelihood ratios); Table 2 (QUADAS-2)

findings.citation: Kutz AM, Marsh AG, Gunderson CG, Maguen S, Masheb RM. Eating disorder screening: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test characteristics of the SCOFF. J Gen Intern Med. 2020;35(3):885-93. doi:10.1007/s11606-019-05478-6
