findings.parameter: SCOFF accuracy in subgroups relevant to an adult app (adults, men, community, binge eating disorder)
findings.value: Adults, mean age >=25 (12 studies): sens 0.84 (0.74-0.94), spec 0.86 (0.79-0.93). Samples <60% female (5): sens 0.75 (0.46-0.91). Community (4): sens 0.71 (0.45-0.96). BED included (6): sens 0.77 (0.60-0.94), spec 0.78 (0.65-0.91); BED vs no-BED difference not significant (p=0.22). North America (4): sens 0.69 (0.43-0.95)
findings.finding: Sensitivity was lower in samples with more men, in community samples, in North America and in studies including binge eating disorder, though the BED difference was not significant. No study tested all DSM-5 eating disorders. A negative SCOFF is not clearance; screening should be one layer of the safety gate.
findings.locator: Table 3 (subgroup analyses); Results (subgroup text); Discussion; Conclusions

findings.citation: Morgan JF, Reid F, Lacey JH. The SCOFF questionnaire: assessment of a new screening tool for eating disorders. BMJ. 1999;319(7223):1467-8. doi:10.1136/bmj.319.7223.1467
findings.population: 116 women aged 18-40 with DSM-IV anorexia or bulimia from a specialist clinic; 96 female college controls aged 18-39; UK
findings.parameter: SCOFF scoring rule and cut-off
findings.value: 5 yes/no items, 1 point per yes; score >=2 = likely anorexia or bulimia. Derivation: sensitivity 100% (95% CI 96.9-100%), specificity 87.5% (95% CI 79.2-93.4%); false-positive rate 12.5%
findings.finding: The SCOFF has five yes/no questions, and two or more yeses flag a likely eating disorder. One item asks about losing more than one stone (about 6.35 kg) in 3 months, so people losing weight on purpose may score higher. Case-control derivation study.
findings.locator: Participants, methods, and results (box of questions and footnote; threshold paragraph); Table

findings.citation: Feltner C, Peat C, Reddy S, Riley S, Berkman N, Middleton JC, et al. Screening for eating disorders in adolescents and adults: evidence report and systematic review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. 2022;327(11):1068-82. doi:10.1001/jama.2022.1807
findings.population: Adults in 10 SCOFF test-accuracy studies (review total 57 studies, N=10773, including adolescents)
findings.parameter: SCOFF (cut point >=2) accuracy in adults
findings.value: Pooled sensitivity 84% (95% CI 74-90%); pooled specificity 80% (95% CI 65-89%); 10 studies, n=3684 adults. No study directly assessed benefits or harms of screening
findings.finding: The USPSTF evidence review found SCOFF accuracy adequate in adults at the >=2 cut point, close to the Kutz estimate, though both pool overlapping validation studies. No study evaluated the benefits or harms of screening itself, so the screen should gate a feature, not act as a treatment. Abstract only.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract (Results; Conclusions); full text not opened (publisher bot check, HTTP 403)

findings.citation: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 clinical practice guideline for the evaluation and management of chronic kidney disease. Kidney Int. 2024;105(4S):S117-S314. doi:10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018
findings.population: Adults with CKD at risk of progression
findings.parameter: protein intake ceiling for adults with CKD at risk of progression
findings.value: >1.3 g/kg body weight/day should be avoided (Practice Point 3.3.1.1; ungraded, expert consensus supported by observational data)
findings.finding: KDIGO advises adults with CKD at risk of progression not to exceed 1.3 g/kg/day of protein, citing hyperfiltration and observational links to faster decline. High-protein goal targets should be blocked, or the user excluded, when CKD is reported.
findings.locator: Chapter 3, section 3.3.1 Protein intake, Practice Point 3.3.1.1 and Key information (pp. S157, S208)

findings.citation: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 clinical practice guideline for the evaluation and management of chronic kidney disease. Kidney Int. 2024;105(4S):S117-S314. doi:10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018
findings.parameter: protein target in adults with CKD G3-G5 (not on dialysis)
findings.value: 0.8 g/kg body weight/day (Recommendation 3.3.1.1, grade 2C: weak recommendation, low-certainty evidence)
findings.finding: For CKD stages G3-G5, KDIGO suggests keeping protein at 0.8 g/kg/day, the same as the WHO allowance for the general population. It is a weak, low-certainty recommendation. It is a clinical target, so the app should refer these users on rather than set it itself.
findings.locator: Recommendation 3.3.1.1 (pp. S157, S208); grading key p. S125; Figure 19

findings.citation: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 clinical practice guideline for the evaluation and management of chronic kidney disease. Kidney Int. 2024;105(4S):S117-S314. doi:10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018
findings.population: Adults and children evaluated for CKD
findings.parameter: CKD definition for an exclusion question
findings.value: Kidney structure or function abnormal for >=3 months: GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 (G3a-G5) and/or albuminuria ACR >=30 mg/g (>=3 mg/mmol), or other damage markers including a history of kidney transplantation. GFR categories: G1 >=90, G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 <15
findings.finding: KDIGO defines CKD as reduced GFR or kidney-damage markers lasting at least 3 months. The app can ask whether a clinician has diagnosed kidney disease, reduced eGFR or albuminuria, or a kidney transplant, and exclude those users from high-protein targets.
findings.locator: CKD nomenclature (p. S126); Table 1 Criteria for CKD and Table 2 GFR categories (p. S137)

findings.citation: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 clinical practice guideline for the evaluation and management of chronic kidney disease. Kidney Int. 2024;105(4S):S117-S314. doi:10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018
findings.parameter: dietary pattern for people with CKD
findings.value: More plant-based than animal-based foods and less ultraprocessed food (Practice Point 3.3.1, ungraded); supported by cohort data, e.g. high vs low DASH adherence HR 0.83 (0.69-0.99) for CKD progression (CRIC, N=2403, observational)
findings.finding: For CKD, KDIGO favours diverse diets that lean toward plant foods and limit ultraprocessed foods, based mainly on cohorts and small RCTs. It also asks for renal-dietitian input. Plant-forward suggestions fit, but CKD users should be referred on rather than managed by the app.
findings.locator: Section 3.3 Diet, Practice Points 3.3.1-3.3.2 (pp. S157, S207); Table 21 (p. S209)

findings.citation: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 clinical practice guideline for the evaluation and management of chronic kidney disease. Kidney Int. 2024;105(4S):S117-S314. doi:10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018
findings.parameter: sodium intake limit in CKD
findings.value: <2 g sodium/day (<90 mmol/day; <5 g sodium chloride/day) (Recommendation 3.3.2.1, grade 2C)
findings.finding: KDIGO suggests people with CKD keep sodium under 2 g/day (under 5 g of salt), except those with sodium-wasting nephropathy. This is a weak, low-certainty recommendation taken from earlier KDIGO guidelines.
findings.locator: Recommendation 3.3.2.1 and Practice Point 3.3.2.1 (pp. S157-S158)

findings.citation: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 clinical practice guideline for the evaluation and management of chronic kidney disease. Kidney Int. 2024;105(4S):S117-S314. doi:10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018
findings.parameter: approximate protein content of common food portions (teaching values)
findings.value: 28 g meat/poultry/fish/seafood = 6-8 g protein; 1 egg = 6-8 g; 250 mL milk/yogurt = 8-10 g; 28 g cheese = 6-8 g; 100 g (0.5 cup) cooked legumes/beans/nuts/seeds = 7-10 g; 100 g (0.5 cup) cooked whole grains/cereals = 3-6 g; starchy vegetables/breads = 2-4 g (no portion size stated); 100 g meat is about 25 g protein
findings.finding: KDIGO gives rough protein amounts per portion so people do not mistake food weight for protein grams. These are approximate teaching values reproduced from KDIGO 2022, not food-composition data. The app should use a licensed food database for real counts.
findings.locator: Section 3.3.1 Key information (p. S208); Figure 20 Average protein content of foods (p. S209)

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) and National Research Council (US) Committee to Reexamine IOM Pregnancy Weight Guidelines; Rasmussen KM, Yaktine AL, editors. Weight gain during pregnancy: reexamining the guidelines. Washington (DC): National Academies Press (US); 2009. doi:10.17226/12584
findings.population: Pregnant women in the US with singleton pregnancies
findings.parameter: recommended total gestational weight gain by pre-pregnancy BMI (singleton)
findings.finding: The official US guideline sets a weight-gain range for every pre-pregnancy BMI category, including obesity. This is incompatible with any deficit or weigh-in-driven loss target, so pregnant users should be excluded. The committee notes the ranges rest on observational data and still need trial validation.
findings.locator: Summary chapter (NAP read-online): Table S-1 (p. 2); Pregnant Adolescents (pp. 3-4); Key Finding S-1 (p. 5); statement on observational basis and need for experimental validation (p. 11); other chapters not read

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) and National Research Council (US) Committee to Reexamine IOM Pregnancy Weight Guidelines; Rasmussen KM, Yaktine AL, editors. Weight gain during pregnancy: reexamining the guidelines. Washington (DC): National Academies Press (US); 2009. doi:10.17226/12584
findings.population: Pregnant women in the US with singleton pregnancies
findings.parameter: weekly gestational weight-gain rate, 2nd and 3rd trimester
findings.value: Mean (range) kg/week: underweight 0.51 (0.44-0.58); normal 0.42 (0.35-0.50); overweight 0.28 (0.23-0.33); obese 0.22 (0.17-0.27). Assumes 0.5-2 kg gain in the first trimester
findings.finding: The guideline sets a positive weekly gain rate for the second and third trimesters in every BMI group. A weight-trend engine aiming for a negative or flat rate would work against it, which confirms pregnancy as a hard exclusion.
findings.locator: Summary chapter, Table S-1 (rate columns and footnote; NAP read-online p. 2)

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) and National Research Council (US) Committee to Reexamine IOM Pregnancy Weight Guidelines; Rasmussen KM, Yaktine AL, editors. Weight gain during pregnancy: reexamining the guidelines. Washington (DC): National Academies Press (US); 2009. doi:10.17226/12584
findings.parameter: provisional gestational weight gain for twin pregnancy
findings.value: At term: normal weight 17-25 kg (37-54 lb); overweight 14-23 kg (31-50 lb); obese 11-19 kg (25-42 lb); no guideline for underweight women (interquartile range of gain in twin births averaging >=2500 g at 37-42 wk)
findings.finding: The committee gave only provisional twin targets, based on the interquartile range of gain in good-outcome twin births, and none for underweight women. This supports excluding all pregnancies rather than handling subtypes.
findings.locator: Summary chapter, Special Populations > Women with Multiple Fetuses (NAP read-online p. 4)

findings.citation: Institute of Medicine (US) and National Research Council (US) Committee to Reexamine IOM Pregnancy Weight Guidelines; Rasmussen KM, Yaktine AL, editors. Weight gain during pregnancy: reexamining the guidelines. Washington (DC): National Academies Press (US); 2009. doi:10.17226/12584
findings.population: Pregnant women, especially those with obesity
findings.parameter: weight loss or low gain during pregnancy
findings.value: The Summary chapter gives no safe rate of weight loss. Research Recommendation S-3 calls for studies of how weight loss or low gain, including prolonged fasting and ketonuria/ketonemia, affect offspring growth, development and long-term neurocognition; Key Finding S-4: evidence insufficient for specific gain targets in obesity classes II-III
findings.finding: The Summary sets no safe rate of weight loss in pregnancy and treats the effects of loss, fasting and ketosis on the offspring as open research questions. Unknown stays unknown, so the app must not offer any deficit to pregnant users.
findings.locator: Summary chapter, Key Finding S-4 (NAP read-online p. 7) and Research Recommendation S-3 (pp. 7-8)

findings.citation: Golden NH, Schneider M, Wood C; Committee on Nutrition; Committee on Adolescence; Section on Obesity. Preventing obesity and eating disorders in adolescents. Pediatrics. 2016;138(3):e20161649. doi:10.1542/peds.2016-1649
findings.parameter: weight-focused vs lifestyle-focused guidance for adolescents
findings.value: No numeric threshold in the abstract. Rule: guidance for adolescents should target healthy habits, not body weight
findings.finding: The AAP report says guidance for teenagers should centre on healthy habits rather than weight, because some teens trying to lose weight go on to develop eating disorders. This supports keeping calorie-deficit targets away from under-18s. The abstract gives no age cut-off.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only; full text not accessed

findings.citation: Golden NH, Schneider M, Wood C; Committee on Nutrition; Committee on Adolescence; Section on Obesity. Preventing obesity and eating disorders in adolescents. Pediatrics. 2016;138(3):e20161649. doi:10.1542/peds.2016-1649
findings.parameter: eating-disorder risk from properly conducted weight management in adolescents
findings.value: Qualitative only: the authors judge that properly run obesity prevention and treatment does not raise eating-disorder risk in adolescents; most adolescents who develop an eating disorder had no prior obesity
findings.finding: The abstract says correctly run obesity prevention and treatment do not appear to predispose teens to eating disorders, while some teens who try to lose weight do develop one. For an unsupervised consumer app, staying adults-only is the safer rule. Abstract only, no numbers.
findings.locator: PubMed abstract only

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.population: People with type 1 diabetes who exercise regularly (youth and adults)
findings.parameter: eligibility exclusion: type 1 diabetes from automated carbohydrate/fuelling targets
findings.value: Rule, not a number: carbohydrate intake around exercise must be matched to individual insulin-dose changes with glucose monitoring, ideally set with a registered dietitian who has diabetes and sports expertise
findings.finding: The consensus treats carbohydrate intake and insulin dosing around exercise in T1D as linked and personal, with glucose checks before, during and after. When exercising to lose weight, it prefers cutting insulin over eating extra carbohydrate. This supports keeping T1D users out of automated fuelling and carbohydrate targets.
findings.locator: Peer-reviewed accepted manuscript (Univ. Dundee Discovery repository), glycaemic-goal text MS p.6-7; 'Nutritional Management - Goals for nutritional management' MS p.8; Table 2 (MS p.16). Published Lancet version returned HTTP 403.

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.population: People with type 1 diabetes who exercise
findings.parameter: pre-exercise blood glucose start range (T1D)
findings.value: 7-10 mmol/L before aerobic exercise lasting up to about 1 h; 5-7 mmol/L acceptable for anaerobic/HIIT; below 5 mmol/L: take 10-20 g glucose and delay until above 5 mmol/L; about 6-8 mmol/L suggested as possibly ideal during exercise
findings.finding: Based on expert agreement, aerobic sessions in T1D should usually start with glucose between 7 and 10 mmol/L. HIIT or anaerobic work can start lower. If glucose is under 5 mmol/L, the person should take glucose and wait. The app should not model these clinical decisions.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript MS p.7 (glycaemic targets paragraph); Table 1 (MS p.15)

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.parameter: exercise contraindication thresholds (T1D)
findings.value: Blood ketones >=1.5 mmol/L: no exercise until treated; >=3.0 mmol/L: immediate clinical care; severe hypoglycaemia (<=2.8 mmol/L or needing help) within the previous 24 h: exercise contraindicated
findings.finding: Exercise should not start in T1D when blood ketones are 1.5 mmol/L or higher. Ketones of 3.0 mmol/L or more need urgent medical care. A severe hypoglycaemic episode in the past 24 hours also rules out exercise. Very low-carbohydrate diets and long endurance events can raise ketones.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript MS p.7-8 'Contraindications and cautions for exercise' A-B; Table 1 (MS p.15)

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.population: Endurance athletes with and without diabetes (performance column)
findings.parameter: intra-exercise carbohydrate g/h by session duration
findings.value: Under 30 min: none needed for performance; 30-60 min: 10-15 g/h may help; 60-150 min: 30-60 g/h; over 150 min: 60-90 g/h from mixed sources using different gut transporters (glucose + fructose), e.g. 20-30 g every 20 min
findings.finding: Table 2's performance column, which applies to athletes with or without diabetes, scales carbohydrate during exercise with session length, rising to 60-90 g/h for sessions over 2.5 h using glucose-fructose mixes. It draws on sports-nutrition references and the authors' expert opinion, not new trials.
findings.locator: Table 2 (MS p.16), 'Endurance exercise performance' column; footnote cites refs 63, 111, 112 plus expert opinion

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.population: Endurance athletes with and without diabetes
findings.parameter: pre-exercise meal carbohydrate g/kg
findings.value: At least 1 g carbohydrate/kg body weight in a low-fat, low-GI pre-exercise meal, scaled to exercise type and intensity; carbohydrate eaten about 4 h before exercise
findings.finding: A low-fat, low-glycaemic-index meal with at least 1 g/kg of carbohydrate is advised before endurance exercise. Carbohydrate should be eaten well before, about 4 h ahead, so muscle and liver glycogen are full.
findings.locator: Table 2 row 'Pre-exercise meal' (MS p.16); Nutritional Management text MS p.8-9

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.population: Endurance athletes with and without diabetes
findings.parameter: post-exercise carbohydrate g/kg
findings.value: 1-1.2 g carbohydrate/kg body weight in the post-exercise meal
findings.finding: To refill glycogen after endurance exercise, the table advises 1-1.2 g/kg of carbohydrate in the post-exercise meal. In T1D this also lowers the risk of late hypoglycaemia, but the insulin dose must be adjusted to match.
findings.locator: Table 2 row 'Post-exercise meal' (MS p.16); 'Nutritional needs for recovery' MS p.9-10

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.population: Athletes with type 1 diabetes (values drawn from athletes without diabetes)
findings.parameter: daily protein g/kg/day (active adults)
findings.value: 1.2-1.6 g/kg body weight/day; possibly higher during injury recovery or energy restriction
findings.finding: For athletes with T1D, daily protein needs are put at 1.2-1.6 g/kg, varying with training type, intensity and carbohydrate availability. More may be needed to protect lean mass during energy restriction. This is a summary of cited sports-nutrition work, not original evidence.
findings.locator: 'Daily energy and macronutrient balance' MS p.9 (refs 63, 70, 71)

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.population: Athletes (evidence mainly from athletes without diabetes)
findings.parameter: post-exercise protein dose g
findings.value: About 20-30 g protein together with carbohydrate after exercise
findings.finding: Eating about 20-30 g of protein with carbohydrate after exercise supports muscle protein synthesis. In athletes without diabetes it does not appear to speed glycogen refilling.
findings.locator: 'Nutritional needs for recovery' MS p.10 (ref 63)

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.parameter: macronutrient distribution % of daily energy
findings.value: 45-65% carbohydrate, 20-35% fat, 10-35% protein; higher protein share for those aiming to lose weight
findings.finding: As a rough guide for active people with T1D, daily energy can be split into 45-65% carbohydrate, 20-35% fat and 10-35% protein, with more protein for weight loss. The best split depends on individual assessment and exercise goals.
findings.locator: 'Daily energy and macronutrient balance' MS p.9 (ref 68)

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.parameter: RMR equation use
findings.value: No specific equation named; predictive resting-energy equations should serve only as a guide because they may over- or underestimate true requirements
findings.finding: Equations that predict resting energy expenditure give only a starting estimate and can be wrong in either direction. This supports an app design that starts from an equation and then adjusts using observed weight trends and logged intake.
findings.locator: 'Daily energy and macronutrient balance' MS p.9 (ref 67)

findings.citation: Riddell MC, Gallen IW, Smart CE, Taplin CE, Adolfsson P, Lumb AN, et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(5):377-90. doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
findings.parameter: sports drink carbohydrate concentration
findings.value: 6-8% carbohydrate with electrolytes for longer, higher-intensity exercise; water is enough for low-intensity or short sessions (about 45 min or less) provided glucose is at or above target (>=7 mmol/L)
findings.finding: Water suits short, easy sessions of about 45 min or less when glucose is at or above 7 mmol/L. For longer or harder sessions, sports drinks with 6-8% carbohydrate and electrolytes supply fluid and fuel and help prevent hypoglycaemia. Over-drinking them can raise glucose in T1D.
findings.locator: 'Fluid Replacement' MS p.10

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.parameter: very-low-energy diet threshold (energy intake floor)
findings.value: Very-low-energy diet = under 800 kcal/day; consider only within a multicomponent strategy in a specialist obesity service, for people with obesity who have a clinically assessed need to lose weight rapidly (e.g. before surgery)
findings.finding: NICE restricts diets under 800 kcal/day to specialist services, for people with obesity who have a clinical need for rapid loss. A consumer app for healthy adults should therefore never propose intakes in this range.
findings.locator: Recommendation 1.16.9 [2025], chapter 'Physical activity and diet' (web chapter; PDF p.77)

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.population: Adults living with obesity, or overweight with type 2 diabetes
findings.parameter: low-energy diet band requiring specialist support (kcal/day)
findings.value: Low-energy diet = 800-1,200 kcal/day; consider only within a multicomponent strategy with long-term support in a specialist obesity service (or a long-term-condition service such as for type 2 diabetes), for people with obesity or with overweight plus type 2 diabetes
findings.finding: NICE defines 800-1,200 kcal/day as a low-energy diet and reserves it for specialist or long-term-condition services with ongoing support. Our inference: an unsupervised app should keep proposed intakes above 1,200 kcal/day.
findings.locator: Recommendation 1.16.8 [2025], 'Low-energy and very-low-energy diets for adults' (PDF p.76)

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.parameter: maximum duration of low-/very-low-energy diets
findings.value: No more than 12 weeks; must be nutritionally complete, with ongoing clinical supervision and dietitian/nutritionist support; not to be used as a long-term strategy
findings.finding: Low- and very-low-energy diets should be nutritionally complete, clinically supervised and last no more than 12 weeks, and are not a long-term strategy. The limit reflects trial durations of 8-16 weeks, most often 12. Risks named include weight cycling and regain, plus constipation, fatigue and hair loss for very-low-energy diets.
findings.locator: Recommendations 1.16.10-1.16.12 [2025] (PDF p.77-78); Rationale 'Low-energy and very-low-energy diets for adults' (PDF p.164-165)

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.population: Adults living with overweight or obesity
findings.parameter: energy deficit kcal/day
findings.value: Trials commonly used a 500-800 kcal/day deficit (or an individualised deficit); NICE chose not to specify a deficit; intake must stay below expenditure
findings.finding: NICE requires only that intake stays below expenditure, and deliberately names no deficit. The evidence it reviewed mostly used 500-800 kcal/day deficits or deficits set per person. The committee also warned that excessive restriction risks poor nutrition and weight cycling.
findings.locator: Recommendation 1.16.3 [2025] (PDF p.75); Rationale 'Dietary approaches for all ages' (PDF p.162)

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.population: Adults living with overweight or obesity
findings.parameter: macronutrient approach for creating the deficit
findings.value: No preferred macronutrient diet; low-fat or low-carbohydrate both acceptable; no evidence identified on plant-based diets for weight loss
findings.finding: The evidence could not separate low-carbohydrate from conventional low-fat diets, so NICE recommends neither over the other. Either can create the deficit. NICE found no weight-loss evidence for plant-based diets. Plans should respect cultural food preferences and a balanced long-term diet.
findings.locator: Recommendations 1.16.1, 1.16.3, 1.16.6 [2025]; Rationale 'Dietary approaches for all ages' (PDF p.162-163); evidence review F

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.population: People living with overweight or obesity
findings.parameter: conditions requiring tailored or specialist dietary care (screening flags)
findings.value: Rule: tailor or refer for eating disorders/disordered eating, type 1 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, MASLD, coeliac disease or other food restrictions; advise against nutritionally unbalanced restrictive diets
findings.finding: Diet plans must allow for conditions including eating disorders, type 1 diabetes, IBD, MASLD and coeliac disease. NICE advises against unbalanced restrictive diets as ineffective long term and possibly harmful. The committee based this on expert opinion because no evidence on tailoring was found.
findings.locator: Recommendations 1.16.1 [2025] (PDF p.75) and 1.16.7 [2025] (PDF p.76); Rationale PDF p.162

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.population: Adults living with overweight or obesity
findings.parameter: intermittent fasting / time-restricted eating
findings.value: No recommendation (research recommendation only)
findings.finding: NICE found that alternate-day fasting and time-restricted eating improved only a few outcomes and were mostly no better than comparators. The studies had quality problems, so NICE made no recommendation. The app should not present fasting schedules as evidence-based.
findings.locator: 'Intermittent fasting in adults (no recommendations)' rationale (PDF p.163)

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.population: People who have lived with obesity and lost weight (regain); general population (obesity prevention)
findings.parameter: physical activity for preventing weight regain after loss
findings.value: People who have lived with obesity and lost weight may need 60-90 min of activity per day to avoid regain; to prevent obesity, most people may need 45-60 min/day of moderate activity (particularly without reducing energy intake)
findings.finding: People who have lived with obesity and lost weight may need 60-90 minutes of activity a day to avoid regaining it. This is a 2006 recommendation carried into NG246 without a 2025 evidence re-review.
findings.locator: Recommendation 1.15.3 [2006] (PDF p.73)

findings.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Overweight and obesity management. NICE guideline NG246. London: NICE; 2025 Jan 14 [updated 2026 Jan 8]. Available from: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246
findings.population: Adults living with overweight or obesity
findings.parameter: self-monitoring and programme structure
findings.value: Programmes should last at least 3 months with weekly or fortnightly sessions, monitor weight throughout, include self-monitoring of weight and behaviours, and set staged weight-loss goals (first weeks, programme end, 1 year)
findings.finding: Adult behavioural programmes should combine diet, activity and behaviour change and run for at least 3 months with weekly or fortnightly contact. They should track weight throughout, encourage self-monitoring and feedback, and set specific energy-intake goals with staged weight targets.
findings.locator: Recommendations 1.19.3-1.19.6 [2014; 1.19.6 amended 2025] (PDF p.99-101)

findings.citation: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA). Scientific Opinion on the essential composition of total diet replacements for weight control. EFSA J. 2015;13(1):3957. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2015.3957
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity using total diet replacement products
findings.parameter: absolute minimum daily energy intake (kcal/day)
findings.value: 2,510 kJ/day (600 kcal/day) minimum for total diet replacements
findings.finding: EFSA set a minimum of 600 kcal/day (2,510 kJ) for products that replace the whole diet, derived from the macronutrient minimums below. This is an absolute lower limit for formula diets, far below any intake a consumer app should propose.
findings.locator: Abstract only (journal abstract via DOAJ record and OpenAlex; citation confirmed via Crossref); full text blocked (HTTP 403 / bot challenge) at EFSA, Wiley and DTU Orbit

findings.citation: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA). Scientific Opinion on the essential composition of total diet replacements for weight control. EFSA J. 2015;13(1):3957. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2015.3957
findings.parameter: minimum protein g/day during severe energy restriction
findings.value: 75 g/day (Population Reference Intake for protein adjusted for overweight/obese adults)
findings.finding: EFSA set a minimum of 75 g/day of protein for total diet replacements, based on the adult protein reference intake adjusted for people with overweight or obesity. This gives an absolute protein floor during severe restriction.
findings.locator: Abstract only (DOAJ record and OpenAlex); full text not opened (HTTP 403)

findings.parameter: minimum carbohydrate g/day
findings.value: 30 g/day (based on the brain's obligatory glucose demand)
findings.finding: EFSA set a minimum of 30 g/day of carbohydrate for total diet replacements, based on the brain's obligatory glucose needs. This gives an absolute carbohydrate floor.

findings.citation: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA). Scientific Opinion on the essential composition of total diet replacements for weight control. EFSA J. 2015;13(1):3957. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2015.3957
findings.parameter: minimum linoleic acid g/day
findings.value: 11 g/day
findings.finding: EFSA set a minimum linoleic acid content of 11 g/day for total diet replacements. This is an essential-fatty-acid floor under severe energy restriction.
findings.locator: Abstract only (DOAJ record and OpenAlex); full text not opened (HTTP 403)

findings.citation: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA). Scientific Opinion on the essential composition of total diet replacements for weight control. EFSA J. 2015;13(1):3957. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2015.3957
findings.parameter: minimum alpha-linolenic acid g/day
findings.value: 1.4 g/day
findings.finding: EFSA set a minimum alpha-linolenic acid content of 1.4 g/day for total diet replacements, alongside micronutrient minimums taken from existing reference values.
findings.locator: Abstract only (DOAJ record and OpenAlex); full text not opened (HTTP 403)

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity (evidence to 2011)
findings.parameter: reduced-calorie intake target kcal/day by sex
findings.value: Women 1,200-1,500 kcal/day; men 1,500-1,800 kcal/day (usually adjusted for body weight)
findings.finding: One of three accepted ways to cut intake is a fixed target of 1,200-1,500 kcal/day for women or 1,500-1,800 kcal/day for men, within a full lifestyle programme. The recommendation has NHLBI grade A (COR I, LOE A), and the underlying evidence statement is rated High.
