findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.parameter: energy deficit kcal/day
findings.value: 500 kcal/day or 750 kcal/day below estimated requirement (ES1 also lists a 30% energy deficit)
findings.finding: Another accepted method is to estimate the person's energy needs and prescribe a deficit of 500 or 750 kcal/day. The evidence statement also allows a 30% deficit. Grade A (COR I, LOE A), evidence rated High.
findings.locator: Table 4 recommendation 3a; section 3.3.1 CQ3 ES1

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.parameter: very-low-calorie diet definition and permitted use
findings.value: VLCD = under 800 kcal/day; use only in limited circumstances by trained practitioners in a medical setting with monitoring and high-intensity lifestyle support (NHLBI grade A; ACC/AHA COR IIa, LOE A)
findings.finding: Diets under 800 kcal/day need medical supervision because weight falls fast and complications can occur. The panel says strong evidence means monitoring is required if a VLCD is used, not that VLCDs should be prescribed. An app must never propose them.
findings.locator: Table 4 recommendation 4e and footnote; section 3.4.7 ES7a

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity and cardiovascular risk factors
findings.parameter: minimum clinically meaningful weight-loss target (% body weight)
findings.value: Sustained loss of 3-5% of body weight; larger losses give larger benefits (NHLBI grade A; COR I, LOE A)
findings.finding: Keeping off 3-5% of body weight meaningfully lowers triglycerides, glucose and HbA1c, and reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes. Larger losses also improve blood pressure and cholesterol and reduce medication needs. This supports a modest default loss goal.
findings.locator: Table 4 recommendation 2; section 3.1 CQ1 ES1-ES4

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity (17 trials in CQ3)
findings.parameter: expected weight-loss trajectory under dietary restriction
findings.value: Loss peaks at about 6 months (4-12 kg), then slow regain: net 4-10 kg at 1 year and 3-4 kg at 2 years
findings.finding: With dietary restriction, average loss peaks at about 6 months and then slowly reverses as treatment tapers. Net loss is 4-10 kg at one year and 3-4 kg at two. Adaptive targets should expect a plateau and some regain. The guideline rates this evidence High.
findings.locator: Section 3.3.2 CQ3 ES3

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity in comprehensive lifestyle programmes
findings.parameter: expected regain rate after the first year
findings.value: About 1-2 kg/year average regain from the 6-12-month low point, even with continued bimonthly (guideline's term) or more frequent contact
findings.finding: In programmes that continue bimonthly (the guideline's term) or more frequent contact after year one, average regain is still 1-2 kg per year from the 6-12-month low point. Long-term losses nonetheless stay larger than with usual care.
findings.locator: Section 3.4.2 CQ4 ES2c

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.population: Adults with overweight or obesity who have lost weight
findings.parameter: weigh-in frequency during weight-loss maintenance
findings.value: Weekly or more often, within a maintenance programme of at least 1 year (face-to-face or telephone, with monthly or more frequent contact with a trained interventionist), 200-300 min/week of physical activity and a reduced-calorie diet (Recs 4f and 4g: NHLBI grade A; COR I, LOE A; CQ4 ES1 strength High)
findings.finding: After weight loss, adults should join a maintenance programme of one year or more: at least monthly contact with a trained interventionist, 200-300 min/week of activity, weekly or more frequent weighing and a reduced-calorie diet. Weighing is one bundled component; no separate effect is reported.
findings.locator: Table 4 recommendations 4f and 4g; section 3.4.1 CQ4 ES1 (weekly weighing for maintenance); section 3.4.8 ES8a-b (maintenance programmes)

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.parameter: expected effect of electronically delivered self-monitoring programmes
findings.value: Up to 5 kg loss at 6-12 months with frequent self-monitoring of weight, food intake and activity plus personalised feedback from a trained interventionist; smaller than face-to-face (Rec 4c grade B; COR IIa, LOE A)
findings.finding: Electronic programmes with frequent self-monitoring of weight, food and activity, plus personal feedback from a trained person, produced up to 5 kg loss at 6-12 months. That beats minimal intervention but is usually less than face-to-face care. An app without human feedback may achieve less.
findings.locator: Section 3.4.3 CQ4 ES3; Table 4 recommendation 4c; section 3.4.11 ES11

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.parameter: protein % of energy during weight loss
findings.value: 25% vs 15% of energy from protein: equivalent weight loss when both diets have a 500-750 kcal/day deficit
findings.finding: Raising protein to 25% of calories gave the same weight loss as a typical 15% protein diet when both had a 500-750 kcal/day deficit. It also brought no extra cardiovascular risk-factor benefit (low-strength evidence). The guideline does not test whether protein spares lean mass.
findings.locator: Section 3.3.4 CQ3 ES5a (strength High) and ES5b (Low)

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.parameter: fat % of energy during weight loss
findings.value: Under 30% vs over 40% of energy from fat: comparable weight loss at 6-12 months with a 500-750 kcal/day deficit
findings.finding: Lower-fat (under 30% of calories) and higher-fat (over 40%) diets with the same 500-750 kcal/day deficit gave similar weight loss at 6-12 months. Lower-fat, higher-carbohydrate diets lowered LDL more but improved triglycerides and HDL less.
findings.locator: Section 3.3.3 CQ3 ES4a and ES4b (strength Moderate)

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.parameter: low-carbohydrate approach for weight loss
findings.value: About 20 g/day carbohydrate for up to 3 months, then raised: no weight-loss difference at 6 months vs a calorie-restricted low-fat diet
findings.finding: A low-carbohydrate diet (about 20 g/day at first, then increased) gave the same 6-month weight loss as a calorie-restricted low-fat diet. There was too little evidence to judge its effect on cardiovascular risk factors.
findings.locator: Section 3.3.5 CQ3 ES6a (strength Low) and ES6b

findings.citation: Jensen MD, Ryan DH, Apovian CM, Ard JD, Comuzzie AG, Donato KA, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline for the management of overweight and obesity in adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society. Circulation. 2014;129(25 Suppl 2):S102-38. doi:10.1161/01.cir.0000437739.71477.ee
findings.parameter: dietary pattern options (vegetarian, vegan, Mediterranean)
findings.value: Energy-restricted Mediterranean, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and low-fat vegan (10-25% of energy from fat) patterns give weight loss comparable to an energy-restricted lower-fat pattern (25-30% fat)
findings.finding: Many calorie-restricted patterns, including Mediterranean, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and low-fat vegan, produce weight loss and heart benefits similar to a standard lower-fat diet, provided the deficit is achieved. This supports letting users choose their pattern.
findings.locator: Section 3.3.1 ES2 (strength High) and section 3.3.8 ES9 (strength Low)

findings.citation: Johansson K, Sundström J, Marcus C, Hemmingsson E, Neovius M. Risk of symptomatic gallstones and cholecystectomy after a very-low-calorie diet or low-calorie diet in a commercial weight loss program: 1-year matched cohort study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2014;38(2):279-84. doi:10.1038/ijo.2013.83
findings.population: Swedish adults (mean age 46, mean BMI 33.4, 83% women) in a commercial weight-loss programme
findings.parameter: energy intake floor (avoid very-low-calorie intakes)
findings.value: 500 kcal/day VLCD vs 1,200-1,500 kcal/day LCD: gallstones needing hospital care 152 vs 44 per 10,000 person-years, HR 3.4 (95% CI 1.8-6.3), NNH 92 (63-168); cholecystectomy HR 3.2 (1.5-6.8), NNH 151 (94-377)
findings.finding: In 3,320 matched pairs, a 500 kcal/day diet roughly tripled the risk of gallstones needing hospital care or gallbladder removal within a year, compared with 1,200-1,500 kcal/day. Absolute risk stayed low. This supports an intake floor well above VLCD levels.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results 'Risk of gallstones requiring hospital care' and 'Risk of cholecystectomy' (PMC3921672 full text)

findings.citation: Johansson K, Sundström J, Marcus C, Hemmingsson E, Neovius M. Risk of symptomatic gallstones and cholecystectomy after a very-low-calorie diet or low-calorie diet in a commercial weight loss program: 1-year matched cohort study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2014;38(2):279-84. doi:10.1038/ijo.2013.83
findings.population: Swedish adults in a commercial weight-loss programme
findings.parameter: weekly weight-loss rate cap (rapid loss as a gallstone risk factor)
findings.value: 3-month loss 12.7 kg (VLCD) vs 7.9 kg (LCD); greater weight loss independently predicted gallstones; adjusting for 3-month loss lowered the gallstone HR to 2.5 (95% CI 1.3-5.1). No weekly rate threshold was reported.
findings.finding: Participants who lost the most weight had more gallstone events, as did women, younger people, those with higher BMI and those with a gallstone history. Accounting for the size of early loss explained only part of the extra VLCD risk. The study gives no numeric weekly-rate cutoff.
findings.locator: Results 'Weight change' and 'Exploratory analysis: predictors of gallstones'; Discussion 'Mechanisms'

findings.citation: Johansson K, Sundström J, Marcus C, Hemmingsson E, Neovius M. Risk of symptomatic gallstones and cholecystectomy after a very-low-calorie diet or low-calorie diet in a commercial weight loss program: 1-year matched cohort study. Int J Obes (Lond). 2014;38(2):279-84. doi:10.1038/ijo.2013.83
findings.population: Swedish adults on a 500 kcal/day formula diet
findings.parameter: minimum dietary fat g/day during very low energy intake
findings.value: The VLCD supplied 7-9 g fat/day; the authors cite 7-10 g/day as a reported threshold for efficient gallbladder emptying and suggest more fat may be needed
findings.finding: The formula diet contained 7-9 g of fat a day, in line with the European 7 g/day guidance, yet gallstone risk was still raised. The authors cite earlier work putting 7-10 g/day as the threshold for gallbladder emptying, and suggest more fat may be needed during severe restriction.
findings.locator: Methods 'Weight loss phase'; Discussion 'Previous research' and 'Mechanisms'

findings.citation: World Health Organization. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. ISBN 978-92-4-007359-3. Available from: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240073593
findings.population: All individuals aged 2 years and older
findings.parameter: preferred carbohydrate food sources
findings.value: Carbohydrate mainly from whole grains, vegetables, fruits and pulses (strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence from 7 systematic reviews); minimally processed foods without added fat, sugars or salt, and intact whole grains, preferred
findings.finding: WHO strongly advises getting carbohydrate mostly from whole grains, vegetables, fruits and pulses, which are linked to lower mortality and NCD risk. Processing should be minimal, with no added fat, sugar or salt, and highly processed 'whole grain' products are discouraged. Food suggestions should rank these sources first.
findings.locator: 'Recommendations and supporting information', recommendation 1 and Remarks (printed pp.22-26; IRIS PDF)

findings.citation: World Health Organization. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. ISBN 978-92-4-007359-3. Available from: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240073593
findings.parameter: minimum vegetables + fruit g/day (adults)
findings.value: At least 400 g/day (strong recommendation); risk kept falling up to 800 g/day, with the steepest drop up to 400 g/day
findings.finding: Adults should eat at least 400 g of vegetables and fruit a day. The threshold comes from a dose-response curve across 95 prospective cohorts: risk kept falling up to about 800 g, but most of the benefit came by 400 g. Evidence certainty was moderate overall.
findings.locator: Recommendation 2 and rationale (printed pp.22, 24); Summary of evidence, Review 4 (printed p.9)

findings.citation: World Health Organization. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. ISBN 978-92-4-007359-3. Available from: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240073593
findings.parameter: minimum dietary fibre g/day (adults)
findings.value: At least 25 g/day of naturally occurring fibre (strong recommendation); dose-response up to 40 g/day, greatest benefit at 25-29 g/day; all-cause mortality high vs low intake RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.79-0.91); per 8 g/day RR 0.93 (0.90-0.95)
findings.finding: WHO advises at least 25 g/day of fibre from food for adults. Benefits rose with intake up to about 40 g/day, and 25-29 g/day helped the most outcomes. The evidence came from 100 cohorts (80 million person-years) and 49 RCTs (3,574 people) and was rated moderate certainty.
findings.locator: Recommendation 4 and rationale (printed pp.22, 24-25); Table 2 and Review 1 in Summary of evidence (printed pp.9, 13)

findings.citation: World Health Organization. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. ISBN 978-92-4-007359-3. Available from: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240073593
findings.parameter: total carbohydrate % of energy
findings.value: No WHO recommendation on amount; carbohydrate should follow from protein and fat recommendations; a 2018 meta-analysis cited: about 40-70% of energy linked to lower mortality than under 40% or over 70%
findings.finding: WHO deliberately sets no total carbohydrate amount; intake should fill the energy left after protein and fat targets. In its remarks it cites a 2018 meta-analysis linking about 40-70% of energy from carbohydrate to lower mortality. That figure comes from one observational synthesis.
findings.locator: Remarks, 'Recommendations and supporting information' (printed p.25) and Executive summary remarks (p.xi)

findings.citation: World Health Organization. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. ISBN 978-92-4-007359-3. Available from: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240073593
findings.parameter: what counts toward fibre and fruit targets
findings.value: Only fibre naturally occurring in foods counts (not extracted/synthetic fibre, supplements, capsules or powders); fresh, cooked, frozen and canned vegetables and fruit are covered, but tinned fruit was linked to higher all-cause mortality and CVD risk in a small number of studies; dried fruit, fruit juice, fruit concentrates and fruit sugars to be consumed within WHO free-sugar guidance; canned vegetables within sodium guidance
findings.finding: The 25 g fibre target covers only fibre naturally present in foods, not supplements or isolated fibres. Fresh, frozen, cooked or canned produce counts, though tinned fruit showed higher risk in a few studies. Juice, dried fruit and fruit concentrates fall under free-sugar limits; canned vegetables under sodium limits.
findings.locator: Remarks (printed p.26; same remarks in executive summary p.xi)

findings.citation: World Health Organization. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. ISBN 978-92-4-007359-3. Available from: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240073593
findings.parameter: glycaemic index/load as a food-selection criterion
findings.value: No recommendation; observational evidence very low to moderate certainty and inconsistent for mortality/NCDs; RCTs showed little to no cardiometabolic improvement
findings.finding: WHO reviewed low-glycaemic-index and low-glycaemic-load diets and found no consistent benefit. It chose fibre and food sources, not GI, as the measures of carbohydrate quality. The app should not rank foods by GI on WHO's authority.
findings.locator: Executive summary 'The evidence' (pp.vii-viii); Table 3 (Summary of evidence); Remarks (printed p.25)

findings.citation: World Health Organization. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. ISBN 978-92-4-007359-3. Available from: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240073593
findings.parameter: publication licence (guideline document, not a dataset)
findings.value: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO
findings.finding: The guideline is published under CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO. Citing its numbers as facts is fine, but copying or adapting its text into the app would bring non-commercial and share-alike terms, which conflict with the repository's licence rule.
findings.locator: Copyright page (PDF p.ii / IRIS page 4)

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.population: Adults free of chronic disease; 185 prospective study publications (~135 million person-years) plus 58 RCTs (4,635 adults)
findings.parameter: dietary fibre minimum intake g/day
findings.value: At least 25-29 g/day total dietary fibre for adults; intakes above 30 g/day confer additional benefit per dose-response. Versus lowest intakes: 25-29 g/day improved 6 of 7 critical outcomes, 20-24 g/day 4 of 7, 15-19 g/day 3 of 7. High vs low fibre: all-cause mortality RR 0.85 (0.79-0.91), GRADE moderate.
findings.finding: WHO-commissioned reviews found the broadest disease-risk reduction when fibre intake reached 25-29 g/day, with dose-response curves still falling beyond 30 g/day, so the authors recommend no less than 25-29 g/day. Evidence is mostly prospective cohorts; GRADE moderate.
findings.locator: Accepted peer-reviewed manuscript (Univ. Dundee Discovery, CC BY-NC-ND): Research in Context; Results 'Dietary fibre' (ms lines 257-261); Discussion (ms lines 313-314, 437-439); Table 1

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.population: Prospective cohorts of adults without pre-existing disease
findings.parameter: risk change per 8 g/day additional dietary fibre
findings.value: Per +8 g/day fibre (linear dose-response): all-cause mortality RR 0.93 (0.90-0.95); CHD incidence RR 0.81 (0.73-0.90); type 2 diabetes RR 0.85 (0.82-0.89); colorectal cancer RR 0.92 (0.89-0.95). Mostly linear, no plateau within observed data.
findings.finding: Each extra 8 g of daily fibre was linked to lower mortality, coronary disease, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer risk, with largely linear curves and no visible ceiling, supporting a 'more fibre is better' scoring slope above the minimum.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Figure 2a-d legends; Results 'Dietary fibre' (ms lines 256-258)

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.population: Adults free of acute/chronic disease (could include prediabetes, mild hypercholesterolaemia/hypertension)
findings.parameter: effect of higher vs lower fibre diet on body weight (RCTs)
findings.value: Body weight MD -0.37 kg (95% CI -0.63 to -0.11); 27 RCTs, 1,294 intervention vs 1,201 control; GRADE high. Also total cholesterol MD -0.15 mmol/L (-0.22 to -0.07), 36 RCTs; systolic BP MD -1.27 mmHg (-2.50 to -0.04), 15 RCTs. Trials >=4 weeks, weight-loss trials and powdered fibre supplements excluded.
findings.finding: In randomised trials of at least four weeks that were not weight-loss trials, higher-fibre diets produced a small but consistent drop in body weight of about 0.37 kg, alongside modest cholesterol and blood-pressure reductions.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Table 1 (rows change in body weight, total cholesterol, systolic BP); Methods 'PICO tables and eligibility criteria'

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.population: Prospective cohorts of adults without pre-existing disease
findings.parameter: whole grain vs refined grain ranking; risk change per 15 g/day whole grains
findings.value: Per +15 g/day whole grains: all-cause mortality RR 0.94 (0.92-0.95); CHD RR 0.93 (0.89-0.98); type 2 diabetes RR 0.88 (0.81-0.95); colorectal cancer RR 0.97 (0.95-0.99). High vs low: all-cause mortality RR 0.81 (0.72-0.90), GRADE low; T2D RR 0.67 (0.58-0.78), GRADE low.
findings.finding: Higher whole-grain intake tracked with roughly 13-33% lower risk of major outcomes and showed dose-response per 15 g/day; authors advise replacing refined grains with whole grains, though cohort certainty was mostly low owing to unexplained heterogeneity.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Figure 3a-d legends; Table 2; Results 'Whole grains' (ms lines 274-285)

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.parameter: effect of higher vs lower whole grain diet on body weight (RCTs)
findings.value: Body weight MD -0.62 kg (95% CI -1.19 to -0.05); 11 RCTs, 498 intervention vs 421 control; GRADE moderate (unexplained heterogeneity). Total cholesterol MD -0.09 mmol/L (-0.23 to +0.04), NS.
findings.finding: Trials that raised whole-grain intake lowered body weight by around 0.6 kg compared with lower intake, graded moderate because results varied between trials; cholesterol change was not significant.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Table 2 (rows change in body weight, total cholesterol)

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.population: Prospective cohorts and RCTs in adults without diabetes or marked hyperlipidaemia
findings.parameter: use of glycaemic index / glycaemic load as a food-selection criterion
findings.value: Low vs high GI: T2D RR 0.89 (0.82-0.97), attenuated to ~5% reduction (13% lower to 4% higher) on sensitivity analysis; CHD RR 0.93 (0.83-1.04); all-cause mortality RR 0.89 (0.70-1.13); stroke mortality RR 0.63 (0.52-0.77), GRADE low; RCT body weight MD -0.29 kg (-0.62 to +0.03). Cohort evidence GRADE low/very low. Rule: do not use GI/GL as a primary ranking criterion; rank on fibre and whole-grain content instead, because some low-GI foods (containing added fructose or sucrose, or combining sugar with saturated fat, e.g. confectionery) lack health benefits. People with diabetes or marked hyperlipidaemia were excluded, so GI use in those groups is not addressed.
findings.finding: Apart from lower stroke mortality, glycaemic index and load predicted outcomes weakly and inconsistently compared with fibre and whole-grain content, and some low-GI foods are unhealthy, so the authors judge GI/GL less useful markers of carbohydrate quality.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Table 3; Results 'Glycaemic index' (ms lines 293-299); Discussion (ms lines 330-337, 366-372, 429-434); Research in Context

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.population: Author interpretation of the pooled evidence base
findings.parameter: naturally occurring vs extracted/added fibre preference
findings.value: Rule (qualitative): favour fibre that occurs naturally in minimally processed whole grains, vegetables and fruit. The pooled evidence comes mostly from studies run before extracted or synthetic fibre was widely added to manufactured foods. Heavily processed 'whole grain' products may not deliver equivalent benefit (limited biomarker evidence; no outcome data).
findings.finding: Because most supporting studies predate widespread use of added fibre, the authors advise emphasising intrinsic fibre from minimally processed whole grains, vegetables and fruit rather than relying on fortified or heavily processed 'whole grain' products.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Discussion (ms lines 406-418)

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.population: General population; caution applies to those with borderline iron/mineral status
findings.parameter: high fibre / whole grain intake caution for borderline iron or mineral status
findings.value: No fibre-related harms emerged in the study types reviewed. Very large whole-grain intakes could worsen iron status where iron/mineral status is already marginal (qualitative caution resting on one cited reference; no threshold given).
findings.finding: The reviews found no fibre-related harms, but the authors caution that very large whole-grain intakes could worsen iron status in people whose iron or mineral status is already marginal; applying this to plant-based users is an app inference, not the authors'.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Discussion (ms lines 426-429)

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.parameter: whole grain serving size (g)
findings.value: 30 g = one serving of whole grains (analytic convention used when studies did not state serving weight)
findings.finding: When studies reported whole grains in servings without weights, the reviewers converted each serving to 30 g, a usable convention for translating servings into grams.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Methods 'Data analysis' (ms line 193)

findings.citation: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Lancet. 2019;393(10170):434-45. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9
findings.parameter: total carbohydrate intake range
findings.value: Not evaluated in this review. Citing other epidemiological evidence, longer-term trials and dietary guidelines, the authors note that many levels of total carbohydrate intake appear acceptable and that the type of carbohydrate matters more than the amount. No numeric range provided.
findings.finding: This review did not test total carbohydrate amount; the authors note that other evidence supports a wide acceptable range, so it cannot supply a carbohydrate percentage or g/kg target for the app.
findings.locator: Accepted manuscript: Discussion (ms lines 402-405)

findings.citation: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, Fadnes LT, Keum N, Norat T, et al. Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality - a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. Int J Epidemiol. 2017;46(3):1029-56. doi:10.1093/ije/dyw319
findings.population: 95 prospective cohort studies (142 publications), mainly adults in Europe, USA, Asia, Australia; up to 2.1 million participants per analysis
findings.parameter: daily fruit and vegetable intake target (g/day)
findings.value: Lowest risk at 800 g/day (~10 servings of 80 g) for CHD, stroke, CVD and all-cause mortality; 550-600 g/day (~7-7.5 servings) for total cancer. Nonlinear, steepest gains at lower intakes. Versus 0-40 g/day: 500 g/day -> RR reductions 16% CHD, 28% stroke, 22% CVD, 13% cancer, 27% all-cause; 800 g/day -> 24%, 33%, 28%, 14%, 31%.
findings.finding: Risk kept falling up to about 800 g/day of combined fruit and vegetables for cardiovascular outcomes and death, and up to 550-600 g/day for cancer, with the largest gains at lower intakes, supporting a tiered daily produce target.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Key Messages; Discussion paragraphs 1-2; Conclusion

findings.citation: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, Fadnes LT, Keum N, Norat T, et al. Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality - a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. Int J Epidemiol. 2017;46(3):1029-56. doi:10.1093/ije/dyw319
findings.parameter: relative risk per 200 g/day fruit and vegetables
findings.finding: Each additional 200 g/day of fruit and vegetables was associated with roughly 8-16% lower cardiovascular risk, 3% lower cancer risk and 10% lower all-cause mortality, although heterogeneity was high for mortality and stroke.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Abstract Results; Results subsections 'Coronary heart disease', 'Stroke', 'Cardiovascular disease', 'Total cancer', 'All-cause mortality'

findings.citation: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, Fadnes LT, Keum N, Norat T, et al. Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality - a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. Int J Epidemiol. 2017;46(3):1029-56. doi:10.1093/ije/dyw319
findings.parameter: separate fruit vs vegetable plateau (g/day)
findings.value: All-cause mortality: 19% lower RR at 600 g/day fruit; 25% lower at 600 g/day vegetables. CVD: 27% lower at 800 g/day fruit; 28% lower at 600 g/day vegetables (vegetable-CVD association approximately linear). CHD: 21% lower up to 750-800 g/day fruit; 30% lower up to 550-600 g/day vegetables. Stroke: 20% lower at 200-350 g/day fruit, 28% at 500 g/day vegetables, little further reduction above. Total cancer: 8% (fruit) and 12% (vegetables) lower at 550-600 g/day.
findings.finding: Analysed separately, fruit and vegetables were each protective. Vegetable benefit mostly levelled off near 500-600 g/day and fruit benefit extended to 600-800 g/day for most outcomes. The exception was stroke, where fruit benefit plateaued at 200-350 g/day. The vegetable-cardiovascular curve was roughly linear.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Results subsections 'Coronary heart disease', 'Stroke', 'Cardiovascular disease', 'Total cancer', 'All-cause mortality'

findings.citation: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, Fadnes LT, Keum N, Norat T, et al. Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality - a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. Int J Epidemiol. 2017;46(3):1029-56. doi:10.1093/ije/dyw319
findings.parameter: fruit/vegetable serving size (g)
findings.value: 80 g = one serving of total fruit or vegetables (convention consistent with previous meta-analyses); 800 g/day = 10 servings, 600 g/day = 7.5 servings, 400 g/day = 5 servings. For specific subtypes the authors used serving sizes from a pooled cohort analysis, and 80 g only where that source gave none.
findings.finding: The reviewers counted one serving of total fruit or vegetables as 80 g, so gram targets convert to servings (400 g = 5, 800 g = 10); subtype analyses instead used serving sizes taken from a pooled cohort analysis.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Methods 'Statistical methods' paragraph 2; Discussion paragraphs 2-3; Conclusion

findings.citation: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, Fadnes LT, Keum N, Norat T, et al. Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality - a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. Int J Epidemiol. 2017;46(3):1029-56. doi:10.1093/ije/dyw319
findings.population: Prospective cohorts, adults; few studies per subtype
findings.parameter: produce subtypes to prioritise in suggestions
findings.value: Inversely associated with CVD and/or all-cause mortality: apples/pears, citrus fruits, green leafy vegetables/salads, cruciferous vegetables, tomatoes, beta-carotene-rich and vitamin C-rich fruit/veg, berries, cooked vegetables, potatoes (all-cause, high vs low). Total cancer: cruciferous and green-yellow vegetables. Subtype increments analysed per 100 g/day.
findings.finding: Several specific produce groups, notably apples/pears, citrus, leafy greens/salads and cruciferous vegetables, showed inverse associations with cardiovascular disease and death; authors warn few studies and possible selective reporting limit these subtype results.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Results subsections (specific types paragraphs); Discussion paragraph 2

findings.citation: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, Fadnes LT, Keum N, Norat T, et al. Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality - a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. Int J Epidemiol. 2017;46(3):1029-56. doi:10.1093/ije/dyw319
findings.parameter: tinned fruit down-weighting
findings.value: CVD: high vs low RR 1.23 (1.06-1.43), 3 risk estimates from 1 publication, I2=0%; per 100 g/day RR 1.30 (0.81-2.08), not significant. All-cause mortality: high vs low RR 1.13 (1.04-1.23), 3 estimates from 1 publication; per 100 g/day RR 1.14 (1.07-1.21), 4 estimates from 2 publications. Total cancer: not significant.
findings.finding: Tinned fruit was the only produce type linked to higher risk: about 23% higher cardiovascular risk and 13% higher all-cause mortality comparing highest with lowest intake, from very few studies, supporting ranking fresh fruit above tinned fruit.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Table 4 and Table 6 (row 'Tinned fruits'); Results 'Cardiovascular disease' and 'All-cause mortality' specific-type paragraphs; Discussion paragraph 2

findings.citation: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, Cai H, Cassimatis T, Chen KY, et al. Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. Cell Metab. 2019;30(1):67-77.e3. doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008
findings.population: Weight-stable adults, mean age 31.2 y, BMI 27 kg/m2, 10 men and 10 women, inpatient; vegetarians/vegans excluded
findings.parameter: ultra-processed vs unprocessed diet effect on ad libitum energy intake and weight
findings.value: Energy intake +508 +/- 106 kcal/day on ultra-processed diet (p=0.0001); final week +459 +/- 105 kcal/day; carbohydrate +280 +/- 54, fat +230 +/- 53, protein -2 +/- 12 kcal/day. Weight +0.9 +/- 0.3 kg (UPF) vs -0.9 +/- 0.3 kg (unprocessed) over 14 days each. Consumed energy density 1.36 vs 1.09 kcal/g.
findings.finding: When diets were matched for presented calories, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fibre, people ate about 500 kcal/day more and gained weight on ultra-processed food, but lost weight on unprocessed food; small, short, inpatient study.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Summary; Results 'Food Intake' and 'Body weight and composition'

findings.citation: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, Cai H, Cassimatis T, Chen KY, et al. Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. Cell Metab. 2019;30(1):67-77.e3. doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008
findings.population: Methodological assumption applied to inpatient adults
findings.parameter: energy density of body tissue change (kcal/kg)
findings.value: Fat mass 9,300 kcal/kg; fat-free mass 1,100 kcal/kg (used to convert DXA body-composition change into change in body energy stores)
findings.finding: To estimate energy-balance from body changes, the investigators valued each kilogram of fat at 9,300 kcal and each kilogram of fat-free mass at 1,100 kcal, constants the app could use when inferring energy balance from weight trends.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): STAR Methods 'Body weight and composition'

findings.citation: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, Cai H, Cassimatis T, Chen KY, et al. Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. Cell Metab. 2019;30(1):67-77.e3. doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008
findings.parameter: weigh-in protocol and trend estimation
findings.value: Daily weight at 06:00 after first void, pre-weighed garment weight deducted; change over each 14-day period estimated by linear regression to damp body-fluid fluctuations. Separately, individual between-diet sodium intake differences (5.8 vs 4.6 g/day) correlated with fat-free mass change (r=0.63) and weight change (r=0.64).
findings.finding: Weight was taken each morning after voiding, minus pre-weighed clothing, and 14-day change was estimated by linear regression to damp fluid fluctuations. Separately, between-diet sodium differences tracked fat-free mass and weight differences, suggesting fluid shifts can move short-term weight.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): STAR Methods 'Body weight and composition'; Results 'Body weight and composition' paragraph 2; Results 'Food Intake' (sodium)

findings.citation: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, Cai H, Cassimatis T, Chen KY, et al. Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. Cell Metab. 2019;30(1):67-77.e3. doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008
findings.population: Inpatient weight-stable adults with mandated light exercise
findings.parameter: physical activity level multiplier (TEE/REE)
findings.value: Measured PAL (DLW TEE / REE) 1.59 +/- 0.06 with 3 x 20 min/day cycling at 30-40% heart-rate reserve; maintenance requirement was estimated a priori as 1.6 x measured REE.
findings.finding: With about an hour of light daily cycling, doubly labelled water gave a physical activity level near 1.6, which matched the 1.6 x resting expenditure the investigators used to estimate maintenance needs.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Results 'Glucose Tolerance' paragraph 3 (PAL); Results and Discussion paragraph 3 (1.6 x REE)

findings.citation: Lane MM, Gamage E, Du S, Ashtree DN, McGuinness AJ, Gauci S, et al. Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ. 2024;384:e077310. doi:10.1136/bmj-2023-077310
findings.parameter: type 2 diabetes risk per 10% increment in ultra-processed food share
findings.value: Dose-response RR 1.12 (95% CI 1.11-1.13) per 10% increase in UPF exposure; 7 cohorts; credibility class I (convincing); GRADE moderate. High vs low OR 1.40 (1.23-1.59), class II, GRADE very low.
findings.finding: Each 10% rise in the share of diet from ultra-processed food was associated with about 12% higher type 2 diabetes risk, the most credible association in the umbrella review, though all evidence is observational.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Results 'Metabolic health' final sentence; Abstract Results

findings.citation: Lane MM, Gamage E, Du S, Ashtree DN, McGuinness AJ, Gauci S, et al. Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ. 2024;384:e077310. doi:10.1136/bmj-2023-077310
findings.parameter: all-cause mortality risk per additional daily serving of ultra-processed food
findings.value: Dose-response RR 1.02 (1.01-1.03) per additional daily UPF serving, 9 cohorts, class III, GRADE moderate (excess significance bias and small-study effects detected). High vs low RR 1.21 (1.15-1.27), 7 cohorts, class II, GRADE low.
findings.finding: Higher ultra-processed food intake was associated with higher all-cause mortality, about 2% per extra daily serving and 21% comparing highest with lowest intake, with signs of reporting bias lowering confidence.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Results 'Mortality'; Results 'Results of syntheses' (bias tests)

findings.citation: Lane MM, Gamage E, Du S, Ashtree DN, McGuinness AJ, Gauci S, et al. Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ. 2024;384:e077310. doi:10.1136/bmj-2023-077310
findings.population: Adults; mostly cross-sectional and mixed designs
findings.parameter: obesity risk associated with ultra-processed food exposure
findings.value: Obesity prevalence: high vs low OR 1.55 (1.36-1.77), class II, GRADE low; per 10% UPF OR 1.07 (1.03-1.11), class III, low (7 cross-sectional studies). Overweight+obesity combined per 10% OR 1.03 (1.01-1.06), class IV, GRADE moderate. Abdominal obesity per 10% OR 1.05 (1.02-1.07).
findings.finding: Greater ultra-processed food intake was associated with higher odds of obesity, mostly from cross-sectional studies, supporting a modest penalty for NOVA-4 items in fat-loss food suggestions.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Results 'Metabolic health'

findings.citation: Lane MM, Gamage E, Du S, Ashtree DN, McGuinness AJ, Gauci S, et al. Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ. 2024;384:e077310. doi:10.1136/bmj-2023-077310
findings.population: Adults and some child/adolescent studies across 45 pooled observational analyses
findings.parameter: cardiovascular disease mortality risk with ultra-processed food exposure
findings.value: High vs low RR 1.50 (1.37-1.63), 5 cohorts, class I, GRADE very low; dose-response RR 1.05 (1.02-1.08), 4 cohorts, class IV, GRADE low. Overall: of 45 pooled analyses, 4 GRADE moderate, 22 low, 19 very low; no pooled RCTs existed.
findings.finding: Highest ultra-processed food intake was associated with 50% higher cardiovascular mortality, statistically convincing but very low GRADE quality; across all 45 outcomes, most evidence was low or very low quality and none was randomised.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Results 'Mortality'; Abstract Results; Discussion 'Principal findings'; Methods 'Inclusion criteria and searches'

findings.citation: Lane MM, Gamage E, Du S, Ashtree DN, McGuinness AJ, Gauci S, et al. Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ. 2024;384:e077310. doi:10.1136/bmj-2023-077310
findings.parameter: ultra-processed subcategory exceptions to down-weighting
findings.value: Rule (qualitative): in an included T2D meta-analysis, some UPF subcategories were inversely associated with T2D: ultra-processed cereals, dark/wholegrain bread, packaged sweet and savoury snacks, fruit-based products, yoghurt and dairy-based desserts. Overall UPF consumption remained associated with higher risk. Secondary report of another meta-analysis.
findings.finding: Not every NOVA-4 subgroup behaved alike: wholegrain bread, yoghurt and some cereals showed lower diabetes risk in one included analysis, so a blanket ultra-processed penalty may misrank these foods.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Discussion 'Strengths and limitations', paragraph 3

findings.citation: Rolls BJ. The relationship between dietary energy density and energy intake. Physiol Behav. 2009;97(5):609-15. doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2009.03.011
findings.population: Narrative review of adult and child feeding studies
findings.parameter: energy density definition and intake equation
findings.value: Energy density (ED) = kcal per gram of food; range 0-9 kcal/g; fat 9 kcal/g, carbohydrate and protein 4 kcal/g. Energy intake = food weight x ED. Worked example: 1,200 g/day x 1.8 kcal/g = 2,160 kcal; lowering ED by 0.1 kcal/g at constant weight -> 2,040 kcal (-120 kcal/day).
findings.finding: Because people tend to eat a fairly constant weight of food, intake can be modelled as grams eaten times energy density, so small reductions in average kcal/g lower daily energy intake.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): section 'What is energy density?'

findings.citation: Rolls BJ. The relationship between dietary energy density and energy intake. Physiol Behav. 2009;97(5):609-15. doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2009.03.011
findings.population: Adults in laboratory feeding studies (lean and obese)
findings.parameter: effect of lowering energy density on ad libitum intake
findings.value: ~30% reduction in ED of entrees (macronutrients and palatability matched) -> ~30% lower cumulative 2-day energy intake with similar food weight and similar hunger/fullness. Manipulating ~50% of meal energy -> 16% lower intake of self-selected foods over 4 days, no compensation, in lean and obese adults.
findings.finding: Controlled feeding studies showed people ate similar food weight regardless of energy density, so lowering kcal/g cut intake substantially without extra hunger, over two to four days; long-term controlled data are limited.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): section 'Energy density and satiation: effects on ad libitum energy intake'

findings.citation: Rolls BJ. The relationship between dietary energy density and energy intake. Physiol Behav. 2009;97(5):609-15. doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2009.03.011
findings.population: Adults in single-meal laboratory preload studies
findings.parameter: low-energy-density first course / preload before a meal
findings.value: Low-ED vegetable soup preload -> total lunch energy intake 20% lower vs no preload (soup form did not matter). Water cooked into soup -> 26% less lunch energy vs same casserole with a 10-oz glass of water. Larger low-ED salad first course reduced meal energy more than smaller one; high-ED salad increased meal energy.
findings.finding: Starting a meal with a low-energy-dense soup or salad reduced total meal energy intake by roughly a fifth, and water incorporated into food was more satiating than drinking water alongside it; high-energy-dense starters increased intake.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): sections 'Consumption of low-energy-dense preloads can enhance satiety' and 'Preload characteristics that can moderate the effect of energy density'

findings.citation: Rolls BJ. The relationship between dietary energy density and energy intake. Physiol Behav. 2009;97(5):609-15. doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2009.03.011
findings.population: Adults in a laboratory preload study
findings.parameter: whole fruit vs puree vs juice preference
findings.value: Whole apple preload (matched for weight, energy, ED and ingestion rate) reduced lunch energy intake by 15% vs no preload and more than applesauce or apple juice; adding naturally occurring fibre levels to juice did not improve satiety.
findings.finding: A whole apple eaten before lunch cut meal energy intake more than applesauce or juice matched for weight, energy, energy density and eating rate, and adding fibre to juice did not help, supporting whole fruit over juice during a deficit.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): section 'Preload characteristics that can moderate the effect of energy density', paragraph 4

findings.citation: Rolls BJ. The relationship between dietary energy density and energy intake. Physiol Behav. 2009;97(5):609-15. doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2009.03.011
findings.population: Overweight/obese adults in clinical trials (as summarised)
findings.parameter: low-energy-density dietary counselling weight loss (12 months)
findings.value: 97 obese women: counselling to add water-rich foods (fruit, vegetables) plus reduce fat lost 17.4 lb (~7.9 kg) vs 14.1 lb (~6.4 kg) for fat reduction plus portion restriction at 12 months (completers); the fruit-and-vegetable group reported eating ~25% more food and less hunger. PREMIER secondary analysis, 6 months: largest ED reduction tertile lost 13 lb vs 9 lb vs 5 lb.
findings.finding: In a year-long trial, advising more fruit and vegetables to lower energy density produced more weight loss than portion restriction while allowing a larger food volume and less hunger; supporting data come from secondary analyses.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): section 'Energy density and body weight', paragraphs 3-4

findings.citation: Rolls BJ. The relationship between dietary energy density and energy intake. Physiol Behav. 2009;97(5):609-15. doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2009.03.011
findings.parameter: dietary fat % energy effect on ad libitum intake when energy density is fixed
findings.value: With ED held constant, varying fat from 20% to 60% of energy did not significantly alter ad libitum energy intake (4 cited studies).
findings.finding: Studies that held energy density constant found that varying fat between 20% and 60% of energy did not change how much energy people ate, suggesting energy density rather than fat share drives overeating.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): section 'Energy density and satiation: effects on ad libitum energy intake', paragraph 1

findings.citation: Stelmach-Mardas M, Rodacki T, Dobrowolska-Iwanek J, Brzozowska A, Walkowiak J, Wojtanowska-Krosniak A, et al. Link between food energy density and body weight changes in obese adults. Nutrients. 2016;8(4):229. doi:10.3390/nu8040229
findings.population: Adults with obesity aged 18-66 y, mostly women, American and European
findings.parameter: body weight change with low-energy-density foods
findings.value: Pooled -0.53 kg (95% CI -0.88 to -0.19; p=0.002; I2=92%); RCT subgroup -0.48 kg (-0.94 to -0.01; I2=93%); cohort subgroup -0.63 kg (-1.1 to -0.16; I2=85%). 13 studies (9 RCTs, 4 cohorts); interventions 8 weeks to 9 months, cohorts up to 6 years. Methods state standardised mean differences were calculated, so the kg unit is ambiguous. Do not use as a quantitative kg parameter.
findings.finding: Low-energy-density eating was associated with roughly half a kilogram more weight loss in adults with obesity, with similar RCT and cohort subgroup estimates. However, heterogeneity was extreme, individual RCTs were inconsistent, and the stated SMD method makes the kg unit doubtful.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Section 2.4 Statistical Approach; Section 3.3; Section 4 Discussion paragraph 2; Abstract

findings.citation: Stelmach-Mardas M, Rodacki T, Dobrowolska-Iwanek J, Brzozowska A, Walkowiak J, Wojtanowska-Krosniak A, et al. Link between food energy density and body weight changes in obese adults. Nutrients. 2016;8(4):229. doi:10.3390/nu8040229
findings.parameter: energy density calculation method (beverage handling)
findings.value: Ello-Martin et al. excluded all beverages (caloric, e.g. milk and juice, and non-caloric) from ED. Poulsen et al. included beverages and reported diet ED about 0.5 kcal/g lower than Ello-Martin's; this compares two different trials, diets and populations, not an isolated method effect. The authors say the calculation method must be considered. Rule: fix one method (e.g., foods only) and track drink energy separately.
findings.finding: Counting beverages or not can shift computed energy density substantially: two included trials differed by about 0.5 kcal/g, only partly because of method. The app should fix one calculation, such as foods only with drinks tracked separately, before scoring meals.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Section 4 Discussion, paragraph 2

findings.citation: Stelmach-Mardas M, Rodacki T, Dobrowolska-Iwanek J, Brzozowska A, Walkowiak J, Wojtanowska-Krosniak A, et al. Link between food energy density and body weight changes in obese adults. Nutrients. 2016;8(4):229. doi:10.3390/nu8040229
findings.parameter: food classes characterising a low-energy-density diet
findings.value: Rule (qualitative): low-ED diets feature more vegetables, fruits and whole-grain products and less fat; most plant foods are low ED except plant oils and nuts. Replacing fat with sugar gives little benefit, unlike replacing it with whole grains or vegetables.
findings.finding: Across included studies, low-energy-density diets were built from more vegetables, fruit and whole grains with less fat, while oils and nuts are energy-dense exceptions among plant foods.
findings.locator: Full text (PMC): Section 1 Introduction paragraph 1; Section 4 Discussion paragraphs 2-3

findings.citation: Lim MT, Pan BJ, Toh DWK, Sutanto CN, Kim JE. Animal protein versus plant protein in supporting lean mass and muscle strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2021;13(2):661. doi:10.3390/nu13020661
findings.population: Adults with mean age >=19 y, with or without resistance training; 18 RCTs reviewed, 16 used across the meta-analyses (the count pooled for absolute lean mass is not given in the text); interventions 14 days to 2 years; four studies in people with medical conditions
findings.parameter: protein source (animal vs plant) effect on absolute lean mass, kg
findings.value: WMD 0.22 kg favouring animal protein (95% CI -0.02 to 0.46), not significant; I2 = 36.1% (p = 0.056); removing any one of three trials (Mobley, Moeller or Thomson) made it significant (WMD 0.25-0.29 kg)
findings.finding: Across the pooled RCTs, absolute lean-mass change did not differ significantly between animal and plant protein when total protein intake was adequate. The null was unstable: dropping any one of three trials made it significant. Most animal protein tested was dairy; most plant protein was soy.
findings.locator: PMC full text, Results 3.4 para 1 (pooled WMD) and para 3 (heterogeneity, leave-one-out); Discussion para 8 (dairy/soy limitation, instability of lean-mass results)

findings.citation: Lim MT, Pan BJ, Toh DWK, Sutanto CN, Kim JE. Animal protein versus plant protein in supporting lean mass and muscle strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2021;13(2):661. doi:10.3390/nu13020661
findings.population: Adults >=19 y, with or without resistance training (RCTs pooled in the meta-analysis); trials were not energy-restricted fat-loss interventions
findings.parameter: protein source (animal vs plant) effect on percent lean mass, %
findings.value: WMD +0.50% favouring animal protein (95% CI 0.05 to 0.95); I2 = 0.0% (p = 0.986); no longer significant if any one of four trials (Hill, Lynch, Mobley, Vupadhyayula) was removed
findings.finding: Animal protein gave a small, statistically significant advantage in percent lean mass over plant protein, but leaving out any one of four trials removed significance. The authors note that no agreed minimal clinically important difference for lean mass exists, so practical relevance is unclear.
findings.locator: PMC full text, Results 3.4 para 1 and para 3; Discussion para 6 (clinical significance)

findings.citation: Lim MT, Pan BJ, Toh DWK, Sutanto CN, Kim JE. Animal protein versus plant protein in supporting lean mass and muscle strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2021;13(2):661. doi:10.3390/nu13020661
findings.population: Adults <50 y vs >=50 y in the pooled RCTs (eight studies had mean/median age >=50 y)
findings.parameter: age as modifier of protein-source effect on lean mass (subgroup <50 y vs >=50 y)
findings.value: <50 y: absolute lean mass WMD +0.41 kg (95% CI 0.08 to 0.74); percent lean mass WMD +0.50% (95% CI 0.00 to 1.01); >=50 y: no difference
findings.finding: In a pre-specified age subgroup, adults under 50 gained slightly more absolute and percent lean mass with animal protein than with plant protein. Older adults showed no difference. This is subgroup evidence and the percent-lean-mass interval reaches zero.
findings.locator: PMC full text, Methods 2.4 (a priori subgroups); Results 3.4 para 1 (age subgroup)

findings.citation: Lim MT, Pan BJ, Toh DWK, Sutanto CN, Kim JE. Animal protein versus plant protein in supporting lean mass and muscle strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2021;13(2):661. doi:10.3390/nu13020661
findings.population: Adults >=19 y in the pooled RCTs, with or without resistance training
findings.parameter: protein source (animal vs plant) effect on muscle strength
findings.value: 1-RM squat WMD -0.94 kg (95% CI -4.57 to 2.70); grip WMD -0.49 kg (-1.28 to 0.30); leg/knee extension WMD -3.01 Nm (-19.25 to 13.23; I2 85.8%); leg/knee flexion WMD 2.93 Nm (-1.70 to 7.56); all not significant. <50 y extension subgroup only: +12.00 Nm (2.04 to 21.96)
findings.finding: No pooled strength outcome differed by protein source, and results were robust in leave-one-out analysis; only knee-extension torque in under-50s favoured animal protein. The authors caution that few studies fed these analyses, so strength equivalence is tentative.
findings.locator: PMC full text, Results 3.4 para 2 (strength WMDs) and para 4 (heterogeneity, robustness); Discussion para 7 (small number of studies limits conclusions)

findings.citation: Lim MT, Pan BJ, Toh DWK, Sutanto CN, Kim JE. Animal protein versus plant protein in supporting lean mass and muscle strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2021;13(2):661. doi:10.3390/nu13020661
findings.population: Adults >=19 y; training and non-training subgroups
findings.parameter: resistance training as modifier of protein-source effect
findings.value: No significant animal-vs-plant difference in absolute or percent lean mass, or in strength, in either the resistance-training or the no-training subgroup (11 of 18 studies included resistance training)
findings.finding: Whether or not participants did resistance training, the protein source did not change lean-mass or strength outcomes. In this evidence base, training status does not justify recommending different protein sources.
findings.locator: PMC full text, Results 3.1 para 1 (11 studies with training); Results 3.4 para 1 and para 2 (training subgroups)

findings.citation: Lim MT, Pan BJ, Toh DWK, Sutanto CN, Kim JE. Animal protein versus plant protein in supporting lean mass and muscle strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2021;13(2):661. doi:10.3390/nu13020661
findings.population: Adults in the included RCTs; intake partly estimated by the authors from reported means
findings.parameter: total protein intake range under which source equivalence was observed, g/kg/day
findings.value: Baseline intakes generally above the RDA of 0.8 g/kg/day; end-of-intervention intake estimated at >=1.0 g/kg/day in all studies; highest reported 3.1 g/kg/day
findings.finding: The animal-versus-plant comparisons were made only at total protein intakes of at least about 1.0 g/kg/day. The authors say source probably matters little when total protein is adequate, so the result should not be applied to intakes below this range.
findings.locator: PMC full text, Results 3.1 para 2 (intake range); Discussion para 3 (adequate total protein); Methods 2.3 (intake estimation method)

findings.value: Custom FSANZ Data User Licence Agreement based on Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Australia (CC BY-SA 3.0 AU). It requires attribution and share-alike for derivative works, plus a mandatory Limitation of Data Statement and a statement that the work is based on Australian data. Implied endorsement is not allowed.
findings.finding: FSANZ licenses the AFCD under an agreement modelled on CC BY-SA 3.0 AU. Redistributors must credit FSANZ, apply the same licence to derivatives, and include both a data-limitation statement and an Australian-data notice. Share-alike data is barred by rule 5. The Release 3 data-files page names no licence.

findings.parameter: dataset data-quality warranty
findings.value: No warranty of accuracy, completeness or comprehensiveness; indicative only; not for medical purposes; data entered by registered contributors (individuals or entities) from product labels and packaging, and the publisher has no obligation to verify it
findings.finding: Contributors (individuals or entities) transcribe data from labels and packaging; the publisher neither verifies nor warrants accuracy, completeness or coverage, calls the data indicative only, and forbids medical use. Because values are label transcriptions, not analytical composition data, they should not serve as reference nutrient values for targets.
